docs.title: Chapter 6: The Aims of Life, Karma and Rebirth
docs.text: karmaṇy evādhikāras te mā phaleṣu kadācana mā karmaphalahetur bhūr mā te saṅgo ’stv akarmaṇi To the deed alone you have a claim, never to what it yields. Let no reward be the reason you act; yet do not cling to doing nothing. — Bhagavadgītā 2.47

docs.title: 6.1 Two Linked Questions
docs.text: This chapter takes up two ideas that are often presented as the core of “the Indian view of life”: that human life has four legitimate aims (puruṣārtha) — dharma, wealth and power (artha), pleasure and love (kāma) and liberation (mokṣa) — and that actions (karma) bear fruit in this life and in future lives, so that beings pass through a beginningless round of rebirth (saṃsāra). Both ideas are old and widely shared. Both also have histories, rival versions and critics, and the comparative interest lies as much in the disagreements as in the agreements.

docs.title: 6.2.1 From three aims to four
docs.text:
The earliest scheme is a triad, the trivarga: dharma, artha and kāma. It appears in the Dharmasūtras, the epics, the Arthaśāstra and the Kāmasūtra, each of which treats one member of the triad as its subject while acknowledging the others. The Arthaśāstra (1.7) advises the king to pursue the three in balance, “not depriving himself of pleasure”, but records Kauṭilya’s own view that artha is primary, “for dharma and kāma are rooted in artha” (Olivelle 2013). The Kāmasūtra attributed to Vātsyāyana (perhaps 3rd century CE) likewise discusses the order of priority among the three and defends the legitimacy of a cultivated life of pleasure (Vātsyāyana 2002). Liberation, mokṣa, was added as a fourth aim later and remained in tension with the others: the three belong to life in the world, whereas mokṣa is release from it. Texts sometimes speak of the “four classes” (caturvarga) of aims, sometimes keep mokṣa apart.

The same triad organised literature outside Sanskrit. The Tamil Tirukkuṟaḷ is divided into three books: on virtue (aṟam), on wealth and polity (poruḷ) and on love (iṉpam or kāmam), corresponding to dharma, artha and kāma. It has no separate book on liberation (vīṭu), although its opening chapters praise God and renunciation (Chapter 5). Later Tamil commentators explained the absence by saying that liberation cannot be taught in words, or that it is the fruit of the other three rightly pursued. Classical Tamil poetics likewise divided poetry into akam (“interior”: love) and puṟam (“exterior”: war, kingship, generosity, death), a division that maps loosely onto kāma and artha. These parallels show that the scheme of the aims of life was a shared South Asian framework for organising knowledge and literature, adapted in different languages and traditions, rather than a purely Brahmanical doctrine.

docs.title: 6.2.2 Each aim and its literature
docs.text:
Dharma.

The first aim is the subject of the literature described in Chapter 5. It is usually ranked first among the three worldly aims, as the regulator of the others: wealth and pleasure pursued against dharma are condemned.

Artha.

Artha covers material prosperity, livelihood, property and, for the king, political power. Indian tradition did not idealise poverty for the householder; the householder’s earnings sustain the other stages of life and the gods through offerings. The Arthaśāstra, a composite treatise of c. 50 BCE–300 CE traditionally ascribed to Kauṭilya, is the classical text of statecraft and political economy (Volume 18). Lakṣmī, the goddess of prosperity and good fortune, embodies this aim in religious life (Figure 6.1).

Figure 6.1. Lakṣmī, goddess of prosperity and good fortune, seated on a lotus and lustrated by elephants that pour water from vessels (Gajalakṣmī; Indian painting, British Museum). Prosperity (artha) was a recognised aim of the householder’s life. Painting: unknown artist, British Museum; public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

Kāma.

Kāma includes erotic love but also, more broadly, the pleasures of the senses and the arts. The Kāmasūtra describes the life of the cultivated man-about-town (nāgaraka) and lists sixty-four arts (kalā) — singing, instrumental music, dance, painting, arranging flowers, making perfumes, word games, carpentry and many more — in which he, and the courtesan, should be skilled. Wendy Doniger and Sudhir Kakar, whose translation is now standard, emphasise that the text is a manual of urban sociability as much as of sex (Vātsyāyana 2002). The aesthetics of rasa, discussed in Chapter 21 and Volume 8, belongs in part to this world.

The legitimacy of kāma as an aim of life is reflected in the place of the erotic in Indian art and literature: in the love poetry of Sanskrit and Tamil, in the theory of the erotic rasa (śṛṅgāra), and in the sculpture of temples such as those at Khajuraho (10th–11th centuries) and Konark (13th century), whose erotic figures embarrassed Victorian visitors and some modern Indian reformers. Scholars have proposed many explanations of these sculptures — auspicious symbolism, tantric ritual, the depiction of the whole of life, royal display — and none has won general agreement. What is clear is that the Indian tradition did not, on the whole, treat sexual pleasure as sinful in itself, though it regulated it closely and regarded celibacy as the higher discipline for those seeking liberation. Women’s perspectives on kāma are harder to recover; the Kāmasūtra discusses the desires and strategies of women, including courtesans and wives, with some sympathy, but it is written for men (Vātsyāyana 2002).

The modern reception of the Kāmasūtra is itself a comparative story. The first English translation, prepared by the Indian scholars Bhagavanlal Indraji and Shivaram Parshuram Bhide for Richard Burton and Forster Fitzgerald Arbuthnot, was printed privately in 1883 by a “Kama Shastra Society” to evade Britain’s obscenity laws. It made the text famous in the West as a sex manual, an image that obscured both its broader concern with the cultivated life and its place in a sophisticated scholarly genre with its own commentaries, notably Yaśodhara’s Jayamaṅgalā (thirteenth century). In India, the text was for a time an embarrassment to reformers who wished to present Indian civilisation as spiritual and chaste; more recently it has been reclaimed as evidence of a frank and sophisticated attitude to pleasure. Both the Victorian exoticism and the nationalist embarrassment, Doniger has argued, misread a work whose subject was the art of living well within the social world of its time.

Mokṣa.

Liberation is understood very differently by different schools, as Table 6.1 shows. What they share is the idea of a final release from the round of rebirth driven by karma.

Table 6.1. Conceptions of final release in the major traditions (simplified) Tradition Conception of liberation Advaita Vedānta realisation that the self (ātman) is identical with Brahman; liberation is not a new state but the removal of ignorance; possible while living (jīvanmukti) Viśiṣṭādvaita (Rāmānuja) the self, a real mode of God, enjoys God’s presence eternally in Viṣṇu’s heaven, retaining its individuality Dvaita (Madhva) the self, eternally distinct from God and dependent on him, enjoys bliss according to its own nature Sāṃkhya–Yoga isolation (kaivalya) of the conscious self from matter Nyāya–Vaiśeṣika cessation of all specific qualities of the self, including pain and pleasure Buddhism nirvāṇa: the “blowing out” of greed, hatred and delusion; not the survival of a self Jainism the soul, freed of all karmic matter, rises to the top of the universe and abides in infinite knowledge, perception, bliss and energy

docs.title: 6.2.3 Artha and Machiavelli
docs.text:
The Arthaśāstra, the principal treatise on statecraft, was lost to modern knowledge until 1905, when a manuscript reached the Oriental Research Institute at Mysore; R. Shamasastry published the text in 1909 and an English translation in 1915. Tradition attributes it to Kauṭilya, minister of Candragupta Maurya; Patrick Olivelle, its most recent translator, argues that the text as we have it is a composite work, put together and revised between about 50 BCE and 300 CE from earlier material (Olivelle 2013). Its frank discussion of espionage, assassination, the manipulation of religious sentiment and the use of deceit in foreign policy startled its first modern readers. Max Weber, in his lecture “Politics as a Vocation” (1919), remarked that by comparison Machiavelli’s The Prince was harmless.

The comparison with Machiavelli is natural and has been made often. Both authors treat politics as a domain with its own rationality, distinct from private morality; both are concerned with the acquisition and preservation of power; both are prepared to recommend deceit and violence when the security of the state requires them. But the differences are significant. The Arthaśāstra is a comprehensive manual of administration — of revenue, mines, forests, trade, law courts and public works — in which the methods of covert action occupy a part; its king is bound to protect his subjects, to maintain the social order of varṇa and āśrama, and to place the welfare of his people above his own pleasure. Machiavelli wrote for a particular Italian situation and was preoccupied with the founding of states and with republican liberty, which the Indian text does not consider. Each is best read as a document of its own world, and the comparison is useful chiefly because it dispels the idea that Indian thought was concerned only with the spiritual.

docs.title: 6.2.4 The stages of life
docs.text:
The aims of life were connected with the system of four “stages” (āśrama): the celibate student, the householder, the forest-dweller and the renouncer. The usual account matches each stage to an aim, with the householder pursuing artha and kāma within dharma and the renouncer pursuing mokṣa (Table 6.2). Patrick Olivelle’s study of the system shows that in the oldest Dharmasūtras the āśramas were alternative, lifelong vocations that a young man chose after his studentship; the familiar sequence of four stages through which one passes was a later “classical” reformulation, designed in part to subordinate renunciation to the householder’s obligations (Olivelle 1993). The tension between world-affirming householder religion and world-renouncing asceticism runs through Indian religious history, and the four-stage model was one way of managing it.

Table 6.2. The four āśramas in the classical scheme (simplified) Stage Ideal way of life Notes student (brahmacārin) celibate study of the Veda in the teacher’s house open in theory to the three higher varṇas; in practice mainly Brahmins; excluded women and Śūdras householder (gṛhastha) marriage, children, ritual duties, earning, hospitality praised by Manu as the stage on which all others depend forest-dweller (vānaprastha) withdrawal to the forest, with or without the wife; austerities rarely practised as described; largely a textual ideal by the classical period renouncer (saṃnyāsin) abandonment of ritual fires, property and social ties; wandering, begging, seeking liberation in the earliest texts an alternative to householdership; later placed last in life

docs.title: 6.2.5 The renouncer and the householder
docs.text: Louis Dumont, in a famous essay on “world renunciation in Indian religions”, argued that the key to Indian religious history lies in the dialogue between the man-in-the-world, bound by the duties of caste and family, and the renouncer, who leaves society to seek liberation as an individual. Most of the new religious ideas of India, on this view, were invented by renouncers — the Upaniṣadic sages, the Buddha, Mahāvīra, the founders of sects — and then adapted for householders (Dumont 1980). The thesis has been criticised as too schematic, and Olivelle’s work on the āśramas shows that the relation between the two ideals was negotiated in different ways at different times (Olivelle 1993). But it captures something important. The Buddhist and Jain monastic orders, the Hindu ascetic orders established in the medieval period and the many independent holy men and women of every century offered an alternative to the life of the householder; and the householder’s religion of ritual, pilgrimage and devotion was shaped by the need to answer the renouncer’s challenge. The Sikh Gurus, by contrast, rejected renunciation and taught that the householder’s life of work and family is the right setting for devotion — another answer to the same question.

docs.title: 6.2.6 Renunciation compared
docs.text: Renunciation of household life for a religious goal is not unique to India, and comparison helps to bring out what was distinctive. Christian monasticism, from the desert fathers of fourth-century Egypt to the Benedictine and later orders of Europe, also involved celibacy, poverty and obedience, and also developed a tension between the contemplative life and life in the world. But Christian monks lived, after the early period, in permanent communities under a written rule, with the eucharist at the centre of their life, and Protestant Christianity rejected monasticism altogether as a superior way. Islam generally discouraged celibate renunciation — a saying attributed to the Prophet declares that there is no monasticism in Islam — though Sufi orders developed forms of discipline and retreat. In India the Buddhist and Jain orders, like the Christian ones, were organised communities with codes of discipline; the Brahmanical renouncer (saṃnyāsin) was in principle a solitary wanderer, though monastic institutions grew up later around figures such as Śaṅkara (Chapter 9). Dumont saw the renouncer as the Indian “individual-outside-the-world”, the one person who stood outside the hierarchical order of caste (Dumont 1980). The comparison suggests that the Indian traditions gave renunciation an unusually central place in their scheme of values, while at the same time — through the doctrine of the aims of life and the stages of life — working hard to keep it in balance with the life of the householder.

docs.title: 6.2.7 Who could pursue the aims?
docs.text: The scheme was formulated for twice-born men. The student stage, the Vedic learning it involved and the right to renunciation were in principle closed to Śūdras and to women. Women’s dharma was defined largely through marriage, and the classical texts gave them little independent access to mokṣa, although devotional and renunciant women — Buddhist nuns, Jain nuns, the Vīraśaiva Akka Mahādēvi, Lal Ded in Kashmir, Mīrābāī in Rajasthan — found their own paths, often in conflict with family and society. The modern habit of presenting the puruṣārthas as a universal model of balanced human flourishing is attractive, but it is a modern universalisation of a scheme that was originally addressed to a privileged minority.

docs.title: 6.2.8 Resolving the tension: the Gītā
docs.text: How can a life in the world be compatible with liberation from it? The Bhagavadgītā’s answer is action without attachment to its fruits (niṣkāma karma), quoted at the head of this chapter: one should do one’s duty, offering the results to God, and such action does not bind. The Gītā combines this “discipline of action” (karmayoga) with the disciplines of knowledge and devotion. It made possible a religious ideal for the householder that did not require renunciation, and it was this teaching that Tilak, Gandhi and Aurobindo made central to their modern reinterpretations (Chapters 11 and 12).

docs.title: 6.2.9 Buddhist and Jain parallels
docs.text: Buddhist and Jain texts do not use the scheme of the four aims, but they address similar questions. The Buddha rejected both sensual indulgence and extreme asceticism in favour of a “middle way”; he gave lay followers practical advice on earning and keeping wealth (the Sigālovāda Sutta, Dīgha Nikāya 31, is a famous example) while teaching that the highest happiness is nibbāna. Right livelihood (sammā ājīva) is one of the eight limbs of the noble path. Jainism distinguished the full vows of monks and nuns from the lesser vows (aṇuvrata) of lay people, who could pursue wealth within limits; Jain merchant communities became among the most prosperous in India. In both traditions the lay life is a legitimate but lesser path, oriented ultimately towards release.

docs.title: 6.3.1 The early Upaniṣads
docs.text: The word karma originally meant “action” and, in the Vedic context, above all ritual action. In the early Upaniṣads it acquires the sense of action that determines a person’s future existence. In the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad (3.2.13), the sage Yājñavalkya takes his questioner aside and tells him privately that “one becomes good by good action and bad by bad action”, as if this were new and secret teaching. Later in the same text (4.4.5) he declares that “as a person acts, as he behaves, so he becomes”. The Chāndogya Upaniṣad (5.10) describes two paths after death — the path of the gods for those who know, and the path of the fathers for those who perform rituals and good works — and adds that those whose conduct here has been pleasant will enter a pleasant womb, while those whose conduct has been foul will enter the womb of a dog, a pig or an outcaste (Olivelle 1998). The combination of karma with a hierarchy of births, including social hierarchy, is present from the beginning.

docs.title: 6.3.2 Debates about origins
docs.text: Where did these ideas come from? Some scholars trace them to developments within Vedic ritual thought, in which the results of sacrifice were stored up for the sacrificer’s future. Others, notably Johannes Bronkhorst, argue that rebirth and karmic retribution belonged originally to the culture of “Greater Magadha” in the eastern Ganges valley — the homeland of the Jains, Buddhists and Ājīvikas — and were absorbed into Brahmanical thought (Bronkhorst 2007). Gananath Obeyesekere has compared Indian ideas of rebirth with those of small-scale societies elsewhere and of ancient Greece, and argued that the distinctive Indian contribution was the “ethicisation” of rebirth, making the quality of the next life depend on moral conduct (Obeyesekere 2002). Wendy Doniger O’Flaherty’s edited volume remains a valuable survey of the classical variety (O’Flaherty 1980). These debates are unresolved; what is clear is that by the time of the Buddha and Mahāvīra the doctrine was common ground among most religious movements of north India.

docs.title: 6.4.1 Buddhist karma: intention without a self
docs.text:
The Buddha redefined karma as intention. “It is intention (cetanā), monks, that I call karma,” he says in a discourse of the Aṅguttara Nikāya (6.63); “having intended, one acts by body, speech and mind.” Unintended harm does not carry the same weight as deliberate harm. Buddhists faced a philosophical difficulty peculiar to their system: if there is no permanent self, who is reborn and who reaps the fruit of an action? The answer, developed in texts such as the Milindapañha, is that rebirth is a continuity of causally connected mental and physical processes, like a flame lit from another flame, so that the reborn being is “neither the same nor another” (Harvey 2013; Gethin 1998). Buddhist texts are not free of the association of karma with social status: a discourse in the Majjhima Nikāya (135) explains poverty, ugliness and low birth as the results of past misdeeds. But the Buddhist emphasis on intention and the denial that birth confers spiritual worth gave the doctrine a different social direction.

In practice, Buddhist lay life has long been organised around the making of merit (puñña). Lay people give food to monks, support monasteries, keep the precepts on holy days and sponsor rituals and buildings, in the expectation that these good actions will bring favourable results in this life and the next. A practice that might seem to contradict the strict doctrine of individual karma — the “transfer” or sharing of merit, in which the donor dedicates the merit of a good deed to deceased relatives or to all beings — became widespread in both Theravāda and Mahāyāna Buddhism, and inscriptions from early Indian Buddhist sites record donations made for the benefit of the donor’s parents. Scholars have debated whether this practice represents a departure from the Buddha’s teaching or a natural development of the idea that the intention of rejoicing in another’s good deed is itself meritorious. Similar tensions between strict individual karma and the desire to help others, especially the dead, appear in Hindu ancestral rites (śrāddha) and in the Mahāyāna ideal of the bodhisattva who gives away his merit. The comparison shows that the doctrine of karma, however rigorous in theory, was everywhere softened in practice by the claims of family, compassion and grace.

docs.title: 6.4.2 Jain karma: a fine matter
docs.text: For the Jains, as Chapter 3 explained, karma is a subtle matter that clings to the soul when it is moved by passion. Every action, intentional or not, involves some harm to living beings and attracts karma, though intentional violence binds far more strongly. Liberation therefore requires not only right intention but the cessation of activity and the burning off of accumulated karma by austerity. The Jain theory is the most systematic and in some ways the most “physical” of the Indian theories; Padmanabh Jaini’s account remains the best introduction (Jaini 1979).

docs.title: 6.4.3 Ājīvika fatalism and Cārvāka denial
docs.text: Not all Indian thinkers accepted the moral efficacy of action. The Ājīvikas, whose leader Makkhali Gosāla was a contemporary and rival of the Buddha and Mahāvīra, taught that everything is determined by fate (niyati) and that beings pass through a fixed number of births before release, whatever they do. The Buddha singled out this doctrine for particular criticism because it denied the value of effort. The materialists known as Cārvākas or Lokāyatas denied rebirth altogether, holding that consciousness arises from the combination of the elements and ends with the body. Their texts survive only in fragments quoted by their opponents, but their presence shows that karma and rebirth were never beyond dispute.

docs.title: 6.4.4 Brahmanical theories
docs.text: Within the Brahmanical schools the mechanism of karma was explained in several ways. The Mīmāṃsā school posited an unseen potency (apūrva) produced by a sacrifice, which persists until it bears fruit. The Nyāya theologians, especially Udayana (11th century), argued that unconscious karma cannot by itself distribute its results justly and that God (īśvara) must be the dispenser of the fruits of action. Vedānta commentators distinguished accumulated karma (sañcita), the portion that has begun to bear fruit in the present life (prārabdha) and the karma being created now (āgāmin or kriyamāṇa); knowledge of Brahman destroys the first and prevents the third, but the second must run its course, which explains why a liberated person continues to live until the body falls away. Wilhelm Halbfass’s essays trace these debates and their philosophical stakes (Halbfass 1991).

docs.title: 6.5.1 Destiny and human effort
docs.text: Does the doctrine of karma imply fatalism? Most Indian thinkers said no. Present circumstances are the results of past actions, but present actions are free and shape the future. The epics and the nīti literature debate the relative weight of “fate” (daiva) and “human effort” (puruṣakāra), and generally come down on the side of effort. A well-known verse in the Hitopadeśa puts it pithily: tasks are accomplished by effort, not by wishing; deer do not walk into the mouth of a sleeping lion. The Yogavāsiṣṭha (Chapter 2) insists that “fate” is nothing but the effort of the past.

docs.title: 6.5.2 Grace
docs.text: Devotional theologies raised a different question: can God’s grace override karma? The answers varied. In the Śrīvaiṣṇava tradition after Rāmānuja, two schools debated the role of the devotee’s own effort in surrender: the northern (Vaṭakalai) school compared the soul to a baby monkey that must cling to its mother, the southern (Teṅkalai) school to a kitten that the mother cat carries without its effort. Śaiva Siddhānta made grace (Tamil aruḷ) the final cause of release. Vallabha’s “path of grace” (puṣṭimārga) taught that grace is unconditioned by merit. The Bhagavadgītā (18.66) itself ends with a promise of release from all sins to the one who takes refuge in Kṛṣṇa alone. Grace in these traditions did not abolish karma, but it qualified the picture of a mechanical moral law (Carman 1974).

docs.title: 6.6 Rebirth in Comparative Perspective
docs.text:
Belief in rebirth is not unique to India. Some ancient Greek thinkers — the Pythagoreans, Empedocles and Plato, whose Republic ends with the myth of Er describing souls choosing their next lives — taught the transmigration of souls; ideas of rebirth are found among many small-scale societies in Africa, the Americas and elsewhere. Obeyesekere argued that what distinguishes the Indian traditions is the systematic linking of rebirth to the ethical quality of actions, and the goal of escaping rebirth altogether (Obeyesekere 2002).

In the twentieth century, some researchers attempted to investigate rebirth empirically. The American psychiatrist Ian Stevenson (1918–2007) of the University of Virginia collected and published, from the 1960s onwards, hundreds of cases, many from India and Sri Lanka, of young children who were said to remember previous lives, and argued that some of them were difficult to explain except by reincarnation. His work was conducted with more care than most writing on the subject, and it was taken seriously by some scholars; but critics pointed out that the cases depended on the testimony of families who often believed in rebirth beforehand, that contamination of the children’s statements by information from adults was hard to exclude, and that the cases were most common in cultures where rebirth was expected. The scientific community has not accepted that rebirth has been demonstrated. The episode is mentioned here because claims that “science has proved” rebirth are often made in popular Indian writing; they rest on this contested body of case studies and on nothing stronger.

Within India, the traditions that came from outside the subcontinent took different views. Islam and Christianity teach a single earthly life followed by resurrection and judgement, and most Indian Muslims and Christians reject rebirth; some Sufis and some Indian Christian thinkers engaged with the idea in dialogue, but it did not become part of their teaching. The Sikh Gurus accepted the round of birth and death and the force of actions, but placed the emphasis on the divine order (hukam) and on God’s gracious glance (nadar), through which the devotee who remembers the divine name is released; for Sikhs, as for the devotional Hindu traditions, karma is real but not the last word. The comparison shows that karma and rebirth, though shared across most Indian religions, were not shared across all the religions of India.

docs.title: 6.7 Modern Reinterpretations
docs.text:
In the late nineteenth and twentieth centuries the doctrines of the aims of life and of karma were reinterpreted to meet the needs of a colonised society seeking self-respect and political action. The decisive text was the Bhagavadgītā. B. G. Tilak, in the Gītā Rahasya (written in Mandalay prison and published in 1915), argued against the dominant renunciatory interpretation that the Gītā teaches above all the discipline of action (karmayoga) — that the enlightened person continues to act for the welfare of the world. Aurobindo’s Essays on the Gita read it as a gospel of divine action in the world. Gandhi, who translated it into Gujarati as Anāsaktiyoga (“The Yoga of Non-attachment”, completed in 1929), read it as teaching selfless service and, allegorically, non-violence. Vivekananda’s Karma Yoga presented work done without attachment as a path to liberation open to all (Chapter 10).

These readings turned a text that had been used to justify renunciation, or the duties of caste, into a charter for social and political activism. Ambedkar dissented sharply. In unfinished writings on the history of ancient India he argued that the Gītā was a defence of the class system against the Buddha’s egalitarian challenge, and that its doctrine of svadharma bound each person to the occupation of his birth. The disagreement between Gandhi’s and Ambedkar’s readings of the same text is a vivid example of the way in which modern Indians argued about their tradition by arguing about the meaning of its scriptures (Chapter 12).

The word “karma” itself has entered English and other languages in a popular sense — something like “what goes around comes around” — that has lost most of its technical meaning. The popular sense is a small example of the global careers of Indian ideas discussed in Part III of this volume.

docs.title: 6.8.1 Karma as theodicy
docs.text:
Max Weber described the doctrine of karma, combined with caste, as “the most consistent theodicy ever produced by history”: it explained every inequality of birth as deserved, and promised that obedience to one’s caste duties would be rewarded in a future life (Weber 1958). The remark is one-sided, but it identifies a real use of the doctrine. Texts from the Chāndogya Upaniṣad onward linked birth in a low caste to past misdeeds, and the doctrine could be, and was, used to justify the suffering of the poor and the outcaste as merited.

Indian critics of caste saw this clearly. The devotional poets denied that God respects caste, and so implicitly denied that low birth reflects spiritual unworthiness. Ambedkar rejected the Brahmanical doctrine of karma as an instrument of caste, and in The Buddha and His Dhamma he reinterpreted the Buddhist doctrine to exclude the transmigration of a soul and to make karma a principle of moral responsibility in this life rather than an explanation of inherited status (Ambedkar 1957). Some Buddhist scholars regard his interpretation as a departure from canonical teaching; it is, in any case, a deliberate and argued response to a real problem.

docs.title: 6.8.2 Other objections
docs.text: Classical and modern critics raised further objections. If the round of rebirth has no beginning, how did inequality first arise? The traditions answered that there was no first moment, so the question does not arise — an answer that satisfies some readers and not others. How can the results of action be stored and transmitted without a mechanism? The Mīmāṃsakas, Naiyāyikas, Buddhists and Jains each proposed one, and each criticised the others’. Can karma be known? Defenders appealed to scripture, to the testimony of yogis said to remember past lives, and to the argument that karma best explains the inequalities of birth; critics, from the Cārvākas to modern sceptics, have found these reasons inadequate. These are live philosophical questions, and the sophistication of the classical debates is one of the treasures of Indian philosophy (Volume 3).

docs.title: 6.8.3 Modern analogies
docs.text: Modern writers have compared the classical theory of latent impressions (saṃskāra) and dispositions (vāsanā) — which in the Yoga and Buddhist traditions are laid down by actions and condition future perception and behaviour — with modern psychological accounts of habit, implicit memory and conditioning. The analogy is suggestive and has been used fruitfully in psychology (Chapter 20 and Volume 22). It should not be pressed too far. The classical theory explains rebirth and liberation; modern psychology does not deal with either, and its accounts of habit rest on experimental evidence of a kind the classical theorists did not seek.

docs.title: 6.9 Assessment
docs.text: The four aims of life and the doctrine of karma were among the most widely shared ideas of pre-modern India, and they shaped Indian ethics, law, literature and religious practice. A comparative account must recognise both their range and their limits. The aims of life were a balanced and humane scheme for the twice-born householder; for others they were partly closed. Karma made moral responsibility central to the understanding of the world; it was also used to justify inequality, and Indians argued about its meaning, mechanism and truth for more than two millennia. Its modern reinterpretations, from Vivekananda’s to Ambedkar’s, belong to the same history of debate.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text:
• Olivelle (1993): the history of the āśrama system.

  • Vātsyāyana (2002) and Olivelle (2013): translations of the Kāmasūtra and the Arthaśāstra.

  • O’Flaherty (1980) and Obeyesekere (2002): karma and rebirth in classical and comparative perspective.

  • Bronkhorst (2007): the case for the eastern origins of karma and rebirth.

  • Halbfass (1991): philosophical essays on karma, dharma and related concepts.

  • Harvey (2000): Buddhist ethics, including intention and karma.

docs.title: Chapter 7: Non-violence and Truth: Ethical Ideals Across Traditions
docs.text: savve pāṇā savve bhūyā savve jīvā savve sattā na hantavvā… esa dhamme suddhe ṇiie sāsae No breathing, existing, living, sentient creature should be killed … This is the pure, unchanging, eternal law. — Ācārāṅga Sūtra 1.4.1 (Jain canon)

docs.title: 7.1 Two Ideals, Many Traditions
docs.text: Non-violence (ahiṃsā) and truthfulness (satya) head almost every Indian list of virtues. They are the first two of the five great vows of Jain monks and nuns, the first two restraints (yama) of Patañjali’s Yoga, and the first two of the common duties in many Brahmanical lists; Buddhist ethics gives them a place in its precepts and in the noble eightfold path; and in the twentieth century Gandhi made them the twin foundations of his politics. It is tempting to conclude that they were the shared core of “Indian ethics”. They were indeed widely shared, but each tradition understood them differently, set different limits to them and argued with the others about those limits. This chapter traces those differences.

docs.title: 7.2.1 Sacrifice and its critics
docs.text:
The Vedic religion centred on sacrifice, and many sacrifices involved killing animals. Already in the later Vedic ritual texts there are signs of unease: animals are killed by suffocation outside the sacred enclosure, the victim’s consent is ritually sought, and some passages speak of the victim taking revenge in the next world. The Chāndogya Upaniṣad lists non-injury (ahiṃsā) among the “gifts” that a person makes as an inner sacrifice, together with austerity, generosity, uprightness and truthful speech (3.17.4), and its final passage praises the householder who “does not harm any creature except at holy places” (8.15) — an exception that shows how the ideal was reconciled with sacrifice (Olivelle 1998).

The decisive impulse came from the renunciant movements of the eastern Ganges valley. Both the Jains and the Buddhists made non-injury fundamental and attacked animal sacrifice as cruel and useless. Ludwig Alsdorf’s classic study argued that the Brahmanical tradition’s growing preference for vegetarianism and its veneration of the cow were in large part responses to this challenge; D. N. Jha has documented the extensive references to meat-eating, including beef, in the Vedic and early Brahmanical texts (Alsdorf 2010; Jha 2002). The history of these practices is contested and politically sensitive in modern India, but the textual evidence that early Vedic religion included animal sacrifice and meat-eating is not in serious dispute among historians.

docs.title: 7.2.2 The Mīmāṃsā defence of sacrifice
docs.text: The Brahmanical exegetes of the Veda did not simply concede the renunciants’ case. The Mīmāṃsā school, whose task was to interpret the Vedic injunctions, faced a direct question: the Veda commands certain animal sacrifices, while a general rule, accepted by the Mīmāṃsakas themselves, forbids injury to any being. How can both be valid? The answer developed by Kumārila Bhaṭṭa (seventh century) and others was that the general prohibition and the specific injunction operate in different domains: the injunction to sacrifice establishes that the sacrifice achieves its ritual result, while the injury involved may still carry its own consequence, or, on another view, injury performed at the Veda’s command is not the forbidden injury at all. A maxim often repeated in later literature put it bluntly: Vedic killing is not killing. The Manusmṛti (5.39, 5.44) adopts this position, declaring that the Self-existent created animals for sacrifice and that injury enjoined by the Veda is to be regarded as non-injury. Buddhists and Jains rejected the argument as a pretext for cruelty, and the materialist Cārvākas, as reported in the fourteenth-century Sarvadarśanasaṃgraha, ridiculed it: if an animal killed in the sacrifice goes to heaven, why does the sacrificer not offer his own father? The exchange is one of the clearest examples of the long argument between the Vedic and renunciant traditions, and it shows that the Brahmanical acceptance of ahiṃsā was gradual and contested rather than original.

docs.title: 7.2.3 Jain non-violence
docs.text:
In Jainism non-violence is the supreme principle from which the other vows follow. The Jain universe is crowded with souls: besides humans and animals, there are souls embodied in earth, water, fire, air and plants, which have only the sense of touch, and myriads of minute creatures. The second chapter of the Tattvārthasūtra classifies living beings by the number of their senses, from one-sensed beings (earth-bodies, water-bodies, fire-bodies, air-bodies and plants) through worms (two senses), ants (three), bees and flies (four) to humans, animals, birds and fish (five) (Umāsvāti 1994). Every action risks harming some of them. Jain monks and nuns therefore carry a whisk (rajoharaṇa) to brush insects from their path, filter their water, do not eat after dark, and in some Śvetāmbara orders wear a cloth over the mouth. Lay Jains take lesser vows that forbid intentional violence to mobile beings while recognising that some harm is unavoidable in worldly life. Jains became strict vegetarians, avoiding also honey, alcohol and, in stricter practice, root vegetables, whose harvesting kills the plant and the many beings in the soil (Dundas 2002; Jaini 1979).

Jain thinkers analysed violence with great subtlety. They distinguished violence by body, speech and mind; violence done, caused to be done and approved; and, above all, the passions — anger, pride, deceit and greed — that make violence binding. Intention mattered; but so did carelessness. The Jain ideal culminates, for a few, in the vow of ending one’s life by gradual fasting (sallekhanā) when death approaches, a practice the community regards as the opposite of suicide because it is undertaken without passion. In 2015 a High Court ruling that it was suicide provoked large Jain protests, and the ruling was stayed by the Supreme Court.

docs.title: 7.2.4 Buddhist non-harming
docs.text:
The first of the five precepts taken by Buddhist lay people is “I undertake the training rule to abstain from taking life”. The Buddha’s emphasis on intention (Chapter 6) shaped Buddhist non-violence: killing is wrong because of the hatred or greed behind it, and its gravity depends on the being killed and the state of mind of the killer. The positive counterpart is loving-kindness (mettā) and compassion (karuṇā). The Karaṇīya Mettā Sutta (Sutta Nipāta 1.8), recited daily in Theravāda countries, wishes that all beings, weak or strong, seen or unseen, near or far, born or yet to be born, may be happy, and asks the practitioner to cultivate towards all a boundless mind, as a mother protects her only child (Harvey 2000).

On diet, Buddhist traditions diverged. The Pali Vinaya allows monks to accept meat provided they have not seen, heard or suspected that the animal was killed for them; the Theravāda tradition has largely followed this rule. Several Mahāyāna sūtras, notably the Laṅkāvatāra, condemn meat-eating, and Chinese Buddhist monasticism became vegetarian. Tibetan Buddhists, living where vegetables were scarce, generally ate meat. The emperor Aśoka, a Buddhist, records in his first rock edict that the animals killed daily for the royal kitchen had been reduced to two peacocks and a deer, and that even these would soon not be killed; his fifth pillar edict lists species protected from slaughter (Thapar 2002).

docs.title: 7.2.5 The Brahmanical synthesis
docs.text: The Dharmaśāstras absorbed the ideal of non-injury while preserving Vedic sacrifice. Manu condemns meat-eating in strong terms — “meat can never be obtained without injury to living beings” (5.48), and the one who permits, cuts, kills, buys, sells, cooks, serves and eats are all “killers” (5.51) — but he also declares that animals were created for sacrifice and that “the injury sanctioned by the Veda” should be regarded as non-injury (5.39, 5.44), and he permits meat in rituals and in times of distress (Olivelle 2005). The tension is left unresolved; the commentators debated it for centuries. The Mahābhārata repeatedly declares that “non-injury is the highest dharma” (ahiṃsā paramo dharmaḥ), particularly in its didactic books, while also telling stories in which killing is a duty. One passage of the Anuśāsanaparvan calls non-injury the highest dharma, the highest self-restraint, the highest gift and the highest austerity. A line often quoted in modern popular sources as the continuation of the phrase — that “violence in defence of dharma is also dharma” — is not found in the critical edition of the epic and appears to be a modern addition; it should not be cited as scripture.

docs.title: 7.2.6 Tamil and other voices
docs.text: The Tamil Tirukkuṟaḷ (c. 5th century), a collection of 1,330 couplets on virtue, wealth and love, gives whole chapters to “abstaining from meat” (chapter 26) and “not killing” (chapter 33); its author’s religious affiliation is disputed, but its ethics shows the influence of Jain ideas (Volume 8). The sant poets of north India were mostly vegetarian and mocked ritual slaughter by Hindus and Muslims alike. The Sikh tradition left diet largely to individual conscience, but the Sikh code of conduct forbids eating meat slaughtered by the Muslim ritual method; and the tenth Guru, Gobind Singh, in the Persian Zafarnāma attributed to him, defended the use of the sword when all other means have failed. At the Mughal court, Jain monks persuaded Akbar to forbid animal slaughter on certain days (Chapter 16).

docs.title: 7.3.1 War and the warrior’s duty
docs.text: None of the Indian traditions except the strictest Jain monastic ideal held that all violence is forbidden to everyone. The Brahmanical texts assigned warfare to the Kṣatriya class and elaborated rules of righteous war (dharmayuddha): warriors should fight only their equals, should not strike the fleeing, the unarmed or those who surrender, and should spare non-combatants. How far these rules were observed is another question, and the Mahābhārata itself shows them being broken by both sides. The ethics of war is discussed in Volume 20. The Bhagavadgītā is set on a battlefield and urges a reluctant warrior to fight; Gandhi read the battle as an allegory of the inner struggle, but most commentators, ancient and modern, have read it as a defence of the warrior’s duty. Buddhist kings fought wars, and Buddhist texts developed justifications for violence in defence of the Dharma. Non-violence was an ideal of great power, but in every tradition it coexisted with an acknowledged place for coercion.

docs.title: 7.3.2 Non-violence as royal policy
docs.text: Before Gandhi, non-violence was occasionally made a principle of state policy, always within limits. Aśoka restricted the killing of animals and renounced wars of conquest while keeping his army and warning the forest peoples of his power (Chapter 5). In twelfth-century Gujarat, the Caulukya king Kumārapāla, influenced by the Jain polymath Hemacandra, is said by Jain chroniclers to have prohibited animal slaughter in his kingdom; the extent of the prohibition is uncertain, but the story shows the influence of the Jain merchant community on royal policy. Mughal emperors, as noted above, made concessions on animal slaughter at the request of Jain monks. None of these rulers abandoned war or the death penalty. The modern Indian state’s Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act (1960) and its laws protecting wildlife belong to a different, largely secular, tradition of animal welfare, though their advocates have often appealed to Indian religious ideals.

docs.title: 7.3.3 Buddhist ethics of war
docs.text: Buddhist texts generally condemn killing, but Buddhist societies faced the same need for defence and punishment as others. Some Mahāyāna texts discuss whether a bodhisattva may kill to prevent a greater evil — for example, to stop a robber about to murder many people — and allow it as an act of compassion that the bodhisattva accepts at the cost of his own karmic suffering. The Sri Lankan chronicle Mahāvaṃsa (c. 5th–6th century) tells how the king Duṭṭhagāmaṇī, troubled by the killing of thousands in his war against the Tamil king Eḷāra, was consoled by monks who told him that only one and a half of those killed had been true Buddhists. The passage has been cited in modern times both as evidence of Buddhist justifications of violence and as a cautionary example. As with the Hindu and Jain cases, the ideal of non-injury coexisted with arguments for exceptions.

docs.title: 7.3.4 Non-violence and diet in modern India
docs.text: In modern India the ideal of non-injury has been linked with vegetarianism and the protection of the cow. Article 48 of the Constitution, one of the non-binding Directive Principles, asks the state to take steps to prohibit cow slaughter, and most states have laws to that effect. In recent decades cow protection has also become the occasion of political mobilisation and of violence, much of it directed against Muslims and Dalits engaged in cattle trade or leather work. It is a sharp irony, and a warning against treating “ahiṃsā” as a simple national virtue, that an ideal of non-injury has been invoked to justify injury.

docs.title: 7.4.1 Ṛta and satya
docs.text:
In the Ṛgveda, truth (satya) is closely linked with cosmic order (ṛta); both are guarded by Varuṇa, and the “truth-act” — a solemn declaration of truth that compels the world to respond — appears in Vedic and later literature, including Buddhist tales. In the Upaniṣads truth becomes a name of ultimate reality itself. The Bṛhadāraṇyaka (1.4.14) identifies dharma with truth. The Taittirīya Upaniṣad’s charge to the departing student (1.11) begins: “Speak the truth; practise dharma; do not neglect your recitation.” The Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad provided the Republic of India with its national motto:

Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.1.6

satyam eva jayate nānṛtaṃ satyena panthā vitato devayānaḥ yenākramanty ṛṣayo hy āptakāmā yatra tat satyasya paramaṃ nidhānam Truth alone prevails, not untruth. By truth is laid out the path to the gods, by which the seers, their desires fulfilled, ascend to where that highest treasure of truth is.

The first words of this verse, satyam eva jayate, were adopted in 1950 as the national motto of the Republic of India and appear beneath the Aśokan lion capital on the state emblem, in Devanāgarī script. The choice is an example of the selective use of tradition discussed in Chapter 5: a phrase from an Upaniṣad, in which truth is the path to the world of the gods and the treasure of the seers, has become a civic maxim about the victory of truth in public life. The reinterpretation is legitimate, and Gandhi’s identification of truth with God gave it a modern meaning that many Indians share; but it is a reinterpretation. In its Upaniṣadic setting the verse concerns the inner discipline of the seeker, not the honesty of governments. That modern India chose a maxim about truth for its motto, and an emblem from a Buddhist emperor’s pillar for its seal, nonetheless says something about the self-image its founders hoped to project: a state founded on truth and righteousness rather than on conquest or faith.

docs.title: 7.4.2 Truth and its competitors
docs.text:
If truth was praised everywhere, the tradition also recognised that truthfulness can conflict with other duties. Manu (4.138) advises: “one should speak the truth, one should speak what is pleasant; one should not speak an unpleasant truth, nor a pleasant falsehood: this is the eternal dharma.” The commentary on the Yogasūtra (c. 325–425 CE) attributed to Vyāsa holds that speech should agree with what has been seen and inferred, and that it should be uttered for the benefit of all beings; speech that harms is not truth but a semblance of virtue. The Mahābhārata tells the story of the ascetic Kauśika, who had vowed always to tell the truth; when robbers asked him which way some fleeing travellers had gone, he told them, the travellers were killed, and Kauśika went to hell. Kṛṣṇa tells the story to persuade Arjuna that dharma cannot be reduced to a rule. The epic also tells, against this, the story of Yudhiṣṭhira’s half-lie and its consequences (Chapter 5).

The most famous Indian exemplar of truth at any cost is King Hariścandra, who in the version of the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa gives up his kingdom, his wife and son and his own freedom rather than break his word. Gandhi records in his autobiography that a play on Hariścandra, seen in his boyhood, haunted him and made him ask why all should not be truthful like him (Gandhi 1927).

docs.title: 7.4.3 Truth in the yoga and Buddhist paths
docs.text:
Patañjali lists truthfulness as the second of the five restraints (yama), after non-injury, and adds that when the restraints are practised without exception of class, place, time or circumstance they constitute the “great vow” (mahāvrata) (Yogasūtra 2.30–31) (Maas 2013). The Buddhist path includes right speech: abstaining from lies, divisive speech, harsh speech and idle chatter. The Buddha’s discourses advise speaking only what is true, beneficial and timely, and sometimes keeping silent even when a statement would be true.

The Jain vow of truthfulness is subordinated explicitly to non-injury. Jain texts on monastic conduct instruct monks and nuns to avoid not only false speech but true speech that would cause harm — harsh words, words that reveal a hiding animal to a hunter, words that provoke violence — and to prefer silence or carefully qualified statements in such cases. The Jain treatment thus resolves in advance the dilemma that the Brahmanical story of Kauśika, discussed above, leaves troubling: where truth and non-injury conflict, non-injury prevails, but the solution is silence rather than a lie. The three traditions agree that truthfulness is a fundamental virtue; they differ, in instructive ways, on what to do when it collides with others.

docs.title: 7.4.4 Truth and many-sidedness
docs.text: The Jains combined the vow of truthfulness with a distinctive epistemology. The doctrine of “non-one-sidedness” (anekāntavāda) holds that reality has infinite aspects, and that every assertion is true only from a particular standpoint (naya); the method of “conditional predication” (syādvāda) expresses this by qualifying statements with “in a certain respect” (syāt) and by a sevenfold scheme of predication. The famous parable of the blind men and the elephant, each of whom describes the animal by the part he touches, is told in Jain, Buddhist and Hindu sources in different forms. Modern Jains often present anekāntavāda as a philosophy of tolerance, and it can support one. Classically, however, it was also a weapon of debate: Jain logicians used it to show that the one-sided views of their opponents were partial, and that the Jain view alone integrated the partial truths (Dundas 2002). It is, in other words, another inclusivism.

docs.title: 7.4.5 Truth in law
docs.text: The legal texts were concerned with truth in a practical setting: the testimony of witnesses. Manu (8.79–101) prescribes how witnesses are to be questioned and solemnly exhorted to tell the truth, and warns of the terrible consequences of false testimony in this life and the next. Yet he also allows (8.103–104) that where telling the truth would lead to the death of a person of any class, a falsehood is to be preferred, and prescribes a small expiation for it. Where evidence failed, the law-books provided for ordeals (divya) — by balance, fire, water or poison — in which the gods were believed to reveal the truth; the Yājñavalkya Smṛti and later digests give detailed procedures (Volume 18). The combination of exhortation, permitted exception and ordeal shows a legal culture that valued truth highly and knew how hard it was to establish.

docs.title: 7.4.6 Truth in philosophy
docs.text:
Indian philosophers also asked what truth is and how it is known; the debate between Nyāya and Mīmāṃsā about whether a cognition’s truth is established from outside or is intrinsic to it, which invites comparison with the correspondence and pragmatist theories of modern Western philosophy, is set out with the theory of the means of knowledge in Chapter 4. Buddhist philosophers distinguished two levels of truth. The Madhyamaka philosopher Nāgārjuna (c. 2nd century CE) wrote:

Nāgārjuna, Mūlamadhyamakakārikā 24.8

dve satye samupāśritya buddhānāṃ dharmadeśanā lokasaṃvṛtisatyaṃ ca satyaṃ ca paramārthataḥ The Buddhas’ teaching of the Dharma rests on two truths: conventional, worldly truth and truth in the ultimate sense.

Conventional truth is the world of persons, things and causes as ordinarily understood; ultimate truth is their emptiness of intrinsic nature. Advaita Vedānta adopted a similar distinction between the empirical and the ultimate standpoints (Chapter 9), with a very different account of what is ultimately real. In both traditions the highest truth was held to be beyond the reach of ordinary language, though not beyond the reach of argument. Mark Siderits’s introduction shows how these Buddhist arguments can be engaged with by contemporary philosophers (Siderits 2007).

docs.title: 7.4.7 Gandhi’s truth
docs.text:
In the twentieth century Gandhi made truth the centre of his religion and politics. He called his autobiography The Story of My Experiments with Truth and named his method of resistance satyāgraha, “holding firmly to truth”. He explained that he had first held that “God is Truth” and later came to say that “Truth is God”, a formulation he thought could be accepted even by an honest atheist. For Gandhi truth and non-violence were inseparable: no one possesses the whole truth, so no one is entitled to impose his truth by violence. This is discussed further in Chapter 12.

Gandhi’s methods had antecedents in Indian practice as well as in his reading of Tolstoy, Ruskin and Thoreau (Chapter 12). Colonial observers described the custom of “sitting dharnā”, in which a creditor or petitioner sat fasting at the door of a debtor or official until his claim was met, and Brahmins in some regions threatened to fast to death to compel kings; Jain ascetics fasted as spiritual discipline, and fasting was a familiar religious practice in Gandhi’s own family. Gandhi transformed these practices by joining them to an explicit ethic of non-injury and truth and by using them in mass political campaigns. The continuity and the transformation are both important: satyāgraha was neither a simple revival of tradition nor an import from the West.

docs.title: 7.4.8 Non-violence and its critics in the freedom struggle
docs.text: Gandhi’s non-violence was never the only strategy of the Indian freedom movement, and Indian critics argued with it vigorously. Revolutionary groups in Bengal, Maharashtra and Punjab from the 1900s onwards used bombs and assassinations, often justifying themselves from the Gītā’s teaching of action without attachment to results. Bhagat Singh (1907–1931), hanged for the killing of a British police officer, wrote while awaiting execution an essay “Why I Am an Atheist” and statements that defended revolutionary violence as a response to the violence of the colonial state; he became, and remains, one of the most popular heroes of the national movement. Subhas Chandra Bose, twice president of the Congress, broke with Gandhi and during the Second World War led the Indian National Army, formed with Japanese support, against the British. Ambedkar criticised Gandhi’s fasts as a form of coercion when directed against the Depressed Classes (Chapter 12). Historians continue to debate how far independence was won by non-violent mass movements, by the threat of violence, or by the weakening of Britain in the Second World War. What is clear is that the Indian tradition of argument about non-violence, traced in this chapter from the Vedic sacrifice to the renouncers, continued vigorously in the twentieth century.

docs.title: 7.5 Comparisons
docs.text:
Comparisons with other traditions help to clarify what is distinctive here. Christian traditions include strong currents of non-retaliation and pacifism, from the Sermon on the Mount through the Anabaptists and Quakers to Tolstoy, who influenced Gandhi directly; but they generally restrict moral concern to human beings. Islamic law developed detailed rules limiting the conduct of war and protecting non-combatants. The Confucian virtue of humaneness (ren) centres on human relationships. What distinguishes the Jain tradition in particular is the sheer extent of the beings it brings within the scope of non-injury, and the rigour with which its monks and nuns tried to live accordingly. What distinguishes the Indian traditions more generally is the long, sophisticated and still unfinished argument among them about where the limits of non-injury should be drawn: between Vedic sacrifice and renunciant critique, between the warrior’s duty and the monk’s vow, between Theravāda and Mahāyāna monks on meat, between Gandhi and his critics on the use of force (Table 7.1). Christopher Chapple’s study of non-violence towards animals, the earth and the self in Asian traditions gives an overview of these debates (Chapple 1993).

Table 7.1. Non-injury in Indian traditions: scope and limits (simplified) Tradition Scope of non-injury Recognised limits or exceptions Jain all living beings, including those with one sense (earth, water, fire, air and plant bodies); intention and carelessness both count lay vows graded; unavoidable harm in household life minimised rather than eliminated Buddhist all sentient beings; the first precept forbids intentional killing intention decisive; Theravāda monks may accept meat not killed for them; debates about war and kingship Brahmanical a general duty (Manu 10.63), increasingly emphasised Vedic sacrifice, the warrior’s duty, punishment by the king Sikh compassion (dayā) as a virtue; the communal kitchen (laṅgar) serves vegetarian food, though views on meat-eating vary armed defence of the oppressed as a last resort Gandhian non-violence in thought, word and deed as a political method and a way of life Gandhi held that violence is preferable to cowardice

docs.title: 7.5.1 Animals in other traditions
docs.text: Concern for animals was not unique to India. In the Greek world, Pythagoras and his followers abstained from meat, partly on the ground that souls pass between human and animal bodies, a doctrine that ancient writers sometimes connected, without good evidence, with India; Empedocles condemned animal sacrifice as the killing of kin; and the Neoplatonist Porphyry (third century CE) wrote a treatise On Abstinence from Animal Food. In the Islamic tradition, the Qurʾān describes animals as communities like human communities, and Islamic law prohibits cruelty to animals and regulates slaughter; but it permits the eating of meat and requires sacrifice at the festival of ʿĪd al-Aḍḥā. In modern Western philosophy, the case for moral concern for animals was made by Jeremy Bentham and, in the twentieth century, by Peter Singer and Tom Regan on the basis of the capacity to suffer or of animals’ inherent value. These arguments are secular and do not depend on rebirth, but modern animal-rights and vegetarian movements in the West have often drawn inspiration from Indian, and especially Jain and Buddhist, examples.

docs.title: 7.5.2 Non-violence as a world tradition
docs.text:
The modern idea of non-violent resistance was formed by exchanges across continents. Gandhi drew on Thoreau’s essay on civil disobedience (1849) and on Tolstoy’s Christian pacifism, whose influence on him is described in Chapter 12; Tolstoy’s “Letter to a Hindu” (1908), written to an Indian revolutionary, urged Indians to free themselves by refusing to cooperate with evil rather than by violence, and Gandhi translated it and corresponded with its author until Tolstoy’s death in 1910. Gandhi’s methods in turn were adopted and adapted by Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan, whose Khudai Khidmatgar (“Servants of God”), founded in 1929, organised Pashtun Muslims in non-violent resistance on the North-West Frontier; by Martin Luther King Jr., who visited India in 1959 and described non-violence as the method and Christian love as the motive of the American civil-rights movement; and by many others discussed in Chapter 12. Non-violence, in its modern political form, is thus a joint creation of Indian, Christian, Muslim and secular traditions, which is itself a good example of what samanvaya can mean.

Truth, too, was argued about. The Indian traditions did not simply praise truthfulness; they asked whether truth must always be spoken, whether it may be withheld for the sake of others, whether any one standpoint can grasp the whole truth, and whether ultimate truth can be expressed in words at all. Those questions remain open, and they are one of the richest legacies of the traditions surveyed in this volume.

docs.text:
