  • Alsdorf (2010) and Jha (2002): the history of vegetarianism and of meat-eating in India.

  • Jaini (1979): the Jain path, including non-violence and many-sidedness.

  • Harvey (2000): Buddhist ethics.

  • Gandhi (1927): Gandhi’s own account of his “experiments with truth”.

docs.title: Chapter 8: Seeing India from Outside: Orientalism and Comparative Philosophy
docs.text: “I have never found one among them who could deny that a single shelf of a good European library was worth the whole native literature of India and Arabia.” — T. B. Macaulay, Minute on Indian Education, 2 February 1835

docs.title: 8.1 Why This History Matters
docs.text: Every description of Indian traditions in English, including the one in this series, inherits categories formed in a long history of encounter: “Hinduism” as a religion with a scripture and a creed, “Indian philosophy” as six orthodox and three heterodox schools, “the Vedic age”, “the caste system”, “the spiritual East”. Some of these categories were coined by outsiders, some by Indians in conversation with outsiders, and most have been contested. A volume that compares Indian traditions with one another and with the thought of other civilisations must therefore look at how such comparisons were made in the past, by whom and for what purposes. This chapter tells that story from the Greek and Chinese visitors of antiquity to the scholarly debates about “Orientalism” at the end of the twentieth century. Table 8.1 gathers some of its landmarks, together with some Indian responses; it is selective, meant to show the pace and sequence of the encounter rather than to list every important work.

docs.title: 8.2.1 Greek and Chinese observers
docs.text:
Greek writers knew of India from the Persian empire and, after Alexander’s campaign in the Indus valley (327–325 BCE), from eyewitnesses. Megasthenes, ambassador of Seleucus to the court of Candragupta Maurya around 300 BCE, wrote an Indica that survives only in fragments quoted by later authors. He described the society he saw as divided into seven hereditary “classes” — philosophers, farmers, herdsmen, artisans, soldiers, overseers and councillors — a description that does not match the Brahmanical four varṇas and has puzzled historians ever since. Greek accounts of the “naked philosophers” (gymnosophistai) and of the Brahmins and śramaṇas reflect real encounters, and the sceptic Pyrrho, who accompanied Alexander, may have been influenced by what he heard in India, though how far is disputed (Thapar 2002).

Chinese Buddhist pilgrims came to India to find texts and visit holy places. Faxian (travelled c. 399–412), Xuanzang (in India c. 630–643) and Yijing (late seventh century) left detailed records of monasteries, kingdoms and customs. Xuanzang studied at Nālandā and returned to China with hundreds of texts, which he spent the rest of his life translating. His account remains one of the most important sources for the history of seventh-century India. These pilgrims came as students, not rulers, and their comparisons were between Indian Buddhism and the Buddhism they knew at home.

docs.title: 8.2.2 Al-Bīrūnī
docs.text:
The most remarkable pre-modern outside study of Indian thought was written by the Central Asian polymath Abū Rayḥān al-Bīrūnī (973–after 1048). Brought to India in the train of Maḥmūd of Ghazna, whose raids devastated temples and cities, al-Bīrūnī learned Sanskrit, translated Patañjali’s Yogasūtra and a Sāṃkhya text into Arabic, and wrote around 1030 a long book on the religion, philosophy, astronomy, calendars, law and customs of the Hindus, known in English as Alberuni’s India (Sachau 1888).

Al-Bīrūnī’s method was explicitly comparative. He set Indian doctrines beside those of the Greeks, the Sufis and the Christians, noting for example the resemblance between the Sāṃkhya and Platonic views of the soul. He distinguished carefully between the ideas of the learned and the beliefs of ordinary people, and he criticised the Purāṇic cosmography in the light of the Indian astronomers’ own spherical Earth (Chapter 2). He also recorded, with some exasperation, the Brahmins’ reluctance to share their knowledge with foreigners and their conviction that no other nation possessed science. He said frankly that the conquests of Maḥmūd had made Hindus hostile to all Muslims. His book is a model of informed, critical and respectful comparison, nearly eight centuries before the European Orientalists.

docs.title: 8.2.3 Persian translations at the Mughal court
docs.text:
The Mughal emperors sponsored an extraordinary programme of translation from Sanskrit into Persian. Under Akbar (r. 1556–1605) the Mahābhārata was translated as the Razmnāma (“Book of War”), and the Rāmāyaṇa, the Yogavāsiṣṭha and many other works followed. Akbar’s great-grandson Dārā Shikoh (1615–1659), whose comparison of Sufi and Vedāntic thought is described in Chapter 16, sponsored in 1657 the Sirr-i Akbar (“The Greatest Secret”), a Persian translation of some fifty Upaniṣads. Audrey Truschke and Supriya Gandhi have shown that these projects were serious intellectual undertakings in which Sanskrit pandits and Persian scholars collaborated (Truschke 2016; Gandhi 2020).

The Sirr-i Akbar had an unexpected European career. In 1801–02 the French scholar Abraham-Hyacinthe Anquetil-Duperron published a Latin translation of it as Oupnek’hat. This was the text through which Arthur Schopenhauer first read the Upaniṣads; in a famous passage of his Parerga and Paralipomena (1851) he called it the consolation of his life and of his death. The first major European encounter with Vedānta thus came through a Mughal prince’s Persian.

docs.title: 8.3 Early Modern Europeans and Their Informants
docs.text:
The first sustained European engagement with Indian knowledge came not from philosophers but from physicians, missionaries and merchants of the Portuguese and Dutch empires, and it depended at every step on Indian informants. Garcia da Orta, a Portuguese physician of Jewish descent in Goa, published there in 1563 his Colóquios dos simples e drogas da Índia, a series of dialogues on Indian drugs and spices that drew on conversations with local practitioners and corrected many errors of the classical European authorities. The Dutch governor of Malabar, Hendrik van Rheede, organised the compilation of the Hortus Malabaricus (twelve volumes, Amsterdam, 1678–1693), a botanical survey of the plants of Kerala with their uses, prepared with the help of the Ezhava physician Itty Achuden and several Konkani Brahmin physicians, whose knowledge is acknowledged in the work itself. Richard Grove has argued that such works, built on Indian ecological and medical knowledge, contributed to the development of European botany and even of early conservation thinking (Grove 1995).

Missionaries learned Indian languages in order to preach, and in doing so produced grammars, dictionaries and literature. The English Jesuit Thomas Stephens composed the Kristapurāṇa (1616), a retelling of the Bible in the form of a Marathi Purāṇa; Roberto de Nobili in Madurai wrote in Tamil and studied Sanskrit (Chapter 16). The Dutch Protestant minister Abraham Rogerius published in 1651 an account of the religion of the Brahmins of the Coromandel coast based on conversations with a Brahmin informant. These works were shaped by the purposes of conversion and trade, but they mark the beginning of European study of Indian knowledge as something to be learned from Indians.

docs.title: 8.4.1 Knowledge for government
docs.text: When the East India Company became a territorial power in Bengal after 1765, its officials needed to know the laws by which their subjects lived. Warren Hastings, Governor of Bengal from 1772 and Governor-General under the Regulating Act of 1773, decided that Hindus and Muslims should be governed by their own laws, which meant identifying and translating the relevant texts. Pandits were commissioned to compile a digest of Hindu law, translated from a Persian version into English by Nathaniel Halhed as A Code of Gentoo Laws (1776). Charles Wilkins published the first English translation of the Bhagavadgītā in 1785, with a preface by Hastings predicting that such works would survive when the British dominion in India had long ceased to exist. Bernard Cohn has analysed how these projects turned Indian knowledge into an instrument of colonial administration, and how, in the process, a few texts such as the Manusmṛti were elevated into authoritative “codes” in a way they had rarely been before (Cohn 1996).

docs.title: 8.4.2 William Jones and the Asiatic Society
docs.text:
Sir William Jones (1746–1794), a judge of the Supreme Court in Calcutta and a gifted linguist, founded the Asiatic Society of Bengal in 1784. Two years later, in his “Third Anniversary Discourse” to the Society, he praised Sanskrit as “of a wonderful structure” and argued that its affinity with Greek and Latin was too strong to be accidental: all three, with Gothic, Celtic and probably Persian, had “sprung from some common source, which, perhaps, no longer exists”. The linguistic consequences of that remark — comparative philology and the Indo-European family — are traced in Volume 10 (Śabda Vidyā). For the history of comparison, what matters is its form. Jones set an Indian language beside the two classical languages on which European education rested and pronounced it their equal or better; the comparison flattered Indians and Europeans alike, and it established kinship, not derivation, as the model for relating India to Europe. Others had noticed some of the resemblances before, but Jones’s prestige and his institution gave the idea its impetus. He also translated Kālidāsa’s Śakuntalā (1789), whose reception in Germany was enthusiastic, and the Manusmṛti (1794), so that a literary masterpiece and a law-book became, side by side, the first “Indian classics” known to Europe. Henry Thomas Colebrooke (1765–1837) followed with careful studies of the Vedas, of Hindu law and of the systems of Indian philosophy, and his essays “On the Philosophy of the Hindus” (1823–27) were for decades the standard European account (Trautmann 1997).

Thomas Trautmann has argued that these men, whatever their colonial purposes, were genuine scholars who admired what they studied and who worked closely with Indian pandits, and that their project should be distinguished from the hostile “Anglicism” that followed (Trautmann 1997). Their admiration was real; so was the asymmetry of power within which it operated.

docs.title: 8.4.3 Images of India
docs.text: European knowledge of India was shaped by pictures as well as texts. The uncle and nephew Thomas and William Daniell travelled through India between 1786 and 1794 and published Oriental Scenery (1795–1808), a series of aquatints of temples, mosques, ruins and landscapes that fixed for British viewers an image of India as a land of picturesque antiquity. Company officials commissioned Indian artists to paint plants, birds, castes and occupations in a hybrid style now called “Company painting”, which combined Indian techniques with European conventions of natural-history illustration. Photography arrived in the 1840s and was used from the 1850s to document monuments and, more troublingly, to compile ethnographic surveys of “types” of Indian people, such as the eight volumes of The People of India (1868–1875). These images, like the texts discussed in this chapter, were produced by collaboration between European patrons and Indian artists and informants, and they served both curiosity and government. Partha Mitter has traced the European reception of Indian art from the early travellers’ horror at “monsters” to the later Romantic admiration (Chapter 21) (Mitter 1977).

docs.title: 8.4.4 Mill, Macaulay and the turn against India
docs.text: In 1817 James Mill, who never visited India, published The History of British India, which devoted hundreds of pages to proving that Hindu civilisation was primitive and that the Orientalists’ admiration for it was misplaced (Mill 1817). The book became a textbook for Company officials. In 1835 Thomas Babington Macaulay, a member of the Governor-General’s council, wrote the Minute on Indian Education quoted at the head of this chapter, arguing that government funds should support English education rather than Sanskrit and Arabic learning, in order to create “a class of persons, Indian in blood and colour, but English in taste, in opinions, in morals, and in intellect”. The English Education Act of the same year adopted his policy. The Anglicist victory shaped Indian education for the next century and is the background to much of the modern Indian resentment of colonial attitudes to Indian knowledge, discussed in Chapter 22.

docs.title: 8.4.5 Counting and classifying: the census and the surveys
docs.text:
Colonial knowledge of India was produced not only by scholars of Sanskrit and Persian but by an apparatus of surveys. The Great Trigonometrical Survey, begun in 1802, mapped the subcontinent; the Archaeological Survey of India, established in 1861 under Alexander Cunningham, recorded and later excavated monuments; district gazetteers described the land, crops, castes and customs of each region; and George Grierson’s Linguistic Survey of India (published 1903–1928) classified hundreds of languages and dialects. The decennial census, conducted throughout British India from 1881 after a less complete enumeration in 1871–72, required every person to be assigned a religion and a caste.

Bernard Cohn and Nicholas Dirks have argued that these exercises did not simply record Indian society but helped to reshape it (Cohn 1996; Dirks 2001). The census made religious communities countable, and so made their relative size a political issue; it turned fluid and locally varying caste identities into fixed categories with all-India names. When the Census Commissioner Herbert Risley attempted in 1901 to rank castes in an order of social precedence — having earlier, in Bengal, tried to correlate caste with physical measurements of the nose and skull — castes across India petitioned to be recorded under higher names, and caste associations formed to press their claims. The classifications of the colonial state thus entered the self-understanding of the people classified. The argument has been criticised for overstating the novelty of colonial categories — caste and religious identity were real before the British counted them — but it has made scholars attentive to the ways in which knowledge and government were intertwined. C. A. Bayly added a further qualification: the Company’s “information order” was built on Indian foundations — the newswriters, runners, clerks (munshī) and pandits of the Mughal and regional states — and British knowledge was weakest, as in the rebellion of 1857, where it had lost touch with these Indian networks (Bayly 1996).

docs.title: 8.5 The Reverse Gaze: Indians in Europe
docs.text:
Europeans were not the only observers. From the late eighteenth century Indians travelled to Britain and wrote about what they saw, and their accounts are a valuable counterweight to the European descriptions of India. Sake Dean Mahomed (1759–1851), from Patna, served in the East India Company’s army, emigrated to Ireland and then England, and published The Travels of Dean Mahomet (1794), the first book written in English by an Indian; he later opened an Indian restaurant in London (1810) and a celebrated “shampooing” bath-house at Brighton. Mirza Abu Taleb Khan, a Persian-writing official from Lucknow, travelled in Britain and Europe between 1799 and 1803 and wrote a Persian account of his journey, admiring British science and public institutions while criticising the pride, irreligion and materialism of the English. Rammohun Roy visited England in 1831 as the envoy of the Mughal emperor, gave evidence to Parliament on the government of India, and died at Bristol in 1833.

In the later nineteenth century the stream of Indian visitors became a flood of students, lawyers, reformers and religious teachers — Gandhi among them — and Indian writers produced a substantial literature of travel and comparison in English, Bengali, Marathi, Urdu and other languages. Tapan Raychaudhuri’s study of Bengali intellectuals’ perceptions of the West shows how their admiration for Western science, literature and liberty coexisted with criticism of its materialism, racism and imperialism, and how the West became for them both a model and a foil (Raychaudhuri 1988). The “spiritual East” contrasted with the “materialist West” was in part an Indian construction, formed in the experience of colonised travellers who found Europe powerful but not admirable in every respect. Recognising this reverse gaze is a necessary part of a comparative history: Orientalism was a two-way conversation, even if the two parties did not speak with equal power.

docs.title: 8.6 Germany, Romanticism and Philosophy
docs.text:
India had a different meaning in Germany, which had no Indian empire. Herder imagined India as the cradle of humanity. Friedrich Schlegel’s Über die Sprache und Weisheit der Indier (“On the Language and Wisdom of the Indians”, 1808) made India the source of European language and religion; his brother August Wilhelm became the first professor of Sanskrit in Germany. Raymond Schwab called this enthusiasm an “Oriental Renaissance”, comparable to the Renaissance rediscovery of Greece (Schwab 1984).

The philosophers were more divided. Hegel, in his lectures on the philosophy of history and of religion, placed India at an early stage of the development of Spirit: a world of dreaming imagination, without history, without the consciousness of individual freedom and without philosophy in the strict sense. Halbfass has shown in detail how Hegel’s judgement, based on wide reading of the available translations, set the terms for the exclusion of India from the history of philosophy as taught in European universities (Halbfass 1988). Schopenhauer, by contrast, saw in the Upaniṣads and in Buddhism confirmations of his own philosophy of the will and of the denial of the will. Nietzsche admired the Manusmṛti as an aristocratic law-code superior to Christianity; European enthusiasm for India was not always for what modern Indians would wish to be admired.

Friedrich Max Müller (1823–1900), a German who spent his career at Oxford, edited the Ṛgveda with Sāyaṇa’s commentary (1849–74) and directed the fifty volumes of The Sacred Books of the East (1879–1910), which made translations of Indian, Chinese and Iranian scriptures widely available (Müller 1879–1910). Paul Deussen’s Sechzig Upanishad’s des Veda (1897) and his systematic studies of Vedānta treated Indian thought as philosophy. Max Müller’s enthusiasm for the “Aryan” heritage and his conviction that the Vedas were the childhood of religion also illustrate the limits of the age: the texts were valued largely as evidence for European origins.

Max Müller never visited India, but he exercised a large influence there. In lectures delivered at Cambridge in 1882 to candidates for the Indian Civil Service, published as India: What Can It Teach Us? (1883), he urged the young administrators to regard the people they would govern with respect, praised the Sanskrit literature as a key to the history of the human mind, and attacked the prejudice that Indians were naturally untruthful. Indian reformers read the lectures with gratitude, and Vivekananda visited him at Oxford in 1896 (Chapter 10). His statement that he would point to India if asked where the human mind had most fully developed some of its choicest gifts is among the most quoted sentences in Indian writing about India; it is usually quoted without the context of his argument, which concerned the value of Sanskrit studies for Europeans. Max Müller’s career thus shows both the generosity and the limits of the Orientalist perspective: admiration was real, but it was admiration for an ancient, textual India, and it was addressed above all to Europe.

docs.title: 8.7 India in American Thought
docs.text: Indian texts reached North America through British translations and German scholarship. The Transcendentalists of New England read them avidly. Ralph Waldo Emerson’s poem “Brahma” (1857), which begins “If the red slayer think he slays, / Or if the slain think he is slain”, paraphrases a passage of the Kaṭha Upaniṣad and the Gītā (2.19); Henry David Thoreau took the Gītā with him to Walden Pond and wrote that he bathed his intellect in its philosophy every morning. Walt Whitman’s Leaves of Grass was later compared by Indian and Western readers to Vedāntic poetry, though his direct knowledge of Indian texts seems to have been slight. These writers read India through the lens of their own Romantic idealism, as the Germans had done; their enthusiasm prepared the ground for the reception of Vivekananda (Chapter 10) and, through Thoreau’s essay on civil disobedience, which Gandhi read, travelled back to India in a new form. The circulation of ideas between India and America is a striking example of how comparisons are made and remade in both directions.

docs.title: 8.8 Aryans, Race and Philology
docs.text: The discovery of the Indo-European language family led, in the course of the nineteenth century, to theories of an “Aryan race” that had spread from a common homeland. In Europe these theories fed racial nationalism and eventually Nazi ideology, which appropriated the word “Aryan” and the svastika. In India they were taken up in contradictory ways. Some British writers used them to claim kinship with upper-caste Indians while justifying rule over others; B. G. Tilak argued in The Arctic Home in the Vedas (1903) that the Aryans had originated near the North Pole; Jotirao Phule turned the theory against the Brahmins, describing them as Aryan invaders who had enslaved the indigenous people (Chapter 14). Thomas Trautmann’s Aryans and British India traces this tangled history (Trautmann 1997). The linguistic and archaeological questions about the spread of Indo-Aryan languages into South Asia are discussed in Volume 1; the point here is that a philological discovery acquired racial and political meanings that its originators did not foresee.

docs.title: 8.9 Sociology: Weber and Dumont
docs.text:
In the early twentieth century, India became a test case for the new sociology of religion. Max Weber, in The Religion of India (first published in German in 1916–17), asked why modern rational capitalism had developed in the Protestant West and not in India. His answer stressed the combination of caste and the doctrine of karma: caste fixed people in hereditary occupations and ritual relations, and karma gave them a religious motive to accept their station and to seek salvation either through ritual conformity or through mystical withdrawal from the world, rather than through the methodical transformation of the world that he associated with Puritanism (Weber 1958). Weber’s analysis was learned and influential, and it identified real features of the Brahmanical texts. It has also been criticised: historians have pointed to the commercial sophistication of Indian merchant communities, Jain and Hindu, whose ethic of thrift and trust Weber himself noted; to the importance of colonial policy in India’s economic history; and to the danger of deriving the behaviour of a whole society from its religious texts.

Louis Dumont’s Homo Hierarchicus (1966; English translation 1970, revised 1980) took a different approach, analysing caste as a system governed by the opposition of the pure and the impure, in which status is separated from and superior to power, and contrasting the “hierarchical” ideology of India with the “individualist” ideology of the modern West (Dumont 1980). Dumont’s work dominated the anthropology of India for a generation and was then criticised for its reliance on Brahmanical texts, its neglect of power and conflict, and its tendency to treat India as the opposite of the West. Both Weber and Dumont illustrate the attraction, and the risk, of comparing civilisations as wholes.

docs.title: 8.10 Theosophy and the “Mystic East”
docs.text:
A different image of India was popularised by the Theosophical Society, founded in New York in 1875 by Helena Petrovna Blavatsky and Henry Steel Olcott, and moved to Adyar, near Madras, in 1882. Theosophy presented India and Tibet as the home of an ancient esoteric wisdom, preserved by hidden masters, that underlay all religions. Its leaders took an active part in Indian public life — Annie Besant founded the Central Hindu College at Banaras and became president of the Indian National Congress in 1917 — and Theosophy helped to restore the self-confidence of many educated Hindus and Buddhists. It also spread a picture of the “mystic East” that was largely a European projection (Figure 8.1). Richard King has analysed how this picture, together with modern Western notions of “mysticism” and “religion”, shaped both Western and Indian accounts of Indian traditions (King 1999). J. J. Clarke’s Oriental Enlightenment surveys the many uses to which Western thinkers, from Leibniz to the counterculture of the 1960s, have put Asian thought, often as a mirror in which to see their own concerns (Clarke 1997).

docs.title: 8.11 Said, Inden and the Critique of Orientalism
8.11.1 The critique
docs.text:
In 1978 Edward Said’s Orientalism argued that Western scholarship about the “Orient” had not been a neutral pursuit of knowledge but a discourse bound up with imperial power, which constructed the Orient as the West’s static, irrational and feminine other (Said 1978). Said wrote mainly about the Arab world, but his argument was soon applied to India. Ronald Inden’s Imagining India (1990) argued that the dominant Western images of India — as a land of caste, of the self-sufficient village, of divine kingship and of otherworldly religion — were “essentialisms” that denied Indians their agency as makers of their own history (Inden 1990). Sheldon Pollock, in an essay provocatively titled “Deep Orientalism?”, pointed out that the relationship between knowledge and domination in India did not begin with the British: Sanskrit learning, including the Dharmaśāstra, had long served to legitimate the power of Brahmins and kings over others (Pollock 1993). A volume edited by Carol Breckenridge and Peter van der Veer collected many of these debates (Breckenridge and van der Veer 1993).

Richard King extended the critique to the very idea of “Hinduism” and of “mysticism” (King 1999). Several scholars argued that “Hinduism” as a single religion was a nineteenth-century construction, produced by colonial census-takers, Orientalist scholars and Indian reformers, out of a great variety of sects and practices; Heinrich von Stietencron called the term “deceptive” (Sontheimer and Kulke 1989).

docs.title: 8.11.2 Critiques of the critique
docs.text:
These arguments have themselves been criticised, and the debate is instructive for anyone engaged in comparison. First, the critique of Orientalism risked repeating the error it denounced, by treating “Orientalism” as a single, all-powerful discourse and the colonised as its passive objects. Indian pandits, munshis and scholars were active participants in the production of colonial knowledge, with their own interests and traditions of learning. Second, David Lorenzen and Andrew Nicholson have shown that the idea of a shared Hindu identity, distinct from Islam and from the heterodox traditions, was not invented by the British: medieval texts in Sanskrit and the vernaculars already used “Hindu” as a self-description, and doxographers and philosophers from the sixteenth century, such as Vijñānabhikṣu, were already constructing a unified “orthodox” philosophy (Lorenzen 1999; Nicholson 2010). Third, the anti-Orientalist argument has been adopted in modern India by Hindu nationalist writers who use it to dismiss all critical scholarship of Indian traditions as colonial, a use its originators did not intend.

The balanced conclusion is that colonial knowledge was a joint production, shaped by unequal power but not determined by it; that it brought real gains — editions, translations, the decipherment of Brāhmī by James Prinsep in 1837, the recovery of Aśoka and of the history of Buddhism in India — as well as distortions; and that both admirers and critics should be read critically.

docs.title: 8.12 Women in the Study of India
docs.text: The history of Indology is usually told as a history of men, but women played a larger part than the standard accounts suggest. Caroline Augusta Foley Rhys Davids (1857–1942) translated Pali texts on Buddhist psychology and served as president of the Pali Text Society; Isaline Blew Horner (1896–1981), a later president, translated the whole of the Vinaya and wrote a pioneering study of women in early Buddhism (1930). The Austrian-born art historian Stella Kramrisch (1896–1993), invited by Tagore to teach at Santiniketan and later professor at the University of Calcutta, wrote The Hindu Temple (1946), still a standard work, before moving to Philadelphia. Indian women entered the field in the twentieth century: Irawati Karve (1905–1970), anthropologist and Sanskritist at Deccan College, wrote on kinship and caste and, in Yuganta (1967), a celebrated Marathi study of the characters of the Mahābhārata; Romila Thapar, whose work on early Indian history is cited throughout this series, has been among the most influential historians of India of her generation (Thapar 2002). Feminist scholars of the late twentieth century, among them Uma Chakravarti and Julia Leslie, opened new questions about women in the texts and in history (Chapter 5). Their work, like that of Indian scholars generally, has changed what Indology studies as well as who studies it.

docs.title: 8.13 Indian Scholars and the Making of Indology
docs.text:
The history of Indology is often told as a history of European scholars, but it was never only that. Behind the British Orientalists stood Indian pandits who taught them Sanskrit and supplied their texts: the digest of Hindu law that Jones commissioned, the Vivādabhaṅgārṇava, was compiled by the aged Bengali scholar Jagannātha Tarkapañcānana and later translated by Colebrooke. In the nineteenth century Indian scholars increasingly worked on their own account. Rādhākānta Deb, a leader of Calcutta’s orthodox Hindus, compiled the great Sanskrit encyclopaedic dictionary Śabdakalpadruma (1822–58). Īśvaracandra Vidyāsāgar reformed the teaching of Sanskrit and Bengali. Rajendralal Mitra catalogued manuscripts and wrote on Indian antiquities. R. G. Bhandarkar (1837–1925) introduced the methods of historical philology into Indian scholarship; the Bhandarkar Oriental Research Institute, founded in Pune in 1917 in his honour, produced under V. S. Sukthankar and his successors the critical edition of the Mahābhārata (1919–1966), one of the great achievements of twentieth-century textual scholarship.

After independence, Indian historians wrote national histories in reply to colonial ones. The multi-volume History and Culture of the Indian People, edited by R. C. Majumdar (1951–77), emphasised the antiquity and achievements of Hindu civilisation; historians such as D. D. Kosambi, R. S. Sharma and Romila Thapar applied materialist and social-historical methods and gave more weight to social conflict, caste and the role of the non-elite (Thapar 2002). The debates among these schools, and between them and later Hindu nationalist histories, continue to shape how India’s past is taught. The lesson for comparison is that “Indian” scholarship, like “Western” scholarship, is plural, and that the nationality of a scholar is no guarantee of either insight or bias.

The independent state also set out to assess the place of classical learning in a modern nation. The Sanskrit Commission appointed by the Government of India in 1956, under the chairmanship of the linguist Suniti Kumar Chatterji, toured the country, took evidence from traditional pandits and university scholars, and reported in 1957 on the condition of Sanskrit education. It recommended support for both the traditional pāṭhaśālās and modern university departments, and the establishment of a central body for Sanskrit, which later became the Rashtriya Sanskrit Sansthan (1970). Its report anticipated many of the questions now raised by the “Indian Knowledge Systems” movement (Chapter 22): how to preserve the oral and textual expertise of traditional scholars, how to join it to modern methods of research, and how to make classical learning available to all citizens rather than to a hereditary few.

docs.title: 8.14.1 From Orientalism to philosophy
docs.text: The academic discipline of “comparative philosophy” emerged in the early twentieth century. The French scholar Paul Masson-Oursel published La philosophie comparée in 1923. The East–West Philosophers’ Conferences at the University of Hawaii, organised by Charles A. Moore from 1939, brought Indian, Chinese, Japanese and Western philosophers together, and their journal, Philosophy East and West, began publication in 1951. Sarvepalli Radhakrishnan held the Spalding Chair of Eastern Religions and Ethics at Oxford from 1936 to 1952 and, with Moore, edited A Source Book in Indian Philosophy (1957), which introduced generations of students to the primary texts (Radhakrishnan and Moore 1957). Early comparative philosophy often sought parallels: Śaṅkara and Kant, Nāgārjuna and Hegel, the Upaniṣads and Plato. The method could illuminate, but it could also reduce Indian thought to a set of anticipations of Western positions.

docs.title: 8.14.2 Halbfass, Matilal and after
docs.text:
Two scholars changed the field in the late twentieth century. Wilhelm Halbfass (1940–2000), in India and Europe (1988) and Tradition and Reflection (1991), wrote a history of how Indians and Europeans had understood — and failed to understand — each other, including a chapter on “traditional Indian xenology”, the classical attitudes to foreigners and foreign thought, which he found to be marked more by self-sufficiency than by curiosity (Halbfass 1988, 1991). Bimal Krishna Matilal (1935–1991), who held the Spalding Chair at Oxford from 1976 until his death, argued that Indian philosophy should be studied with the tools of modern analytic philosophy, because it was concerned with the same problems — perception, inference, meaning, the self — and had developed rigorous arguments about them (Matilal 1971, 1986). His students and successors, among them Jonardon Ganeri, Arindam Chakrabarti and Mark Siderits, have made Indian philosophy part of the international philosophical conversation, sometimes as historical study, sometimes as what Siderits has called “fusion philosophy”, using Indian arguments to address contemporary problems (Ganeri 2011; Siderits 2007).

Indian philosophers within India were often sceptical of comparative philosophy’s assumptions. K. C. Bhattacharya, in a lecture of about 1930 entitled “Swaraj in Ideas”, warned against a “cultural subjection” that led educated Indians to echo Western ideas without assimilating them, and Daya Krishna questioned the received picture of Indian philosophy itself as a fixed set of schools devoted to liberation (Chapter 15).

docs.title: 8.15 Lessons for Comparison
docs.text: This history bears directly on the rest of the volume. It shows that every comparison of India with Europe was made by someone for some purpose — to govern, to convert, to admire, to criticise or to defend — and that images travelled in both directions, so that the “spiritual East” was a joint creation of European Romantics and Indian reformers. It shows, too, that the opposite of a colonial stereotype is not the truth: correcting the picture of India as backward does not require a picture of India as uniquely wise. And it suggests where the best comparisons lie. Al-Bīrūnī setting Sāṃkhya beside Plato, Matilal setting Nyāya beside Russell on perception, Halbfass tracing the history of a single concept: such particular comparisons have taught more than any number of contrasts between “Indian” and “Western” thought in general, and they are the model that the rules set out in Chapter 1 try to follow.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text:
• Halbfass (1988): the fundamental history of the encounter between Indian and European thought.

  • Schwab (1984) and Clarke (1997): European enthusiasm for Asian thought.

  • Said (1978), Inden (1990), King (1999) and the essays in Breckenridge and van der Veer (1993): the critique of Orientalism and its critics.

  • Trautmann (1997), Cohn (1996) and Bayly (1996): British Orientalism, colonial knowledge and the Aryan idea.

  • Sachau (1888): al-Bīrūnī’s study of India.

docs.title: Chapter 9: Vedānta, Reform and Neo-Vedānta
docs.text: sa ya eṣo ’ṇimaitadātmyam idaṃ sarvaṃ tat satyaṃ sa ātmā tat tvam asi śvetaketo That which is the finest essence — this whole world has that as its self. That is the truth; that is the self. And that is how you are, Śvetaketu. — Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.7

docs.title: 9.1 Introduction
docs.text: In the nineteenth and twentieth centuries one Indian philosophical tradition, Advaita Vedānta, came to be presented to the world — and to many Indians — as the essence of Hinduism and even as the meeting point of all religions. This chapter explains how that happened. It begins with Vedānta as a classical school, one among several and itself divided, and then follows the reform movements of colonial India, from Rammohun Roy to Radhakrishnan, which reinterpreted it. The two following chapters are devoted to the most influential reinterpreters, Vivekananda and Aurobindo. The classical schools are treated more fully in Volume 3 and the Upaniṣads in Volume 2.

docs.title: 9.2.1 The three foundations and Śaṅkara
docs.text:
Vedānta (“the end of the Veda”) is the school of interpretation that takes the Upaniṣads as its primary source. Its classical authors commented on three “foundations” (prasthānatraya): the principal Upaniṣads, the Bhagavadgītā and the Brahmasūtra. The earliest surviving complete commentaries on all three are those of Śaṅkara (c. 700–750 CE; traditional dates 788–820), the founder of Advaita, “non-dual”, Vedānta.

Śaṅkara taught that Brahman, pure being and consciousness, is the only reality; that the individual self (ātman) is identical with Brahman; and that the world of many things and persons, though real for practical purposes, is not ultimately real. The appearance of multiplicity is due to a beginningless ignorance (avidyā) which “superimposes” (adhyāsa) the properties of the non-self on the self, as a rope is mistaken for a snake. Śaṅkara distinguished the standpoint of ordinary experience (vyāvahārika), at which the world, the Vedic injunctions and the personal God are real, from the standpoint of ultimate truth (pāramārthika), at which only Brahman is; later Advaitins added a third level, that of mere illusion (prātibhāsika). Liberation comes from knowledge of Brahman, which removes ignorance; it is not produced by action, since what is produced by action is impermanent. For Śaṅkara this knowledge arises from scripture: the “great sentences” (mahāvākya) of the Upaniṣads, such as “that is how you are” (tat tvam asi) of the Chāndogya, rightly understood by a qualified student under a teacher, are the means of knowing Brahman. Anantanand Rambachan has emphasised that for Śaṅkara scripture, not mystical experience, is the decisive means of knowledge (pramāṇa) (Rambachan 1991; Potter 1981).

docs.title: 9.2.2 How Śaṅkara argued
docs.text:
Śaṅkara’s commentary on the Brahmasūtra opens with a celebrated preface on superimposition. The subject (“I”) and the object (“you”) are opposed like light and darkness, so that the properties of one cannot belong to the other; yet in ordinary experience we constantly confuse them, saying “I am fat” or “I am blind”, attributing to the self the properties of the body and senses. This confusion, he argues, is beginningless and natural, and all the distinctions of ordinary life — between knower and known, agent and action, even between the injunctions of the Veda and those to whom they apply — presuppose it. The purpose of the Upaniṣads is to remove it by teaching the self’s identity with Brahman.

The argument is subtle. Śaṅkara does not deny that the Vedic rituals, the castes and stages of life, the gods and the world are real for all practical purposes; he insists that they are, and that they must be respected by those who live within them. He denies only that they are ultimately real. This allowed him to combine a radical metaphysics with a conservative social teaching: renunciation of ritual and caste duties was open, on his view, only to Brahmin men, and he excluded Śūdras from the study of the Upaniṣads, though not from liberation through other means. Modern admirers of Advaita have often drawn egalitarian conclusions from the identity of all selves in Brahman; Śaṅkara did not.

docs.title: 9.2.3 Divisions within Advaita
docs.text: After Śaṅkara the school divided over several questions. Is ignorance located in the individual self or in Brahman? Vācaspati Miśra (10th century), in his commentary called the Bhāmatī, held that the individual self is the locus of ignorance and Brahman its object; Prakāśātman’s Vivaraṇa school, building on Śaṅkara’s pupil Padmapāda, held that Brahman is both locus and object. Another pupil, Sureśvara, and the independent thinker Maṇḍana Miśra developed other positions. The debates continued for centuries and produced some of the most rigorous dialectical works in Indian philosophy. Eliot Deutsch’s reconstruction offers an accessible philosophical account of the system (Deutsch 1969).

docs.title: 9.2.4 Rival Vedāntas
docs.text:
Advaita was never the only Vedānta. Rāmānuja (traditionally 1017–1137) commented on the same texts and found in them a “qualified non-dualism” (viśiṣṭādvaita): Brahman is the personal God Viṣṇu–Nārāyaṇa, and the world and selves are real, forming his body, inseparable from him as attributes from their substance. In his Śrībhāṣya he raised a series of objections to the Advaita doctrine of ignorance: where could it reside, if Brahman is pure knowledge? how could it be neither real nor unreal? John Carman’s study remains the standard account of his theology (Carman 1974). Madhva (c. 1238–1317; traditional dates 1199–1278) taught a thoroughgoing dualism (dvaita) based on five real differences — between God and selves, God and matter, self and self, self and matter, and matter and matter — and held that selves are eternally graded in their capacity for bliss (Sharma 1962). Nimbārka, Vallabha and the Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇavas following Caitanya developed further Vedāntas, most of them devotional. For most of their history the Vedāntas argued fiercely with one another, and with the Buddhists, Jains, Mīmāṃsakas and Naiyāyikas.

Table 9.1 summarises the main positions. It simplifies a large literature, but it shows how far apart the schools that all called themselves Vedānta could be.

docs.title: 9.2.5 Classical synthesisers
docs.text: Some classical thinkers did attempt broad syntheses. The fourteenth-century Sarvadarśanasaṃgraha of Mādhava ranges the schools in an order that leads towards Advaita (Chapter 1). Madhusūdana Sarasvatī (16th century) combined Advaita with devotion to Kṛṣṇa; Vijñānabhikṣu (16th century) argued that Sāṃkhya, Yoga, Nyāya, Vaiśeṣika and Vedānta were in harmony when properly understood, and that their apparent disagreements arose from addressing different audiences. Madhusūdana also wrote a short work, the Prasthānabheda (“The Divisions of the Sciences”), which surveys the branches of learning — the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, the Purāṇas, logic, exegesis, law, medicine, archery, music, statecraft and the philosophical systems — and argues that all of them, rightly understood, serve the single purpose taught by Vedānta. It is in effect a classification of Indian knowledge systems with an Advaitic summit, and a precursor of the modern idea, examined in Chapter 22, of “Indian knowledge” as a unified whole. Andrew Nicholson has argued that such works show that the idea of a unified “orthodox” Hindu philosophy predates colonial rule, even if colonial categories later reinforced it (Nicholson 2010).

docs.title: 9.2.6 Advaita and Buddhism
docs.text: The relation of Advaita to Buddhism was a matter of controversy in classical India and remains one in modern scholarship. The Māṇḍūkyakārikā attributed to Gauḍapāda, which Śaṅkara’s tradition regards as the work of his teacher’s teacher, teaches that nothing is ever really born (ajātivāda) and uses arguments and vocabulary closely resembling those of the Madhyamaka and Yogācāra Buddhists; its fourth chapter even appears to praise the Buddha. Śaṅkara himself attacked the Buddhist schools at length, especially the Yogācāra view that only consciousness exists, insisting that external objects are given in perception and that the self is permanent. Yet his opponents among the theistic Vedāntins accused him of being a “crypto-Buddhist” (pracchanna-bauddha): his doctrine of illusion, they argued, was the Buddhist doctrine of emptiness in Vedic dress. A verse of the Padma Purāṇa that makes this charge was quoted by Vijñānabhikṣu and others. Modern scholars generally conclude that early Advaita absorbed Buddhist methods and concepts while rejecting the Buddhist denial of a permanent self, and that the borrowing was one of many in the long argument among the Indian schools. Here, as often, a tradition defined itself partly by what it took from, and what it rejected in, its rivals.

docs.title: 9.2.7 Monasteries and legend
docs.text: According to tradition, Śaṅkara founded four monasteries (maṭha) at the four corners of India — Śṛṅgeri in the south, Dvārakā in the west, Purī in the east and Jyotirmaṭh near Badrinath in the north — and organised the renouncers of his tradition into ten orders (the Daśanāmīs). The heads of these monasteries, and of the Kāñcī monastery whose claim to Śaṅkara’s foundation is disputed, bear the title Śaṅkarācārya and are influential religious figures. Historians have pointed out that the accounts of these foundations come from hagiographies, collectively called “Śaṅkara’s conquest of the quarters” (Śaṅkaradigvijaya), the earliest of which date from centuries after his death, and that the institutional history of the monasteries can be traced with confidence only from the late medieval period, when Śṛṅgeri enjoyed the patronage of the Vijayanagara kings. The legend of a single founder who unified India’s renouncers by travelling its length is nonetheless significant: it expresses an idea of the subcontinent as a single sacred space that long predates modern nationalism.

docs.title: 9.2.8 Vedānta in the regional languages
docs.text: Vedānta was not confined to Sanskrit. The Marathi Jñāneśvarī (1290), a verse commentary on the Gītā by the young poet-saint Jñāneśvar, combined non-dualist metaphysics with devotion and the imagery of the Nāth yogis, and became the foundational text of the Vārkarī tradition. In the Hindi-speaking north, the Vicārasāgara of Niścaldās (nineteenth century), an exposition of Advaita in Hindi, was widely read among ascetics and lay people; Vivekananda is said to have called it one of the most influential books in India. Tamil, Kannada and Telugu works carried Vedānta into the devotional and monastic cultures of the south. These vernacular texts show that Advaita was a living tradition among people who knew no Sanskrit long before the English-language Neo-Vedānta of the colonial period.

docs.title: 9.3.1 Rammohun Roy
docs.text:
Rammohun Roy (1772–1833) is usually called the father of modern India, a title that reflects the range of his activity. Born into a Brahmin family in Bengal, he learned Persian and Arabic as well as Sanskrit, and his earliest surviving work, the Tuhfat al-muwaḥḥidīn (“A Gift to Monotheists”, c. 1804), written in Persian with an Arabic preface, argued on rational grounds for belief in one God and against the irrational practices of all religions. After moving to Calcutta in 1814 he published Bengali and English translations of several Upaniṣads and an abridgement of the Brahmasūtra, arguing that the Vedānta taught the worship of one formless God and condemned image-worship. He studied Hebrew and Greek, published The Precepts of Jesus (1820), a selection of Jesus’s moral teachings without the miracles, and became embroiled in controversy with the Baptist missionaries of Serampore over the Trinity. He campaigned against the burning of widows (satī), which the government prohibited in 1829, and founded in 1828 the Brahmo Sabha, the forerunner of the Brahmo Samaj. He died in Bristol in 1833 (Killingley 1993; Kopf 1979).

Rammohun’s reading of the Upaniṣads was selective: he found in them a monotheism close to Unitarian Christianity and to the rational theism of the Islamic tradition he had studied. Dermot Killingley has shown how he drew at once on Hindu, Islamic and Christian traditions of thought. His appeal to the Upaniṣads as the authentic core of Hinduism, against later “corruptions”, set a pattern that many reformers followed.

docs.title: 9.3.2 The Brahmo Samaj after Rammohun
docs.text: Debendranath Tagore (1817–1905), the father of Rabindranath, gave the Brahmo Samaj a firmer organisation, founded the Tattvabodhinī Sabhā (1839) and its journal, and, after sending scholars to Banaras to study the Vedas, concluded in the 1840s that the Vedas could not be regarded as infallible. The Brahmo faith was then grounded on reason and the intuition of the heart, supported by selected Upaniṣadic texts. Keshab Chandra Sen (1838–1884) moved the movement in a more universalist and Christian-influenced direction, and in 1880 proclaimed a “New Dispensation” (Navavidhān) that aimed to harmonise all religions in a single church, with readings from many scriptures. The Brahmo movement split more than once, but its influence on the educated classes of Bengal — in social reform, women’s education and the abolition of caste distinctions within the Samaj — was out of proportion to its small numbers (Kopf 1979; Jones 1989).

docs.title: 9.3.3 The Arya Samaj
docs.text:
Not all reformers were inclusivists. Dayānanda Sarasvatī (1824–1883), a Gujarati renouncer, founded the Arya Samaj in Bombay in 1875 and set out his teaching in the Satyārth Prakāś (“Light of Truth”, 1875). He held that the four Vedic Saṃhitās alone were revealed scripture, containing all true knowledge; he rejected image-worship, the Purāṇas, polytheism and caste by birth, while accepting a varṇa order based on merit. The later chapters of his book attacked Jainism, Buddhism, Christianity and Islam in uncompromising terms. The Arya Samaj, strongest in Punjab and the north, founded schools and colleges, promoted widow remarriage and developed a ritual of “purification” (śuddhi) to bring converts to other religions back into Hinduism, which brought it into conflict with Muslims, Christians and Sikhs (Jones 1989). Its example shows that the modern Hindu reform movements were plural: some sought harmony with other religions, others sought to defend Hinduism against them.

Dayānanda’s method of interpretation deserves notice in a comparative account. He read the Vedic hymns not as liturgies addressed to many gods but as teachings about a single God and about the natural world, interpreting the names of the gods as names of the one God or of natural forces, and he found in them references to sciences such as electricity and telegraphy. This reading, which he justified by the etymological method of the old Vedic lexicon, was rejected by Western Vedic scholars and by most traditional Brahmin authorities alike. It was nonetheless the first systematic attempt to claim that the Veda contains modern knowledge, and it stands at the head of the “Vedic science” literature discussed in Chapter 19. The Arya Samaj divided in 1893 into a “college” party, which supported English and scientific education in its Dayanand Anglo-Vedic schools, and a “Gurukul” party, which founded the Gurukul Kangri near Haridwar in 1902 to revive Vedic education in Sanskrit; the two strategies represent two answers, still debated, to the question of how a tradition should meet modern learning.

docs.title: 9.3.4 Other movements
docs.text:
In western India the Prarthana Samaj (1867), associated with M. G. Ranade and R. G. Bhandarkar, combined theism with social reform, drawing on the Marathi devotional poets. Jotirao Phule’s Satyashodhak Samaj (1873) rejected Brahmin authority altogether (Chapter 14). Orthodox Hindus organised too: the Dharma Sabha of Calcutta (1830) petitioned against the abolition of satī, and late nineteenth-century sanātana dharma associations defended image-worship, caste and the authority of the Purāṇas against the reformers. Tapan Raychaudhuri’s study of how nineteenth-century Bengali intellectuals perceived the West shows how varied the responses were (Raychaudhuri 1988). Figure 9.1 sets these movements beside the Muslim, Sikh, Buddhist, Jain and anti-caste movements of the same century, which are discussed in later chapters; the parallels in timing are not accidental, since all of them answered the same colonial state, the same missionary criticism and the same new world of print.

Figure 9.1. Some reform, revival and community movements discussed in this volume, by community, 1828–1956. Dates are those of founding or first organisation; the columns are a convenience, since many movements, the anti-caste ones above all, crossed the boundaries of religious communities.

docs.title: 9.4 Rāmakṛṣṇa
docs.text: Rāmakṛṣṇa (Gadādhar Chattopādhyāy, 1836–1886), priest of the Kālī temple at Dakshineswar near Calcutta, was neither a scholar nor a reformer. He was a devotee of the goddess who, according to the accounts of his disciples, also practised Vaiṣṇava, tantric and Advaita disciplines under various teachers and, for short periods, Islamic and Christian devotion, and declared that all had led him to the same God. His conversations were recorded by Mahendranath Gupta in Bengali as the Śrīśrīrāmakṛṣṇa Kathāmṛta, translated as The Gospel of Sri Ramakrishna (Gupta 1942). Educated Brahmos, including Keshab Chandra Sen, were drawn to him, and among the young men who gathered round him was Narendranath Datta, the future Vivekananda. Rāmakṛṣṇa’s sayings about many paths to one goal — “as many faiths, so many paths” — became the experiential foundation on which Vivekananda built the modern doctrine of the harmony of religions.

docs.title: 9.5.1 Hacker’s thesis
docs.text:
The German Indologist Paul Hacker coined the term “Neo-Hinduism” for the reinterpretation of Hindu tradition that he found in Vivekananda, Aurobindo, Gandhi and Radhakrishnan. He argued that these thinkers had taken Western values — social activism, nationalism, a universal ethics — and read them back into Indian texts, using Advaita as a framework in which everything could be included. Hacker’s tone was often polemical, and Halbfass, who edited his essays, moderated his conclusions; but the analysis identified real features of the modern movement (Hacker 1995; Halbfass 1988). They can be summarised as follows:

  • Advaita as the essence of Hinduism. The diverse Hindu traditions are presented as stages on the way to, or expressions of, the non-dual truth of Vedānta.

  • Religion as experience. The final authority in religion is direct spiritual experience (anubhava), of which scripture is a record, rather than scripture interpreted by tradition.

  • The harmony of religions. All religions are paths to the same goal, with Vedānta best able to recognise this.

  • Practical Vedānta. The identity of all selves in Brahman grounds an ethic of social service, which classical Advaita had not emphasised.

  • Hinduism as tolerant and scientific. Hinduism, so understood, is uniquely tolerant and in harmony with modern science, in contrast to dogmatic Western religions.

docs.title: 9.5.2 Continuity or rupture?
docs.text: Was Neo-Vedānta a betrayal of the classical tradition or a legitimate development? Rambachan argued that Vivekananda’s appeal to experience departed significantly from Śaṅkara’s view that scripture is the means of knowing Brahman (Rambachan 1994). Others point out that Indian traditions had always reinterpreted their texts, that classical Advaitins also wrote for their own times, and that inclusivism itself was classical. The question cannot be settled by asking which version is “authentic”; it is better to see Neo-Vedānta as a new school, with its own arguments and its own historical context, standing in a recognisable relation to the old.

docs.title: 9.5.3 What Neo-Vedānta left out
docs.text: The cost of making Advaita the essence of Hinduism was that much else was pushed to the margins: the theistic Vedāntas of Rāmānuja and Madhva, which reject the unreality of the world; the Śaiva and Śākta tantric traditions; Mīmāṃsā ritualism; the devotional traditions of temple and pilgrimage; and the countless local and caste-specific religious practices of rural India. Buddhism was often presented as a reform movement within Hinduism and the Buddha as a Hindu sage, a presentation that Buddhists, and especially Ambedkarite Buddhists, have rejected (Chapter 18). Sikhs, Jains, Muslims and Christians were assured that their religions were true, but true as approximations to a Vedāntic truth they did not themselves accept. These are not reasons to dismiss Neo-Vedānta, but they are reasons not to mistake it for a neutral account of Indian religion.

docs.title: 9.6 Radhakrishnan
docs.text:
Sarvepalli Radhakrishnan (1888–1975) was the most influential academic exponent of Neo-Vedānta. Trained at Madras Christian College, where he encountered missionary criticism of Hinduism, he wrote his master’s thesis on the ethics of the Vedānta in reply. His two-volume Indian Philosophy (1923, 1927) presented Indian thought to English-speaking readers as a philosophical tradition comparable in depth to that of Europe (Radhakrishnan 1923–1927). The Hindu View of Life (1927), An Idealist View of Life (1932) and Eastern Religions and Western Thought (1939) argued that the core of religion is intuitive experience of the spirit, which the Upaniṣads expressed with unique clarity, and that Hinduism, with its tolerance and its hospitality to all forms of worship, offered a model for the reconciliation of religions in the modern world (Radhakrishnan 1927, 1932, 1939). He held the Spalding Chair at Oxford, was Vice-Chancellor of Andhra and Banaras Hindu Universities, chaired the University Education Commission (1948–49), and served as Vice-President (1952–62) and President (1962–67) of India.

Radhakrishnan’s presentation was eloquent and influential, and it gave Indian philosophy a place in the curricula of the world. It has also been criticised on several grounds. His history of Indian philosophy reads every school as a stage on the way to Vedānta, a “Vedāntic teleology” that later historians have abandoned. His appeal to intuition made religious experience the arbiter of truth in a way that philosophers such as Matilal and Daya Krishna found unhelpful. And his treatment of caste in The Hindu View of Life defended varṇa as an ideal division of society by aptitude while deploring its rigid hereditary form — a defence that critics of caste found insufficient. Like Vivekananda, he spoke of Hinduism as more “a way of life” than a creed, a phrase that has since been used for many purposes.

docs.title: 9.7 Hindu Nationalism
docs.text:
A different modern answer to the question “what is Hinduism?” was given by the Hindu nationalist movement. Its classic statement is V. D. Savarkar’s Hindutva (written in prison and published in 1923; later titled Essentials of Hindutva). Savarkar, himself an atheist, distinguished “Hindutva”, the cultural and national identity of the Hindus, from “Hinduism” as a religion. A Hindu, he argued, is one who regards India as both fatherland (pitṛbhū) and holy land (puṇyabhū). The definition included Sikhs, Jains and Buddhists, whose holy places are in India, and excluded Muslims and Christians, whose holy lands lie elsewhere, however long their families had lived in India. The Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS), founded in Nagpur in 1925 by K. B. Hedgewar, and the Hindu Mahasabha organised Hindus on this basis (van der Veer 1994; Jaffrelot 1996).

Hindu nationalism shares some features with Neo-Vedānta — the idea of a single Hindu civilisation, pride in its antiquity — but differs from it fundamentally. Vivekananda and Radhakrishnan claimed that Hinduism accepted all religions as true; Savarkar’s definition made territory and ancestry, not belief, the test of belonging, and placed India’s largest religious minority outside the nation. Gandhi, a devout Hindu, rejected this politics and was assassinated by Nathuram Godse, a Hindu nationalist who had been associated with both the RSS and the Hindu Mahasabha. Many Sikhs, Jains and Buddhists, for their part, reject their inclusion as “Hindus” in Savarkar’s sense, for reasons discussed in Chapters 16 and 18.

docs.title: 9.7.1 Hindu nationalist thought after 1947
docs.text:
The movement’s intellectual history did not end with independence. M. S. Golwalkar (1906–1973), head of the RSS from 1940 to 1973, had argued in We or Our Nationhood Defined (1939) that the nation was a unity of territory, race, religion, culture and language, and that the minorities must adopt Hindu culture or live in India wholly subordinated to the nation; the book cited Germany’s treatment of its Jews as a lesson, and the RSS later ceased to treat it as authoritative. His speeches, collected as Bunch of Thoughts (1966), described Hindu society as an organic whole whose classes were complementary limbs, and named Muslims, Christians and Communists as threats to the nation. The RSS was banned after Gandhi’s assassination, from 1948 to 1949, and then rebuilt itself as the centre of a family of organisations among students, workers, peasants and Adivasis.

The fullest statement of the movement’s social and economic philosophy came from Deendayal Upadhyaya (1916–1968), a leader of the Bharatiya Jana Sangh, the party founded in 1951. In lectures delivered in Bombay in 1965 and published as Integral Humanism, he rejected both capitalism and socialism as Western systems that treated the person as a merely economic being. Each nation, he argued, has an innate character or “soul” (citi); its institutions should be governed by dharma, understood not as a religion but as the principles that sustain a society; the individual should be understood as an integrated whole of body, mind, intellect and soul; and the economy should be decentralised and self-reliant. The Jana Sangh adopted the doctrine, and its successor, the Bharatiya Janata Party (1980), later named integral humanism its basic philosophy. Its call for a distinctively Indian (bhāratīya) framework of values and knowledge, in place of borrowed categories, makes it one of the intellectual ancestors of the policies discussed in Chapter 22. The Vishva Hindu Parishad, founded in 1964 to bring together Hindu religious leaders and sects, gave the movement a religious organisation, and its campaign from the 1980s for a temple at Ayodhya, on the site of the Babri Masjid demolished in December 1992, made Hindu nationalism a mass movement.

Scholars have analysed these developments from several angles. Walter Andersen and Shridhar Damle’s study of the RSS, written with access to its leaders, describes it as a movement of character-building and social organisation rather than of doctrine (Andersen and Damle 1987). Christophe Jaffrelot has argued that Hindu nationalism practised a “strategic syncretism”, modelling a unified Hindu community on the organisation and scriptural coherence it attributed to its Muslim and Christian rivals (Jaffrelot 1996); Thomas Blom Hansen has read its rise after 1980 as a response of the middle classes to the uncertainties of mass democracy (Hansen 1999). Its defenders present Hindutva as a cultural nationalism open to all who accept India’s civilisational inheritance; its critics, including many Hindus, reply that defining the nation by the culture of one community makes citizens of other faiths conditional members. Christophe Jaffrelot’s anthology of primary texts allows readers to judge the arguments in the movement’s own words (Jaffrelot 2007).

In 1995 the Supreme Court of India described Hindutva as “a way of life” rather than a religion, in judgments on election law that have been much debated. Since the 1980s Hindu nationalist parties have become the dominant force in Indian politics, and the interpretation of India’s traditions — including many of the subjects of this series — has become a matter of intense political contest. A comparative study cannot settle that contest, but it can insist that the traditions be described accurately, including the parts of them that no political programme finds convenient.

docs.title: 9.8 Vedānta and Western Philosophy
docs.text: Comparisons between Vedānta and Western philosophy have been made since Schopenhauer, and some have been illuminating. Śaṅkara and Kant both argued that the forms in which we know the world — for Kant space, time and the categories, for Śaṅkara the distinctions produced by ignorance — do not reveal reality as it is in itself; but Kant held that the thing in itself is unknowable, while Śaṅkara held that Brahman is known, indeed is knowledge, when ignorance is removed by the teaching of the Upaniṣads. Spinoza’s single substance with infinite attributes has been compared with Brahman and with Rāmānuja’s view of the world as God’s body. Hegel’s absolute, which realises itself through history, has been compared — mostly by Indian idealists of the early twentieth century — with the Vedāntic absolute, though Hegel himself regarded Indian thought as an early and inadequate stage of spirit (Chapter 8). Bradley’s distinction between appearance and reality made him a favourite of Indian philosophers trained in British idealism. Eliot Deutsch’s reconstruction of Advaita and the essays of Halbfass show how such comparisons can be pursued carefully, as philosophical dialogue rather than as a search for anticipations (Deutsch 1969; Halbfass 1991). The less careful versions — claims that Advaita “anticipated” modern physics or neuroscience — are discussed in Chapter 19.

docs.title: 9.9 Comparisons: Perennialism and Its Critics
docs.text:
Neo-Vedānta had a counterpart in the West. Aldous Huxley’s The Perennial Philosophy (1945), drawing heavily on Vedāntic sources mediated by the Vedanta Society of Southern California, argued that the mystics of all traditions had discovered the same truth: the identity of the soul with the divine ground (Huxley 1945). The view was influential in the counterculture of the 1960s and remains popular. In the 1970s philosophers of religion led by Steven Katz argued against it that mystical experiences are always shaped by the concepts and practices of particular traditions, so that there is no “pure” experience common to all (Katz 1978). John Hick developed a more cautious pluralism, holding that the religions are different human responses to a transcendent Real that none fully grasps (Hick 1989).

The debate between perennialists, constructivists and pluralists is unresolved, and this volume does not attempt to resolve it. What can be said is that the claim that “all religions are one” is a philosophical and theological position with a definite history, not a neutral description of the religions; that many members of the religions concerned reject it; and that a comparative study must report their rejection as faithfully as it reports the claim.

docs.text:

  • Carman (1974): the theology of Rāmānuja.

  • Killingley (1993) and Kopf (1979): Rammohun Roy and the Brahmo Samaj.

  • Jones (1989): the reform movements of British India.

  • Hacker (1995), Halbfass (1988) and Rambachan (1994): Neo-Vedānta and its critics.

  • Nicholson (2010): pre-colonial efforts to unify Hindu philosophy.

docs.title: Chapter 10: Swami Vivekananda: Vedānta for the Modern World
docs.text: “Each soul is potentially divine. The goal is to manifest this Divinity within by controlling nature, external and internal. Do this either by work, or worship, or psychic control, or philosophy — by one, or more, or all of these — and be free.” — Swami Vivekananda, Raja Yoga (1896)

docs.title: 10.1 Introduction
docs.text: Swami Vivekananda (1863–1902) was the first Indian religious teacher to win a large following in the West, and the most influential single formulator of modern Hindu self-understanding. His address to the World’s Parliament of Religions in Chicago in 1893, his books on the four yogas, his “Practical Vedānta” and the Ramakrishna Math and Mission that he founded shaped the way Hinduism was presented abroad and understood by educated Indians for a century. He is honoured in India as a patriot-saint; his birthday, 12 January, has been celebrated as National Youth Day since 1985. He has also been the subject of critical scholarship that questions some of his claims and examines the uses made of him. This chapter attempts to do justice to both.

docs.title: 10.2 Life
docs.text:
Narendranath Datta was born in Calcutta in 1863 into a prosperous Kāyastha family. He studied Western philosophy at the General Assembly’s Institution (later Scottish Church College), read Mill, Spencer and Hume, and attended meetings of the Brahmo Samaj. In 1881 he met Rāmakṛṣṇa at Dakshineswar (Chapter 9). After initial scepticism he became his most prominent disciple, and after Rāmakṛṣṇa’s death in 1886 he and a group of fellow disciples took monastic vows. From 1888 to 1893 he travelled as a wandering monk across India, an experience that brought him face to face with the poverty of the country and convinced him that religion without service to the poor was hollow.

In 1893, with the support of the Raja of Khetri and of friends in Madras, he sailed to the United States to attend the World’s Parliament of Religions, held in Chicago in conjunction with the Columbian Exposition. His success there led to more than three years of lecturing in America and England. He founded the Vedanta Society of New York (1894), returned to India in 1897 to an enthusiastic reception, delivering a series of lectures from Colombo to Almora, and on 1 May 1897 founded the Ramakrishna Mission Association. The monastery at Belur, on the Ganges near Calcutta, was established in 1898. After a second journey to the West (1899–1900), he died at Belur on 4 July 1902, aged thirty-nine. His lectures, letters and conversations fill the nine volumes of his Complete Works (Vivekananda 1992).

docs.title: 10.3 Chicago, 1893
docs.text:
The World’s Parliament of Religions opened on 11 September 1893. Delegates included Christians of many denominations, Jews, Muslims, Buddhists (among them Anagārika Dharmapāla from Ceylon), the Jain lay scholar Virchand Gandhi, and Brahmo representatives such as P. C. Mozoomdar. Vivekananda’s brief opening address began with the words “Sisters and Brothers of America”, which drew prolonged applause. He continued:

I thank you in the name of the most ancient order of monks in the world; I thank you in the name of the mother of religions; and I thank you in the name of millions and millions of Hindu people of all classes and sects. … I am proud to belong to a religion which has taught the world both tolerance and universal acceptance. We believe not only in universal toleration, but we accept all religions as true.

He illustrated his theme with two quotations: a verse from the Śivamahimnaḥ Stotra comparing the different paths of human beings, straight or crooked, to streams that all reach the ocean, and the Bhagavadgītā’s declaration (4.11) that the Lord meets people by whatever path they approach him. In his longer “Paper on Hinduism” he presented Hinduism as a religion grounded in the Vedas, the eternal laws of spiritual life discovered by the sages, and as a hierarchy of spiritual stages in which even image-worship had its place as a step towards higher realisation.

The success of the address owed much to its moment: a Western audience curious about “Oriental” religions and increasingly uncertain about its own, and a speaker of great presence who answered missionary caricatures with confidence. The claims it made — that Hinduism is the “mother of religions” and that it uniquely accepts all religions as true — were rhetorical as much as historical, and other delegates at the Parliament, Buddhist and Jain among them, did not regard their traditions as offspring of Hinduism.

docs.title: 10.4 The Other Indians at Chicago
docs.text: Vivekananda was not the only Indian at the Parliament, and the presence of the others is a useful corrective to accounts that present him as India’s sole voice. Pratap Chandra Mozoomdar spoke for the Brahmo Samaj, as he had already done on an earlier American tour, and presented a liberal, theistic Hinduism close to Unitarian Christianity; he later became critical of Vivekananda. Anagārika Dharmapāla represented Theravāda Buddhism (Chapter 18); Virchand Gandhi spoke for the Jains; B. B. Nagarkar of Bombay for the Prarthana Samaj; and G. N. Chakravarti and Annie Besant appeared for the Theosophical Society. Christian speakers from India also took part. The Parliament itself, organised by liberal American Protestants, was designed to display the religions of the world as approaching, by different routes, the truths best expressed in Christianity, and several of its organisers expected the “Oriental” speakers to confirm this. Vivekananda’s success lay partly in reversing the expected hierarchy, presenting Vedānta as the most universal religion and Christianity as one of its partial expressions — an inclusivism that mirrored that of his hosts.

docs.title: 10.5 The American Setting
docs.text:
Vivekananda’s success in America is easier to understand when one remembers what his audiences already knew. The Transcendentalists, Emerson and Thoreau, had read the Bhagavadgītā and other Indian texts in translation earlier in the century (Chapter 8). Unitarian and liberal Protestant circles were open to the idea that truth could be found in many religions; the “New Thought” movement taught the power of mind over body; and the Theosophical Society had popularised the idea of an ancient Eastern wisdom (Chapter 8). Many of Vivekananda’s most devoted supporters were educated women, such as Sara Bull and Josephine MacLeod, who financed his work and later supported the Ramakrishna movement in India.

His audiences also brought stereotypes, which he exploited and resisted. He was received as an exotic sage, and some of his success depended on his presence and eloquence as much as his arguments. He used his platform to attack the work of Christian missionaries in India: at the Parliament he told his hearers that what India needed was not religion, of which it had plenty, but bread, and that it was an insult to a starving people to offer them doctrine. Missionaries and some Indian Christians responded critically, and controversies about his statements followed him through his American years. His lectures, collected in the Complete Works, show him adapting his message to audiences in New York, London and Madras with considerable skill (Vivekananda 1992).

docs.title: 10.6 Vivekananda on Other Religions
docs.text:
Vivekananda’s attitudes to the other religions he encountered were generous but not neutral. He admired the Buddha intensely, calling him the greatest of men and the model of selfless work, and lectured on him in America and India. But he described Buddhism, in a speech at the Parliament, as the “fulfilment” of Hinduism and elsewhere as its “rebel child”, and attributed its disappearance from India partly to its own decadence and partly to its reabsorption into Hinduism. Dharmapāla, whom he met at Chicago, insisted on the contrary on the independence of the Buddha’s teaching (Chapter 18), and the question — reformer within Hinduism, or founder of a separate tradition? — still shapes how Buddhists in modern India, including the followers of Ambedkar, understand themselves. He admired Jesus and quoted the Gospels often, while denying that Christianity had any monopoly of truth. He praised Islam for practising the equality that Vedānta taught in theory, but he also repeated, in some lectures, the common nineteenth-century picture of Muslim rule in India as a period of oppression.

These views were shaped by his framework. In a hierarchy in which the Vedānta is the most comprehensive religion, other religions could be honoured as true, and even as necessary for the peoples who held them, while remaining partial. The framework enabled him to speak respectfully of all religions to audiences used to missionary polemic; it also made it hard for him to hear them on their own terms. This is the inclusivism discussed in Chapter 1, in one of its most attractive forms.

docs.title: 10.7 Practical Vedānta and Service
docs.text:
Vivekananda’s most original contribution was his insistence that Advaita Vedānta had practical, social consequences. If every being is in essence Brahman, then the poor, the hungry and the outcaste are God in disguise, and to serve them is to worship God. His lectures on “Practical Vedānta” in London (1896) argued that the Vedānta should be brought “from the forest” into ordinary life, into the market-place and the home. He popularised the term daridranārāyaṇa, “God in the form of the poor”, later taken up by Gandhi. The Ramakrishna Mission’s motto, “for one’s own liberation and for the welfare of the world” (ātmano mokṣārthaṃ jagaddhitāya ca), expresses the combination. The Mission’s hospitals, schools, colleges and famine and disaster relief, begun in his lifetime, made it one of the best-known service organisations in India.

Hacker and others have pointed out that classical Advaita did not draw this conclusion: for Śaṅkara the liberated sage has transcended action, and service is at most a preparation for knowledge (Hacker 1995). Vivekananda’s ethic owed as much to the Christian and humanitarian ideals of nineteenth-century Bengal as to Śaṅkara. That does not make it less valuable; it does make it new.

docs.title: 10.8 The Four Yogas
docs.text:
Vivekananda organised religious practice under four “yogas”, each suited to a different temperament: karmayoga, the path of selfless work; bhaktiyoga, the path of devotion; jñānayoga, the path of philosophical discrimination; and rājayoga, the path of meditation, which he identified with Patañjali’s Yogasūtra. He published books on each, based on his lectures in America and England, the most influential being Raja Yoga (1896), which included a translation and commentary on the Yogasūtra (Vivekananda 1992).

The Bhagavadgītā had already discussed action, knowledge and devotion as disciplines (yoga), but Vivekananda’s fourfold scheme, with the paths presented as complementary and ideally combined, was his own systematisation. His Raja Yoga was particularly consequential.
