Elizabeth De Michelis has shown that it presented Patañjali’s yoga as a “science” of the mind, verifiable by experiment, in terms shaped by Western esotericism, Unitarianism and the “New Thought” movement of his American audiences, and that it became the founding text of what she calls “modern yoga” (De Michelis 2004).

The book departs from its classical source in ways worth noting. Patañjali’s Yogasūtra is a dualist work in the Sāṃkhya tradition, whose goal is the isolation (kaivalya) of the conscious self from matter, not union with an absolute; Vivekananda read it through his Vedāntic universalism, so that the goal of yoga became the realisation of the divinity of the soul. He gave great prominence to prāṇa, which he explained in the language of nineteenth-century physics as a universal energy, whereas the classical commentators Vyāsa and Vācaspati Miśra had located yoga within a scheme of scriptural authority, ritual purity and renunciation. The postures (āsana) that dominate yoga today play almost no part in his account; for him, as for Patañjali, āsana meant a steady seat for meditation. None of this makes Raja Yoga a fraud — every interpreter reads an ancient text in the light of his own concerns, and this reading proved enormously fruitful — but it means that the “yoga” Western readers met through him was already a modern synthesis. Its later history is taken up in Chapter 20.

docs.title: 10.9 Religion as Experience and as Science
docs.text:
Vivekananda argued that religion, like science, rests on experience: the sages had experienced the truths they taught, and anyone who followed their methods could verify those truths for himself. Religion should therefore be “scientific”, and the Vedānta, being based on experience rather than on dogma or on historical events, was the religion best suited to the scientific age. He drew analogies between Vedāntic monism and the physics of his time, especially the conservation of energy, and taught that behind all forces there is one cosmic energy (prāṇa) and behind all matter one universal substance (ākāśa). A letter of 1896 records his meeting with the inventor Nikola Tesla, who, he wrote, was interested in these ideas.

Physics has not developed in the direction Vivekananda expected, and his specific analogies are now of historical interest only. The more lasting issue is philosophical. Rambachan has shown that Vivekananda’s appeal to experience as the final authority reverses Śaṅkara’s view that the Upaniṣads are the means of knowing Brahman, and that the scriptures are for Vivekananda secondary records of the sages’ experience (Rambachan 1994). The appeal to experience made the Vedānta attractive to modern audiences and compatible with the idea of a universal mysticism; it also exposed it to the objection, discussed in Chapter 9, that there is no experience independent of the concepts of a tradition.

docs.title: 10.10 The Harmony of Religions
docs.text:
Vivekananda’s doctrine of the harmony of religions drew on Rāmakṛṣṇa’s example and on Advaita. Because the ultimate reality is infinite, no single religion can exhaust it; each religion expresses some aspect of the truth suited to a particular people and temperament; therefore all should be accepted, not merely tolerated. At the same time, he held that the Vedānta, which recognised the impersonal Absolute behind all personal gods, was the most comprehensive religion and could provide the philosophical basis for a universal religion.

He did not think that India’s own communities should simply merge. In a letter of 1898 to Mohammed Sarfaraz Husain of Naini Tal, he wrote that mankind should be led to the place where there is “neither the Vedas, nor the Bible, nor the Koran”, but that this should be done by harmonising them, and that the hope of India lay in “Vedanta brain and Islam body” — the philosophy of Vedānta joined to the practical equality of Islam (Vivekananda 1992). The letter shows both the generosity of his vision and its characteristic hierarchy, in which the brain is Vedāntic.

docs.title: 10.11 Society, Caste and Nation
docs.text:
Vivekananda was a fierce critic of the social practices of his day. He mocked the orthodox preoccupation with ritual purity as “don’t-touchism”, condemned the oppression of the lower castes and the neglect of the poor, and urged the education of women and of the masses. He supported the girls’ school that his disciple Sister Nivedita opened in Calcutta (see below). On caste he was less radical than some of his admirers suppose: he sometimes defended caste as originally a natural division of labour corrupted over time, and he proposed raising the lower castes to the cultural level of the Brahmins rather than abolishing caste distinctions altogether.

His call to national self-respect — “Arise, awake, and stop not till the goal is reached”, adapted from the Kaṭha Upaniṣad (1.3.14) — inspired a generation of nationalists, including the revolutionaries of Bengal, Aurobindo and Subhas Chandra Bose. Tapan Raychaudhuri has shown that his attitude to the West combined admiration for its energy, organisation and science with contempt for its materialism and resentment of its imperialism (Raychaudhuri 1988). His image has since been claimed by many political movements, including Hindu nationalist organisations that emphasise his patriotism and his defence of Hinduism while giving less weight to his universalism and his social criticism.

docs.title: 10.12 The Bengali Writings
docs.text: Vivekananda’s English lectures are well known; his Bengali writings, addressed to his own countrymen, are less so outside Bengal, and they show a sharper social analysis. In Bartamān Bhārat (“Modern India”, 1899) he offered a theory of Indian history as a succession of dominant classes: first the priests, whose power rested on knowledge and ritual; then the warriors, whose power rested on arms; then, under British rule, the merchants, whose power rested on wealth. Each had risen by drawing on the strength of the labouring masses and had then exploited them; he foresaw a time when the Śūdras, the labouring people, would themselves rise to power, and he called on educated Indians to identify with them. In Prācya o Pāścātya (“East and West”), he compared Indian and European customs, food, dress and ideals with humour and some acerbity, criticising both. These writings reveal a thinker who could combine his Vedāntic universalism with a materialist sense of social power, and they help to explain why Indian socialists as well as religious nationalists have claimed him (see below).

docs.title: 10.13 Education
docs.text: Vivekananda wrote no treatise on education, but his scattered remarks were later collected and have been very influential. He defined education as “the manifestation of the perfection already in man” and contrasted the “man-making” education he wanted with the clerk-making education of colonial schools. In a lecture he said that education is not information put into the brain that “runs riot there, undigested, all your life”, and that a person who has assimilated five ideas and made them his life and character has more education than one who has learned a whole library by heart. He stressed self-confidence (śraddhā), concentration, physical strength and service, and favoured teaching in the mother tongue. His ideas are often cited in support of India’s National Education Policy of 2020, discussed in Chapter 22.

docs.title: 10.14 Vivekananda and the Orientalists
docs.text: Vivekananda’s relation to European scholarship was close and ambivalent. In 1896 he visited Max Müller at Oxford and was moved by the old scholar’s devotion to India; Müller, for his part, published an essay on Rāmakṛṣṇa and in 1898 a book, Rāmakrishna: His Life and Sayings, based partly on material supplied by Vivekananda’s circle. Vivekananda praised Müller and Paul Deussen, whom he also visited in Germany, as true friends of India who had understood the Vedānta better than many Indians. At the same time he rejected the Orientalists’ historical criticism of the Veda and their theories of Indian history, and he insisted that the authentic interpretation of Indian religion belonged to those who lived it. His career illustrates the point made in Chapter 8: modern Hindu self-understanding was shaped in dialogue with European scholarship, appropriating its admiration while resisting its authority.

docs.title: 10.15 Women, Disciples and Sister Nivedita
docs.text:
Vivekananda’s work in the West drew a circle of disciples and supporters, many of them women, who played a large part in establishing his movement. Sara Bull, the widow of the Norwegian violinist Ole Bull, and Josephine MacLeod became lifelong supporters; Josiah John Goodwin, an English stenographer, recorded many of the lectures that survive. The most important of these disciples was Margaret Noble (1867–1911), an Irish schoolteacher who met Vivekananda in London in 1895, came to India in 1898 and took the name Nivedita (“dedicated”). In November 1898 she opened a school for girls in the Bagbazar quarter of Calcutta, and she spent the rest of her life in India, writing on Indian society and religion (The Web of Indian Life, 1904), supporting the scientific work of Jagadish Chandra Bose (Chapter 19), encouraging the artists of the Bengal School (Chapter 21) and moving, after Vivekananda’s death, into open sympathy with the nationalist movement, which led her to separate formally from the Ramakrishna Order.

Vivekananda’s views on women combined reform and conservatism in ways typical of his period. He insisted that the condition of Indian women was one of the causes of India’s decline, called for their education, and envisaged a monastic order for women; the Sri Sarada Math, named after Rāmakṛṣṇa’s wife Sāradā Devī, was eventually established in 1954. At the same time he idealised the self-sacrificing Hindu wife and mother, defended many existing customs against missionary criticism, and held that Indian women must solve their own problems in their own way, without foreign interference. Historians of gender in colonial India have placed him within the wider nationalist reconstruction of the “Indian woman” as the guardian of spiritual tradition (Chakravarti 2003).

docs.title: 10.16 Uses of Vivekananda
docs.text: Few modern Indians have been claimed by so many different movements. Bengali revolutionaries of the early twentieth century read his call for strength and fearlessness as a summons to political action; Subhas Chandra Bose acknowledged him as a formative influence. Socialists and secular nationalists admired his concern for the poor and his attack on priestcraft; Nehru wrote of him with respect in The Discovery of India (Nehru 1946). Hindu nationalist organisations have made him a central figure: the Vivekananda Rock Memorial at Kanyakumari, inaugurated in 1970, was built by a committee led by Eknath Ranade, a senior worker of the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh, and his image is widely used in their publications. Scholars have noted that these uses select different parts of a large and sometimes inconsistent body of speeches and letters — the universalist and the nationalist, the defender of Hinduism and its severe critic. A careful reading of the Complete Works does not support any single appropriation; it shows a man of strong and changing views, speaking to different audiences, whose thought cannot be reduced to a slogan.

docs.title: 10.17 After Vivekananda: Indian Teachers in the West
docs.text:
Vivekananda opened a path that many Indian teachers followed, with very different teachings. Paramahansa Yogananda (1893–1952) arrived in Boston in 1920 for a congress of religious liberals, stayed in America, founded the Self-Realization Fellowship in Los Angeles and taught a technique he called Kriya Yoga; his Autobiography of a Yogi (1946) became one of the most widely read books on Indian spirituality. A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda (1896–1977) founded the International Society for Krishna Consciousness in New York in 1966, bringing the devotional Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇavism of Bengal — a tradition that explicitly rejects Advaita — to young Westerners. Maharishi Mahesh Yogi (c. 1917–2008) taught Transcendental Meditation, a simple mantra technique, to millions from the late 1950s, and attracted the Beatles to his ashram at Rishikesh in 1968. Swami Chinmayananda (1916–1993) founded the Chinmaya Mission in 1953 to teach Advaita Vedānta in English to the urban middle class in India and the diaspora.

These movements differ from one another in doctrine as much as any of the classical schools did: some are non-dualist, some devotional and theistic, some centred on technique. They share a modern form — an international organisation, publications in English, a teacher presented as a guide for people of any background — that owes much to Vivekananda’s example. Several of them also produced scandals and controversies over authority, money and the treatment of followers, as new religious movements in every tradition have done. Their history is part of the global life of Indian religions, and it shows that “Hinduism abroad” was never a single message.

docs.title: 10.18 Who Is a Hindu? The Mission and the Courts
docs.text: The universalism of the Ramakrishna movement produced a curious legal episode, which illustrates the difficulty of defining religious identity in modern India. In the 1980s the Ramakrishna Mission, seeking the protection given by the Constitution to educational institutions run by religious minorities, argued before the courts that its followers constituted a distinct religion, “Ramakrishnaism”, rather than a Hindu sect, since they accepted all religions as true. The Calcutta High Court accepted the argument, but in 1995 the Supreme Court reversed the decision and held that the Mission was a Hindu religious denomination. The case shows how an inclusivist claim — that one’s own tradition embraces all others — can turn into a claim to be outside every particular tradition, and how the courts, like the census, are compelled to draw boundaries that the traditions themselves leave vague.

docs.title: 10.19 Influence and Assessment
docs.text:
Vivekananda’s influence in the West was considerable but specific. The Vedanta Societies remained small, but their members and associates included writers such as Christopher Isherwood and Aldous Huxley, whose Perennial Philosophy drew on Vedāntic sources (Chapter 9). William James quoted Vivekananda’s lectures in The Varieties of Religious Experience (1902). Through Raja Yoga he gave the West its first widely read presentation of yoga as a practical discipline.

In India his influence was immense and continues. Admirers see in him the man who restored Hindu self-confidence, joined spirituality to social service and gave India a voice in the world. Critics have pointed out the historical claims that do not stand up (Hinduism as “the mother of religions”, Buddhism as a branch of Hinduism), the departure from classical Advaita that his “experience” and “service” represent, and the ease with which his rhetoric of Hindu pride could be used for exclusive nationalism. Both views can be held at once. Vivekananda was a creative reformer who used the resources of his tradition to answer the questions of his time; his synthesis is best understood, and best honoured, as one argued position among others, not as the final truth about Indian religion.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text:
• Vivekananda (1992): the collected works.

  • Harris (2022): a recent biography that places Vivekananda in his global setting.

  • Raychaudhuri (1988): Vivekananda and other Bengali intellectuals on the West.

  • Rambachan (1994): Vivekananda’s reinterpretation of the authority of the Vedas.

  • De Michelis (2004): Vivekananda and the origins of modern yoga.

  • Hacker (1995): essays on Neo-Vedānta and its classical background.

docs.title: Chapter 11: Sri Aurobindo: Nationalism, Evolution and Integral Yoga
docs.text: “In the right view both of life and of Yoga all life is either consciously or subconsciously a Yoga.” — Sri Aurobindo, The Synthesis of Yoga, Introduction

docs.title: 11.1 Introduction
docs.text: Aurobindo Ghose (1872–1950), known after his withdrawal from politics as Sri Aurobindo, was successively a classically educated product of Victorian England, a radical nationalist leader, a political prisoner and, for the last forty years of his life, a yogi and philosopher in the French enclave of Pondicherry. His major works — The Life Divine, The Synthesis of Yoga, The Human Cycle, The Ideal of Human Unity, The Secret of the Veda and the epic poem Savitri — constitute the most ambitious attempt of modern India to reinterpret the Vedic and Vedāntic tradition as a philosophy of evolution and world-affirmation. This chapter outlines his life, his thought and his legacy, and considers how it stands as a “synthesis”. Peter Heehs’s biography is the fullest critical account (Heehs 2008).

docs.title: 11.2 Life
docs.text:
Aurobindo was sent to England at the age of seven by his anglicised father, with instructions that he should have no contact with Indian culture. He studied classics at St Paul’s School, London, and at King’s College, Cambridge, passed the examination for the Indian Civil Service but failed to present himself for the riding test and was not appointed. He returned to India in 1893 to serve the Maharaja of Baroda, where he learned Sanskrit, Bengali and Marathi and began reading the Indian classics. From 1906 he was in Bengal, as principal of the new Bengal National College and as a leading voice of the “extremist” wing of the Indian National Congress, writing in the newspaper Bande Mataram. He advocated complete independence and the boycott of British goods, and in his pamphlet The Doctrine of Passive Resistance (1907) he argued for organised non-cooperation while refusing to rule out other means.

In 1908 he was arrested in connection with the Alipore bomb case, in which his younger brother Barindra was a leading conspirator. He spent a year in jail before being acquitted, and later described spiritual experiences in prison that changed the direction of his life. In 1910, to avoid further arrest, he moved secretly to Pondicherry, then French territory, where he remained until his death in 1950. From 1914 to 1921 he published the monthly Arya, in which most of his major works first appeared serially. Mirra Alfassa (1878–1973), born in Paris to Jewish parents from Turkey and Egypt, whom he first met in 1914 and who settled in Pondicherry in 1920, became his closest collaborator, known as “the Mother”. After 1926 Aurobindo withdrew into seclusion and the Mother organised the Sri Aurobindo Ashram.

docs.title: 11.3 Religious Nationalism
docs.text: Aurobindo’s early nationalism was explicitly religious. In the pamphlet Bhawani Mandir (1905) he proposed a temple and an order of renouncers dedicated to the Mother-goddess as the embodiment of India, and described the nation not as a piece of earth or a figure of speech but as a mighty power (śakti) made up of the energies of its millions of people, as the goddess Durgā had been formed from the energies of the gods. In a speech at Uttarpara in 1909, shortly after his release from prison, he declared that “it is the Sanatan Dharma which for us is nationalism”, and described India’s mission as the preservation and spread of that eternal religion. These texts made him a hero of later Hindu nationalism. They also show a problem that recurs throughout this volume: a nationalism defined by the religion of the majority could not easily include India’s Muslims, Sikhs and Christians on equal terms. In his later writings, especially The Ideal of Human Unity, Aurobindo moved towards a vision of world union in which nations would be stages in the evolution of humanity, and in 1947 he welcomed independence while lamenting partition.

docs.title: 11.4 The Life Divine
docs.text:
The Life Divine, serialised in the Arya (1914–1919) and revised as a book in 1939–40, is Aurobindo’s principal philosophical work (Aurobindo 1970a). Its starting point is a rejection of what he calls two “negations”. The materialist negation denies the reality of spirit; the ascetic negation, of which he took Śaṅkara’s Advaita and Buddhism to be the extreme forms, denies the reality or value of the world. Both, he argues, are one-sided. Reality is saccidānanda — existence, consciousness and bliss — which has “involved” itself in matter, so that matter is a form of concealed consciousness; evolution is the progressive unfolding of what has been involved, from matter to life and from life to mind. Mind is not the last term. Above it lie a series of higher levels of consciousness — higher mind, illumined mind, intuition and overmind — culminating in “supermind” (vijñāna), a truth-consciousness in which the One knows itself as the Many without division. The next stage of evolution, Aurobindo held, would be the emergence of a supramental consciousness on earth and the transformation of human nature, and eventually of the body itself.

Aurobindo reinterpreted māyā: not illusion, but the creative power of the divine to measure out forms, a meaning he found in the Ṛgveda. Against Śaṅkara he held that the world is real as a manifestation of Brahman, a position closer to the “real transformation” (pariṇāma) views of earlier Vedāntins than to Advaita’s “appearance” (vivarta). His system is thus a Vedānta, but an evolutionary and world-affirming one, consciously addressed to the questions raised by Darwin, Bergson and Nietzsche.

docs.title: 11.5 Integral Yoga
docs.text: The Synthesis of Yoga (serialised 1914–1921) set out a “yoga” corresponding to this metaphysics (Aurobindo 1970b). Aurobindo surveyed the paths of works, knowledge and devotion described in the Gītā, the rājayoga of Patañjali, haṭhayoga and tantra, and argued that each takes up one part of human nature. An “integral” yoga would take up all of them, and would aim not at the individual’s escape from the world but at the transformation of the whole being — body, life, mind and soul — and, through it, of terrestrial life. Its means are aspiration, the rejection of the movements of the lower nature, and surrender to the Divine Mother; its stages, in his later formulation, are a “psychic” transformation, in which the inmost soul (the “psychic being”) comes forward, a “spiritual” transformation, in which the higher levels of consciousness descend, and a “supramental” transformation. Aurobindo was sober about the dangers of the path: his letters warn repeatedly against mistaking vivid inner experiences in what he called the “intermediate zone” for genuine realisation.

docs.title: 11.6 The Veda, Society and Poetry
docs.text:
The Veda.

In The Secret of the Veda, also first published in the Arya, Aurobindo argued that the Ṛgvedic hymns had an inner, psychological meaning: Agni was the divine will, Soma the delight of existence, the cows of the Aṅgirases the rays of illumination. The interpretation is ingenious and has been influential among his followers, but it has not been accepted by Vedic scholars, who read the hymns in the context of the ritual and society that produced them (Volume 1).

Society and politics.

The Human Cycle interprets social history as a movement from symbolic and conventional ages through an age of individualism and reason towards a “subjective” and finally spiritual age; The Ideal of Human Unity, written during the First World War, foresees a world-union of free nations. Both drew on European social thought, including Karl Lamprecht’s theory of historical stages, which Aurobindo acknowledged.

The Gītā.

In Essays on the Gita, also serialised in the Arya, Aurobindo read the Bhagavadgītā as a synthesis of the paths of works, knowledge and devotion, culminating in the surrender of the whole being to the Divine and in action as the Divine’s instrument. He rejected both Śaṅkara’s view that the Gītā ultimately subordinates action to knowledge and renunciation, and the purely ethical reading of those who saw in it a gospel of duty; and he treated the setting on the battlefield as part of the teaching, not as an allegory to be explained away, since the Gītā accepts that the world includes struggle and destruction. His reading thus differed both from Tilak’s activism and from Gandhi’s non-violent allegory (Chapter 6).

Translations.

Aurobindo was also a translator. In his Baroda years he translated Kālidāsa’s play Vikramorvaśīya into English verse as The Hero and the Nymph, and passages of the epics; later he translated and commented on the Īśa, Kena and other Upaniṣads, and on hymns of the Ṛgveda in the light of his psychological interpretation. His translations are free and literary rather than philological, and they show the same tendency as his commentaries to read the texts as expressions of his own spiritual vision. They also show a poet’s engagement with Sanskrit literature that was unusual among the religious teachers of his generation.

Savitri.

Aurobindo’s longest work is Savitri: A Legend and a Symbol, an epic in English blank verse of some 24,000 lines on which he worked from about 1916 until his death. It retells the story from the Mahābhārata of the princess Sāvitrī who wins back her husband Satyavān from Death, and makes it a symbol of the soul’s victory over death and ignorance. His followers regard it as a revelation; literary critics have been more divided, some admiring its visionary sweep and others finding its diction archaic.

docs.title: 11.7 The Arya and the Defence of Indian Culture
docs.text:
Almost all of Aurobindo’s major prose works first appeared in the Arya, a monthly “review of pure philosophy” that he published from Pondicherry between August 1914 and January 1921, initially with Paul and Mirra Richard. Each issue carried instalments of several works at once — The Life Divine, The Synthesis of Yoga, The Secret of the Veda, Essays on the Gita, the essays later collected as The Human Cycle and The Ideal of Human Unity — so that the whole system was composed in parallel, over six and a half years, in a journal with a few hundred subscribers.

Among the last series in the Arya was a response to the English drama critic William Archer, whose India and the Future (1917) had dismissed Indian civilisation as barbarous and its religion and art as obstacles to progress. Aurobindo’s reply, later published as The Foundations of Indian Culture, defended Indian religion, art, literature and polity, arguing that each must be judged by its own aims rather than by the standards of nineteenth-century European rationalism. The work belongs to a genre familiar from Chapter 8: the Indian answer to European disparagement. It is eloquent and often penetrating, especially on Indian art, where Aurobindo drew on Havell and Coomaraswamy; it also shares the genre’s tendency to set an idealised “spiritual” India against a “materialist” West, a contrast that later scholars on both sides have questioned.

docs.title: 11.8 Aurobindo and European Philosophy
docs.text:
Aurobindo was educated in England, read Greek and Latin fluently, and knew European literature and philosophy well. His system invites comparison with three European thinkers in particular.

Hegel.

Like Hegel, Aurobindo describes reality as Spirit that realises itself through a historical and cosmic process, and like Hegel he treats earlier philosophies as partial truths taken up into a larger whole. The difference is that Aurobindo’s Spirit is known in the last resort not through dialectical reason but through spiritual experience, and that his process is not complete in the present: the supramental stage lies ahead.

Bergson.

Henri Bergson’s Creative Evolution (1907) presented evolution as the work of a vital impulse (élan vital) and contrasted analytic intellect with intuition. Aurobindo used similar language of intuition and of a creative evolutionary force, but he regarded Bergson’s “life” as only one level in an ascending series that continues beyond mind.

Nietzsche.

Aurobindo’s “superman” or supramental being has been compared with Nietzsche’s Übermensch. Aurobindo himself discussed Nietzsche, admiring his vision of human self-surpassing but rejecting the ideal of power without spiritual transformation.

Such comparisons were made by Aurobindo’s early interpreters, including S. K. Maitra, and they remain useful as long as they are not turned into claims of priority. Aurobindo did not anticipate Hegel or Bergson; he read them and others, and built something new from European and Indian materials together. That is itself a form of samanvaya.

docs.title: 11.9 The Message of 15 August 1947
docs.text: India became independent on 15 August 1947, Aurobindo’s seventy-fifth birthday. At the request of All India Radio he wrote a message for the occasion, in which he described the coincidence as a sign and set out five “dreams” that he had held since his youth: a free and united India; the resurgence and liberation of the peoples of Asia; a world-union forming the outer basis of a fairer and nobler life for all humanity; the spiritual gift of India to the world; and a new step in the evolution of consciousness. He regarded the partition of the country, then taking place, as a settled fact that must not be accepted as final, and expressed the hope that it would in some way disappear. The message shows the continuity in Aurobindo’s thought between the nationalism of his youth and the evolutionary internationalism of his later works, and it also shows the limits of prophecy: partition did not disappear, and the conflicts it produced were bloodier than almost anyone foresaw.

docs.title: 11.10 The Ashram and Auroville
docs.text: The Sri Aurobindo Ashram in Pondicherry grew under the Mother’s direction into a large community with its own farms, workshops, press and, from 1943, a school that became the Sri Aurobindo International Centre of Education, known for its emphasis on physical education and the arts. In 1968, five years before her death, the Mother founded Auroville, an international township on a barren plateau north of Pondicherry, intended as a place where people of all nations could live in harmony beyond religion and politics. Its inauguration was supported by UNESCO, and its residents, now numbering a few thousand from several dozen countries, have reforested much of the land and experimented with renewable energy, architecture and education. Disputes between the residents and the Sri Aurobindo Society led the Government of India to take over its administration, and the Auroville Foundation Act of 1988 placed it under a governing board; tensions over development and governance have continued.

docs.title: 11.11 Aurobindo and His Contemporaries
docs.text:
Aurobindo’s relations with the other major figures of his time illuminate his position. In 1907, when Aurobindo was on trial for sedition, Rabindranath Tagore published a Bengali poem saluting him as the voice of India’s soul. Aurobindo shared with Tilak, his ally in the extremist wing of the Congress, the conviction that the Gītā taught action in the world, and with Vivekananda the belief that India had a spiritual mission. With Gandhi he had little personal contact, and he did not share Gandhi’s commitment to non-violence as an absolute principle: in his political years he refused to rule out armed resistance, and from Pondicherry he supported the Allies in the Second World War and in 1942 urged acceptance of the Cripps proposals for Indian self-government, which the Congress rejected. In his later works he regarded nationalism, and politics generally, as a stage in the evolution of a spiritual humanity rather than an end.

Aurobindo’s partnership with the Mother was itself unusual. After 1926 she, a woman and a European, directed the Ashram and was regarded by its members as an embodiment of the divine Mother; Aurobindo wrote a short work, The Mother (1928), explaining her role. In a tradition in which spiritual authority had mostly been held by men, and in a period of nationalist assertion against Europe, the arrangement was a notable departure.

docs.title: 11.12 The Mother’s Later Teaching
docs.text: After Aurobindo’s death in 1950, the Mother led the Ashram for another twenty-three years and continued, in her own way, the work he had described. She announced to the Ashram that on 29 February 1956 the “supramental” consciousness had manifested in the earth’s atmosphere, an event that her followers commemorate and that others have no means of assessing. In her last years she described, in conversations with her disciple Satprem later published in many volumes as Mother’s Agenda, an experimental yoga of the cells of the body, aimed at a physical transformation that would overcome death. She died in 1973. Her role as a spiritual authority in her own right — a European woman leading an Indian religious community, and regarded by its members as divine — made the Pondicherry Ashram unusual among modern Indian movements. After her death the Ashram, the Sri Aurobindo Society and Auroville entered a period of disputes over property and authority, a common fate of religious communities after the death of a charismatic founder. For a comparative account, the Mother’s teaching illustrates once again how modern Indian spirituality was shaped by persons from several cultures, and how claims of extraordinary experience, which cannot be checked, sit beside institutions that can be studied historically.

docs.title: 11.13 Integral Education
docs.text: The Mother developed, on the basis of Aurobindo’s thought, a theory of “integral education” that aimed at the development of the whole person in five aspects: physical, vital (emotional and energetic), mental, psychic and spiritual. The Ashram school, later the Sri Aurobindo International Centre of Education, emphasised physical education for both girls and boys, the arts and a “free progress” system in which students chose their own subjects and pace, without competitive examinations. Similar ideas have influenced schools in India and elsewhere. Like Tagore’s Santiniketan and Gandhi’s “basic education”, the experiment was a criticism of the examination-centred colonial system, and it is often cited in support of the holistic aims of India’s National Education Policy of 2020 (Chapter 22).

docs.title: 11.14 Influence
docs.text: Aurobindo’s influence has been strongest among his own followers in India and abroad, in the field of “integral” education, and in some Western movements. Haridas Chaudhuri, a Bengali philosopher influenced by Aurobindo, founded in San Francisco in 1968 the institute that became the California Institute of Integral Studies; Michael Murphy, co-founder of the Esalen Institute, had spent time at the Pondicherry Ashram; and the American writer Ken Wilber developed an “integral theory” that cites Aurobindo among its inspirations. Commentators have often compared his evolutionary spirituality with that of the Jesuit palaeontologist Pierre Teilhard de Chardin, whose The Phenomenon of Man (published 1955) also described evolution as the ascent of consciousness towards a divine goal; the two developed their ideas independently, and the parallel says more about the intellectual climate of the early twentieth century, shaped by Bergson and by the challenge of Darwin, than about direct influence.

docs.title: 11.15 Four Modern Syntheses Compared
docs.text:
Aurobindo’s synthesis is best understood beside the others discussed in this part of the volume. Table 11.1 compares four of the most influential modern Indian visions on a few central questions. The summaries simplify large bodies of work, and each thinker changed his views over time.

Table 11.1. Four modern syntheses compared (simplified) Vivekananda Aurobindo Radha­krishnan Gandhi Ultimate reality Brahman of Advaita, approached by many paths Saccidānanda unfolding in evolution Spirit known in intuitive experience Truth, which is God The world real for practice; field of service real; to be divinised real; a stage for spiritual growth real; field of service and non-violent action Other religions all true, Vedānta the most universal partial expressions of one spiritual truth expressions of one experience; Hinduism the most tolerant all true and all imperfect; equal respect Caste criticised hereditary privilege; idealised varṇa a stage of social evolution ideal varṇa by aptitude untouchability a sin; varṇa long defended Politics national regeneration through character revolutionary nationalism, then world union liberal internationalism non-violent mass action; village self-rule Method experience and service integral yoga philosophical reflection experiments with truth

The table shows how much these visions differ beneath their common vocabulary of spirituality and harmony. It also shows what all four share and what their critics, above all Ambedkar, rejected: the conviction that India’s renewal would come through a reinterpretation of its spiritual tradition rather than through a break with it (Chapter 12).

docs.title: 11.16 Assessment
docs.text:
Aurobindo’s synthesis is a philosophical vision on a grand scale, written with great erudition and literary power. As philosophy, it can be compared with the speculative systems of Hegel, Bergson and Whitehead, and judged by the same criteria of coherence and illumination. Several points need to be made in a comparative account.

  • It is not a scientific theory. Aurobindo’s evolution of consciousness is a metaphysical interpretation of evolution, not an alternative biological mechanism. It cannot be tested by the methods of biology, and comparisons with recent philosophical critiques of materialism, such as Thomas Nagel’s, are comparisons between philosophical positions.

  • It is a new Vedānta. Aurobindo’s world-affirming, evolutionary reading of the Upaniṣads is his own; it departs from Śaṅkara as consciously as Rāmānuja did, and it draws heavily on European thought. Its value does not depend on its being the “true” meaning of the Veda.

  • Its politics changed. The religious nationalism of 1905–09 and the internationalism of the later works coexist in his writings, and those who invoke his authority today tend to select one or the other.

  • History and hagiography. The publication of Heehs’s documented biography in 2008 provoked protests from some devotees who objected to its treatment of their master as a historical figure. Writers on other modern Indian religious teachers, whose followers often regard critical history as disrespect, have met the same difficulty.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text:
• Heehs (2008): the standard critical biography.

  • Aurobindo (1970a) and Aurobindo (1970b): the principal philosophical and yogic works.

  • Bhushan and Garfield (2011): an anthology of Indian philosophy in English from the colonial period, with selections from Aurobindo.

docs.title: Chapter 12: Gandhi and Ambedkar: Non-violence, Caste and Justice
docs.text: “On the 26th of January 1950, we are going to enter into a life of contradictions. In politics we will have equality and in social and economic life we will have inequality.” — B. R. Ambedkar, speech to the Constituent Assembly, 25 November 1949

docs.title: 12.1 Two Founders
docs.text: Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi (1869–1948) and Bhimrao Ramji Ambedkar (1891–1956) are the two most influential Indian political thinkers of the twentieth century. Both drew on Indian traditions to answer the questions of their age; both were also profoundly shaped by Western thought, Gandhi through Tolstoy, Ruskin and the New Testament, Ambedkar through John Dewey and liberal constitutionalism. They disagreed fundamentally about caste, about the village, about the authority of Hindu scripture and about the means of achieving justice, and their disagreement remains one of the central debates of Indian public life. This chapter presents each in turn and then compares them. To treat Ambedkar merely as a footnote to Gandhi, as many older accounts did, is to repeat the exclusion he spent his life fighting.

docs.title: 12.2.1 Life
docs.text: Gandhi was born in Porbandar, in Kathiawar, into a family of Vaiṣṇava Baniyas in a region where Jain influence was strong. He studied law in London (1888–91), where he read the Bhagavadgītā for the first time, in Edwin Arnold’s English version, with Theosophist friends, and encountered vegetarian and Christian circles. In South Africa (1893–1914), where he went as a lawyer, his experience of racial discrimination turned him into a political organiser. There he founded the Natal Indian Congress (1894), the Phoenix Settlement (1904) and Tolstoy Farm (1910), and developed the method he called satyāgraha in campaigns against discriminatory laws from 1906 onwards. Returning to India in 1915, he led local campaigns in Champaran (1917) and Kheda (1918), the nationwide Non-Cooperation Movement (1920–22), the Salt March (1930) and the Quit India Movement (1942). He opposed the partition of India, spent the months around independence trying to stop communal violence in Bengal and Delhi, and was assassinated on 30 January 1948 (see below) (Brown 1989; Guha 2018).

docs.title: 12.2.2 Sources
docs.text: Gandhi wrote in his autobiography that the Gītā became his “dictionary of daily reference”. He read it, against most traditional commentators, as an allegory: the battle of Kurukṣetra was the struggle within the human heart, and the teaching of action without attachment to its fruits (anāsakti) was its essence. The Jain jeweller and poet Raychandbhai (Śrīmad Rājacandra), with whom he corresponded from South Africa, was, he wrote, one of the three modern people who had most influenced him. The other two were Tolstoy, whose The Kingdom of God Is Within You (1894) confirmed him in the conviction that evil must not be resisted by force, and John Ruskin, whose Unto This Last (1860), read on a train journey in 1904, convinced him that the life of manual labour was the life worth living and that the good of the individual is contained in the good of all. He paraphrased Ruskin in Gujarati under the title Sarvodaya, “the welfare of all”. He also admired Thoreau’s essay on civil disobedience and the Sermon on the Mount (Gandhi 1927).

docs.title: 12.2.3 Hind Swaraj
docs.text: In November 1909, on a voyage from London to South Africa, Gandhi wrote in Gujarati, in about ten days, the short dialogue Hind Swaraj (“Indian Home Rule”). Its argument is that the enemy is not the British but “modern civilisation” — the civilisation of railways, lawyers, doctors and machinery, which multiplies wants and makes people slaves of their bodies — and that true self-rule (svarāj) is the rule of oneself, achieved by “soul-force” rather than “brute force”. Gandhi later moderated some of its positions, but never repudiated it. Anthony Parel’s edition is the standard English text (Gandhi 1997). The book’s critique of industrial civilisation has been admired by environmentalists and critics of modernity; it has also been criticised as romanticising a village life that was, for many Indians, a life of poverty and caste oppression — a criticism Ambedkar made with particular force.

docs.title: 12.2.4 Satyāgraha
docs.text:
Satyāgraha, “holding firmly to truth”, was Gandhi’s name for a method of resistance that was neither violent nor merely “passive”. Its principles can be summarised as follows. No one possesses the whole truth, so no one may impose his view on another by violence; the resister must therefore accept suffering rather than inflict it. The aim is not to defeat or humiliate the opponent but to convert him, by appealing to his conscience and by making the injustice visible. The means must be as pure as the end, since “the means may be likened to a seed, the end to a tree”. And the satyāgrahī must be disciplined — truthful, fearless, non-possessive and, in Gandhi’s view, celibate. Fasting was the extreme form of self-suffering, used to move opponents and, more often, followers (Parekh 1989).

Gandhi’s ashrams were governed by a set of vows that expressed this discipline: truth, non-violence, chastity, control of the palate, non-stealing, non-possession, bread labour, fearlessness, equal respect for all religions, use of local goods (svadeśī) and the removal of untouchability.

docs.title: 12.2.5 The constructive programme
docs.text: For Gandhi, resistance to injustice had to be accompanied by the reconstruction of society. His Constructive Programme (1941) listed its items: communal unity, removal of untouchability, prohibition of alcohol, hand-spun cloth (khādī) and village industries, village sanitation, “basic education” through productive work (nayī tālīm), adult education, the uplift of women, education in health, provincial languages and a national language, economic equality, and work among peasants, labourers, tribal people (ādivāsī), lepers and students (Gandhi 1941). His ideal political order was a federation of self-governing village republics. In 1946 he described it as “not a pyramid with the apex sustained by the bottom” but “an oceanic circle whose centre will be the individual”, ever ready to sacrifice for the village, the village for the circle of villages, and so on outwards. On property he proposed “trusteeship”: the rich should regard their wealth as held in trust for the community. A saying widely attributed to him, that the earth provides enough for everyone’s need but not for everyone’s greed, has become a slogan of the environmental movement.

docs.title: 12.2.6 Religion and the communities
docs.text: Gandhi described himself as a Sanātanī Hindu, but his Hinduism was idiosyncratic: he rejected the authority of any text that conflicted with reason and morality, and he held that all the great religions were true but imperfect. His prayer meetings included readings from the Gītā, the Qurʾān, the Bible and other scriptures. He made Hindu–Muslim unity central to his politics, supporting the Khilafat agitation of Indian Muslims in 1919–22 and spending the last months of his life trying to quell communal violence, with fasts in Calcutta in 1947 and Delhi in January 1948. His inclusive Hinduism was rejected both by Muslim separatists, who saw it as a Hindu claim to speak for all, and by Hindu nationalists, who saw it as a betrayal.

docs.title: 12.2.7 Conversion
docs.text: Gandhi’s pluralism had a firm limit: he opposed religious conversion. Since all religions were, in his view, true but imperfect, there was no reason to change one’s religion, and he regarded the work of Christian missionaries among the poor and the untouchables as an exploitation of their misery. He told missionaries that they should serve without seeking converts, and he resisted Ambedkar’s threat to lead the untouchables out of Hinduism. Indian Christians and Muslims pointed out that this position, however sincerely held, left them in an uncomfortable place: their faiths were accepted as true, but their freedom to share them was not. The Constitution guarantees the right to “profess, practise and propagate” religion (Article 25), and the question of conversion has remained politically contested, with several states passing laws to regulate it.

docs.title: 12.2.8 Gandhi on caste
docs.text: Gandhi’s views on caste changed over his life. In the early 1920s he defended varṇāśrama as a natural division of hereditary occupations, compatible with equality of status, while condemning untouchability as a sin. He called untouchables harijan, “people of God”, a name many Dalits came to reject as patronising. He campaigned for temple entry and founded the Harijan Sevak Sangh (1932) and the weekly Harijan (1933). In his last years he went further, approving of inter-caste marriages and saying he would attend only weddings between “Harijans” and caste Hindus. But he never accepted that untouchability required the destruction of Hinduism’s scriptural authority, and he opposed the political separation of the Depressed Classes from the Hindu community. On these points he clashed with Ambedkar.

docs.title: 12.2.9 Temple entry
docs.text: The campaign for the entry of untouchables into Hindu temples, and for their use of the roads around them, shows both the reach and the limits of Gandhian methods. At Vaikom in the princely state of Travancore, in 1924–25, a satyagraha was organised to open the roads near the temple to the lower castes, who were forbidden to use them. Gandhi lent his support, visited Vaikom and negotiated a compromise by which some roads were opened; the Tamil leader E. V. Ramasamy (Periyar), then still in the Congress, took part and was imprisoned. A later satyagraha at Guruvayur (1931–32) was led by K. Kelappan. In 1936 the Maharaja of Travancore issued a proclamation opening the state’s temples to all Hindus, and other states and provinces followed. Supporters of the movement saw it as proof that caste Hindus could be persuaded to change; Ambedkar, who had led the Kalaram campaign at Nashik, concluded by the mid-1930s that temple entry was a secondary goal and that the untouchables needed political power, education and economic independence more than access to the temples of a religion that degraded them.

docs.title: 12.2.10 Women in the movement
docs.text: Gandhi’s campaigns drew women into public life on an unprecedented scale. Women picketed liquor shops and foreign-cloth shops, joined the Salt Satyagraha of 1930 — the poet Sarojini Naidu led the raid on the Dharasana salt works after Gandhi’s arrest — and went to jail in thousands. Gandhi regarded women as especially suited to non-violent resistance, because of their capacity for suffering and self-sacrifice. His views were nevertheless conservative in other respects: he idealised the self-sacrificing wife of the epics, opposed artificial contraception and placed great emphasis on celibacy. Feminist historians have noted both the opportunities his movement opened and the limits of the roles it offered.

docs.title: 12.2.11 Gandhian economics
docs.text: Gandhi’s economic ideas, scattered through his journalism, were systematised by his associate J. C. Kumarappa (1892–1960), an economist trained at Syracuse and Columbia, who argued in Economy of Permanence (1945) for a decentralised economy of self-sufficient villages, based on handicrafts and local resources, in harmony with the cycles of nature. Gandhi’s doctrine of “trusteeship” held that the owners of wealth should regard themselves as trustees holding it for the benefit of society, and should be persuaded rather than compelled to do so. Independent India, under Nehru, chose state-led industrialisation instead, though it gave a place to khadi and village industries through a statutory commission. The Gandhian critique of industrial civilisation found a later echo in the West: the economist E. F. Schumacher, who had worked as an adviser in Burma and visited India, advocated “intermediate technology” and a “Buddhist economics” of sufficiency in Small Is Beautiful (1973), citing Gandhi among his inspirations (Schumacher 1973). Ambedkar, as noted below, took the opposite view, seeing industrialisation as the way to free Dalits from the village economy. The disagreement remains alive in Indian debates about development and the environment (Chapter 21).

docs.title: 12.2.12 Partition and the last years
docs.text: The last years of Gandhi’s life were overshadowed by the communal violence that accompanied the end of British rule. After the riots in Calcutta in August 1946 and the attacks on Hindus in Noakhali in eastern Bengal later that year, Gandhi spent four months walking from village to village in Noakhali, attempting to restore confidence between Hindus and Muslims. He opposed partition to the end but did not resist the decision of the Congress leaders to accept it. On 15 August 1947, while Delhi celebrated independence, he was in Calcutta, where his presence and his fast in early September were credited with ending the killing in the city. In January 1948 he fasted again in Delhi for communal peace and the safety of Muslims in the capital; during the fast the government of India agreed to pay Pakistan its withheld share of the cash balances of undivided India, a decision for which his opponents blamed him. On 30 January 1948 he was shot dead at a prayer meeting in Delhi by Nathuram Godse (Chapter 9), who held him responsible for the concessions to Muslims and to Pakistan. Gandhi’s death was the culmination of a life spent insisting that Hindus and Muslims, and all the communities of India, belonged to a single nation, a conviction that his assassin rejected.

docs.title: 12.3.1 Life
docs.text: Bhimrao Ramji Ambedkar was born in 1891 at Mhow, in central India, into a family of the Mahar caste, regarded as untouchable in Maharashtra; his father was a subedar in the army. As a schoolboy he experienced the humiliations of untouchability — being made to sit apart, denied water from the common tap. With scholarships from the Maharaja of Baroda he studied at Columbia University in New York, where he was taught by the philosopher John Dewey and the economist E. R. A. Seligman, and at the London School of Economics; he became a barrister at Gray’s Inn. Back in India he founded journals and organisations, led the Mahad satyagraha of 1927 for the right of untouchables to draw water from a public tank, publicly burned the Manusmṛti in the same year, and led a campaign for entry to the Kalaram temple at Nashik (1930). He represented the Depressed Classes at the Round Table Conferences in London (1930–32), founded the Independent Labour Party (1936) and later the Scheduled Castes Federation, and served as Labour Member of the Viceroy’s Executive Council (1942–46). In independent India he was the first Law Minister and chairman of the drafting committee of the Constitution. He resigned from the cabinet in 1951 when the Hindu Code Bill, which would have given Hindu women rights of inheritance and divorce, was shelved. On 14 October 1956 at Nagpur he converted to Buddhism together with several hundred thousand followers, and he died on 6 December 1956 (Zelliot 1992; Jaffrelot 2005).

docs.title: 12.3.2 Ambedkar and Dewey
docs.text: Ambedkar’s thought was itself a synthesis, though not of the kind usually celebrated. At Columbia he studied with John Dewey, the leading American philosopher of pragmatism and democracy, and he acknowledged his debt to Dewey throughout his life. In Annihilation of Caste he quoted Dewey on the need for a society to select and preserve what is good in its past and discard what is harmful, and he defined democracy, in terms close to Dewey’s, as not merely a form of government but primarily a mode of associated living, of conjoint communicated experience. For Ambedkar, as for Dewey, the test of a social order was whether it permitted free communication and shared interests among all its members; caste failed the test because it divided society into isolated, graded groups. Scott Stroud has traced in detail how Ambedkar adapted Dewey’s pragmatism (Stroud 2023), and other scholars how he combined this pragmatist conception of democracy with his reading of the Buddha, and with the constitutional traditions of Britain and the United States, to produce a political philosophy grounded in Indian experience but addressed to universal questions (Jaffrelot 2005). His example shows that a synthesis of Indian and Western thought need not take the form of Neo-Vedānta; it could equally take the form of a democratic and egalitarian critique of tradition.

docs.title: 12.3.3 Caste and the Hindu scriptures
docs.text: Ambedkar’s analysis of caste combined social science with textual criticism. In a paper written at Columbia in 1916, “Castes in India”, he argued that caste is fundamentally a system of endogamy, maintained by the control of women’s marriage. In Annihilation of Caste (1936), written as the presidential address for a conference of the Jat-Pat-Todak Mandal of Lahore — which cancelled the conference when it saw the text — he argued that caste was not merely a division of labour but a division of labourers, graded one above another; that it destroyed public spirit and made a Hindu society impossible; and that because it was sanctioned by the śāstras, it could not be abolished without destroying the authority of the śāstras themselves. “Caste is a notion; it is a state of the mind,” he wrote, and the mind could be changed only if people ceased to believe in the sanctity of the texts that taught it (Ambedkar 1936). In Who Were the Shudras? (1946) and The Untouchables (1948) he offered historical theories of the origin of the lowest classes, which later historians have debated but which opened new questions (Ambedkar 1946).

docs.title: 12.3.4 The village
docs.text: In the Constituent Assembly, on 4 November 1948, Ambedkar replied to those who wished to make the village the basic unit of the Constitution: “What is the village but a sink of localism, a den of ignorance, narrow-mindedness and communalism?” He was glad that the draft Constitution had discarded the village and adopted the individual as its unit. The remark was directed at Gandhian ideals, and it expressed the experience of untouchables for whom the village was the place where caste was most strictly enforced.

docs.title: 12.3.5 Constitutional democracy
docs.text: Ambedkar’s political philosophy rested on the three principles of liberty, equality and fraternity, which he said he had derived not from the French Revolution but from the teaching of the Buddha. He argued that political democracy could not last unless it rested on social democracy, a way of life that recognised these principles, and he warned in his final speech to the Constituent Assembly, quoted at the head of this chapter, that India was entering a life of contradictions in which political equality coexisted with social and economic inequality. He insisted on “constitutional morality” — respect for constitutional forms and the renunciation of unconstitutional methods once constitutional ones were available — and warned against hero-worship in politics. The Constitution abolished untouchability (Article 17), prohibited discrimination and provided for reserved seats in legislatures and positions in public employment for the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Jaffrelot 2005).

docs.title: 12.3.6 Religion, the state and Pakistan
docs.text: Ambedkar wrote on many subjects besides caste. In Thoughts on Pakistan (1940), later revised as Pakistan or the Partition of India (1945), he analysed the demand of the Muslim League with detachment, setting out the arguments of both sides; he concluded that if Muslims as a community were determined to have a separate state, it would be better to concede it than to keep an unwilling community within a single state, and he discussed the exchange of populations that this might require. The book was read by leaders of both the Congress and the League. In the Constituent Assembly he argued for a secular state, in the sense that the state should not establish or favour any religion, while defending the power of the state to reform religious practices that violated equality. His posthumously published Riddles in Hinduism, a sharply critical examination of Hindu doctrines and myths, provoked protests in Maharashtra when it was issued by the state government in 1987 as part of his collected works; the episode shows that Ambedkar remains a living and contested voice, not merely a revered founder.

docs.title: 12.3.7 Economist and planner
docs.text: Ambedkar’s training was in economics as much as in law. His Columbia doctoral dissertation, later published as The Evolution of Provincial Finance in British India (1925), and his London thesis, The Problem of the Rupee (1923), dealt with public finance and currency. He wrote on the problems of small agricultural holdings and argued that the remedy for rural poverty lay in industrialisation, which would draw surplus labour from the land and break the economic dependence of untouchables on caste Hindu landowners. In a memorandum submitted to the Constituent Assembly in 1947, States and Minorities, he proposed that key industries and agricultural land be owned by the state, a form of state socialism to be written into the Constitution itself. The Assembly did not adopt the proposal, but the memorandum shows that his vision of justice extended from social equality to economic organisation.

docs.title: 12.3.8 Buddhism
docs.text: In 1935, at Yeola, Ambedkar announced that although he had been born a Hindu he would not die one. He considered Sikhism, Islam and Christianity before choosing Buddhism, which he presented as a rational, egalitarian and Indian religion. His Buddhism, set out in The Buddha and His Dhamma (published posthumously in 1957), reinterpreted the tradition: it emphasised social liberation, treated the four noble truths and the doctrines of karma and rebirth in ways that differed from canonical teaching, and rejected the idea of a soul that transmigrates (Ambedkar 1957). At the conversion ceremony he administered twenty-two vows, which included explicit rejections of belief in Hindu gods, in the avatāras and in the idea that the Buddha was an incarnation of Viṣṇu. Ambedkarite Buddhism, often called Navayāna, is now the largest Buddhist community in India (Chapter 18) (Omvedt 2003).

docs.title: 12.3.9 The Buddha or Karl Marx
docs.text: One of Ambedkar’s last essays, “Buddha or Karl Marx”, written shortly before his death and published posthumously, compared the two teachers whom he regarded as the most important for the modern world. He agreed with Marx that the purpose of philosophy is to reconstruct the world rather than to explain it, that private property and exploitation produce suffering, and that society must be reorganised to abolish them. He found these aims anticipated in the Buddha’s teaching on suffering and in the communal life of the Buddhist monastic order, which held no private property. But he rejected the Marxist means — violence and the dictatorship of the proletariat — on the ground that a society transformed by force must be held together by force, and he argued that the Buddha’s method of persuasion, moral training and voluntary change would produce a more lasting equality and would preserve liberty. The essay shows Ambedkar choosing Buddhism, in part, as an alternative to communism, at a time when many educated Dalits were attracted to the Left; and it shows that his religious choice was also a political philosophy.

docs.title: 12.4 Religion in the Constituent Assembly
docs.text:
The Constituent Assembly that sat from December 1946 to January 1950 had to decide how the new state would treat the religions of its citizens, and its debates show the ideas of this chapter at work. Three issues were especially contested.

Propagation.

Article 25 guarantees to all persons freedom of conscience and the right freely to “profess, practise and propagate” religion. Some members wished to omit the right to propagate, fearing missionary conversion; Christian members and others insisted on it as part of religious freedom; the word was retained. The question of conversion has nonetheless remained contentious, and several states have since passed laws regulating conversion by “force, fraud or inducement”.

Reform and personal law.

The Constitution empowers the state to regulate secular activities associated with religion, to provide for social welfare and reform, and to throw open Hindu religious institutions of a public character to all classes of Hindus. It directs the state to endeavour to secure a uniform civil code, but leaves personal laws in place. Ambedkar, as Law Minister, sought to reform Hindu personal law through the Hindu Code Bill; Nehru’s government later enacted its main provisions in separate acts in 1955–56, while Muslim, Christian and Parsi personal laws were left to their communities. The arrangement reflected both the reforming ambitions of the framers and their caution in dealing with minorities.

Cow protection.

Some members pressed for a ban on cow slaughter as a fundamental right. The compromise was a Directive Principle (Article 48) asking the state to organise agriculture and animal husbandry on modern scientific lines and to take steps for preserving breeds and prohibiting the slaughter of cows and calves and other milch and draught cattle. The wording placed the matter on economic rather than religious grounds, while leaving it to the states. The history of non-violence and diet traced in Chapter 7 thus entered the Constitution in a carefully secular form.

The Assembly’s work shows that Indian secularism, as its framers designed it, was not a strict separation of religion and state on the American or French model but a principled distance: the state would protect all religions, reform some of their practices in the name of equality, and favour none. Whether that balance has held is a matter of continuing debate.

docs.title: 12.5.1 The Poona Pact
docs.text: The sharpest confrontation came in 1932. The British Communal Award granted the Depressed Classes separate electorates, as Ambedkar had demanded. Gandhi, then in Yeravda jail, announced a fast unto death against the separation of the untouchables from the Hindu electorate. Under intense pressure, with Gandhi’s life at stake, Ambedkar agreed to the Poona Pact (24 September 1932), which abandoned separate electorates in favour of a larger number of seats reserved for the Depressed Classes within joint electorates. Gandhi regarded the pact as saving the unity of Hindu society; Ambedkar regarded it as having been extracted by coercion, and later wrote in What Congress and Gandhi Have Done to the Untouchables (1945) that the fast had been a form of political blackmail.

docs.title: 12.5.2 Annihilation of Caste and Gandhi’s reply
docs.text: When Annihilation of Caste was published, Gandhi replied in Harijan (July 1936). He argued that the śāstras should be judged by the conduct of the saints rather than by texts of doubtful authority, that caste had nothing to do with religion, and that varṇa, rightly understood as a law of hereditary vocation without superiority, was not the same as caste. Ambedkar’s rejoinder, appended to later editions, asked how a Hindu could reject the scriptures while claiming to be a Hindu, and why the saints, however personally free of caste feeling, had never attacked the system (Ambedkar 1936).

docs.title: 12.5.3 Comparison
docs.text:
Table 12.1 summarises the main points of difference.

Table 12.1. Gandhi and Ambedkar compared (simplified) Question Gandhi Ambedkar Untouchability a sin to be removed by a change of heart among caste Hindus a structure of domination to be abolished by law, organisation and the rejection of its scriptural basis Varṇa defensible as hereditary vocation without hierarchy (in his earlier and middle writings) inseparable from caste; to be rejected Scripture to be judged by reason and the conduct of the saints its authority must be destroyed, since it sanctions caste Political representation joint electorates to preserve Hindu unity separate representation for the Depressed Classes; accepted reserved seats under pressure Village the basis of a just, non-violent society “a sink of localism” and the stronghold of caste Modern state suspicious of centralised power and industry constitutional democracy, rule of law, state action for social justice Religion reformed Hinduism; equal respect for all religions Buddhism as a rational and egalitarian dhamma Means non-violent resistance, fasting, constructive work constitutional methods, education, organisation (“educate, agitate, organise”)

Christophe Jaffrelot and Eleanor Zelliot, among others, have shown that the two men shared more than their quarrel suggests: both condemned untouchability, both sought a moral basis for politics, both drew on Indian religious traditions to articulate it (Jaffrelot 2005; Zelliot 1992). But they spoke from different places. Gandhi spoke as a caste Hindu asking his own community to repent; Ambedkar spoke as an untouchable demanding rights. The comparison is a lesson in why the identity of the speaker matters in any synthesis.

docs.title: 12.6 After Gandhi: Nehru, Vinoba, Lohia and Jayaprakash Narayan
docs.text:
The debate between Gandhi and Ambedkar was overlapped by a third vision, that of Jawaharlal Nehru. Nehru admired Gandhi and followed him politically, but he did not share his suspicion of industry, the modern state or science. As Prime Minister he pursued planned industrialisation, built dams that he called “the temples of modern India”, and founded institutes of science and technology. On this question he was closer to Ambedkar than to Gandhi, though Ambedkar left Nehru’s cabinet in 1951 over the delay in passing the Hindu Code Bill and over policy towards the Scheduled Castes. Gandhi’s economics survived in the village and cottage industries programmes and in later movements for decentralised and sustainable development.

His most direct heir was Vinoba Bhave (1895–1982), whose “land gift” (bhūdān) campaign began in Telangana in 1951 and, over the following years, persuaded landowners across India to give land to the landless, later extending to the gift of whole villages (grāmdān). Vinoba presented the campaign as a non-violent alternative to the communist uprisings of the same region and period; much of the land given proved poor or was never distributed, but the movement was the largest attempt to apply Gandhi’s “trusteeship”. His description of the Emergency of 1975–77 as a “time of discipline” estranged many of his followers.

Two socialists gave Gandhian ideas a different political form. Ram Manohar Lohia (1910–1967), who studied in Berlin and was a founder of the Congress Socialist Party in 1934, argued in Marx, Gandhi and Socialism (1963) for a socialism equidistant from capitalism and communism, built on small machines, a decentralised “four-pillar” state of village, district, province and centre, and civil disobedience as a permanent right. He made caste central to socialist politics, as few Marxists of his generation did, demanding preferential opportunity for the backward castes, Dalits, Adivasis, women and poor minorities, and he campaigned against the dominance of English in public life. His followers carried these ideas into the politics of the “backward classes” in north India. Jayaprakash Narayan (1902–1979), educated in the United States and a Marxist in his youth, joined Vinoba’s movement in 1954, and in A Plea for Reconstruction of Indian Polity (1959) proposed a “communitarian” democracy built upward from village assemblies, without the competition of parties. In 1974 he led the student movement in Bihar under the slogan of “total revolution” (sampūrṇa krānti); the agitation it inspired was one of the occasions of the Emergency, and its defeat of the Congress in 1977 restored parliamentary democracy. Thomas Pantham and Kenneth Deutsch’s collection places these thinkers within the wider history of modern Indian political thought (Pantham and Deutsch 1986).

The relation between these visions — village and city, tradition and modern science, moral transformation and state action — remains one of the central arguments of Indian public life. The Hindu nationalist philosophy of Deendayal Upadhyaya, which drew on some of the same Gandhian themes of decentralisation and self-reliance for different ends, is discussed in Chapter 9.

docs.title: 12.7.1 Gandhi in the world
docs.text:
Gandhi’s methods were adopted, adapted and argued about across the world: by Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan on the North-West Frontier and by Martin Luther King Jr. from the Montgomery bus boycott (1955–56) onwards (Chapter 7), and by many others. In South Africa the African National Congress used non-violent campaigns in the 1950s before turning to armed struggle in 1961; Nelson Mandela later described non-violence as a tactic rather than a principle for his movement. The American scholar Gene Sharp systematised the techniques of non-violent action, many drawn from Gandhi’s campaigns (Sharp 1973), and Erica Chenoweth and Maria Stephan, studying more than three hundred resistance campaigns between 1900 and 2006, found that non-violent campaigns had succeeded about twice as often as violent ones (Chenoweth and Stephan 2011). Gandhi’s critique of industrial civilisation influenced E. F. Schumacher’s Small Is Beautiful (1973) and the environmental movement, including the Chipko movement in India (Chapter 21).

Gandhi has also been reinterpreted and criticised. Faisal Devji has read his thought as an engagement with violence rather than simply a rejection of it, and Shruti Kapila has placed him among Indian political thinkers who made the relation between fraternity and violence the central problem of the new nation (Devji 2012; Kapila 2021). Critics have pointed to his early statements about black Africans in South Africa, which Ashwin Desai and Goolam Vahed have documented (Desai and Vahed 2015); for his treatment of the women around him and his experiments in celibacy; for his opposition to modern technology; and, by Ambedkar and the Dalit movement, for his defence of varṇa. An honest account must include these criticisms alongside the admiration.

docs.title: 12.7.2 Ambedkar in India and beyond
docs.text:
Ambedkar’s reputation grew enormously after his death. The Dalit Panthers of Maharashtra (1972), inspired partly by the Black Panthers, took his name as their banner; Dalit literature, beginning in Marathi with writers such as Namdeo Dhasal and spreading to other languages, has made his thought the centre of a new literary tradition (Volume 8); and the political mobilisation of the Scheduled Castes, notably through the Bahujan Samaj Party founded by Kanshi Ram in 1984, has transformed Indian elections. His image, usually in a blue suit holding a copy of the Constitution, stands in villages across India. Internationally, he is increasingly read as a theorist of democracy and social justice, and his critique of caste has informed movements against discrimination by descent among South Asian diaspora communities.

Gail Omvedt and others have placed Ambedkar at the culmination of a long line of Indian critics of Brahmanical tradition that begins with the Buddha (Omvedt 2003). Whether or not one accepts that reading of history, a volume concerned with synthesis must take his challenge seriously: that a tradition which claims to see the divine in all beings must be judged by how it has treated the least of them.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text:
• Gandhi (1997): Hind Swaraj with related writings and a valuable introduction.

  • Parekh (1989) and Brown (1989): Gandhi’s political philosophy and life.

  • Ambedkar (1936): Annihilation of Caste, with Gandhi’s reply and Ambedkar’s rejoinder in later editions.

  • Zelliot (1992) and Jaffrelot (2005): Ambedkar and the Dalit movement.

  • Omvedt (2003): Buddhism and anti-caste thought in India.

  • Chenoweth and Stephan (2011): the effectiveness of non-violent resistance.

docs.title: Chapter 13: Tagore and His Contemporaries: Poets, Nationalists and Independent Thinkers
docs.text: Where the mind is without fear and the head is held high; Where knowledge is free; Where the world has not been broken up into fragments by narrow domestic walls … — Rabindranath Tagore, Gitanjali (1912), no. 35

docs.title: 13.1 Introduction
docs.text: The thinkers discussed in the previous three chapters were religious teachers and political leaders who reinterpreted the Vedāntic and Gandhian inheritance. Modern India also produced poets, scholars, novelists and independent teachers who responded to the encounter with the West in other ways, and some who rejected the religious framing of the question altogether. This chapter begins with Rabindranath Tagore, whose universalism was the most sustained alternative to nationalism in colonial India, and sets beside him three writers who shaped how modern Indians imagined their past: the sceptical scholar Vidyāsāgar, the novelist Bankimchandra and Jawaharlal Nehru. It then turns to four figures who stood outside every school: Jiddu Krishnamurti, Ramana Maharshi, the psychoanalyst Girindrasekhar Bose and the radical humanist M. N. Roy. The thinkers who spoke for those excluded from the high tradition — anti-caste intellectuals, women writers and Adivasi leaders — are the subject of Chapter 14; the academic philosophers of Chapter 15; and the Muslim thinkers of the same years, among them Sayyid Ahmad Khan, Abul Kalam Azad and Muhammad Iqbal, of Chapter 17. Nalini Bhushan and Jay Garfield’s anthology and study of Indian philosophy in English in the colonial period are indispensable guides (Bhushan and Garfield 2011; Bhushan and Garfield 2017).

docs.title: 13.2.1 Life and work
docs.text: Rabindranath Tagore (1861–1941) was born in Calcutta into the wealthy and cultivated family of Debendranath Tagore, the leader of the Brahmo Samaj (Chapter 9). He wrote poems, songs, novels, short stories, plays and essays in Bengali, composed more than two thousand songs which form the tradition of Rabīndrasaṅgīt, and in his late sixties began to paint. The English Gitanjali (1912), a selection of 103 prose poems translated by himself from several Bengali collections and introduced by W. B. Yeats, won him the Nobel Prize for Literature in 1913, the first awarded to an Asian (Tagore 1913). He was knighted in 1915 and renounced the knighthood in 1919 in protest at the massacre at Jallianwala Bagh in Amritsar. Two of his songs are the national anthems of India and Bangladesh. Krishna Dutta and Andrew Robinson’s biography gives a balanced account of his life (Dutta and Robinson 1995).

docs.title: 13.2.2 Religion of Man
docs.text: Tagore’s religious thought grew from the Upaniṣadic theism of the Brahmo Samaj, from the Vaiṣṇava poetry of Bengal and from the songs of the Bāuls, wandering singers who sought the divine “man of the heart” (maner mānuṣ) within the human body and rejected caste and scripture. His poems speak of a “lord of life” (jīvandevatā), an intimate divine presence encountered in nature, love and creative work rather than in temple or doctrine. In his Hibbert Lectures at Oxford, published as The Religion of Man (1931), he argued that the divine is realised in humanity’s capacity for creative surplus, for love and for the ideal, and devoted a chapter to the Bāul singers (Tagore 1931). He drew on Indian sources, but his humanism also owed much to European Romanticism and to his conversations with Western friends.

docs.title: 13.2.3 Critique of nationalism
docs.text: Tagore supported Indian freedom, wrote patriotic songs during the agitation against the partition of Bengal in 1905, and then withdrew from the movement when it turned to violence and to the boycott of everything foreign. His novel Ghare Baire (The Home and the World, 1916) dramatises the corruption of a household by the passions of nationalist politics. In lectures delivered in Japan and America in 1916–17 and published as Nationalism (1917), he distinguished the life of a people from “the Nation” as an organisation of power, which he regarded as the great menace of the modern age (Tagore 1917). The Japanese audiences who had welcomed him as an Asian sage were not pleased to hear their own imperial nationalism criticised.
