Ashis Nandy has argued that Tagore’s refusal of nationalism was a deliberate defence of a civilisational, plural self against the homogenising state, and that it has proved more prophetic than its contemporaries believed (Nandy 1994).

docs.title: 13.2.4 Tagore and Gandhi
docs.text: Tagore and Gandhi admired each other, and their disagreements were conducted in public with remarkable courtesy. During the Non-Cooperation Movement Tagore published “The Call of Truth” (1921), questioning the burning of foreign cloth, the boycott of government schools and the demand that everyone spin. Gandhi replied in “The Great Sentinel”, defending non-cooperation as a discipline of self-purification. In “The Cult of the Charka” (1925) Tagore returned to the charge, arguing that mechanical spinning could not be the path to freedom of mind. In 1934, when Gandhi described the Bihar earthquake as a divine chastisement for the sin of untouchability, Tagore protested that such a view was unscientific and unworthy, since natural disasters do not discriminate between the guilty and the innocent. Sabyasachi Bhattacharya’s edition of their letters and debates shows two thinkers who shared the goal of an India free in spirit and differed about almost everything else (Bhattacharya 1997). Amartya Sen has called Tagore a defender of reason and freedom who resisted both colonial domination and the cultural nationalism that answered it (Sen 2005).

docs.title: 13.2.5 Santiniketan and Visva-Bharati
docs.text: In 1901 Tagore founded a school at Santiniketan, the retreat his father had established in rural Bengal, where classes were held outdoors, the arts were central and examinations were not. In 1921 he founded Visva-Bharati, a university intended as a meeting-place of the cultures of the world, taking as its motto a line from the Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā of the White Yajurveda (32.8): yatra viśvaṃ bhavaty ekanīḍam, “where the whole world becomes one nest”. Scholars from Europe, China, Japan and elsewhere taught there; the Englishman Leonard Elmhirst helped him found the institute of rural reconstruction at Sriniketan, and later founded Dartington Hall in England on principles learned from him. The ideal was a synthesis in which each culture contributes its own gifts, not one in which all are dissolved into one. Tagore also travelled widely — to Japan, China, Southeast Asia, Latin America, the Soviet Union and Iran — and his conversation with Albert Einstein near Berlin in 1930, on whether truth exists independently of the human mind, was published and remains much discussed. His last public essay, “Crisis in Civilisation” (1941), written as the world war raged, condemned the betrayal of Western civilisation’s ideals in imperialism while affirming his faith in humanity.

docs.title: 13.3 Vidyāsāgar: Reform Without Metaphysics
docs.text: Īśvaracandra Vidyāsāgar (1820–1891), principal of the Sanskrit College of Calcutta, is remembered for his campaign for widow remarriage (Chapter 5), for his work for the education of girls and for his Bengali primer, Varṇaparicay (1855), from which generations of Bengali children learned to read. He is less often remembered as a sceptic in philosophy. A master of Sanskrit learning, he nevertheless argued, in a letter of 1853 to the colonial Council of Education, that Vedānta and Sāṃkhya were false systems of philosophy which had to be taught at the Sanskrit College for the sake of scholarship, and that students should be given Western philosophy, such as Mill’s logic, to counteract their influence. Unlike Rammohun and the Brahmos, he made no attempt to found a reformed religion; unlike Vivekananda, he did not claim that Vedānta was the summit of human thought. He grounded his reforms in compassion, in common sense and, where it served his purpose, in the interpretation of the śāstras. Vidyāsāgar shows that nineteenth-century Indian reform included a secular and sceptical strand, often overshadowed in later accounts by the religious reformers, and that a scholar could know the tradition intimately while rejecting much of it.

docs.title: 13.4 Bankimchandra and Nehru: Two Nationalist Readings of the Past
docs.text:
Two other writers shaped the way modern Indians imagined their civilisation, and they make a useful contrast with Tagore. The Bengali novelist Bankimchandra Chattopadhyay (1838–1894) wrote the novel Ānandamaṭh (1882), which contains the hymn “Vande Mātaram” (“I bow to thee, Mother”) addressed to the motherland as goddess; the song became the anthem of the nationalist movement, and the novel’s depiction of Hindu ascetics fighting Muslim rulers has made it a contested text. In Kṛṣṇacaritra (1886) Bankim applied the methods of historical criticism to the Kṛṣṇa legends, rejecting the miraculous and the erotic as later accretions and presenting Kṛṣṇa as an ideal man and statesman. Partha Chatterjee has analysed how Bankim’s rationalised Hinduism combined a critique of Western power with an acceptance of Western forms of knowledge (Chatterjee 1986).

Jawaharlal Nehru (1889–1964), who became India’s first Prime Minister, wrote The Discovery of India (1946) while in prison during the Second World War. A self-described agnostic educated at Harrow and Cambridge, he presented India as a civilisation that had absorbed many peoples and cultures — Vedic, Buddhist, Islamic, European — in successive layers, comparing it to an ancient palimpsest, and found in this capacity for synthesis the basis of a composite national identity in which no religious community had priority (Nehru 1946). Nehru’s “unity in diversity” became an official ideal of independent India, embodied in the secular Constitution. It was an inclusivism of a different kind from Vivekananda’s: civilisational rather than Vedāntic, and aimed at a modern, scientific state. Hindu nationalists criticised it for neglecting the Hindu majority, and Muslim separatists for disguising Hindu dominance; historians have praised its breadth and noted its romanticism.

docs.title: 13.5 Jiddu Krishnamurti
docs.text: Jiddu Krishnamurti (1895–1986) occupies a unique place among modern Indian thinkers. Born in Andhra Pradesh, he was taken up as a boy by the leaders of the Theosophical Society, who proclaimed him the vehicle of a coming “World Teacher” and founded an organisation, the Order of the Star in the East, to prepare for his mission. In 1929 he dissolved the Order, declaring that “truth is a pathless land” which cannot be approached by any religion, sect or organisation, and spent the rest of his life travelling and speaking in India, Europe and America without disciples or doctrines. He taught that psychological freedom comes from “choiceless awareness” of the workings of one’s own mind, and that all authority in spiritual matters — of gurus, scriptures and traditions — is an obstacle. His dialogues with the physicist David Bohm are mentioned in Chapter 19, and the schools he founded in India and England pursued his ideal of education free from fear and competition. Krishnamurti rejected the labels “Hindu” and “Indian philosopher”, and in his teaching the modern Indian response to tradition took the form of a radical refusal of all tradition.

docs.title: 13.6 Ramana Maharshi
docs.text: Venkataraman Iyer (1879–1950), known as Ramana Maharshi, left his home in Madurai at the age of sixteen after an overwhelming experience of the deathless self, and lived for the rest of his life at the sacred hill of Arunachala at Tiruvannamalai in Tamil Nadu. He wrote little, mostly short verse works in Tamil, and taught chiefly through silence and through answers to visitors’ questions. His central teaching was the practice of self-enquiry (ātma-vicāra): to ask persistently “Who am I?” and to trace the sense of “I” back to its source, where, he taught, the individual ego disappears and the self alone remains. His teaching is close to Advaita, but it gives little place to the study of scripture that Śaṅkara regarded as essential, and it made direct inquiry available to anyone, without distinction of caste, sex or learning. Ramana became known in the West through the British journalist Paul Brunton’s A Search in Secret India (1934), and he was visited by many seekers and writers; Somerset Maugham’s novel The Razor’s Edge (1944) drew on a visit. Ramana illustrates a different modern pattern from that of Vivekananda or Aurobindo: not a synthesis of traditions, nor a programme for society, but a traditional ascetic’s teaching that reached a global audience largely through the interest of others.

docs.title: 13.7 Indian Psychoanalysis
docs.text: The encounter between Indian thought and modern psychology began early. The Calcutta physician Girindrasekhar Bose (1887–1953), who took a doctorate in psychology at the University of Calcutta, founded the Indian Psychoanalytical Society in 1922 and corresponded with Sigmund Freud from 1921 until the 1930s. Bose accepted much of psychoanalysis but proposed his own theory of “opposite wishes”, according to which every wish is accompanied by its repressed opposite, and he argued that the Oedipus complex did not have the central place in Indian patients that Freud gave it in European ones. He also wrote on the Yogasūtra and the Gītā in psychological terms. Freud’s replies were courteous but sceptical. The episode is an early example of the attempt, continued later in the work of Sudhir Kakar, to test a Western theory of the mind against Indian experience and to ask how far its claims are universal (Kakar 1982). Kakar’s studies of Indian childhood, family and religious healing have argued that psychoanalysis can illuminate Indian experience if its culture-bound assumptions are recognised, and that Indian materials can in turn enrich psychoanalytic theory. The exchange shows comparative thinking at its most useful: neither side’s theory is accepted as given, and each is tested against the other’s evidence.

docs.title: 13.8 M. N. Roy and Radical Humanism
docs.text: Not every modern Indian thinker sought to renew religion. Manabendra Nath Roy (1887–1954), born Narendranath Bhattacharya in Bengal, began as a revolutionary nationalist, travelled to Mexico, where he helped to found the Mexican Communist Party in 1919, and became a leading figure in the Communist International, debating with Lenin on the colonial question in 1920. Expelled from the International in 1929, he returned to India, was imprisoned by the British, and gradually broke with Marxism. In the 1940s he developed a philosophy he called Radical or New Humanism, which placed the free individual at the centre of political life, rejected both nationalism and communist dictatorship, and called for a decentralised democracy of people’s committees. He was a severe critic of the idea that India had a special “spiritual” civilisation, which he regarded as an obstacle to the scientific and secular modernisation the country needed, and he wrote on the history of materialism in India and elsewhere. Roy’s influence was small in numbers but significant among Indian rationalists and civil-liberties activists, and it gave secular humanism a place in modern Indian thought.

docs.title: 13.9 Modern Indian Thinkers at a Glance
docs.text:
Table 13.1 brings together some of the modern Indian thinkers discussed in Part II of this volume, with the question each pressed most insistently. The list is far from complete, and each entry simplifies a large body of work; its purpose is to show the range of positions rather than to rank them.

Table 13.1. Some modern Indian thinkers and their central questions Thinker Central concern Rammohun Roy (1772–1833) rational monotheism from the Upaniṣads; reform of social custom Sayyid Ahmad Khan (1817–1898) reconciling Islam with modern science and Western education Jotirao Phule (1827–1890) caste as Brahmin domination; education of Śūdras, Ati-Śūdras and women Iyothee Thass (1845–1914) the untouchables as the original Tamil Buddhists Narayana Guru (1856–1928) one caste, one religion, one God; Advaita from below Pandita Ramabai (1858–1922) the Dharmaśāstra as the source of high-caste women’s subjection Rabindranath Tagore (1861–1941) the “religion of man”; critique of nationalism Vivekananda (1863–1902) Vedānta as a universal religion and a call to service M. K. Gandhi (1869–1948) truth and non-violence as the basis of politics and life Aurobindo (1872–1950) evolution of consciousness; integral yoga K. C. Bhattacharya (1875–1949) philosophy as the study of the subject; “swaraj in ideas” Muhammad Iqbal (1877–1938) reconstructing Islamic thought; the dynamic self E. V. Ramasamy, Periyar (1879–1973) self-respect; rationalism against caste and religion Rokeya Sakhawat Hossain (1880–1932) seclusion as a denial of knowledge to women M. N. Roy (1887–1954) radical humanism; secular modernity S. Radhakrishnan (1888–1975) Hinduism as a religion of experience and tolerance B. R. Ambedkar (1891–1956) annihilation of caste; constitutional democracy; Buddhism J. Krishnamurti (1895–1986) freedom from all spiritual authority Daya Krishna (1924–2007) questioning received pictures of Indian philosophy B. K. Matilal (1935–1991) Indian philosophy as rigorous argument in a world conversation

docs.title: 13.10 Assessment
docs.text: The writers of this chapter did not agree with one another, and their disagreements are their most valuable legacy. Tagore’s religion of man was a universalism without a nation; Bankim’s rationalised Kṛṣṇa and Nehru’s palimpsest were two different nationalisms built from the same past; Vidyāsāgar reformed custom without a metaphysics, Roy rejected the idea of a spiritual India altogether, and Krishnamurti refused every tradition, his own included. Ramana’s self-enquiry and Bose’s psychoanalysis, at opposite ends of the century’s interest in the mind, both made inner experience a field of inquiry rather than of inherited doctrine. None of these answers converges on Vedānta, and a synthesis that admitted only those that did would leave them all out. The voices that challenged the tradition from below, examined in the next chapter, widen the range further.

docs.text:

  • Bayly (2012): modern Indian political and social thought in its liberal and imperial contexts.

docs.title: Chapter 14: Voices from Below: Anti-Caste Thinkers, Women Writers and Adivasi Movements
docs.text: na jaccā vasalo hoti, na jaccā hoti brāhmaṇo kammunā vasalo hoti, kammunā hoti brāhmaṇo Not by birth is one an outcaste, not by birth a Brahmin. By deeds one is an outcaste, by deeds a Brahmin. — Sutta Nipāta 1.7 (Vasala Sutta)

docs.title: 14.1 Introduction
docs.text: The reformers and philosophers of the preceding chapters mostly argued about the Indian inheritance from within it, as heirs who wished to renew it. This chapter turns to thinkers who stood where the classical texts had placed those they excluded: the castes ranked lowest, women, and the forest and hill peoples who were not ranked at all. The chapter treats four anti-caste intellectuals — Jotirao Phule, Iyothee Thass, Narayana Guru and Periyar — and compares their counter-histories with Ambedkar’s; three women writers who asked who had made the rules they lived under; and the religious and political movements through which Adivasi communities, in central India and the North-East, answered missionaries, Hindu reformers and the state. The verse at the head of the chapter, from one of the oldest Buddhist collections, shows how old the argument against birth-rank is; its earlier history is told in Chapter 5.

docs.title: 14.2 Anti-Caste Thought on Its Own Terms
docs.text: The reformers of the Brahmo, Prarthana and Arya Samajes (Chapter 9) argued about caste from within the Sanskrit tradition, usually by claiming that hereditary rank was a later corruption of a purer Vedic or Upaniṣadic past. A second current of modern thought, rooted in the communities that the tradition ranked lowest, argued against that tradition or from outside it. Its thinkers wrote mostly in Marathi, Tamil and Malayalam rather than in English, for audiences of cultivators, labourers and artisans, and they did not regard themselves as contributors to a Hindu synthesis. Gail Omvedt called them “anticaste intellectuals” and took the title of her study from Ravidās’s song of Begumpurā, the city without sorrow, where no one is ranked above another; she argued that, for all their differences, they shared the hope of such a society and a habit of reading the Indian past against its Brahmanical narrators (Omvedt 2008). Their predecessors, the Buddhist, Vīraśaiva and sant critics of birth-rank, are described in Chapter 5, and Ambedkar in Chapter 12. This section treats four of them as thinkers, not only as organisers of reform.

docs.title: 14.2.1 Jotirao Phule: a counter-history
docs.text:
Jotirao Phule (1827–1890) belonged to the Mālī caste of Pune, a Śūdra community of cultivators and market-gardeners. He was educated at a Scottish mission school, where he read Thomas Paine’s Rights of Man, and from 1848 he and his wife Savitribai opened the schools for girls, and then for children of untouchable castes, that are described in Volume 22 (Manas and Śikṣā). His importance for a comparative history is that he wrote one of the first systematic counter-histories of India from the standpoint of the lower castes (O’Hanlon 1985).

Gulāmgirī (“Slavery”, 1873) is a dialogue in Marathi between Jotirao and a young questioner, Dhoṇḍībā, with an English preface; Phule dedicated it to “the good people of the United States” for their sacrifice in abolishing Black slavery, and so placed caste beside slavery as a single kind of injustice. Its argument takes up the Orientalist story of an Aryan migration (Chapter 8) and reverses its values. The Brahmins, in Phule’s account, descend from invaders who conquered the original inhabitants of the land, the ancestors of the Śūdras and Ati-Śūdras, and kept them subject by force and then by fraud. The Purāṇic avatāras become veiled memories of that conquest: Vāmana’s trick, by which the dwarf obtained three paces of land from the generous king Bali and then took the whole world, is the type of the Brahmin’s deceit, and Bali becomes the just king of the cultivators. Phule found confirmation in a Marathi saying recited at the Bali festival during Divāḷī, a wish that “troubles and sorrows go and Bali’s kingdom come”. The law-books and Purāṇas, on this reading, were composed to keep the conquered in ignorance, and the denial of education to Śūdras and women was the mechanism of their enslavement (Deshpande 2002).

As history the racial part of this account is no better than the Aryan theories it inverts; modern scholarship does not support a conquest of Śūdras by Brahmins (see Volume 1 on the spread of Indo-Aryan languages). Its force lay elsewhere. Phule treated sacred narratives as records of power and asked who had written them and for whom, a question that the reformers who sought a purer Vedic past did not ask. He also gave the lower castes a collective identity and heroes of their own: his ballad (povāḍā) of 1869 presented Śivājī as a king of the peasants, not of Brahmins. In Śetkaryācā Asūḍ (“The Cultivator’s Whipcord”, written in 1883) he extended the analysis to the agrarian economy, describing how the peasant was squeezed by the Brahmin village accountant, the moneylender and the colonial revenue and forest departments together. His last work, Sārvajanik Satyadharma Pustak (published in 1891, after his death), sets out a universal ethical religion of a single creator, without priests or exclusive scriptures, in which men and women are equal; Phule applied the same scepticism to the revealed books of Christianity and Islam as to the Vedas.

The Satyashodhak Samaj (“Truth-Seekers’ Society”, 1873) put these ideas into practice, conducting marriages and other rites in Marathi without Brahmin priests. Its successors formed the non-Brahmin movement of western India in the early twentieth century. Ambedkar dedicated Who Were the Shudras? (1946) to Phule’s memory, calling him the greatest Śūdra of modern India, and regarded him, with the Buddha and Kabīr, as one of his three teachers.

docs.title: 14.2.2 Iyothee Thass and the Tamil Buddhist past
docs.text:
Iyothee Thass (Ayōttitācar, 1845–1914), a practitioner of Siddha medicine and a Tamil scholar from the Paraiyar community of Madras, worked out the most elaborate counter-history of the south. Active from the 1880s in Paraiyar associations and journals, he concluded that the communities treated as untouchable in the Tamil country were not outcastes but the descendants of the land’s original Buddhists. In his account, Brahmins whom he called “false Brahmins” (vēṣa pirāmaṇar), Brahmins by dress and claim rather than by conduct, had destroyed Tamil Buddhism and degraded those who refused to abandon it; untouchability was the punishment of the faithful. He insisted that his people were “casteless Dravidians” and “original Tamils”, not a caste at the bottom of a Hindu hierarchy (Aloysius 1998).

In 1898, with the help of the Theosophist Henry Steel Olcott, Thass and his associates received the Buddhist precepts in Ceylon and founded in Madras the Sakya Buddhist Society, which had branches among Tamil labourers as far away as the Kolar Gold Fields. From 1907 he edited a weekly, Oru Paicā Tamiḻaṉ (“The One-Paisa Tamilian”), soon renamed Tamiḻaṉ, in which he reread the Tirukkuṟaḷ, the verses attributed to Auvaiyār and popular festivals as residues of a Buddhist culture, and argued that Indra (Tamil Intiraṉ) had been in origin an epithet of the Buddha. His Buddhism, like Dharmapāla’s (Chapter 18), was rationalist and critical of ritual; unlike Dharmapāla’s, it was a Buddhism of caste memory, which G. Aloysius has called an “emancipatory identity”.

Thass anticipated by nearly half a century Ambedkar’s thesis, in The Untouchables (1948), that the untouchables were descended from Buddhists who had refused Brahmin supremacy, and by nearly sixty years Ambedkar’s conversion; whether Ambedkar knew his work is not established. V. Geetha and S. V. Rajadurai have traced a line from Thass’s Tamil Buddhism to Periyar’s non-Brahmin radicalism (Geetha and Rajadurai 1998). After Thass’s death the society declined, and his writings were largely forgotten until Dalit scholars recovered them in the 1990s.

docs.title: 14.2.3 Narayana Guru
docs.text:
In Kerala, Sree Narayana Guru (1856–1928), born into the Ezhava community, which was regarded as polluting by the upper castes, became the leader of a movement of religious and social reform. In 1888 at Aruvippuram he consecrated an image of Śiva himself, defying the rule that only Brahmins could do so. According to the account preserved by his followers, when orthodox critics objected he replied that he had consecrated an Ezhava Śiva, not a Brahmin one. He wrote philosophical hymns in Sanskrit and Malayalam in an Advaitic idiom, but drew from them a radical conclusion summed up in his teaching of “one caste, one religion, one God for humanity”. The Sree Narayana Dharma Paripalana Yogam (1903) spread education and temple reform among Ezhavas and transformed Kerala society. Narayana Guru is an example of the Advaita tradition being used from below, against caste.

His philosophical writing is more substantial than his reputation as a social reformer suggests. The Malayalam Ātmopadeśaśataka (“One Hundred Verses of Self-Instruction”) and the Sanskrit Darśanamālā (“Garland of Visions”) restate non-dualism in his own terms, and the short prayer Daivadaśaka (“Ten Verses to God”) is still recited in many Kerala homes and schools. In a brief Sanskrit poem on caste, the Jātinirṇaya (“Determining Kind”), he made an argument with a long Indian pedigree. In the Nyāya–Vaiśeṣika theory of universals, jāti means a natural kind, a universal shared by all members of a class. Humanness, he argued, is the jāti of human beings as cowness is of cows; since a Brahmin is born of a human being in the same way as a Paraiyar, there is only one human jāti. The argument is close to the Buddha’s in the Vāseṭṭha Sutta (Chapter 5), and it turns the technical vocabulary of the schools against the social meaning of the word.

His later temples expressed the same thought in stone and glass. In some he installed a lamp or a tablet of moral precepts instead of an image, and at Kalavamkodam in 1927, according to the standard accounts, a mirror, so that the worshipper saw his own face where the deity should be. In 1924 he convened at his ashram at Aluva a conference of religions whose motto, inscribed at the venue, declared that the participants had met not to argue and win but to know and to make known. The movement he founded did not remain of one mind. His disciple Sahodaran K. Ayyappan organised in 1917 a shared meal of Ezhavas with Pulayas, who stood below them in the local hierarchy, and recast the Guru’s motto as “no caste, no religion, no God for humanity”; the poet Kumaran Āśān, the Yogam’s first general secretary, carried the Guru’s thought into Malayalam literature; and the Yogam itself became, as Filippo and Caroline Osella have shown, a vehicle for the social mobility of one community as much as for the abolition of caste (Osella and Osella 2000).

docs.title: 14.2.4 Periyar
docs.text:
E. V. Ramasamy (1879–1973), called Periyar, “the great one”, left the Indian National Congress in 1925 to found the Self-Respect Movement in the Tamil country. He attacked Brahmin dominance, caste, the subordination of women and religion itself as instruments of oppression, promoted “self-respect marriages” without Brahmin priests, and championed Tamil identity against what he saw as the imposition of Sanskrit and Hindi. His rationalist atheism and his critique of the epics, especially the Rāmāyaṇa, made him the most radical opponent of Brahmanical tradition in modern India, and the Dravidian parties that descend from his movement have governed Tamil Nadu since 1967.

Periyar’s thought is best read as a theory of dignity. “Self-respect” (cuyamariyātai) named both the goal and the method: a person who accepts an inferior birth because a scripture or a priest says so has given up his self-respect, and no political freedom can restore it to him. He spread the argument through his Tamil weekly Kuṭi Aracu (from 1925) and through the Self-Respect conferences, the first of which, at Chengalpattu in 1929, called for the abolition of caste titles and for women’s rights to divorce and to property. He led the agitation against compulsory Hindi in 1937–39, became president of the Justice Party in 1938, and in 1944 turned it into the Dravidar Kazhagam; the title “Periyar” was conferred on him by a women’s conference in Madras in 1938. His essays on women, collected under the title “Why Did Woman Become a Slave?”, attacked chastity (kaṟpu) as a virtue demanded of women alone, and defended divorce, widow remarriage and contraception. Self-respect marriages, solemnised by an exchange of garlands and a declaration without Sanskrit mantras, were given legal validity in Tamil Nadu by an amendment to the Hindu Marriage Act in 1967.

His counter-history was political rather than theological. Unlike Narayana Guru he did not seek a truer religion; unlike Phule and Thass he did not seek an original faith to restore. The opposition of Aryan and Dravidian, which M. S. S. Pandian has traced to colonial philology (beginning with Robert Caldwell’s Comparative Grammar of the Dravidian or South-Indian Family of Languages, 1856) as well as to Tamil revivalism, served him as a frame for a contemporary struggle over education, office and language (Pandian 2007). His readings of the Rāmāyaṇa, which made Rāvaṇa a Dravidian king wronged by northern invaders, belong to the long history of counter-tellings of the epic described in Volume 7 (Itihāsa–Purāṇa). Dalit critics have since pointed out that the non-Brahmin movement benefited the intermediate landowning castes more than it benefited those below them.

docs.title: 14.2.5 Counter-histories compared
docs.text:
Table 14.1 sets four of these thinkers beside Ambedkar. Three of them, like Ambedkar, answered the Brahmanical account of the Indian past with a rival history of loss: a just order or a true religion of the people that had been destroyed by fraud and force and could be recovered. Phule’s lost order was Bali’s kingdom of cultivators, Thass’s and Ambedkar’s a Buddhist past, Periyar’s a Dravidian self-respect that had never needed Sanskrit gods. Narayana Guru is the exception. He offered no history of conquest, and argued instead from the concept of jāti itself that there was only one human kind; his method was conceptual where theirs was genealogical.

Table 14.1. Anti-caste counter-histories compared Thinker The excluded were originally Remedy proposed Jotirao Phule the cultivators of Bali’s just kingdom, conquered by Aryan Brahmins education; a priestless religion of one creator (Satyashodhak Samaj) Iyothee Thass the original Buddhists of the Tamil land return to Buddhism; a casteless Dravidian identity Narayana Guru no counter-history: there is only one human jāti temples, schools and organisation open to all; Advaita Periyar self-respecting Dravidians subjected to Aryan religion rationalism; rejection of religion; self-respect marriage B. R. Ambedkar Buddhist “Broken Men” (1948); the Śūdras as degraded Kṣatriyas (1946) constitutional democracy; conversion to Buddhism

The genealogical histories share the weakness of their Orientalist models: they read myth as coded history and project modern categories of race and nation onto the distant past, and specialists do not accept them as accounts of what happened. They share also the strength of a hermeneutics of suspicion, the recognition that the texts which classified people were written by some of those people about others. For a volume on samanvaya they pose a direct challenge. The classical ideal of harmonising the scriptures assumed that the scriptures were the measure; these thinkers asked who had made the measure, and they found the harmony of the texts to be the harmony of a ruling voice.

docs.title: 14.2.6 Dalit and Bahujan thought after Ambedkar
docs.text: Ambedkar’s critique has been continued and extended by later Dalit and Bahujan (“majority”, that is, non-elite) thinkers. Kancha Ilaiah’s Why I Am Not a Hindu (1996) contrasted the productive, egalitarian culture of the labouring castes of Andhra Pradesh with what he called the “spiritual fascism” of Brahmanical Hinduism, in a polemic that provoked fierce debate (Ilaiah 1996). The political scientist Gopal Guru and the philosopher Sundar Sarukkai, in The Cracked Mirror (2012), asked who has the right to theorise experience in India, and argued that the social sciences had treated Dalits as objects of study rather than as thinkers; they called for a philosophy that takes the experience of humiliation and exclusion as its starting point (Guru and Sarukkai 2012). Dalit autobiographies and literature in Marathi, Tamil, Kannada, Hindi and other languages have become one of the most important sources for Indian thought about caste. These writers do not regard themselves as contributors to a “synthesis” of Indian traditions; they regard themselves as critics of a tradition that excluded them. A volume on synthesis must give their criticism its full weight.

docs.title: 14.3 Women Thinkers Answering the Śāstras
docs.text: The reform debates of the nineteenth century were conducted mostly by men about women. Reformers and their orthodox opponents argued over satī, widow remarriage and the age of marriage by quoting the śāstras at one another, and both sides tended to locate the ideal Indian woman in an imagined Vedic past of learned wives such as Gārgī and Maitreyī. Some women answered for themselves, and they asked a different question: not what the texts permitted, but who had written them. The legal history of these debates is told in Volume 18 (Rājanīti and Dharmaśāstra), the history of women’s schooling in Volume 22, and women’s writing in the regional literatures in Volume 8 (Kāvya Kalpalatā); this section treats three women as thinkers who compared and judged traditions. In western India the questioning began early. In 1855 Mukta Salve, a fourteen-year-old Māṅg girl at one of the Phules’ schools, wrote an essay on the sufferings of the Māṅgs and Mahārs, published in a missionary journal, which asked what religion the Māṅgs and Mahārs could call their own if the Vedas belonged to the Brahmins alone. Savitribai Phule (1831–1897), Jotirao’s wife, who taught in these schools from 1848, published two books of Marathi verse, Kāvyaphule (1854) and Bāvanakaśī Subodharatnākar (1892), and died in 1897 while nursing victims of plague.

docs.title: 14.3.1 Tarabai Shinde
docs.text:
Little is known of Tarabai Shinde (c. 1850–1910) beyond her single book. She was the daughter of Bapuji Hari Shinde, a Maratha clerk in the revenue office at Buldhana, in Berar, who was a member of Phule’s Satyashodhak Samaj and who taught her to read. Strī Puruṣ Tulanā (“A Comparison of Women and Men”, 1882) was provoked by a case reported in the Marathi press in 1881: a young Brahmin widow, Vijayalakshmi, was convicted at Surat of killing her newborn illegitimate child and sentenced to death, a sentence later commuted to transportation for life. The newspapers moralised about the wickedness of women. Tarabai asked why the woman was punished while the man who had seduced her went unnamed, and turned the case into a general comparison of the vices of the two sexes (O’Hanlon 1994).

Her method was inversion. A long literary tradition in Sanskrit and Marathi catalogued the faults of women, their fickleness, deceit and lust; Tarabai catalogued the faults of men, from the drinking, gambling and whoring of the idle to the hypocrisy of English-educated reformers who demanded learned wives while keeping their own habits. She turned the epic exemplars of the devoted wife (pativratā) against the men who held them up, asking which husband had shown the constancy that the stories demanded of wives, and she described the condition of widows, forbidden remarriage, often tonsured and treated as a burden, as the creation of men who had written the rules for their own convenience. The Pune press received the book with hostility, and Phule defended it. Rosalind O’Hanlon, who translated it, reads it as one of the earliest sustained feminist arguments in a modern Indian language and stresses that it criticised Brahmanical patriarchy and the new reforming patriarchy together.

docs.title: 14.3.2 Pandita Ramabai
docs.text:
Pandita Ramabai (1858–1922), a Brahmin woman who mastered Sanskrit and was given the title “Pandita” by the scholars of Calcutta, criticised the treatment of women in the Dharmaśāstras in The High-Caste Hindu Woman (1887), converted to Christianity and founded the Mukti Mission for widows and destitute women near Pune. Uma Chakravarti’s study shows how her life was shaped by the conflict between her learning and the restrictions placed on women (Chakravarti 1998).

Her father, Anant Shastri Dongre, had taught Sanskrit to his wife and daughter against the custom of his caste, and the family lived as wandering reciters of the Purāṇas until her parents and a sister died, within a short time of one another, in the famine years of the 1870s. After the recognition in Calcutta in 1878 Ramabai married a Bengali lawyer of the Kāyastha caste, a marriage across caste and region that orthodox opinion condemned, and was widowed with an infant daughter in 1882. In the same year she founded the Arya Mahila Samaj in Pune and published Strīdharmanīti (“Morals for Women”), a Marathi conduct book that urged women to educate themselves and to become self-reliant. The High-Caste Hindu Woman, written in the United States, was organised by the stages of a woman’s life, childhood, marriage and widowhood, and quoted the law-books against themselves; its argument was that the treatment of high-caste widows was not a corruption of the tradition but was prescribed by it. Its sale and the American association formed to support her paid for the Sharada Sadan, a residential school for widows opened in Bombay in 1889 and moved to Pune in the following year (Kosambi 2000).

Ramabai’s Christianity was as independent as her Hinduism had been. Baptised in England in 1883, she disputed doctrine and obedience with the Anglican sisters who sponsored her, and wrote that having freed herself from one priestly authority she would not submit to another. Nationalist critics in Pune, among them the editors of the Kesari, accused the Sharada Sadan of converting its pupils, and in America in 1894–95 supporters of her mission were among Vivekananda’s critics, the two offering American audiences opposed pictures of Hindu womanhood (Chapter 10). After the famine of 1896–97 she built the Mukti Mission at Kedgaon, and in her last years she completed a translation of the Bible into Marathi from the Hebrew and Greek. Chakravarti argues that she was written out of the nationalist history of reform because she had converted, and that her critique of Brahmanical patriarchy was more searching than that of most male reformers.

docs.title: 14.3.3 Rokeya Sakhawat Hossain
docs.text:
Rokeya Sakhawat Hossain (1880–1932) grew up in a landed Muslim family of Rangpur in northern Bengal, where girls were kept in strict seclusion; an elder brother taught her English and Bengali secretly at night. Her husband, a deputy magistrate in Bhagalpur, encouraged her writing, and after his death in 1909 she used his bequest to found a school for Muslim girls, first at Bhagalpur and from 1911 in Calcutta. In 1916 she founded the Anjuman-e-Khawateen-e-Islam, an association of Muslim women in Bengal (Ray 2002).

Sultana’s Dream, written in English and published in 1905 in the Indian Ladies’ Magazine of Madras, is a short utopia. The narrator dreams that she walks through Ladyland, where the men live in seclusion in the mardāna and the women govern. Women scientists in the two women’s universities have learned to draw water from the clouds and to collect the heat of the sun, and the country won its only war by turning concentrated sunlight on the invaders after the men had failed; crime has nearly disappeared, and the religion of the land is one of love and truth (Hossain 1988). The satire turns on a simple inversion of purdah, but its argument is about knowledge: seclusion is an arrangement of power, sustained by keeping women from science. Rokeya’s Bengali writing was more direct. Her essay “Our Degradation” (Āmāder abanati), first published in the Calcutta journal Nabanūr in 1904 and reprinted in revised form as “The Degradation of Women” (Strījātir abanati) in Motīcūr, argued that religious scriptures had been used by men to keep women in subjection; its most outspoken passages on religion were omitted from the reprint. Her novel Padmarāg (1924) imagines a refuge run by women in which women of every religion live and work together, and the sketches of Abarodhbāsinī (“The Secluded Ones”, 1931) record, with deadpan precision, the injuries and absurdities that purdah produced.

docs.title: 14.3.4 Three strategies compared
docs.text: The three women wrote from different religious worlds, Tarabai from a Marathi non-Brahmin Hindu household, Ramabai from Brahmin learning that led her to Christianity, Rokeya from Bengali Muslim gentility, and they used different means: satire and inversion, scholarly exegesis and institution-building, and a scientific utopia. They agreed on one point that set them apart from most male reformers. They located women’s subordination not in a decline from a golden age but in the texts and customs that men had made and continued to make, Hindu, Muslim and modern alike. In this they stand in sharp contrast to the idealised images of ancient Indian womanhood promoted by many reformers and nationalists, and they anticipate the questions that Uma Chakravarti and other historians have since asked of the Dharmaśāstra tradition (Chakravarti 2003), discussed in Chapter 5.

docs.title: 14.4 Adivasi Religion and Thought
docs.text: The communities now called Adivasis (“original inhabitants”, a name that came into political use in Chotanagpur in the 1930s) or, in the language of the Constitution, Scheduled Tribes, are the part of India’s population least represented in its written traditions. Their knowledge of forests, plants, animals and crafts is the subject of Volume 23 (Jana–Jāti). This section is concerned with Adivasi religion as a tradition with its own voice, and with the arguments of Adivasi leaders and their interlocutors about what their place in India should be.

docs.title: 14.4.1 Sacred groves and Sarna
docs.text: Most Adivasi religions of central and eastern India centre on a supreme being associated with the sun or the sky, on ancestral and village spirits, and on sacred places, above all the grove. Among the Munda, Ho and Oraon of Jharkhand the grove is the sarnā, the site of the village’s festivals and sacrifices (Chapter 21); the supreme being is called Singbonga by the Munda and Dharmes by the Oraon. In the twentieth century these practices were organised into a self-conscious religion, “Sarna”, distinct from both Hinduism and Christianity, and Sarna associations have long asked that the census record it as a religion in its own right rather than counting its followers as Hindus or under “other religions”. In 2020 the Jharkhand Legislative Assembly passed a resolution supporting that demand. The question is the one that this volume meets among Sikhs, Jains, Buddhists and Ambedkarites: whether a community’s own account of its religion, or an outside classification, decides what it is.

docs.title: 14.4.2 Prophets and rebellions
docs.text:
Adivasi religious thought often found expression in movements that were at once religious reforms and revolts. The Santal rising of 1855–56, led by the brothers Sidhu and Kanhu, began with a vision in which they were commanded to free the Santals from moneylenders, landlords and officials. In the 1890s Birsa Munda (c. 1875–1900), who had been educated at a mission school, proclaimed himself a prophet among the Munda, taught the worship of one god, Singbonga, and the abandonment of sacrifice and of the fear of spirits, and called on his followers to reclaim the land from outsiders (diku); his teaching drew on Munda tradition, on Christianity and on Vaiṣṇava ideas of purity, and it ended in the armed rising (ulgulān) of 1899–1900. Birsa died in prison at Ranchi in 1900, and the Chotanagpur Tenancy Act of 1908 was in part a response to the grievances his movement had expressed. K. Suresh Singh’s study remains the standard account (Singh 1966). Among the Oraon, the Tana Bhagat movement that began in 1914 combined a reformed, sober and vegetarian discipline with the refusal of rent and labour dues, and many of its members later joined Gandhi’s campaigns. In south Gujarat in 1922–23 a goddess was believed to speak through mediums who commanded Adivasis to give up liquor and meat and to boycott the liquor-dealers and moneylenders; David Hardiman has shown how this “coming of the Devi” turned a religious movement into an assertion of economic and political independence (Hardiman 1987).

These movements are often read either as primitive rebellions or as early stages of nationalism. They are better read, as their historians suggest, as Adivasi arguments about legitimate authority, conducted in a religious idiom: who owns the land, which god is to be served, and whether the rules of outsiders bind the community. Their prophets borrowed from Christianity and Hinduism as Indian reformers borrowed from European thought, to answer questions of their own.

docs.title: 14.4.3 Elwin, Ghurye and the question of assimilation
docs.text:
In the 1940s the place of the tribal peoples in a future India became the subject of a sharp public argument. Verrier Elwin (1902–1964), an English missionary who left the church, lived for many years among the Gond and Baiga of central India and wrote ethnographies of them, argued that tribal cultures had their own values and should be protected from exploitation by traders, moneylenders, officials and missionaries, and from the contempt of reforming Hindus; in his early writing he proposed protected areas within which tribal life would be shielded from outside pressure. The sociologist G. S. Ghurye (1893–1983) replied in The Aborigines — “So-called” — and Their Future (1943) that the tribes were “backward Hindus”, long integrated into the social and religious life of their Hindu neighbours, and that the remedy for their poverty was assimilation into the wider society, not isolation (Ghurye 1943). Ramachandra Guha’s biography of Elwin shows that the two positions were less opposed than their rhetoric suggested — Elwin abandoned the idea of isolation, and Ghurye did not deny exploitation — but the argument set the terms of the later debate between protection and integration (Guha 1999). After independence Elwin became adviser on tribal affairs for the North-East Frontier Agency, and Jawaharlal Nehru’s principles for tribal policy, which called for development along the lines of the people’s own genius and respect for tribal rights in land and forests, drew on his views.

Adivasi leaders spoke for themselves. Jaipal Singh Munda (1903–1970), educated at Oxford and captain of the Indian hockey team that won the Olympic gold medal in 1928, led the Adivasi Mahasabha of Chotanagpur and argued in the Constituent Assembly that the Adivasis, as the oldest inhabitants of the land, had been dispossessed by the rest of India and needed safeguards rather than paternal improvement. The Constitution responded with the Fifth Schedule, which gives special responsibilities for Scheduled Areas, and the Sixth Schedule, which created autonomous district councils in the hill areas of the North-East; later laws on self-government in Scheduled Areas (1996) and on forest rights (2006; Chapter 22) extended these protections. Their uneven enforcement, and the displacement of Adivasis by dams, mines and conservation projects, remain among the gravest failures of Indian democracy.

docs.title: 14.4.4 The North-East
docs.text:
The hill peoples of the North-East met the colonial and national states later than those of central India, and their religious history took a distinctive course. In the Brahmaputra valley the Vaiṣṇava teacher Śaṅkaradeva had already, in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries, drawn people of many communities, including tribal ones, into a devotional order of village prayer-halls and monasteries (Chapter 16). In the hills, Baptist and Presbyterian missions of the nineteenth and twentieth centuries led to large-scale conversion, so that Christians now form the majority in Nagaland, Mizoram and Meghalaya, and Christianity there became a vehicle of literacy, of written languages and of new ethnic identities. Indigenous religions answered in their own ways. In the Khasi Hills the Seng Khasi, founded at Shillong in 1899, set out to preserve the Khasi religion and customs against conversion. Among the Zeme, Liangmai and Rongmei Nagas, the movement begun by Jadonang and continued after his execution in 1931 by Gaidinliu (1915–1993) reformed the indigenous religion as Heraka and opposed both British rule and the Christian missions; Gaidinliu, imprisoned from 1932 until independence and later honoured as “Rani”, became a national figure, and her later association with Hindu organisations has made her legacy contested among Nagas. In Arunachal Pradesh, movements of the late twentieth century have organised the worship of Donyi-Polo, the sun and moon, among the Adi and neighbouring peoples as a self-conscious indigenous religion.

These developments show that Adivasi religion is not a static substratum beneath the “great” traditions, as older scholarship often assumed, but a set of living traditions that have argued with Hinduism, Christianity and the state, borrowed from them and resisted them. For many of their adherents the most important question is not whether they share the ideas of their neighbours but whether they may keep their land, their gods and their own name for themselves.

docs.title: 14.5 Assessment
docs.text: The anti-caste thinkers, the women writers and the Adivasi leaders of this chapter worked in different places and languages and rarely read one another. They shared a starting point: each spoke from a position that the classical texts had defined from outside — as Śūdra or outcaste, as wife or widow, as forest-dweller beyond the four varṇas — and each refused that definition. Their methods differed: counter-history, conceptual argument, satire, scholarly exegesis, prophecy, rebellion and constitutional bargaining. For a volume on synthesis they pose the most direct challenge of all, set out above in the comparison of counter-histories, and it applies to the women writers and the Adivasi leaders as much as to the anti-caste thinkers: the classical texts are evidence about a tradition, not the measure of who belongs to it.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text:
• Omvedt (2008): the anti-caste intellectuals from Phule to Ambedkar.

  • O’Hanlon (1985) and Deshpande (2002): Phule’s thought, and his writings in translation; the Marathi collected works are edited by Phadke (1991).

  • Aloysius (1998), Geetha and Rajadurai (1998) and Pandian (2007): Iyothee Thass, Periyar and the Tamil non-Brahmin movement.

  • O’Hanlon (1994), Chakravarti (1998) and Kosambi (2000): Tarabai Shinde and Pandita Ramabai.

  • Hossain (1988) and Ray (2002): Rokeya Sakhawat Hossain.

  • Singh (1966), Hardiman (1987) and Guha (1999): Birsa Munda, the Devi movement, and Elwin and the tribal question.

docs.title: Chapter 15: Philosophy in the Indian Academy: From “Swaraj in Ideas” to Saṃvāda
docs.text: pramāṇa-prameya-saṃśaya-prayojana-dṛṣṭānta-siddhānta-avayava-tarka-nirṇaya-vāda-jalpa-vitaṇḍā-hetvābhāsa-chala-jāti-nigrahasthānānāṃ tattvajñānān niḥśreyasādhigamaḥ The highest good is attained from knowledge of the truth about the means of knowledge, the objects of knowledge, doubt, purpose, example, established doctrine, the members of an inference, hypothetical reasoning, ascertainment, debate, disputation, cavil, pseudo-reasons, quibbling, futile rejoinders and the grounds of defeat. — Nyāyasūtra 1.1.1

docs.title: 15.1 Introduction
docs.text:
The modern Indian thinkers of the previous chapters were, for the most part, teachers, reformers, poets and political leaders who wrote for a wide public. Alongside them a smaller group of professional philosophers worked in the universities that colonial rule had created and that independent India greatly enlarged. Their audience was narrower and their influence less visible, but they faced the question that runs through this volume in its sharpest form. They were trained to teach Locke, Kant and Bradley in English; many of them had also been brought up in, or later sought out, the Sanskrit śāstras taught by pandits in their own way and in their own language. What would it mean to do philosophy, rather than merely to report on it, as an Indian in that situation?

The chapter follows their answers from the colonial university to the end of the twentieth century. It treats the historians who fixed the modern picture of the “six systems”, the original philosophers of the colonial period, of whom K. C. Bhattacharya is the most important, the critics who rejected Radhakrishnan’s spiritual India from the left and from the analytic side, the attempts to make pandits and professors argue with one another as equals, and the phenomenologists and analytic philosophers who carried Indian arguments into international debate. Radhakrishnan himself is discussed in Chapter 9, and the international rise of comparative philosophy, with the work of Halbfass and Matilal abroad, in Chapter 8. The classical schools themselves are the subject of Volume 3 (Darśana Darpaṇa). Nalini Bhushan and Jay Garfield’s anthology and study are indispensable for the colonial period (Bhushan and Garfield 2011; Bhushan and Garfield 2017), and A. Raghuramaraju’s Debates in Indian Philosophy stages the arguments of the modern thinkers against one another (Raghuramaraju 2006).

docs.title: 15.2 The Colonial University and Its Philosophers
docs.text:
Philosophy was taught in Indian universities from the late nineteenth century, largely as Western philosophy in English. The Indian Philosophical Congress was founded in 1925, with Tagore presiding over its first session in Calcutta. Brajendranath Seal (1864–1938) pioneered a comparative method in his studies of Vaiṣṇavism and Christianity and his The Positive Sciences of the Ancient Hindus (1915). Radhakrishnan’s histories made Indian philosophy a subject of study (Chapter 9). Many of the philosophers of this period were idealists, influenced by Hegel and the British idealists, and found in Vedānta a congenial counterpart.

The universities of Calcutta, Bombay and Madras, founded in 1857, began as examining bodies on the model of the University of London, and for decades their courses in “mental and moral philosophy” followed British textbooks. Indian philosophy entered the syllabus slowly and, at first, as a historical subject. Two scholars did most to give it a modern shape. Surendranath Dasgupta (1887–1952), who taught at Chittagong and Calcutta and studied at Cambridge, wrote A History of Indian Philosophy in five volumes (1922–1955, the last published after his death), which remains the fullest survey in English and gives the Buddhist, Jain and medical traditions a place beside the Brahmanical schools (Dasgupta 1922–1955). M. Hiriyanna (1871–1950) of Mysore wrote in Outlines of Indian Philosophy (1932) a shorter and still much-used account, careful in its presentation of arguments; his essays on aesthetics treated rasa theory as a philosophy of art (Hiriyanna 1932). Together with Radhakrishnan’s two volumes these histories fixed the picture, still found in examination syllabi, of Indian philosophy as a set of “systems”, six orthodox and three heterodox, each with a fixed doctrine.

Outside the universities, the Indian Institute of Philosophy at Amalner in Khandesh, endowed in 1916 by the mill-owner Pratap Seth for the study of Advaita, gave a small group of philosophers fellowships and a journal, the Philosophical Quarterly, edited for many years by G. R. Malkani. In 1936 Radhakrishnan and J. H. Muirhead published Contemporary Indian Philosophy, in which Indian professors set out their own positions rather than the doctrines of the ancients (Radhakrishnan and Muirhead 1936). Bhushan and Garfield have recovered from these and other sources a lively debate, conducted in English, between idealists such as Hiralal Haldar and A. C. Mukerji, critics of idealism, and thinkers who tried to say what was distinctive about Indian thought without turning it into a national property.

docs.title: 15.3 K. C. Bhattacharya
docs.text:
Krishnachandra Bhattacharya (1875–1949), who taught at Calcutta University, was the most original Indian academic philosopher of the colonial period. In The Subject as Freedom (1930) he developed, in dialogue with Kant and with Vedānta, an account of the subject as that which can never be an object, and of philosophy as the progressive realisation of the subject’s freedom from objectivity (Bhattacharya 1930). He wrote original interpretations of Sāṃkhya, Vedānta and the Jain theory of many-sidedness, and of aesthetic experience.

His essay “The Concept of Philosophy”, contributed to Radhakrishnan and Muirhead’s volume of 1936, distinguished grades of theoretical consciousness. Science deals with facts that can be perceived and spoken of; philosophy begins where we speak of what is not a fact in that sense, and it has three regions: the philosophy of the object, the philosophy of the subject and the philosophy of truth. Each is reached by a kind of reflection that cannot be reduced to the one below it, and the higher regions can be spoken of only in symbols and denials. In another essay, “The Alternative Forms of the Absolute”, he argued that the absolute can be conceived as truth, as freedom or as value, according as the knowing, willing or feeling side of the subject is taken as primary, and that these are genuine alternatives, none of which can be shown to be the only correct one. The idea of alternation was itself an Indian borrowing used for a modern purpose: he found its model in the Jain doctrine that a thing may be described from several standpoints, and he insisted that such a doctrine was not a vague tolerance but a logical thesis that had to be made precise. His son Kalidas Bhattacharyya (1911–1984) developed the theme in Alternative Standpoints in Philosophy (1953).

His lecture “Swaraj in Ideas”, delivered around 1930 (it is dated variously to 1928 and 1931) and published only after his death, is the most penetrating Indian diagnosis of intellectual colonialism. Bhattacharya argued that political subjection was less dangerous than “cultural subjection”, the unconscious adoption by educated Indians of Western ideas that they had not assimilated and could not genuinely criticise; that the remedy was neither rejection of the West nor uncritical traditionalism but a reflective reckoning with both; and that genuine freedom in ideas would require Indians to think from within their own traditions while honestly confronting Western thought. Bhushan and Garfield have shown that the philosophers of this period, far from being mere imitators, were engaged in exactly this work (Bhushan and Garfield 2017).

The lecture is often quoted as a charter for a nativist programme, and that reading misses its point. Bhattacharya did not ask Indians to stop reading Western philosophy; he asked them to stop accepting it, or rejecting it, without thinking it through in terms that were genuinely their own. The same discipline, he implied, applied to the Indian inheritance: a traditional doctrine repeated without reflection was no more an exercise of freedom than an imported one. His own work, which reads Kant through Sāṃkhya and Sāṃkhya through Kant, is the best illustration of what he meant.

docs.title: 15.4 Reading the Classical Schools
docs.text:
The generation after Bhattacharya produced interpretations of the classical schools that are still read. T. R. V. Murti (1902–1986), who taught at Banaras Hindu University, published The Central Philosophy of Buddhism (1955), which presented the Madhyamaka of Nāgārjuna as a “dialectic” that criticises all views without holding one of its own, compared it at length with Kant’s antinomies, and argued that it was the pivot around which later Buddhist and Vedāntic thought turned (Murti 1955). The book did much to make Madhyamaka a subject for philosophers rather than only for philologists. Later scholars have objected that it reads Nāgārjuna through Kant and through an Advaitic expectation of an absolute beyond words, for the comparisons of this generation carried their own frames with them (Chapter 18 describes the later career of Buddhist philosophy in world philosophy).

In Banaras, Gopinath Kaviraj (1887–1976), principal of the Government Sanskrit College from 1923 to 1937, combined the methods of a modern historian of texts with a life of religious practice under tantric teachers; his studies of the history of Nyāya–Vaiśeṣika and of tantric literature, many of them in Hindi and Bengali, mark a different kind of bridge between the pandit’s learning and the university’s (Volume 6, Tantra–Āgama). In Calcutta the training of philosophers in Navya-Nyāya by traditional teachers continued, and it was from such teachers that B. K. Matilal and others learned the technical language they later brought to analytic philosophy.

docs.title: 15.5 Against the Spiritual Picture
docs.text: Radhakrishnan’s presentation of Indian philosophy as a religion of the spirit culminating in Vedānta (Chapter 9) met resistance from several sides, and the resistance itself became one of the main currents of Indian philosophy after independence.

docs.title: 15.5.1 Materialist and Marxist readings
docs.text:
Debiprasad Chattopadhyaya (1918–1993) set out to recover the tradition that the spiritual picture left out. In Lokāyata: A Study in Ancient Indian Materialism (1959) he argued that the materialism of the Cārvākas, known almost entirely from the refutations of its opponents, was the learned form of a much older and wider popular outlook, rooted in agricultural fertility rites and preserved in parts of tantric practice, and that its suppression by the priestly schools was a social as well as an intellectual event (Chattopadhyaya 1959). In later books he examined the place of observation and experiment in the medical texts of Caraka and Suśruta and asked, in What Is Living and What Is Dead in Indian Philosophy (1976), which parts of the inheritance could support a secular and scientific culture. Many of his specific reconstructions are speculative, and specialists in the Cārvāka sources have questioned his use of ethnography to fill the gaps in the texts. His lasting achievement was to show that the classical record was a record of arguments between rival schools, some of which lost, rather than a single spiritual tradition.

The historian and mathematician D. D. Kosambi (1907–1966), son of the Buddhist scholar Dharmanand Kosambi (Chapter 18), made a similar point about the texts most often used to define the tradition. In Myth and Reality (1962) he read the Bhagavadgītā as a text whose synthesis of ways of salvation, and whose ideal of devotion to a lord, suited a society of overlords and dependants, and he argued that the ability of the Gītā to reconcile everything was also its weakness (Kosambi 1962). Readers who do not share Kosambi’s Marxism have still found his method valuable: it asks what work a doctrine did in the society that preserved it.

docs.title: 15.5.2 Three myths about Indian philosophy
docs.text:
Daya Krishna (1924–2007), who taught at Jaipur, was the most provocative of these thinkers. In an essay of 1966, “Three Myths about Indian Philosophy”, reprinted in Indian Philosophy: A Counter Perspective (1991), he challenged what he regarded as myths about Indian philosophy: that it was essentially spiritual and directed towards liberation, that its “orthodox” schools derived their doctrines from the authority of the Veda, and that it was organised into fixed “schools” each with an unchanging position (Daya Krishna 1991). He organised dialogues between traditional pandits and modern philosophers on philosophical questions, and argued that Indian philosophy should be treated as a living tradition of argument, open to questions its classical authors had not asked. His work is a direct challenge to the Neo-Vedāntic picture described in Chapter 9.

His arguments were deliberately sharp. If liberation was the goal of every school, he asked, why did the Nyāya and Mīmāṃsā texts spend so little space on it and so much on inference, meaning and the authority of testimony? If the schools were fixed systems, why did their later authors disagree so openly with the founders whose sūtras they claimed to explain? And if the “orthodox” schools rested on the authority of the Veda, why did the Nyāya, Vaiśeṣika and Sāṃkhya texts make so little use of it in their arguments? He did not deny that Indian philosophers cared about liberation; he denied that this concern told us what their arguments were worth.

docs.title: 15.5.3 Ambedkar as a philosopher of religion
docs.text: The most searching critic of the spiritual picture was not a professional philosopher at all, and for decades philosophy departments did not teach him. B. R. Ambedkar (Chapter 12) trained in economics and law at Columbia and London, but his unfinished and undated essay “Philosophy of Hinduism”, published only in the collected edition of his writings, set out a criterion for judging any religion that most philosophers of religion in India had avoided. A religion’s philosophy, he argued, should be judged not by the sublimity of its metaphysics but by the society it sanctions, and the test was justice, understood as liberty, equality and fraternity, together with social utility; by that test a doctrine of the oneness of all selves that coexisted with untouchability had failed, whatever its speculative merits. His later writings on the Buddha (Chapter 18) applied the same criterion in a positive direction. Since the 1990s Ambedkar has been read increasingly as a philosopher in his own right, and his challenge — that the ethical worth of a tradition is shown by how it treats those it excludes — is now part of the academic discussion of Indian philosophy.

docs.title: 15.6 The Sanskrit Institutions After Independence
docs.text:
The traditional schools did not disappear when the professor displaced the pandit at the centre of intellectual life. Independent India created institutions for them: the Government Sanskrit College at Banaras, where Gopinath Kaviraj had taught, became the core of a Sanskrit university in 1958, now the Sampurnanand Sanskrit University; the Rashtriya Sanskrit Sansthan, founded in 1970 and since 2020 the Central Sanskrit University, maintains campuses in several states; and other Sanskrit universities were founded in later decades. In these institutions Nyāya, Mīmāṃsā, Vedānta, Vyākaraṇa and Jyotiṣa continued to be taught in Sanskrit, through the classical texts and commentaries, and scholars continued to write treatises and commentaries in the classical forms. The government also honoured eminent pandits with presidential awards.

These institutions preserved skills that would otherwise have been lost, above all the ability to read the technical literature of the later schools with its own teachers’ understanding. Their weakness, which their own scholars have often acknowledged, was isolation: few of their graduates learned the languages and methods of modern scholarship, few university philosophers learned Sanskrit well enough to read with them, and the employment open to their students was narrow. The dialogues described in the next section were an attempt to bridge this gap; the recent policy of bringing “Indian knowledge” into all university courses (Chapter 22) has given it a new urgency, since the courses can be taught well only by people who can read the sources.

docs.title: 15.7 Pandits and Professors: The Experiment of Saṃvāda
docs.text:
The separation of the pandit and the professor was one of the strangest legacies of colonial education. The pandit, trained in Sanskrit in a traditional school or a Sanskrit college, could read Gaṅgeśa or Śaṅkara with a precision that few university philosophers could match, but usually knew no Western philosophy and had no place in its institutions; the professor, trained in English, often knew the Indian schools only through the histories of Dasgupta and Radhakrishnan. Each regarded the other with some condescension.

From the 1980s a group of philosophers set out to bring them together. In 1983 a week-long seminar, planned by M. P. Rege, was held at Pune at which Sanskrit pandits trained in the traditional śāstras and philosophers trained in the Western tradition discussed a single question: whether, to explain how we understand sentences that are false or whose truth is unknown, we must suppose that there are “propositions” as entities distinct from sentences and facts. The proceedings were transcribed from the tapes and published as Saṃvāda: A Dialogue between Two Philosophical Traditions (1991), edited by Daya Krishna, M. P. Rege, R. C. Dwivedi and Mukund Lath (Daya Krishna et al. 1991). The question had been formulated in Western terms and was translated into the categories of the Sanskrit schools, and the pandits answered it from within their own theories of verbal knowledge (śābdabodha). The book records misunderstandings as well as agreements, which is part of its value. Its premise was that the pandits were not informants about a dead tradition but philosophers whose answers to a live question deserved to be heard.

The Indian Council of Philosophical Research, registered in 1977 and active from 1981, became the main sponsor of such work. Its journal, edited from 1990 until his death by Daya Krishna, opened sections for discussion and debate and for agendas of research, and carried exchanges in which classical Indian positions were treated as contributions to current questions. The same council’s founding chairman, the philosopher D. P. Chattopadhyaya (1933–2022), not to be confused with the author of Lokāyata, later directed the Project of History of Indian Science, Philosophy and Culture, launched around 1990, which commissioned many volumes from scholars of different disciplines on the history of Indian thought, science and society; its volumes are uneven, but they brought historians of philosophy, of science and of society into one enterprise, and one of them, edited by Daya Krishna, surveyed Indian philosophy from the eighteenth century onwards, a period that the standard histories had passed over. The experiment did not reverse the decline of traditional learning, and the number of pandits who could take part has fallen since; but it established a method — the dialogue of equals across languages and institutions — that is perhaps the most practical form of samanvaya described in this volume.

docs.title: 15.8 Phenomenology and Hermeneutics
docs.text:
After 1947 Indian philosophy developed in several directions. Jitendranath Mohanty (1928–2013), trained in both Nyāya and Husserlian phenomenology, moved between the two traditions with unusual ease. His Gaṅgeśa’s Theory of Truth (1966) edited and translated the discussion of the validity of cognitions (prāmāṇyavāda) in Gaṅgeśa’s Tattvacintāmaṇi, the foundational text of Navya-Nyāya, with an introduction that set the Nyāya view, that the validity of a cognition is established from outside it, by a further inference, beside the Mīmāṃsā view that cognitions are intrinsically valid (Mohanty 1966). At the same time he wrote studies of Husserl’s theory of meaning and taught for many years in the United States. In Reason and Tradition in Indian Thought (1992) (Mohanty 1992) and later essays, written against the stereotype of Indian philosophy as anti-rational, he argued that the centre of Indian philosophy was the theory of the means of knowledge (pramāṇa), not a set of metaphysical conclusions, and that the soteriological framing of the texts did not prevent their arguments from being rational in the ordinary sense. He asked, as a phenomenologist would, how the Indian schools understood the relation between consciousness and its objects, and he found in them positions — the self-luminosity of consciousness in Advaita and Prābhākara Mīmāṃsā, its intentionality in Nyāya — that could be argued about with Husserl and his critics.

Jarava Lal Mehta (1912–1988), who taught at Banaras and later at Harvard’s Center for the Study of World Religions, wrote one of the first comprehensive studies of Heidegger and used Heidegger’s and Gadamer’s hermeneutics to ask how a modern Indian could understand a tradition that was both his own and alien to him. Ramchandra Gandhi (1937–2007), a grandson of the Mahatma who studied at Oxford, wrote on the conditions of communication and religious language in The Availability of Religious Ideas (1976), and in Sita’s Kitchen (1992), written in response to the dispute at Ayodhya, read Advaita as a philosophy of the self’s openness to others (Gandhi 1976).

docs.title: 15.9 Matilal and the Analytic Turn
docs.text:
Bimal Krishna Matilal (1935–1991), trained by Navya-Nyāya pandits in Calcutta and then at Harvard, where he came into contact with W. V. O. Quine, showed in a series of books that Indian logic and epistemology could be studied with the tools of analytic philosophy (Chapter 8). Epistemology, Logic, and Grammar in Indian Philosophical Analysis (1971) showed how Nyāya, Buddhist and grammatical theories of meaning and inference could be stated precisely and compared with modern logic (Matilal 1971). Perception (1986) reconstructed the long debate between Nyāya realists and Buddhist idealists and phenomenalists about whether we perceive external objects, and treated it as a contribution to the same problem that occupied Russell and his successors (Matilal 1986). The Word and the World (1990) did the same for the philosophy of language (Matilal 1990). In 1970 he founded the Journal of Indian Philosophy, which became the main international forum for such work. His later essays on the moral dilemmas of the Mahābhārata and on the ethics of the epics (Matilal 1989; Matilal 2002) argued that the epic’s refusal to give simple answers was itself a form of ethical thought, and that Indian ethics had been neglected because it was conducted in narrative rather than in treatises.

Matilal’s programme was sometimes criticised from two sides: by traditional scholars who felt that it translated the schools into an idiom that changed what they said, and by philosophers who felt that it treated Indian arguments as early versions of Western ones. Matilal’s answer was that every interpretation translates, and that the alternative — treating the texts as inaccessible or merely religious — denied their authors the respect due to fellow philosophers. His insistence that “mysticism” was the wrong category for most Indian philosophy, and that its rigour should be shown rather than asserted, shaped the work of his students and successors, including Jonardon Ganeri and Arindam Chakrabarti.

docs.title: 15.10 Is There an Indian Way of Thinking?
docs.text:
In a well-known essay, the poet and scholar A. K. Ramanujan asked whether there is “an Indian way of thinking”. He suggested that classical Indian culture tended to be “context-sensitive”, formulating rules for particular persons, places and times (as in the dharma of class and stage of life), where modern Western thought aspired to context-free universals, and that modern India was moving between the two (Ramanujan 1989). The essay is tentative and playful, and Ramanujan was careful to call his generalisation a tendency, not an essence. It is the kind of comparison this volume tries to make: a hypothesis about patterns, offered for testing against particular cases, rather than a claim about a fixed national mind.

Its question has received two very different kinds of answer since. One, associated with the critics of the previous sections, holds that there are Indian philosophers and Indian arguments but no Indian way of thinking, any more than there is a single European one; the search for a national mind repeats the Orientalist habit of describing civilisations by their essences. The other, associated with some recent writing in the “Indian Knowledge Systems” movement (Chapter 22), holds that Indian thought has a distinctive and unified character that colonial education obscured. Ramanujan’s own answer lay between them: patterns can be real without being essences, and the test of any such claim is whether it helps us read particular texts better.

docs.title: 15.11 Recent Directions
docs.text:
Since the end of the twentieth century the study of Indian philosophy has moved in several new directions. Jonardon Ganeri’s The Lost Age of Reason (2011) turned attention to the Navya-Nyāya philosophers of the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, above all Raghunātha Śiromaṇi of Navadvīpa, and argued that they had opened a “new reason” that broke with the authority of earlier masters in ways comparable to the early modern philosophers of Europe (Ganeri 2011). The work belongs to a wider recovery of the period immediately before colonial rule, which had often been dismissed as an age of mere commentary. The Dalit philosopher’s question about who is entitled to theorise experience, raised by Gopal Guru and Sundar Sarukkai (Chapter 14), has asked the profession to examine its own social composition. And the growth of “cross-cultural” or “fusion” philosophy abroad has made it common to use Indian arguments on contemporary problems of the self, consciousness and knowledge, sometimes without much concern for the history from which they came.

The public thinkers of the previous chapters have also become subjects of academic philosophy. Raghavan Iyer’s The Moral and Political Thought of Mahatma Gandhi (1973) treated Gandhi’s ideas of truth, non-violence, means and ends and individual conscience as a systematic political philosophy rather than as the sayings of a saint (Iyer 1973), and Bhikhu Parekh’s critical examination of his political philosophy did the same with greater scepticism (Parekh 1989) (Chapter 12). Later philosophers have read Gandhi’s refusal to generalise his own moral choices into rules for others as a distinctive account of moral judgement by example, and have taken Tagore’s arguments against nationalism and Ambedkar’s against caste as contributions to political theory. The boundary between “Indian philosophy” and “modern Indian thought” that the colonial university drew has thus become less sharp.

Within India, departments of philosophy have struggled for students and posts, and the gap between Sanskrit scholarship and university philosophy, which Saṃvāda tried to bridge, has in many places widened again. The movement for “Indian Knowledge Systems” has created new courses and funds, and has also revived the question that Bhattacharya posed a century ago: whether an inheritance can be made one’s own by celebration, or only by thinking it through.

Table 15.1. Some Indian academic philosophers of the twentieth century Philosopher Representative work Approach Surendranath Dasgupta (1887–1952) A History of Indian Philosophy (1922–1955) comprehensive history of the schools, including medicine M. Hiriyanna (1871–1950) Outlines of Indian Philosophy (1932) exposition of arguments; aesthetics K. C. Bhattacharya (1875–1949) The Subject as Freedom (1930) original metaphysics in dialogue with Kant and Vedānta; “swaraj in ideas” T. R. V. Murti (1902–1986) The Central Philosophy of Buddhism (1955) Madhyamaka as dialectic, compared with Kant Debiprasad Chattopadhyaya (1918–1993) Lokāyata (1959) materialist and Marxist recovery of suppressed traditions Daya Krishna (1924–2007) Indian Philosophy: A Counter Perspective (1991) critique of received pictures; dialogue with pandits J. N. Mohanty (1928–2013) Reason and Tradition in Indian Thought (1992) phenomenology; pramāṇa theory as the core B. K. Matilal (1935–1991) Perception (1986) analytic reconstruction of Indian epistemology and logic

docs.title: 15.12 Assessment
docs.text: Table 15.1 lists some of the philosophers discussed in this chapter. Their work refutes two common assumptions: that modern Indian philosophy consisted of Neo-Vedāntic apologetics, and that the only alternative to apologetics was imitation of the West. Bhattacharya’s alternation of standpoints, Chattopadhyaya’s materialism, Daya Krishna’s dialogues, Mohanty’s phenomenology and Matilal’s analysis were different ways of claiming the freedom in ideas that Bhattacharya had asked for. None of them treated the classical schools as a single wisdom to be admired; all of them treated the schools as arguments to be understood, tested and continued. That, more than any thesis about an Indian way of thinking, is their legacy for a volume on samanvaya.

docs.text:
