  • Frykenberg (2008): Christianity in India.

docs.title: Chapter 17: Muslim Thought in Modern India: Reformers, Revivalists and Their Critics
docs.text: inna llāha lā yughayyiru mā bi-qawmin ḥattā yughayyirū mā bi-anfusihim God does not change what is in a people until they change what is in themselves. — Qurʾān 13:11

docs.title: 17.1 Introduction
docs.text:
The Qurʾānic verse above was often quoted by the Muslim reformers of modern India. Thinkers of very different persuasions cited it to argue that the decline of Muslim power was not a divine decree but the consequence of Muslims’ own neglect, and that recovery depended on their own effort; they disagreed, often bitterly, about what that effort should be. This chapter is concerned with their arguments, and compares them with the Hindu, Sikh and anti-caste debates described elsewhere in this volume.

The movements themselves can be listed briefly. Shāh Walī Allāh of Delhi (Chapter 16), whose Persian Qurʾān let educated Muslims read scripture without depending on the ʿulamāʾ, left descendants and pupils who shaped Indian Islamic learning for a century. After the revolt of 1857, which ended the Mughal dynasty, the seminary founded at Deoband in 1866 trained ʿulamāʾ in a reformist curriculum; the followers of Aḥmad Riḍā Khān of Bareilly defended the veneration of the Prophet and the saints against it; Sayyid Ahmad Khan’s college at Aligarh (1875; a university from 1920) sought to combine Islamic loyalty with Western education; the Nadwat al-ʿUlamāʾ at Lucknow (1894) attempted a middle path; the Aḥmadiyya movement (1889) made claims about its founder that most Muslims rejected; the Tablīghī Jamāʿat (1926) began a lay preaching movement; and Mawdūdī founded the Jamāʿat-i Islāmī (1941) to work for an Islamic state (Figure 9.1). These movements did not form a single “Muslim response”; they disagreed with one another about law, devotion, education and politics as sharply as Hindu reformers did. During the Khilafat movement of 1919–24, when Indian Muslims campaigned to defend the Ottoman caliphate, many of them joined Gandhi’s Non-Cooperation Movement in the most extensive Hindu–Muslim political cooperation of the colonial period; its collapse was followed by a decade of communal riots.

Four questions ran through the debates. The first concerned authority: whether Muslims should follow the established schools of law and their scholars (taqlīd, “imitation”), or return to the Qurʾān and the reports of the Prophet’s sayings and practice (ḥadīth) and reason from them afresh (ijtihād). The second concerned reason and revelation: how far the findings of modern science and history could require the reinterpretation of scripture. The third concerned the status of India itself after the loss of Muslim rule: a famous legal opinion of the early nineteenth century, attributed to Shāh ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz of Delhi, held that a land governed by Christians under their own law had ceased to be an “abode of Islam”, and the question of what Muslims owed to such a state, and later to a secular democracy in which they were a minority, was never settled. The fourth concerned women: their education, seclusion and rights under Islamic law. Aziz Ahmad’s survey, Ayesha Jalal’s study of the tension between individual and community, and Muhammad Qasim Zaman’s work on the ʿulamāʾ are the best guides (Ahmad 1967; Jalal 2000; Zaman 2002).

docs.title: 17.2 Aligarh: Reason, Nature and the Community
17.2.1 Sayyid Ahmad Khan as theologian
docs.text:
Sayyid Ahmad Khan (1817–1898), a former official of the Company, concluded after 1857 that Muslims must embrace Western education and science if they were to recover. The Muhammadan Anglo-Oriental College that he founded at Aligarh in 1875, which became Aligarh Muslim University in 1920, is usually remembered as an educational project, and so it was; David Lelyveld has shown that its purpose was as much to form a self-conscious Muslim gentry able to hold its own in colonial India as to teach Western knowledge (Lelyveld 1978). Behind the college lay a theology. After the revolt of 1857 Sayyid Ahmad wrote an essay on its causes, arguing that the government’s ignorance of its subjects’ feelings, not a Muslim conspiracy, had brought it about; from 1862 he published a commentary on the Bible, often described as the first by a Muslim, intended to show that Muslims and Christians shared more than either supposed. A visit to England in 1869–70 convinced him that Indian Muslims needed both a new education and a new theology, and on his return he founded the journal Tahzīb al-Akhlāq (“The Refinement of Morals”) to argue for both.

In his commentary on the Qurʾān he argued that the word of God (scripture) and the work of God (nature) cannot contradict each other, so that apparent conflicts between the Qurʾān and science must be resolved by reinterpretation. The principle, which parallels the rationalism of the Brahmo reformers in Bengal, led him further than most of his contemporaries were willing to go. He treated many traditional reports of the Prophet as historically unreliable, accepted only those that met strict criteria, interpreted the angels of scripture as natural forces and Satan as the evil disposition within human beings, and read the miracles in ways consistent with natural law. Christian Troll’s study shows that this was a reinterpretation of Muslim theology from within, using the methods of the classical commentators for new ends, not a simple adoption of European rationalism (Troll 1978). His followers were nicknamed nēcharī, “naturalists”, and the name stuck.

docs.title: 17.2.2 The Aligarh circle
docs.text:
Sayyid Ahmad’s associates developed his ideas in different directions. Chirāgh ʿAlī (1844–1895), an official of the Hyderabad state, argued in A Critical Exposition of the Popular “Jihád” (1885) that the wars of the Prophet had been defensive and that the Qurʾān did not command aggressive war, and in other works that Islamic law was not a closed code but could be reformed by the community. Altāf Ḥusain Ḥālī (1837–1914) wrote the most influential poem of the movement, the Musaddas (“The Flow and Ebb of Islam”, 1879), a lament in six-line stanzas for the greatness of early Islam and the decline of Indian Muslims, which ended in a call to education and effort (Shackle and Majeed 1997); in his Muqaddama-i Shiʿr-o-Shāʿirī (1893) he argued that Urdu poetry should turn from the artifice of the ghazal to the truthful description of nature and society. Nazīr Aḥmad (1831–1912) wrote novels for the instruction of Muslim girls, beginning with Mirʾāt al-ʿArūs (“The Bride’s Mirror”, 1869), which made the educated, capable housewife a model of reformed Muslim domesticity.

The movement’s most formidable critic from outside was Jamāl al-Dīn al-Afghānī (1838/39–1897), the itinerant pan-Islamic activist, who wrote a treatise against the nēcharīs in Persian while living in Hyderabad around 1881, later known in its Arabic version as the Refutation of the Materialists. He accused Sayyid Ahmad of dissolving religion into naturalism and of serving British interests by teaching Muslims to accept their rule. The exchange set a pattern that would recur: a reformer who sought accommodation with the colonial state was attacked both by the traditional ʿulamāʾ for his theology and by anti-colonial activists for his politics.

docs.title: 17.3 Shiblī Nuʿmānī and the Defence of Islamic History
docs.text:
Shiblī Nuʿmānī (1857–1914) taught Arabic and Persian at Aligarh from 1883 to 1898 and was close to Sayyid Ahmad and to the British orientalist Thomas Arnold, who taught there; but he came to disagree with the Aligarh programme. Where Sayyid Ahmad reinterpreted theology in the light of modern science, Shiblī sought to renew the classical scholarly tradition from within and to defend Islamic civilisation against the charges of its European critics. He wrote biographies of the great figures of early Islam — al-Fārūq, on the caliph ʿUmar, is the best known — and began the Sīrat al-Nabī, a multi-volume life of the Prophet completed after his death by his pupil Sayyid Sulaimān Nadvī. In essays on the library of Alexandria and on the poll-tax (jizya) he argued that European accusations against early Muslim rule rested on late and unreliable sources, and in ʿIlm al-Kalām and al-Kalām (1903–04) he proposed a new theology (kalām) that would answer modern objections as the classical theologians had answered those of their day. His history of Persian poetry, Shiʿr al-ʿAjam, remains a landmark of Urdu criticism.

From 1905 Shiblī directed studies at the Nadwat al-ʿUlamāʾ in Lucknow, which aimed to train scholars who knew both the religious sciences and something of modern learning, and he planned the academy of writers (Dār al-Muṣannifīn) at Azamgarh, founded in the year of his death, which continued his historical work. His career shows a third way between Aligarh and the traditional seminaries: modernisation through history and scholarship rather than through natural theology, and a confidence in the Islamic past that answered European contempt with evidence.

docs.title: 17.4 Deoband: Reform Through the ʿUlamāʾ
docs.text:
The seminary at Deoband (Chapter 16) is often contrasted with Aligarh as tradition against modernity. Barbara Metcalf’s study shows that it was itself a modern institution of reform (Metcalf 1982). Its founders, Muḥammad Qāsim Nānautavī (1832/33–1880) and Rashīd Aḥmad Gangohī (d. 1905), adopted the organisation of a British college — a fixed curriculum, examinations, a library, salaried teachers — and financed it not by grants from a ruler or by endowments but by annual contributions from ordinary believers, which made it independent of both the colonial state and the old aristocracy. Its scholars answered questions sent by Muslims all over India in legal opinions (fatwā), many of them printed, and so built up a body of practical guidance that reached far beyond the seminary. They taught that the law of the Ḥanafī school should be followed faithfully, and they attacked as innovations (bidʿa) many customs at saints’ shrines, extravagant weddings and death rites, and practices shared with Hindus. Nānautavī took part in public religious debates with Christian missionaries and Arya Samajists at religious fairs held at Chandapur near Shahjahanpur in the 1870s, a sign that the new public arena of print and debate shaped the ʿulamāʾ as much as it shaped the reformers they opposed.

The most widely read Deobandi work was written for women. Ashraf ʿAlī Thānawī (1863–1943) wrote the Bihishtī Zēwar (“Heavenly Ornaments”), first published in the early twentieth century, a comprehensive guide to belief, ritual, law, household management, letter-writing and health, intended to enable women to read and to practise their religion correctly without depending on custom (Metcalf 1990). It assumed that women and men had the same moral capacity and the same obligations to God, and it taught women to reject many customs that men regarded as harmless; it also took for granted seclusion and the authority of husbands. Metcalf reads it as a work that “perfected” women by making them reformed Muslims like men, a very different strategy from Rokeya’s (Chapter 14). It is still given to brides in many South Asian families.

In politics, many Deobandi scholars opposed British rule. Their association, the Jamʿiyyat-i ʿUlamāʾ-i Hind (1919), supported the Khilafat movement and then allied with the Congress against the demand for Pakistan, a choice whose theological defence is discussed below.

docs.title: 17.5 Devotion Defended: Barelwīs, Ahl-i Ḥadīth and Aḥmadīs
docs.text:
The Deobandi critique of shrine customs provoked a vigorous defence. Aḥmad Riḍā Khān of Bareilly (1856–1921), a prolific jurist and poet, defended the veneration of the Prophet as a being of light with knowledge of the unseen, the intercession of saints, the celebration of the Prophet’s birthday and the annual commemorations at saints’ tombs; he regarded these not as innovations but as expressions of love sanctioned by the tradition. In 1906 he obtained the endorsement of scholars in Mecca and Medina for a legal opinion declaring certain Deobandi leaders and Mirzā Ghulām Aḥmad to be unbelievers, and the bitterness between the two schools has lasted to the present. Usha Sanyal has shown that his movement was no less a modern reform than Deoband’s, using print, organisation and the training of scholars to define a “devotional Islam” that most South Asian Muslims recognised as their own (Sanyal 1996).

At the other extreme, the Ahl-i Ḥadīth (“People of the Ḥadīth”), led by scholars such as Nawāb Ṣiddīq Ḥasan Khān of Bhopal (1832–1890), rejected adherence to any of the four schools of law and insisted that every practice be justified directly from the Qurʾān and authenticated reports, a position close to that of the Wahhābīs of Arabia. And in the Punjab Mirzā Ghulām Aḥmad of Qadian (c. 1835–1908), who first became known for his defence of Islam against Christian and Arya Samaj polemic in the Barāhīn-i Aḥmadiyya (1880–84), went on to claim that he was the promised Messiah and Mahdī. His followers understood his status in different ways, and they divided in 1914 into the Qadian and Lahore branches; the Lahore branch regarded him as a renewer rather than a prophet. Yohanan Friedmann has shown how the Aḥmadī idea of a continuing, subordinate prophecy drew on medieval Sufi and theological sources (Friedmann 1989). Most other Muslims rejected the claim, and in Pakistan the Aḥmadīs were declared non-Muslims by constitutional amendment in 1974; in India they are a small community that regards itself as Muslim.

These disputes are sometimes treated as sectarian quarrels of no wider interest. They were in fact arguments about the same questions that divided Hindu reformers: the authority of custom against scripture, the place of saints and intermediaries, the continuity of revelation, and who had the right to interpret.

docs.title: 17.6 Preachers, Sufis and Poets
docs.text:
Not all the important movements of the period were led by theologians or politicians. In 1926 Mawlānā Muḥammad Ilyās (1885–1944), a scholar trained in the Deobandi tradition, began a movement of lay preaching among the Meos of Mewat, south of Delhi, a community that had kept many customs shared with its Hindu neighbours. His method was simple: groups of ordinary Muslims would leave home for a few days or weeks, at their own expense, to travel to other Muslims and invite them to the basic practices of prayer and remembrance, learning by teaching. The Tablīghī Jamāʿat that grew from this beginning deliberately avoided political questions and doctrinal controversy, and became, after partition, one of the largest Muslim movements in the world, with its centre still at the Nizamuddin quarter of Delhi. The most widespread form of Muslim revival in modern South Asia was thus pietist and apolitical, not Islamist.

Sufism, attacked by reformers of several kinds, also found modern spokesmen. The shrines of Delhi, Ajmer and many other places continued to draw pilgrims of every community (Chapter 22), and writers attached to them defended their customs in print against Deobandi and Ahl-i Ḥadīth criticism. A different path was taken by Hazrat Inayat Khan (1882–1927), a musician of Baroda initiated into the Chishtī order, who travelled to the United States in 1910 and spent the rest of his life teaching in Europe and America. He presented Sufism as a universal path of love, harmony and beauty, open to members of every religion and not bound to the observance of Islamic law, and founded an order for his Western followers. His universalism, like Vivekananda’s Vedānta, was a modern reformulation for a Western audience, and it had a similar double reception: admired abroad as the essence of a tradition, and regarded by many in that tradition as a departure from it.

The poets who had served the Aligarh movement were followed by poets and writers who rejected religious authority altogether. In 1932 four young writers, among them Sajjad Zaheer and Rashid Jahan, published Angāre (“Embers”), a collection of Urdu stories that satirised the hypocrisy of clerics and the seclusion of women; it provoked protests and was banned by the government of the United Provinces in the following year. Its authors were among the founders of the Progressive Writers’ Association, whose first conference at Lucknow in 1936 was presided over by Premchand. The progressive writers, Muslim and non-Muslim, made Urdu literature a vehicle of socialist and secular thought for a generation, and they stand at the beginning of the secular Muslim voices discussed below.

docs.title: 17.7 Regional Voices: Bengal and Kerala
docs.text:
Most accounts of modern Indian Islam are written from the Urdu-speaking north, where the great seminaries, Aligarh and the political leadership were concentrated. But most Indian Muslims lived elsewhere, and the regional languages produced debates of their own. In Bengal, where Muslims formed a majority of the population, a Bengali Muslim literature grew up in the late nineteenth century; Mir Mosharraf Hossain’s Biṣād Sindhu (“The Ocean of Sorrow”, 1885–91), a prose epic on the martyrdom of Ḥusain at Karbala, showed that Islamic sacred history could be told in the literary Bengali shaped largely by Hindu writers. Kazi Nazrul Islam (1899–1976), the “rebel poet”, wrote both Islamic devotional songs and songs to the goddess Kālī, attacked religious hypocrisy in Hindus and Muslims alike, and became after 1971 the national poet of Bangladesh; his work is the most vivid example in the twentieth century of a Muslim writer who used the whole religious vocabulary of his region without surrendering his own.

In 1926 a group of Muslim teachers and students of the new University of Dhaka, among them Abul Hussain and Kazi Abdul Wadud, formed the Muslim Sāhitya Samāj (“Muslim Literary Society”) and published the journal Śikhā. Their programme, which they called the emancipation of the intellect (buddhir mukti), asked Bengali Muslims to judge custom and religious authority by reason and to take part in a common Bengali culture of letters. The movement was small and met the hostility of religious leaders, but it was an early statement of the rationalist and linguistic Bengali Muslim identity that later shaped the politics of East Pakistan and Bangladesh.

In Kerala, where Islam had arrived by sea and the Māppiḷa community spoke Malayalam (Chapter 16), reform took a different course. Sanāullāh Makti Taṅṅaḷ (1847–1912) answered Christian missionary polemic in Malayalam, and Vakkom Abdul Khadir Maulavi (1873–1932) founded the newspaper Svadēśābhimāni (1905), later famous for its criticism of the Travancore government under its editor K. Ramakrishna Pillai, and campaigned for modern and religious education, for the use of Malayalam in religious instruction and against customs he regarded as un-Islamic. The reform associations that followed from the 1920s combined Islamic reform with the movement for education and social uplift that was transforming Kerala society as a whole, and they show the same pattern as Narayana Guru’s movement among the Ezhavas (Chapter 14): religious reform as a path to modern education and public life.

docs.title: 17.8 Boundaries Drawn in Court: The Khojas and the Aga Khan Case
docs.text:
The questions of identity that the reformers argued in print were sometimes settled in the colonial courts, and one case shows the process with unusual clarity. The Khojas, a trading community of Gujarat, Kutch and Sindh, had for centuries followed the Satpanth (“true path”), a tradition of devotional hymns (ginān) in Gujarati, Sindhi and related languages attributed to Ismāʿīlī preachers (pīr). The gināns expressed the teaching of the Shīʿa Imām in the vocabulary of the region; one of them, the Dasa Avatāra, presented the Imām ʿAlī as the tenth avatāra of Viṣṇu, completing the series that Hindu tradition expected. Many Khoja families also followed Hindu customs of inheritance.

When the first Aga Khan, Ḥasan ʿAlī Shāh, the hereditary Imām of the Nizārī Ismāʿīlīs, settled in Bombay in the 1840s and claimed the community’s allegiance and dues, a group of Khojas resisted, arguing that they had always been Sunnī Muslims. In 1866 Justice Joseph Arnould of the Bombay High Court decided the case in the Aga Khan’s favour: relying largely on the gināns, he held that the Khojas were and always had been Shīʿa Imāmī Ismāʿīlīs, owing allegiance to the Aga Khan as their Imām. Teena Purohit has argued that the judgment fixed a single religious identity on a community whose practice had been plural, and that it read a local, vernacular Islam through the categories of Middle Eastern sectarian history (Purohit 2012); other historians have shown that divergent practices, especially in inheritance, persisted long afterwards. Some Khojas became Sunnī or Ithnāʿasharī (Twelver) Shīʿa, and the Ismāʿīlī community under the third Aga Khan, Sulṭān Muḥammad Shāh (1877–1957), developed its own institutions of education and welfare and a modern constitution. The case is a parallel to the Singh Sabha debates over Sikh identity (Chapter 16) and to the census classifications described in Chapter 8: in each, a colonial institution asked a community to state what it had always been, and the answer changed the community.

docs.title: 17.9 Women’s Rights in Muslim Reform
docs.text:
Muslim reformers, like Hindu ones, debated the education and status of women, and here too the most radical positions came from unexpected quarters. Sayyid Mumtāz ʿAlī (1860–1935), a scholar trained in the religious sciences, wrote Ḥuqūq-i Niswāṅ (“The Rights of Women”, published in 1898), which argued from the Qurʾān and the law that men were not superior to women, that the seclusion practised in India went beyond what scripture required, and that women were entitled to education, to choice in marriage and to the rights that the law gave them over property and divorce. According to Gail Minault’s account, Sayyid Ahmad Khan, shown the manuscript, was so disturbed by it that he tore it up, and Mumtāz ʿAlī published it only after the older man’s death. With his wife, Muḥammadī Bēgam, he founded in the same year Tahzīb-i Niswāṅ, a weekly for women that ran for decades (Minault 1998).

Minault shows a spectrum of positions among the reformers of women’s education, from Nazīr Aḥmad’s capable housewife and Thānawī’s reformed believer to Mumtāz ʿAlī’s equality under scripture and the schools founded by reforming couples and by women themselves, such as the school for girls at Aligarh founded in 1906 by Shaikh Abdullah and Wahid Jahan Begum, which grew into a women’s college, and Rokeya’s school in Calcutta. As with the Hindu reformers and the women writers (Chapter 14), the decisive questions were who was to define women’s proper knowledge, and whether reform meant a return to scripture, an accommodation with custom or a challenge to both.

docs.title: 17.10 Muhammad Iqbal: The Self and the Reconstruction of Religious Thought
docs.text:
Muhammad Iqbal (1877–1938), born in Sialkot in Punjab, studied philosophy at Cambridge and in Germany, where he wrote a dissertation on the development of metaphysics in Persia (1908). In Urdu and Persian poetry he became the leading voice of Indian Muslims; his early poem “Tarāna-e-Hind” (1904), beginning sāre jahāṃ se acchā hindostāṃ hamārā, is still sung in India. His Persian poems, notably Asrār-i Khudī (“The Secrets of the Self”, 1915), developed a philosophy of the self (khudī) as a creative, striving individuality, against what he saw as the passive, self-annihilating mysticism of later Sufism and the Vedāntic doctrine of the illusory self (Chapter 4). In lectures delivered in Madras, Hyderabad and Aligarh in 1928–29 and published as The Reconstruction of Religious Thought in Islam, he engaged with Bergson, Whitehead, Nietzsche and modern physics in an attempt to reformulate Islamic theology for the modern age, arguing for the principle of independent reasoning (ijtihād) (Iqbal 1934). His presidential address to the Muslim League at Allahabad in 1930, proposing a consolidated Muslim state in north-western India, made him a founding figure of the idea of Pakistan.

Iqbal was one of the most original philosophers of modern India, whose engagement with European thought paralleled and rivalled that of Aurobindo and Radhakrishnan, and his rejection of the Vedāntic dissolution of the self, made from within a South Asian Islamic tradition, shows that Neo-Vedānta’s harmony of religions was not accepted by all Indians. His politics drew him into the debate about the nation that is the subject of the next section.

docs.title: 17.11 Composite Nationalism and Its Critics
docs.text:
The most consequential Muslim debate of the late colonial period concerned the nation. Maulana Abul Kalam Azad (1888–1958), a religious scholar and journalist who was twice president of the Congress and became independent India’s first Minister of Education, argued in his Urdu commentary on the Qurʾān, Tarjumān al-Qurʾān (1930s), that the essential teaching of all prophets was the same — belief in one God and righteous action — and that the religions differed in law and ritual rather than in their core. His “unity of religion” was argued from within the Qurʾānic tradition, not from Vedānta, and it shows that Indian ideas of religious harmony had Islamic as well as Hindu sources. In politics he moved from the pan-Islamism of his journal al-Hilāl (from 1912) to a lifelong defence of a united India in which Muslims were full partners. He is remembered for declaring, at a special session of the Congress in 1923, that Hindu–Muslim unity mattered more to him than the immediate gift of self-rule, and in his presidential address to the Congress at Ramgarh in 1940 he described the Muslim inheritance as an inseparable part of a common Indian nationality built up over a thousand years.

The theological case for this position was made by Ḥusain Aḥmad Madanī (1879–1957), from 1927 the senior teacher of ḥadīth at Deoband and later president of the Jamʿiyyat-i ʿUlamāʾ-i Hind. In Muttaḥida Qaumiyat aur Islām (“Composite Nationalism and Islam”, 1938) he argued that a qaum, a nation, could be formed by a shared homeland, and was not the same as the millat, the community of faith; Muslims could therefore belong to a territorial Indian nation together with Hindus and others while remaining fully Muslim in religion. He found a precedent in the compact by which the Prophet at Medina had joined the Muslims and the Jewish tribes of the city in a single political community. Barbara Metcalf’s study shows that Madanī’s nationalism was grounded not in secularism but in an Islamic understanding of a plural polity, in which Muslims would be free to follow their law (Metcalf 2009).

Iqbal, by then the leading intellectual voice of Muslim separatism, attacked Madanī’s view in Persian verses in which he accused him of not understanding the faith if he taught that nations were made by homelands. A mutual acquaintance, Ṭālūt, intervened by correspondence; Madanī explained that he had described the political facts, not prescribed a religious ideal, and Iqbal, shortly before his death in April 1938, publicly withdrew his personal criticism while maintaining his view that Islam could not be subordinated to territorial nationalism. The exchange is one of the clearest statements on both sides of the argument that ended in partition, and it shows that Muslim opposition to Pakistan, like Muslim support for it, was argued in Islamic terms.

docs.title: 17.12 The Two-Nation Argument
docs.text:
The argument that Madanī opposed had a history. In speeches of the 1880s Sayyid Ahmad Khan warned that representative institutions on the British model, in which a majority ruled, would place Muslims permanently under a Hindu majority, and he spoke of Hindus and Muslims as two “nations” with distinct interests, though he used the word loosely and also described them as the two eyes of a single India. The separate electorates introduced in 1909, after a Muslim deputation to the Viceroy at Simla in 1906 led by the Aga Khan, gave the idea of a distinct Muslim political community a legal form. Iqbal’s Allahabad address of 1930 (Section 17.10) proposed a consolidated Muslim state in the north-west within or outside the empire, and in 1933 the Cambridge student Choudhary Rahmat Ali coined the name “Pakistan”.

The decisive formulation came from Muhammad Ali Jinnah, a secular lawyer who had once been hailed as an ambassador of Hindu–Muslim unity. In his presidential address to the Muslim League at Lahore in March 1940, the session that adopted the resolution demanding independent states in the Muslim-majority regions, he argued that Hindus and Muslims belonged to two different religious philosophies, social customs and literatures, rarely intermarried or ate together, and drew their inspiration from different histories and heroes, so that to yoke them in a single state under a numerical majority would end in discontent and destruction. The argument was, in form, a theory of civilisations rather than of theology; Jinnah himself was no religious scholar. The ʿulamāʾ were divided: Madanī and most of the Jamʿiyyat-i ʿUlamāʾ-i Hind opposed him, while other Deobandi scholars, among them Thānawī and Shabbīr Aḥmad ʿUthmānī, supported the League; Mawdūdī rejected his secular leadership for different reasons. Historians continue to debate how far the Lahore resolution was a bargaining position for a federal settlement and how far a demand for full separation (Jalal 2000). For a volume on samanvaya, the two-nation argument is the starkest modern denial that the traditions of India could share a political home, and it was answered, on Islamic grounds, by Muslims as well as by others.

docs.title: 17.13 Mawdūdī and the Islamic State
docs.text:
A third position rejected nationalism of every kind. Abul Aʿlā Mawdūdī (1903–1979), born in Aurangabad and trained as a journalist and in the religious sciences largely by private study, first became known for al-Jihād fī al-Islām (serialised in 1927), a defence of the Islamic law of war against the charge that Islam was spread by the sword. From 1932 his monthly Tarjumān al-Qurʾān developed the ideas for which he is known. Islam, he argued, was not a private religion but a complete order of life (niẓām); sovereignty (ḥākimiyya) belonged to God alone, so that a state whose laws were made by human majorities, whether Indian or Muslim, set up humans as rivals to God; and the four key terms of the Qurʾān — God (ilāh), lord (rabb), worship (ʿibāda) and religion (dīn) — had to be understood in this comprehensive, political sense. On these grounds he opposed both the Congress’s composite nationalism and the Muslim League’s demand for a state of Muslims led by secular politicians. In 1941 he founded the Jamāʿat-i Islāmī at Lahore as a disciplined vanguard of the “Islamic revolution”; after partition he moved to Pakistan, where he campaigned for an Islamic constitution and developed the idea of a “theo-democracy” in which an elected government ruled within the limits of divine law (Nasr 1996).

Mawdūdī’s writings were translated into Arabic and read across the Muslim world, and they influenced the Egyptian thinker Sayyid Quṭb and later Islamist movements. Within South Asia his systematic and lucid prose made him one of the most widely read Muslim authors of the century. His critics, Muslim and non-Muslim, have argued that his conception of a total Islamic order was itself modern, closer to the ideologies of the twentieth century than to the plural legal and political practice of the Islamic past, and that it left no place for those who did not share it.

docs.title: 17.14 Critics of Political Islam and the Jamāʿat in Indian Democracy
docs.text:
The sharpest critique of Mawdūdī came from within his own movement. Mawlānā Waḥīduddīn Khān (1925–2021), for fifteen years a member of the Jamāʿat-i Islāmī Hind, corresponded with Mawdūdī in 1962–63 and then published Taʿbīr kī Ghalaṭī (“The Error of Interpretation”, 1963). He argued that Mawdūdī had inverted the order of the Qurʾān: by reading the faith as a political system he had made the state the goal of religion, whereas the Qurʾān’s centre was the individual’s relation to God, from which a just society might follow. He left the Jamāʿat, and over the following decades, through his monthly al-Risāla (from 1976) and many books, developed a theology of patience, dialogue and peace that urged Indian Muslims to give up the politics of grievance. The scholar Abul Ḥasan ʿAlī Nadwī (1914–1999), rector of the Nadwa, also criticised the political reading of Islam, while founding in 1974 a movement for goodwill between communities, Payām-i Insāniyat (“The Message of Humanity”).

The Jamāʿat itself changed. Reconstituted in India in 1948 as the Jamāʿat-i Islāmī Hind, it at first regarded participation in a secular state as illegitimate and forbade its members to vote. Irfan Ahmad has traced how, over the following decades, it came to accept secular democracy as the best available protection for Indian Muslims, permitted voting from the 1980s and eventually supported a political party of its own; he argues that participation in democratic politics transformed an Islamist movement more than the movement transformed politics (Ahmad 2009). The Indian case is one of the clearest examples of a revivalist organisation remade by the constitutional order it once rejected.

docs.title: 17.15 Secular and Liberal Voices After 1947
docs.text:
Independence and partition left Indian Muslims a much smaller minority, deprived of much of their educated leadership, and under suspicion of divided loyalty. Several thinkers tried to define a place for them in a secular republic. Mohammad Mujeeb (1902–1985), for a quarter of a century vice-chancellor of the Jamia Millia Islamia — the university founded in 1920 by nationalist Muslims who left Aligarh during the Non-Cooperation movement — wrote in The Indian Muslims (1967) a history that emphasised their roots in Indian society and their contributions to a shared culture (Mujeeb 1967). Asaf A. A. Fyzee (1899–1981), a jurist and scholar of Ismāʿīlī law, argued in A Modern Approach to Islam (1963) that the moral and spiritual teaching of Islam should be distinguished from the historical law built upon it, so that the law could be reformed while the faith was kept.

The most radical reformer was the Marathi writer Hamid Dalwai (1932–1977). In April 1966 he led seven women who had been divorced by unilateral repudiation (ṭalāq) to the government secretariat in Bombay to demand a reform of Muslim personal law, and in 1970 he founded at Pune the Muslim Satyashodhak Mandal, whose name deliberately recalled Phule’s Truth-Seekers’ Society (Chapter 14). Dalwai argued for a common civil code and for the secular reform of the community from within; he was attacked by religious leaders as an enemy of Islam and is now claimed by many Indian liberals as a pioneer. Asghar Ali Engineer (1939–2013), a reformer within the Dāʾūdī Bohra community, wrote extensively on communal violence and on the rights of women, arguing in The Rights of Women in Islam (1992) that the Qurʾān’s ethical intent favoured equality and that much of the law of marriage and divorce reflected the patriarchal societies in which it had been formulated (Engineer 1992). The controversy over the Shah Bano judgment of 1985 and the law that followed it (Volume 18, Rājanīti and Dharmaśāstra) showed how sharply these questions divided the community and how readily they became instruments of national politics. Mushirul Hasan’s study traces these post-independence debates (Hasan 1997).

docs.title: 17.16 Muslim and Hindu Reform Compared
docs.text:
The parallels between Muslim and Hindu reform in colonial India were noticed at the time, and Kenneth Jones’s survey treats them together (Jones 1989). Table 17.1 sets out some of them. The parallels arise from shared conditions — a colonial state that claimed neutrality in religion while classifying communities, missionary criticism, printing presses, English education and a new public sphere of journals and debates — rather than from imitation, and each tradition worked them out in its own vocabulary. The parallels also had a darker side: reformers on each side defined their communities more sharply against one another, and the competitive mobilisation of religious identities that resulted is part of the history of partition (Chapter 16).

Table 17.1. Some parallel positions in Hindu and Muslim reform, c. 1860–1970 Position Hindu examples Muslim examples Return to scripture against custom Arya Samaj (the Vedas alone) Deoband (the Ḥanafī law, purified of custom); Ahl-i Ḥadīth (Qurʾān and ḥadīth alone) Reason and science as the test of interpretation Brahmo Samaj; Vidyāsāgar Sayyid Ahmad Khan; Chirāgh ʿAlī Defence of devotional custom Sanātana Dharma associations Aḥmad Riḍā Khān and the Barelwīs Renewal through history and scholarship Bankimchandra’s Kṛṣṇacaritra; the Orientalist-trained historians Shiblī Nuʿmānī; the Nadwa Composite nationalism Gandhi; Nehru Azad; Ḥusain Aḥmad Madanī Religion as the basis of political community Savarkar’s Hindutva (a cultural nation) Mawdūdī (the sovereignty of God); Iqbal (a Muslim homeland) Social reform against religious authority Phule’s Satyashodhak Samaj Mumtāz ʿAlī; Hamid Dalwai’s Muslim Satyashodhak Mandal

The table simplifies, and several of its pairings are imperfect. Savarkar’s Hindutva was a theory of a cultural and territorial nation and did not require religious belief, while Mawdūdī rejected nationalism altogether in the name of divine sovereignty; they belong in the same row only because both made religion, in different senses, the basis of political belonging. The comparison is useful because it shows that “the Muslim response” to modernity was as plural as “the Hindu response”, and that the lines of disagreement within each community often ran parallel to those within the other.

docs.title: 17.17 Assessment
docs.text: Modern Indian Muslim thought produced, within a century, a natural theology (Sayyid Ahmad), a historical apologetics (Shiblī), a reform of the ʿulamāʾ (Deoband), a defence of devotional Islam (Aḥmad Riḍā Khān), a philosophy of the creative self (Iqbal), a theology of composite nationalism (Madanī), an Islamist ideology (Mawdūdī) and its critique from within (Waḥīduddīn Khān), and a secular reformism (Fyzee, Dalwai, Engineer). These positions were argued with the same seriousness, and against the same pressures, as the Hindu positions that dominate most accounts of modern Indian thought. A history of Indian ideas that omitted them would be not only incomplete but distorted, for many of the debates described in this volume — about the nation, about scripture and reason, about women, about the relation of religion to the state — were conducted on both sides at once, sometimes in conversation and sometimes in opposition.

docs.text:

  • Lelyveld (1978) and Troll (1978): Aligarh and Sayyid Ahmad Khan’s theology.

  • Metcalf (1982), Sanyal (1996) and Zaman (2002): Deoband, the Barelwīs and the ʿulamāʾ.

  • Metcalf (1990) and Minault (1998): women and Muslim reform.

  • Metcalf (2009) and Nasr (1996): Madanī and Mawdūdī.

  • Tareen (2020): the Deobandi and Barelwī debates about the Prophet.

  • Ahmad (2009) and Hasan (1997): Indian Muslims since independence.

docs.title: Chapter 18: Buddhism and Jainism in the Modern World
docs.text: vayadhammā saṅkhārā appamādena sampādethā All conditioned things are subject to decay. Strive on with diligence. — The last words of the Buddha, Mahāparinibbāna Sutta (Dīgha Nikāya 16)

docs.title: 18.1 Introduction
docs.text: Buddhism and Jainism are among India’s oldest living religious traditions, and both are treated historically in Volume 4. This chapter is concerned with their modern histories: the near-disappearance of Buddhism from India and its revival; the global spread of Buddhism and its encounter with Western science and psychology; the Ambedkarite conversion movement; and the modern life of the Jain community in India and abroad. Both traditions are frequently described in Hindu writing as “offshoots” or “reform movements” of Hinduism. Their adherents generally reject that description, and this chapter follows them in treating Buddhism and Jainism as independent traditions with their own histories.

docs.title: 18.2 The Decline and Rediscovery of Buddhism in India
18.2.1 Decline
docs.text: Buddhism flourished in India for some fifteen centuries after the Buddha. By the thirteenth century it had all but disappeared from most of the subcontinent, surviving mainly in the Himalayan regions and in small pockets elsewhere. Historians have proposed several causes, which probably worked together. Buddhism depended heavily on large monasteries supported by royal and merchant patronage, and lost that patronage as kings turned to Śaiva and Vaiṣṇava devotional religion. The devotional and tantric forms of Hinduism absorbed many Buddhist practices and figures, including the Buddha himself as an avatāra of Viṣṇu, and offered lay people religious resources that the monastic tradition did not. Brahmanical polemic and, in some regions, persecution played a part. Finally, the great monasteries of the east, already in decline, were destroyed in the course of the Turkish conquests: Nālandā was sacked around 1200 in the campaigns associated with Bakhtiyār Khaljī (c. 1193–1205), as was Vikramaśīla. The Tibetan pilgrim Dharmasvāmin, who visited Nālandā in 1234, found a few monks still teaching amid the ruins. Ambedkar emphasised Brahmanical hostility and the Muslim invasions; most historians now see a longer and more complex process (Omvedt 2003; Harvey 2013). Volume 4 discusses the evidence, and also corrects the popular myth that Nālandā’s library held “nine million” manuscripts, a figure for which there is no early source.

docs.title: 18.2.2 Rediscovery
docs.text: Buddhism’s Indian past was recovered in the nineteenth century largely by European scholars and by Buddhists from other Asian countries. James Prinsep’s decipherment of the Brāhmī script in 1837 made the edicts of Aśoka legible; Alexander Cunningham, first director of the Archaeological Survey of India (1861), used the travel records of the Chinese pilgrims Faxian and Xuanzang to identify the sites of the Buddha’s life. The Mahābodhi temple at Bodh Gaya was restored in the 1880s. Edwin Arnold’s poem on the life of the Buddha, The Light of Asia (1879), was a best-seller in Britain, America and India. Philip Almond has shown how Victorian Britain “discovered” Buddhism as a textual religion, often contrasting a pure, rational “original” Buddhism found in the Pali texts with the living Buddhism of Asia (Almond 1988).

docs.title: 18.2.3 Monuments and art
docs.text: The monuments of Indian Buddhism were rediscovered in the same period. The painted caves of Ajanta, abandoned for more than a millennium, were found in 1819 by a party of British officers hunting in the Waghora valley; copies of the paintings made in the following decades, many of them later destroyed by fire, brought them to international attention. The great stūpa at Sanchi, surveyed in 1818, was excavated carelessly and then restored under John Marshall, Director-General of the Archaeological Survey from 1902, who also excavated at Taxila and Sarnath and later at the Indus cities. The Gandhāra sculptures of the north-west, with their Greco-Roman features, fascinated colonial scholars, some of whom argued that Indian art owed its finest achievements to Greek influence — a view that Indian and other historians of art, including Coomaraswamy, later contested by tracing the independent development of the Buddha image at Mathurā (Chapter 21). The archaeological recovery of Buddhist India had political consequences too: the Aśokan lion capital excavated at Sarnath in 1905 became the emblem of the Indian republic.

docs.title: 18.2.4 Anagārika Dharmapāla
docs.text: The Sri Lankan reformer Anagārika Dharmapāla (1864–1933), inspired partly by the Theosophists Blavatsky and Olcott, founded the Maha Bodhi Society in 1891 and campaigned for the return of Bodh Gaya, then controlled by a Hindu abbot, to Buddhist management. He spoke at the Chicago Parliament of 1893 alongside Vivekananda. The dispute over Bodh Gaya lasted more than half a century; the Bodh Gaya Temple Act of 1949 placed the temple under a committee of four Buddhists and four Hindus, with the district magistrate as chairman. Dharmapāla’s Buddhism was an example of what David McMahan calls “Buddhist modernism”: a reformulation of the tradition that emphasised its rationality, its compatibility with science, its ethics and its meditation, and played down ritual, cosmology and the supernatural (McMahan 2008).

docs.title: 18.3 Buddhism in Modern India
docs.text:
The 2011 census recorded about 8.4 million Buddhists in India, about 0.7 per cent of the population. Three groups account for most of them.

Ambedkarite Buddhists.

The largest group, concentrated in Maharashtra, consists of Dalits who followed B. R. Ambedkar into Buddhism at Nagpur on 14 October 1956 and in the conversions that have continued since (Chapter 12). Their Buddhism, often called Navayāna, is centred on Ambedkar’s The Buddha and His Dhamma, on the twenty-two vows he administered and on the anniversary of the conversion, celebrated at the Dīkṣābhūmi in Nagpur. It is a Buddhism of social liberation and dignity, critical of Hinduism and of caste, and it has produced a vigorous literature and political movement (Omvedt 2003; Zelliot 1992).

Ambedkarite Buddhism has its own festivals, pilgrimages and literature. Every year on the anniversary of the conversion, hundreds of thousands of people gather at the Dīkṣābhūmi in Nagpur, and on 6 December, the anniversary of Ambedkar’s death, at his memorial in Mumbai. Dalit Buddhist writers in Marathi — poets such as Namdeo Dhasal and autobiographers such as Daya Pawar — made Buddhism a literary as well as a religious identity. The movement has also produced debates within itself: about the relation of Ambedkar’s Navayāna to the Theravāda and Mahāyāna traditions of other countries, about ritual and monasticism, and about the relation between religious conversion and political mobilisation. It has spread beyond Maharashtra, to Dalit communities in Uttar Pradesh, Punjab, Karnataka and elsewhere, and to the diaspora.

Himalayan and Tibetan Buddhists.

The Buddhist communities of Ladakh, Sikkim, Arunachal Pradesh and other Himalayan regions belong to the Tibetan traditions. After the Chinese takeover of Tibet and the flight of the Fourteenth Dalai Lama in 1959, India gave refuge to many thousands of Tibetans; the Dalai Lama’s government in exile is based at Dharamsala in Himachal Pradesh, and Tibetan monasteries have been re-established in Karnataka and elsewhere. India thus became a centre of Tibetan Buddhist learning.

The Vipassanā movement.

S. N. Goenka (1924–2013), born in Burma to an Indian family and trained by the Burmese lay teacher Sayagyi U Ba Khin, began teaching ten-day silent retreats in India in 1969 and established the centre Dhamma Giri at Igatpuri, Maharashtra. His non-sectarian presentation of Theravāda insight meditation spread throughout India and the world, attracting many people who would not call themselves Buddhists.

The modern Indian state has also used the Buddhist heritage. The Aśokan lion capital became the state emblem and the Dharma wheel appears on the national flag. A new Nālandā University was established by Act of Parliament in 2010 near the ancient site, with the support of several East Asian governments, and began teaching in 2014. India’s diplomatic outreach to Buddhist Asia draws on the pilgrimage sites of Bodh Gaya, Sarnath, Kushinagar and (across the border in Nepal) Lumbini.

docs.title: 18.3.1 Buddhist studies in modern India
docs.text: The modern study of Buddhism in India owes much to Indian scholar-monks and laymen as well as to Europeans. Dharmanand Kosambi (1876–1947), a Goan Brahmin who learned Pali in Sri Lanka, where he entered the Buddhist order, and later lived as a monk in Burma, taught Pali at Calcutta, Pune and Harvard, edited Buddhaghosa’s Visuddhimagga for the Harvard Oriental Series, and wrote in Marathi on the Buddha’s life and on non-violence; his son was the historian D. D. Kosambi. The monk Jagdish Kashyap (1908–1976) founded the Nava Nalanda Mahavihara near the ancient site in 1951 and directed the publication of the Pali canon in Devanāgarī script, making it accessible to Indian readers for the first time in centuries. The Vipassana Research Institute at Igatpuri later produced an electronic edition of the canon based on the Burmese Sixth Council text. These efforts show that the “rediscovery” of Buddhism in India was not only a colonial enterprise but also an Indian and Asian one.

docs.title: 18.3.2 Buddhism, Hinduism and the avatāra question
docs.text: Relations between modern Buddhists and Hindus have often turned on a single question: is the Buddha an avatāra of Viṣṇu? From about the sixth century CE several Purāṇas include the Buddha among Viṣṇu’s descents, sometimes with the explanation that he came to mislead the wicked with false doctrine, sometimes as a teacher of compassion and non-violence; Jayadeva’s Gītagovinda (twelfth century) praises him for abolishing animal sacrifice. Many modern Hindus regard the doctrine as a sign of respect and of the unity of Indian traditions. Many Buddhists regard it as an act of absorption that denies the independence of their tradition. Among the twenty-two vows that Ambedkar administered at Nagpur in 1956 was a refusal to believe that the Buddha was an incarnation of Viṣṇu, and Ambedkarite Buddhists regard the doctrine as part of the process by which Buddhism was erased in India. The disagreement is a clear instance of the inclusivism discussed in Chapter 1: a gesture of inclusion from one side can be an act of appropriation from the other.

docs.title: 18.3.3 Women in modern Buddhism
docs.text: The order of fully ordained nuns (bhikkhunī) died out in the Theravāda countries many centuries ago and was never established in Tibet, although it survived in China, Korea, Taiwan and Vietnam. Since the late twentieth century, Buddhist women and their supporters have worked to restore it. An ordination of Sri Lankan women held at Sarnath in 1996 with the assistance of Korean nuns and monks was one of the first steps in a revival that has since spread in Sri Lanka and elsewhere, though it remains contested by conservative monastic authorities in several countries. India, as the land where the Buddha first admitted women to the order, has thus again become a site of debate about the tradition’s treatment of women.

docs.title: 18.4.1 The traditions
docs.text:
Buddhism spread from India across Asia in three broad streams (Table 18.1). Theravāda, “the teaching of the elders”, using the Pali canon, was established in Sri Lanka by the third century BCE (by tradition through the mission of Aśoka’s son Mahinda) and later became dominant in Myanmar, Thailand, Laos and Cambodia. Mahāyāna Buddhism reached China in the first centuries CE along the trade routes of Central Asia, and from China passed to Korea, Japan and Vietnam, where it developed schools such as Chan (Zen), Pure Land, Tiantai and Huayan. The tantric Buddhism of the late Indian monasteries (Vajrayāna) was transmitted to Tibet from the eighth century onwards, and from Tibet to Mongolia. The word “Hīnayāna” (“lesser vehicle”), used polemically in Mahāyāna texts for the older schools, is now generally avoided. Estimates of the number of Buddhists in the world are uncertain because of the overlap of Buddhist, Confucian, Daoist and Shinto practice in East Asia; the Pew Research Center’s estimate for 2010 was about 490 million.

docs.title: 18.4.2 South Asian Buddhism beyond India
docs.text:
Two South Asian Buddhist communities outside India are of particular interest for the history traced in this chapter. In the Kathmandu valley of Nepal, the Newar Buddhists preserved a Sanskrit-based Mahāyāna and Vajrayāna tradition continuously from the period of the great Indian monasteries. Their householder priests (vajrācārya), married and hereditary rather than celibate, perform rituals in Sanskrit, and their libraries preserved many Sanskrit Buddhist manuscripts lost in India; it was from Nepal that the British resident Brian Houghton Hodgson sent Sanskrit Buddhist texts to Calcutta, London and Paris in the 1820s and 1830s, enabling Eugène Burnouf’s pioneering study of Indian Buddhism (1844). In the twentieth century Theravāda missionaries from Sri Lanka and Burma established a reform movement among Newars, so that both forms of Buddhism now coexist in the valley.

Bhutan, the only state in which a form of Tibetan Buddhism (the Drukpa Kagyu school) is the state religion, has drawn international attention for its policy of “Gross National Happiness”, a phrase associated with its fourth king in the 1970s and later developed into a set of indicators of well-being. The policy is often described as an application of Buddhist values to economics; observers have also noted the expulsion of many Nepali-speaking Lhotshampa residents from southern Bhutan in the early 1990s, which shows that the ideal and the practice of a Buddhist state can diverge, as they did in the reign of Aśoka.

docs.title: 18.4.3 Buddhism in the West
docs.text: Buddhism entered Western intellectual life through scholarship in the nineteenth century and through Asian teachers and Western converts in the twentieth. D. T. Suzuki’s writings popularised Zen; the Beat writers Jack Kerouac, Allen Ginsberg and Gary Snyder drew on it; Japanese and Tibetan teachers founded centres in America and Europe; and the Vietnamese monk Thich Nhat Hanh (1926–2022), exiled in France, developed an “engaged Buddhism” that applied mindfulness and compassion to social and political action (Queen and King 1996). Engaged Buddhism also took other forms in Asia, among them the Sarvodaya movement of Sri Lanka, which drew on Gandhi, and the Ambedkarite movement in India.

docs.title: 18.4.4 Buddhism and science
docs.text:
Since the late nineteenth century, Buddhist modernists have presented Buddhism as the religion most compatible with science, because it rejects a creator god, emphasises causation and invites investigation. The Fourteenth Dalai Lama has made dialogue with scientists a central part of his work. The Mind and Life Institute, founded in 1987 by the Dalai Lama, the lawyer and entrepreneur Adam Engle and the neuroscientist Francisco Varela, has organised dialogues with physicists, psychologists and neuroscientists and supported research on meditation. In The Universe in a Single Atom (2005), the Dalai Lama wrote that if science conclusively disproved a Buddhist claim, Buddhists should abandon the claim, and gave as his example the Meru-centred cosmology of the Abhidharma (Chapter 3) (Dalai Lama XIV 2005). Research on the effects of meditation is discussed in Chapter 20.

Donald Lopez has traced the long history of claims that Buddhism is “scientific”, from nineteenth-century Asian reformers and Western Theosophists to modern neuroscience, and has shown how much each version reshaped Buddhism to fit the science of its day (Lopez 2008). His critique does not imply that the dialogue is worthless; it implies that it should be conducted without the assumption that the tradition must turn out to have been right all along.

docs.title: 18.4.5 Recovering the Indian Buddhist heritage
docs.text: Much of the Sanskrit literature of Indian Buddhism had been lost in India and survived only in Tibetan and Chinese translation, or in manuscripts carried to Nepal and Tibet. In the 1930s the scholar and traveller Rahul Sankrityayan (1893–1963; Section 18.6) made several journeys to Tibet and brought back photographs of Sanskrit manuscripts of important Buddhist works, including texts of the logician Dharmakīrti, that were thought to be lost. After 1959 the Tibetan exile community made India once again a centre of Buddhist learning: the Central Institute of Higher Tibetan Studies at Sarnath (founded in 1967, now a university) and the Library of Tibetan Works and Archives at Dharamsala (1970) teach and preserve the tradition, and Tibetan scholars have collaborated with Indian ones to translate lost Sanskrit works back from Tibetan.

docs.title: 18.4.6 Buddhist philosophy in world philosophy
docs.text: Buddhist philosophy has become one of the most active fields of cross-cultural philosophy. Nāgārjuna’s arguments for emptiness have been compared with Wittgenstein, Derrida and contemporary anti-realism; the Yogācāra analysis of consciousness with phenomenology; Dharmakīrti’s epistemology with modern theories of perception and inference; and the Buddhist denial of a self with debates about personal identity initiated by Derek Parfit. Jay Garfield’s translation of Nāgārjuna’s Mūlamadhyamakakārikā, published as The Fundamental Wisdom of the Middle Way, with a philosophical commentary, and Mark Siderits’s introduction, are examples of this work (Nāgārjuna 1995; Siderits 2007). Here, as elsewhere, the most fruitful comparisons are between particular arguments rather than between “Buddhism” and “the West”.

docs.title: 18.4.7 Buddhism and nationalism
docs.text: Modern Buddhism is not only a religion of peace and meditation. In Sri Lanka and Myanmar, Buddhist nationalist movements, some led by monks, have supported violence against Tamil, Muslim and Rohingya minorities. These movements are a reminder, parallel to the Hindu examples discussed in Chapter 7, that no tradition’s ideals guarantee the conduct of those who claim them.

docs.title: 18.5.1 The community
docs.text: The 2011 census recorded about 4.5 million Jains in India, concentrated in Gujarat, Rajasthan, Maharashtra, Madhya Pradesh and Karnataka; there are significant communities abroad, in Britain, North America and East Africa. The community is divided between the Śvetāmbara (“white-clad”) and Digambara (“sky-clad”) traditions, which differ on the nudity of monks, the possibility of liberation for women and the authority of the canon; the Śvetāmbaras are further divided into image-worshipping (mūrtipūjaka) and non-image-worshipping (Sthānakavāsī and Terāpanthī) traditions. Most Jains are lay people, many of them in commerce; monks and nuns, though few, are central to the community’s religious life. John Cort’s study of Jain lay and monastic values in Gujarat and Jeffery Long’s introduction are good guides (Cort 2001; Long 2009). The Government of India recognised the Jains as a national minority community in 2014.

docs.title: 18.5.2 Monks, nuns and the question of women
docs.text: The ascetic community remains the centre of Jain religious life. Among the Śvetāmbaras, nuns substantially outnumber monks; they preach, teach and travel on foot like their male counterparts, though they are formally subordinate to monks. The Digambara tradition has historically held that a woman cannot attain liberation in a female body, since liberation requires complete nudity and women cannot practise it; Digambara women may become renunciants of a lower grade (āryikā). The question of the liberation of women (strīmukti) was debated between the two traditions in medieval philosophical texts, the Śvetāmbaras affirming that women can be liberated and that the nineteenth Tīrthaṅkara, Mallī, was a woman (Jaini 1979; Dundas 2002). The debate is one of the most interesting cases in Indian thought of a philosophical argument conducted explicitly about gender.

docs.title: 18.5.3 Jain identity and the law
docs.text: The legal position of the Jains illustrates the problem of classification that runs through this volume. Under Article 25 of the Constitution, for the purpose of laws on religious institutions, “Hindus” is defined to include “persons professing the Sikh, Jaina or Buddhist religion”, and the Hindu Code laws of the 1950s applied to Jains, Buddhists and Sikhs. Many Jains objected that this treated them as a Hindu sect. The question of whether they should be recognised as a minority community was contested in the courts and in state legislation for decades before the central government’s notification of 2014. Jains themselves have been divided: some emphasise their distinct identity, others their close social and family ties with Hindu merchant communities, with whom intermarriage has been common in some regions.

docs.title: 18.5.4 Libraries and learning
docs.text: Jain communities were among the great preservers of Indian manuscripts. From the medieval period, monks and wealthy lay patrons maintained libraries (jñāna bhaṇḍāra) attached to temples and monasteries, notably at Patan and Cambay in Gujarat and at Jaisalmer in Rajasthan, where palm-leaf and paper manuscripts were copied, stored in sealed rooms and protected from damp and insects. These collections preserved not only Jain canonical and philosophical works but also Brahmanical and Buddhist texts on logic, poetics, grammar and other sciences, some of which survive nowhere else. Jain scholars were prolific authors in Sanskrit, Prakrit and the regional languages: Hemacandra (1088/89–1172), at the court of the Caulukya kings of Gujarat, wrote on grammar, lexicography, poetics, logic and Jain doctrine and composed a universal history of the Jain heroes. In the twentieth century, the Jain monks Muni Puṇyavijaya and Muni Jinavijaya catalogued and edited many of these collections, and Jain foundations continue to support manuscript conservation. The history of Indian learning as a whole owes much to these libraries.

docs.title: 18.5.5 Modern Jain figures
docs.text: Jainism’s modern history includes figures who made it known beyond the community. The German Indologist Hermann Jacobi (1850–1937), who translated Jain canonical texts for The Sacred Books of the East, established that Jainism was an independent tradition and not, as earlier European scholars had supposed, an offshoot of Buddhism. Virchand Gandhi (1864–1901) represented the Jains at the Chicago Parliament of 1893 and lectured in America and Britain. Śrīmad Rājacandra (1867–1901), a Jain jeweller, poet and mystic, was one of the strongest influences on the young M. K. Gandhi (Chapter 12). In 1949 Ācārya Tulsī, head of the Terāpanthī order, launched the Aṇuvrata movement, which invited people of every religion to adopt small vows of non-violence and honesty in daily life.

docs.title: 18.5.6 Temples, pilgrimage and festivals
docs.text: Jain religious life centres on temples and pilgrimage as well as on ascetic teachers. The temple-cities on the hills of Śatruñjaya near Palitana in Gujarat and Girnar near Junagadh, the marble temples of Dilwara at Mount Abu (eleventh to thirteenth centuries) and the great four-faced temple at Ranakpur in Rajasthan (fifteenth century) are among the finest monuments of Indian architecture, built largely with the donations of merchant families. Digambara pilgrims travel to Shravanabelagola in Karnataka, where the colossal monolithic image of Bāhubali, erected in the late tenth century, is anointed in a great ceremony (mahāmastakābhiṣeka) roughly every twelve years, and to Sammeta Śikhara in Jharkhand, the hill of the Tīrthaṅkaras’ liberation (Chapter 3). The festival of Paryuṣaṇa (for Digambaras, Daśalakṣaṇa), held during the rainy season, is a period of fasting, scripture reading and confession that ends with the asking and granting of forgiveness among family, friends and community. These practices show that Jainism, often described abroad only through its doctrines of non-violence and many-sidedness, is also a richly ritual and devotional religion (Cort 2001).

docs.title: 18.5.7 Jains abroad
docs.text: Gujarati Jain traders settled in East Africa from the late nineteenth century, and after the expulsions and emigrations of the 1960s and 1970s many moved to Britain; others emigrated to North America from the 1960s. Diaspora communities have built temples — often shared between Śvetāmbara and Digambara worshippers, and sometimes housing images of several traditions in one building — and have adapted Jain practice to new circumstances, for example by emphasising the tradition’s ethical and environmental teachings for a generation brought up outside India. Long’s and Cort’s studies discuss these developments (Long 2009; Cort 2001).

docs.title: 18.5.8 Jain ethics and modern concerns
docs.text: Jain ideas have entered modern conversations in three main areas. Jain non-violence and vegetarianism have influenced animal-welfare and environmental movements; Jain institutions run hospitals for birds and animals (pāñjrāpoḷ), and Jain scholars have presented the tradition as an ecological ethic, a presentation that is partly a modern interpretation of an ethic originally directed at the soul’s liberation. The doctrine of many-sidedness (anekāntavāda) has been presented as a philosophy of tolerance and dialogue; Chapter 7 noted that it was classically also a technique of debate. And the practice of fasting to death (sallekhanā) has raised legal and ethical questions about the right to die. In each case the modern presentation adapts an old idea to new questions; the adaptation is legitimate, but it should be acknowledged as an adaptation.

docs.title: 18.6 Modern Buddhist and Jain Thinkers
docs.text: The institutional histories above can hide the fact that modern Buddhism and Jainism in India produced thinkers of their own, who reinterpreted their traditions for a new age as boldly as the Hindu and Muslim reformers did theirs. Ambedkar’s Navayāna is described in Chapter 12; this section treats some of the others. Several of them knew one another or one another’s work, and together they show that the modern Indian argument about religion, reason and caste was not conducted only in Vedāntic terms.

docs.title: 18.6.1 Lakshmi Narasu: a rationalist Buddhism
docs.text: P. Lakshmi Narasu (1861–1934), a teacher of science in Madras who was associated with Iyothee Thass’s Sakya Buddhist Society (Chapter 14), published The Essence of Buddhism in 1907, with an introduction by Dharmapāla. It presented the Buddha’s teaching as a rational ethics that required no creator, no soul and no priesthood, compatible with modern science and opposed in principle to caste; a later book, A Study of Caste (1922), turned the same rationalism on the institution itself. Narasu’s Buddhism was closer to the Victorian rationalists than to the living Buddhism of Sri Lanka or Burma, and it shared the limits of Buddhist modernism described above. Its importance lies in its afterlife: Ambedkar reissued the book in 1948 with a preface praising it as the best book on Buddhism, and it was one of the sources from which he built his own interpretation.

docs.title: 18.6.2 Dharmanand Kosambi: Buddhism, non-violence and socialism
docs.text: Dharmanand Kosambi (1876–1947), whose work as a scholar of Pali is described above, was also a thinker who tried to bring together the Buddha, Gandhi and socialism. His Marathi writings, collected and translated by his granddaughter Meera Kosambi, include a life of the Buddha written for the general reader, an autobiography and studies of the history of non-violence (Kosambi 2010). He argued that ahiṃsā had entered Indian culture through the śramaṇa traditions of the Buddha and Mahāvīra rather than through the Vedic sacrificial religion, and he was critical of the Bhagavadgītā’s justification of war, a point on which he differed from Gandhi while admiring him. He taught Pali for a time in Leningrad in 1929, took part in the salt satyagraha, and saw in the early Buddhist community a model of a society without private property. In 1947, having decided to end his life by fasting in the manner that both Buddhist and Jain traditions allow to the dying, he did so at Gandhi’s ashram at Sevagram. Kosambi’s synthesis of Buddhist ethics, Gandhian method and socialist aims was idiosyncratic, but it anticipated the engaged Buddhism of later decades, and through his son D. D. Kosambi (Chapter 15) it entered the Marxist historiography of India.

docs.title: 18.6.3 Rahul Sankrityayan: Buddhism and Marxism
docs.text: Rahul Sankrityayan (1893–1963), whose journeys to Tibet in search of Sanskrit manuscripts are described above, passed through more of modern India’s religious options than any other thinker of his time. Born Kedarnath Pandey in a Brahmin family of eastern Uttar Pradesh, he became a Vaiṣṇava ascetic, then an Arya Samaj preacher, then, after studying Pali in Sri Lanka, a Buddhist monk under the name by which he is known, and finally a Marxist and a member of the Communist Party, without ceasing to call himself a follower of the Buddha’s method. He wrote more than a hundred books in Hindi, among them translations of Pali suttas, a survey of world philosophy, Darśan-Digdarśan, and Volgā se Gaṅgā (1943), both written in prison in the early 1940s, the second a cycle of stories that follows a human community from the prehistoric steppes to modern India and treats religion and caste as historical creations. He read the Buddha as an empiricist who rejected authority and speculation and taught that all things are impermanent and conditioned, and he regarded the Buddhist analysis of change as a precursor of dialectical thinking. His Buddhism, like Narasu’s, was selective; unlike Narasu’s, it was subordinated to a theory of history.

docs.title: 18.6.4 Śrīmad Rājacandra and the inward path
docs.text: Among Jain thinkers the most influential of the period was Śrīmad Rājacandra (1867–1901), the Gujarati jeweller and poet whose influence on Gandhi is noted in Chapter 12. Known in his youth for feats of memory and attention (avadhāna), he turned to a life of introspection while continuing in business. His Ātmasiddhi Śāstra (“The Treatise on Self-Realisation”, 1896), 142 verses in Gujarati, sets out six fundamental propositions — that the soul exists, that it is eternal, that it is the agent of its actions, that it experiences their fruits, that liberation exists and that there is a path to it — and defends each against objections in the manner of a classical dialogue. Gandhi had sent him a series of questions from South Africa in 1894 about religion, God, the soul and the claims of Christianity, and Rājacandra’s replies, which advised him to look for the truth within his own tradition before changing it, are among the documents of Gandhi’s formation. Rājacandra was critical of sectarian divisions among Jains and of ritual without understanding, and the communities of his followers, which are not attached to either the Śvetāmbara or the Digambara order, have spread in India and abroad.

docs.title: 18.6.5 Kanji Swami and the Digambara revival
docs.text: A different kind of inward turn produced the largest new Jain movement of the twentieth century. Kanji Swami (1890–1980), a Sthānakavāsī monk in Saurashtra, was drawn to the Samayasāra of the Digambara teacher Kundakunda, with its distinction between the conventional standpoint (vyavahāra-naya), from which the soul acts and is bound, and the ultimate standpoint (niścaya-naya), from which the pure soul is untouched by karma. In 1934 or 1935 at Songadh he gave up his monastic status and declared himself a lay follower of the Digambara teaching; he never took Digambara ascetic initiation, and the movement that grew around him remained largely a lay movement, centred on the study of Kundakunda and on the realisation of the soul’s pure nature. Digambara monks and scholars criticised it for neglecting the conventional discipline of vows and asceticism on which the tradition had always insisted, and the controversy recalls older Indian debates about whether insight can make practice unnecessary (Dundas 2002).

docs.title: 18.6.6 Jain scholarship and the modern self-image
docs.text: Jain learning also entered the modern academy. Pandit Sukhlāl Saṅghavī (1880–1978), blind from his youth, taught Jain philosophy at Banaras Hindu University and with Becardās Dośī edited Siddhasena Divākara’s Sanmatitarka, a foundational work of Jain logic; in Gujarati and Hindi essays he presented Jain thought historically, as a tradition that had changed through argument with Buddhists and Brahmanical schools, rather than as a timeless system. English-language writers, among them the barrister Champat Rai Jain, presented Jainism to Western and Indian readers in the vocabulary of comparative religion, and in the Terāpanthī order Ācārya Mahāprajña developed from the 1970s a system of meditation, prekṣā dhyāna, that drew on the canonical texts and on modern psychology. These efforts produced the image of Jainism, now familiar worldwide, as a religion of non-violence, many-sidedness and ecological restraint. As with the other modernisms of this chapter, the image selects from a larger tradition, much of which — the temple ritual, the cosmology, the place of renunciation — it leaves in the background.

docs.title: 18.7 Assessment
docs.text: The modern histories of Buddhism and Jainism illustrate the themes of this volume. Both were reinterpreted in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries in conversation with Western scholarship, Theosophy and science; both produced “modernist” versions emphasising reason, ethics and meditation; both have been claimed by Hindu writers as parts of a larger Hindu or “Indic” whole, and both have resisted that claim. Ambedkar’s conversion made Buddhism once again a living Indian religion of the poor and the excluded, and it did so in explicit opposition to Hinduism. A synthesis that respects these traditions must allow them to speak for themselves, including when what they say is a refusal.
