docs.title: Chapter 19: Indian Thought and Modern Science: History, Analogy and Overreach
docs.text: anulomagatir nausthaḥ paśyaty acalaṃ vilomagaṃ yadvat acalāni bhāni tadvat samapaścimagāni laṅkāyām As a man in a boat moving forward sees the stationary objects on the shore moving backward, so are the stationary stars seen by people at Laṅkā as moving exactly westward. — Āryabhaṭa, Āryabhaṭīya, Golapāda 9 (499 CE)

docs.title: 19.1 Two Kinds of Story
docs.text:
Two quite different stories are told about Indian knowledge and modern science, and they are often confused. The first is a story of history: of results, methods and instruments that were developed in India, transmitted to other cultures and eventually became part of the science of the whole world. The decimal place-value numerals with zero are the most important example; trigonometry, astronomical tables, medical knowledge and the analysis of language are others. This story is true, well documented, and told in detail in Volumes 10–14 of this series.

The second is a story of anticipation: that the Vedas, Upaniṣads, Purāṇas or Jain and Buddhist texts already contained the discoveries of modern physics, cosmology, genetics or computing, or that modern scientists found in them the inspiration for their theories. This story, in most of its forms, is false. It has been repeated in popular books and in speeches by public figures, and it has done real damage, because it discredits the genuine achievements of Indian science and diverts attention from the actual history. This chapter examines both stories, and then asks what kinds of comparison between Indian thought and modern science are legitimate.

docs.title: 19.2.1 Numerals and zero
docs.text:
The decimal place-value system with a symbol for zero developed in India in the first millennium CE. Positional notation with zero is clearly attested in Indian texts from the fifth and sixth centuries, and in inscriptions somewhat later; a well-known inscription of 876 CE in the Caturbhuj temple at Gwalior uses a small circle for zero. Brahmagupta’s Brāhmasphuṭasiddhānta (628 CE) gave the first systematic rules for calculating with zero and with negative quantities (“debts” and “fortunes”), including the rule that a number added to zero is unchanged and that a number multiplied by zero is zero; he also stated that zero divided by zero is zero, which modern mathematics does not accept (Plofker 2009). In 662 the Syrian bishop Severus Sebokht praised the Indian method of calculation with nine signs. The Baghdad scholar al-Khwārizmī wrote around 825 a treatise on arithmetic with Indian numerals, which survives in a Latin version beginning Dixit Algorizmi; from his name comes the word “algorithm”. Leonardo of Pisa (Fibonacci), who learned the “Indian figures” in North Africa, introduced them to Latin Europe in his Liber Abaci (1202), and they slowly replaced Roman numerals over the following centuries (Joseph 2011). Volume 11 traces this history in detail.

The adoption of the new numerals in Europe was neither quick nor uncontested. Merchants valued them for calculation, but they were easier to falsify than Roman numerals, and in 1299 the bankers’ guild of Florence forbade its members to use them in account books. Counting boards and Roman numerals remained common in Europe until the sixteenth century. The spread of a superior technique depended on institutions and habits, not only on its merits.

docs.title: 19.2.2 Astronomy and trigonometry
docs.text: Indian astronomical works were translated into Arabic at Baghdad in the late eighth century; a version of Brahmagupta’s work became known as the Sindhind. Indian astronomers had replaced the Greek table of chords with a table of half-chords, or sines, and the Sanskrit word for the sine, jyā or jīvā (“bowstring”), was transliterated into Arabic as jība, read as jayb (“fold” or “pocket”), and translated into Latin as sinus — the origin of the English “sine”. Āryabhaṭa (499 CE) taught that the apparent daily westward motion of the stars is caused by the Earth’s rotation, as the verse quoted at the head of this chapter shows; most later Indian astronomers did not follow him on this point (Volume 12).

docs.title: 19.2.3 Two-way traffic
docs.text: Transmission did not run only from India outwards. Indian astronomy itself had absorbed Babylonian and Greek elements: the zodiac of twelve signs, the planetary week and much of the technical apparatus of horoscopic astrology entered India from the Hellenistic world in the early centuries CE, as the Greek loanwords in Sanskrit astrological texts show (horā from Greek hōra, kendra from kentron, jāmitra from diametron) (Pingree 1981). A verse in Varāhamihira’s Bṛhatsaṃhitā (sixth century), attributed there to the older authority Garga, declares that the Greeks (yavana), though foreigners, are to be honoured like sages because this science is well established among them. In the second millennium, Islamic astronomy reached India in its turn: Persian and Arabic astronomical tables (zīj) were used at the courts of the sultans and Mughals, the astrolabe was adopted and described in Sanskrit, notably in Mahendra Sūri’s Yantrarāja (1370), and Sanskrit scholars at Jai Singh’s court in the eighteenth century translated works of Islamic and European astronomy (Chapter 16). The history of Indian astronomy is thus a history of exchange, and Indian astronomers were most creative when they engaged with other traditions rather than when they ignored them.

docs.title: 19.2.4 The Kerala school
docs.text: Between the fourteenth and sixteenth centuries, a lineage of astronomers in Kerala beginning with Mādhava of Saṅgamagrāma (c. 1340–1425) found infinite series for the sine, cosine and arctangent and for \(\pi\), together with corrections that accelerate their convergence. Their results were set out with demonstrations in Nīlakaṇṭha’s Tantrasaṅgraha (1500) and above all in Jyeṣṭhadeva’s Yuktibhāṣā (c. 1530), written in Malayalam. These results were achieved two to three centuries before Gregory, Newton and Leibniz found the same series in Europe, and they rest on careful arguments about sums of increasingly fine divisions that historians compare with the methods of early calculus. They were first brought to European attention by Charles Whish in a paper of 1835. Whether they reached Europe earlier, through Jesuit missionaries active on the Kerala coast in the sixteenth century, has been argued but not demonstrated; there is no documentary evidence of transmission (Plofker 2009; Joseph 2011). The achievement does not depend on transmission: it is one of the great independent discoveries in the history of mathematics.

docs.title: 19.2.5 Medicine
docs.text: Sanskrit medical works, including those of Caraka and Suśruta, were translated into Arabic in Baghdad in the eighth and ninth centuries, and Indian physicians worked at the Abbasid court. In the colonial period, European surgeons learned from Indian practice: a letter in the Gentleman’s Magazine of London in 1794 described the reconstruction of a nose with a forehead flap by an Indian practitioner near Poona, and the English surgeon Joseph Carpue, who studied the method, performed and published such operations in 1816. The relation between classical Āyurveda and the modern Āyurvedic industry is discussed in Chapter 20 and Volume 13 (Wujastyk 2003).

docs.title: 19.2.6 Craft knowledge: inoculation and steel
docs.text: Some of the knowledge that Europeans learned from India in the colonial period was not textual but practical. In 1767 John Zephaniah Holwell, a surgeon of the East India Company, presented to the College of Physicians in London an account of the inoculation against smallpox practised in Bengal by itinerant Brahmin specialists, who introduced material from smallpox pustules into a small cut and prescribed a regimen for the patient; similar methods were known in Turkey, China and Africa, and had been introduced into England from Constantinople earlier in the century. The Indian practice was later suppressed by the colonial government in favour of Jenner’s cowpox vaccination, which was safer. Indian crucible steel, known in Europe as “wootz”, was examined by members of the Royal Society in the 1790s, who were impressed by its quality; its high carbon content made it the raw material of the famous “Damascus” blades of the Middle East. Dharampal collected many such British accounts to show the range of eighteenth-century Indian technology (Dharampal 1971). Such knowledge was held by craftsmen and practitioners, not recorded in Sanskrit treatises, and its history depends on the testimony of outsiders and on modern metallurgical and historical research.

docs.title: 19.2.7 Language
docs.text: The European discovery of Pāṇini’s grammar transformed nineteenth-century linguistics. Franz Bopp and the comparative philologists used Sanskrit and the Indian grammatical analysis of roots and suffixes to reconstruct the Indo-European languages; the American linguist Leonard Bloomfield called Pāṇini’s grammar “one of the greatest monuments of human intelligence”. In 1967 the computer scientist Peter Ingerman suggested that the notation for describing programming-language syntax known as Backus–Naur form be renamed Pāṇini–Backus form, in recognition of the formal similarity. Paul Kiparsky has analysed the architecture of the Aṣṭādhyāyī as a formal system with ordered and interacting rules (Kiparsky 2009). These are genuine and precise comparisons. The popular claim that Sanskrit is “the best language for computers”, often attributed to NASA, rests on a misreading of a 1985 article by Rick Briggs, a NASA researcher, on knowledge representation in the technical Sanskrit of the grammarians; neither Briggs nor NASA claimed that Sanskrit was used, or should be used, for programming. Volume 10 discusses Pāṇini’s grammar.

docs.title: 19.2.8 Logic
docs.text: A less familiar Indian contribution to the history of rigorous thought is the “new reason” (Navya-Nyāya) that grew out of the work of Gaṅgeśa (14th century) in Mithilā and flourished in Bengal, especially at Navadvīpa, in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries. To avoid ambiguity in philosophical argument, its authors developed a technical Sanskrit in which the relations between a property, its bearer and the conditions under which it holds are specified with great precision, with the help of such concepts as the “limitor” (avacchedaka) of a property or relation. The language was adopted by grammarians, legal scholars and poeticians, and it became the standard idiom of Sanskrit intellectual life in the early modern period. Matilal and Ganeri have shown that Navya-Nyāya invites comparison with modern formal logic, though it is not a symbolic logic and was designed for different purposes (Matilal 1971; Ganeri 2011). Raghunātha Śiromaṇi (c. 1460–1540), one of its boldest thinkers, revised the categories of the Vaiśeṣika ontology in ways that Ganeri describes as part of a “lost age of reason” in early modern India.

docs.title: 19.3 Encounters with Modern Science
docs.text: The story of Indian thought and modern science is not only one of Western scholars discovering Indian achievements; it is also one of Indians choosing what to take from European science. In 1823 Rammohun Roy wrote to the Governor-General, Lord Amherst, protesting against the government’s plan to found a Sanskrit college in Calcutta and asking instead for instruction in “Mathematics, Natural Philosophy, Chemistry, Anatomy, with other useful Sciences”. In the 1830s and 1840s the British political agent Lancelot Wilkinson at Sehore in central India and the astronomer Bāpūdeva Śāstrī (1821–1900) taught Copernican astronomy to traditional scholars through Sanskrit, comparing it point by point with the siddhānta tradition; Bāpūdeva later taught mathematics at the Sanskrit College of Banaras and wrote textbooks in Sanskrit and Hindi. At Delhi College in the 1830s and 1840s, scholars translated European works on mathematics and science into Urdu. In 1876 the physician Mahendralal Sircar founded the Indian Association for the Cultivation of Science in Calcutta, with the aim of enabling Indians to pursue science independently; C. V. Raman’s discovery of the effect named after him was made in its laboratories in 1928. Gyan Prakash has shown that Indian intellectuals of the period debated whether modern science was foreign or could be claimed as a continuation of their own tradition (Prakash 1999). Both answers had political uses; neither required the claim that the ancient texts already contained modern science.

docs.title: 19.4 Science in Colonial and Modern India
docs.text:
Modern science came to India through colonial institutions, but Indians quickly made it their own. Jagadish Chandra Bose (1858–1937) did pioneering work on radio waves and on the responses of plants to stimuli; his later claims that plants and metals share a common “responsiveness” were influenced by his Vedāntic convictions and were not accepted by most physiologists. Prafulla Chandra Ray (1861–1944), founder of Bengal Chemicals, wrote A History of Hindu Chemistry (1902–09), an early attempt to recover the history of Indian science that combined careful scholarship with nationalist purpose (Volume 14). C. V. Raman won the Nobel Prize for physics in 1930; Meghnad Saha and Satyendra Nath Bose made fundamental contributions to astrophysics and quantum statistics; Srinivasa Ramanujan (1887–1920), self-taught in Kumbakonam and brought to Cambridge by G. H. Hardy, produced results in number theory that mathematicians are still exploring (Kanigel 1991). Gyan Prakash has shown how Indian scientists and nationalists of this period sought to present science as compatible with, and even rooted in, Indian tradition, partly to claim it as Indian rather than colonial (Prakash 1999). That project produced both serious history of science and much of the “anticipation” literature discussed below.

Not all Indian scientists welcomed the attempt to find modern science in ancient texts. The astrophysicist Meghnad Saha (1893–1956), whose ionisation equation transformed the study of stellar atmospheres, ridiculed the claim that “everything is in the Vedas” in a much-read exchange in the Bengali press in the late 1930s, and as chairman of the government’s Calendar Reform Committee (1952–55) proposed a unified national calendar based on modern astronomy rather than on the traditional siddhāntas. Jawaharlal Nehru made the cultivation of a “scientific temper” a theme of his writings and of national policy, and in 1976 the Constitution was amended to make it a fundamental duty of every citizen “to develop the scientific temper, humanism and the spirit of inquiry and reform” (Article 51A(h)). The tension between this ideal and the celebration of ancient science has run through Indian public life ever since.

docs.title: 19.4.1 Indian contributions to modern science
docs.text: The contributions of Indian scientists to modern science in the first half of the twentieth century were substantial and are easily documented. In 1924 Satyendra Nath Bose sent Einstein a paper deriving Planck’s radiation law by a new method of counting states of indistinguishable particles; Einstein translated it into German, had it published and extended the method, giving rise to Bose–Einstein statistics, and particles that obey them are called bosons. Meghnad Saha’s ionisation equation (1920) made it possible to read the temperatures of stars from their spectra. C. V. Raman’s discovery of the inelastic scattering of light (1928) won the Nobel Prize in 1930. Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar (1910–1995), Raman’s nephew, calculated in 1930, while sailing to England to study at Cambridge, the upper limit of mass for a stable white dwarf star, now called the Chandrasekhar limit, and received the Nobel Prize in 1983. P. C. Mahalanobis (1893–1972) founded the Indian Statistical Institute in 1931 and introduced the generalised distance measure that bears his name; Homi Bhabha worked on cosmic-ray showers before building India’s nuclear programme. These achievements were made with the methods of modern physics and mathematics, often in institutions founded by Indians to escape the limitations of colonial science, and they are the strongest answer to the colonial claim that Indians were unfit for science.

docs.title: 19.4.2 Scientists and their faiths
docs.text: Indian scientists of the colonial and early independent periods held a wide range of religious views, and their lives show that personal belief and scientific practice could be combined in many ways. Ramanujan was a devout Brahmin who, according to his friends and his biographer, attributed some of his mathematical insights to the family goddess Namagiri of Namakkal (Kanigel 1991); his results, however, stand or fall by their proofs, and Hardy, an atheist, valued them on those terms. J. C. Bose’s Vedāntic convictions shaped the questions he asked about the responses of living and non-living matter, though not, in his best work, the experimental methods he used. P. C. Ray was a member of the Brahmo Samaj; Meghnad Saha was a rationalist critic of religious claims in science; C. V. Raman spoke of science as a kind of worship of truth while keeping it strictly separate from scripture. Many later Indian scientists have combined religious practice in private life with uncompromising scientific method in the laboratory, a combination common among scientists in every country. What the history does not support is the claim that any of their discoveries depended on, or confirmed, the doctrines of a particular tradition.

docs.title: 19.4.3 Women in Indian science
docs.text: The history of modern Indian science also includes women who entered it against considerable obstacles. Anandibai Joshi (1865–1887) graduated in medicine from the Woman’s Medical College of Pennsylvania in 1886 and died the next year, shortly after returning to India; Kadambini Ganguly (1861–1923) qualified in medicine in Calcutta in the same period and practised for decades. Kamala Sohonie (1912–1998), refused admission to research at the Indian Institute of Science by C. V. Raman on account of her sex until she persuaded him to admit her on probation, went on to earn a doctorate in biochemistry at Cambridge in 1939. E. K. Janaki Ammal (1897–1984) became a leading cytogeneticist and plant breeder, developing sugarcane hybrids at Coimbatore and later working at the Botanical Survey of India; Asima Chatterjee (1917–2006) did important work on the chemistry of medicinal plants, including alkaloids used against epilepsy and malaria. Their careers show both the opening of modern science to women in India and the resistance they met, from colonial institutions and from Indian scientists alike.

docs.title: 19.4.4 Science and the new state
docs.text: After independence, the Indian state invested heavily in science and technology. The Council of Scientific and Industrial Research (established 1942) built a network of national laboratories; Homi Bhabha founded the Tata Institute of Fundamental Research in 1945 and led the atomic energy programme; the first Indian Institute of Technology opened at Kharagpur in 1951; and Vikram Sarabhai led the space programme, organised from 1969 as the Indian Space Research Organisation. The Scientific Policy Resolution of 1958, passed by Parliament on Nehru’s initiative, committed the state to “foster, promote and sustain” the cultivation of science in all its aspects. These institutions are the real foundation of India’s scientific achievements in the twentieth and twenty-first centuries, from the Green Revolution to the Mars orbiter of 2013–14. They were built by applying modern science, not by recovering ancient science, and their success is no less Indian for that.

docs.title: 19.4.5 People’s science movements
docs.text: The cultivation of a scientific temper in India has also been the work of voluntary movements. The Kerala Sastra Sahitya Parishad (“Kerala Science Literature Society”), founded in 1962 by writers and teachers who wished to publish science in Malayalam, grew into a mass movement that ran village science classes, campaigned on public health and literacy and played a prominent part in the campaign to save the Silent Valley forest (Chapter 21). Similar “people’s science” organisations formed in other states and joined in an all-India network in the 1980s; they took part in the national literacy campaigns of the late 1980s and 1990s. The government’s own agency for science communication, Vigyan Prasar, was established in 1989. These movements insisted that science should be available in the Indian languages and addressed to the problems of ordinary people, and they combined scientific method with social criticism. They represent a strand of Indian modernity that neither rejects tradition wholesale nor seeks modern science in ancient texts, but tries to make science part of the culture of the people.

docs.title: 19.5.1 What is documented
docs.text:
Several twentieth-century physicists did take an interest in Indian philosophy, and their interest is worth recording accurately.

Erwin Schrödinger.

Schrödinger read the Upaniṣads, largely through Schopenhauer and Paul Deussen, and was drawn to the idea that individual minds are aspects of a single consciousness. He expressed this in an essay written in 1925 and published in 1961 as My View of the World, in the epilogue to What Is Life? (1944), where he wrote of the Upaniṣadic identity of ātman and Brahman, and in Mind and Matter (1958), where he argued that consciousness is singular and that its apparent plurality is an illusion of the kind the Hindus call māyā (Schrödinger 1944, 1958). His biographer Walter Moore documents how important these ideas were to him (Moore 1989). But Schrödinger presented them as his personal philosophy of mind, not as consequences of quantum mechanics, and he did not claim that Indian thought had anticipated his physics. A text often quoted under the title “The Vedantic Vision” and attributed to him does not correspond to any of his published works in that form and should not be cited.

J. Robert Oppenheimer.

Oppenheimer studied Sanskrit at Berkeley in the 1930s with Arthur Ryder and read the Bhagavadgītā in the original. In a television interview in 1965 he recalled that at the first atomic test in 1945 he had thought of the line in which Kṛṣṇa reveals himself as Time, the destroyer of worlds (Gītā 11.32). In his lectures Science and the Common Understanding (1954) he remarked that the general notions about human understanding suggested by atomic physics were not wholly new and had a place in Buddhist and Hindu thought. He did not say that the Vedas contained quantum mechanics, and statements to that effect attributed to him in popular sources are not genuine.

Niels Bohr.

When Bohr was awarded the Danish Order of the Elephant in 1947, he chose for his coat of arms the Chinese taiji (yin–yang) symbol with the motto contraria sunt complementa, “opposites are complementary”. The symbol is Chinese, not Indian, and expresses Bohr’s own principle of complementarity; it is sometimes misreported as evidence of Indian influence.

Werner Heisenberg.

The story that Heisenberg, after conversations with Rabindranath Tagore in 1929, found that ideas of quantum physics “suddenly made much more sense” derives from Fritjof Capra’s later recollections of his own conversations with Heisenberg, published in Uncommon Wisdom (1988). Heisenberg’s autobiographical Physics and Beyond (1969 in German, 1971 in English) contains no such account. The anecdote cannot be verified and should not be presented as fact; quotations from Physics and Beyond about Indian philosophy, which circulate widely, do not appear in that book. Tagore, it may be added, was a poet, not a physicist, as some versions of the story claim.

David Bohm.

The physicist David Bohm developed a holistic interpretation of quantum theory, with the notion of an “implicate order” in which all things are enfolded, and held extended dialogues with the Indian teacher Jiddu Krishnamurti, published as The Ending of Time (1985) (Bohm 1980). Bohm’s interpretation of quantum mechanics is a minority view among physicists; his dialogues with Krishnamurti were a philosophical and personal exchange, not a scientific collaboration.

docs.title: 19.5.2 Capra and the “new physics” literature
docs.text:
Fritjof Capra’s The Tao of Physics (1975) argued that the worldview of modern physics, especially quantum field theory, converged with the worldviews of Hinduism, Buddhism and Daoism: both saw reality as dynamic, interconnected and beyond ordinary concepts (Capra 1975). The book was enormously popular and inspired a genre of similar works. In 2004 the Government of India presented a statue of Śiva Naṭarāja to CERN, the European laboratory for particle physics near Geneva, where it stands with a plaque quoting Capra’s comparison of the cosmic dance of Śiva with the “dance” of subatomic particles (Figure 19.1).

Figure 19.1. Śiva as Naṭarāja, Lord of the Dance, within a ring of flames, trampling the dwarf of ignorance. Bronze, Tamil Nadu, Cōḻa period (c. 10th–11th century). A modern statue of this type was presented by India to CERN in 2004. Sculpture: Chola bronze, c.950-1000, LACMA M.71.82; photograph: LACMA, public domain via Wikimedia Commons

Critics, including sociologists of science such as Sal Restivo and many physicists, pointed out that the parallels depended on loose analogies between verbal descriptions, that the same Eastern texts could be paired with very different physical theories, and that the mathematics, which is the substance of physics, played no part in the comparison (Restivo 1983). Meera Nanda has argued that the “Vedic science” literature in India, which borrows heavily from this genre, serves to legitimise religious nationalism under the authority of science (Nanda 2003). The Naṭarāja at CERN is best understood as what Capra intended: a metaphor offered by a writer, which many people have found beautiful, not a claim that Cōḻa sculptors knew particle physics.

docs.title: 19.5.3 “Quantum consciousness”
docs.text: A related literature claims that quantum mechanics shows consciousness to be fundamental, and that this vindicates Advaita Vedānta or Buddhism. It usually relies on the idea that observation by a conscious observer “collapses” the wave function. This idea was proposed by some physicists in the mid-twentieth century, notably Eugene Wigner, but it is a minority interpretation, later abandoned by Wigner himself; in the standard practice of physics the “observer” is any measuring interaction, and no conscious mind is required. Books such as Amit Goswami’s The Self-Aware Universe (1993) present a speculative interpretation as if it were established physics. Whatever one thinks of the philosophical question of consciousness, quantum mechanics does not settle it in favour of any Indian school.

docs.title: 19.6 Documented Transmissions and Popular Claims Compared
docs.text:
Table 19.1 sets some of the documented achievements and transmissions discussed in this chapter beside popular claims that are not supported by evidence. The contrast is the main lesson of the chapter: the real history is more interesting than the myths, and it can be checked.

Table 19.1. Documented history and unsupported claims (selected) Claim Status Evidence or reason Decimal place-value with zero developed in India documented Sanskrit texts from the 5th–6th c.; Brahmagupta (628); Gwalior inscription (876); Arabic and Latin transmission Sine function via Indian astronomy documented jyā–jība–sinus; Arabic translations of Sanskrit works Kerala infinite series for \(\pi\) and sine documented Tantrasaṅgraha (1500), Yuktibhāṣā (c. 1530) Kerala series transmitted to Europe not demonstrated no documentary evidence of transmission Rhinoplasty learned from Indian practitioners documented 1794 report; Carpue (1816) Smallpox inoculation practised in Bengal documented Holwell (1767) Sanskrit “best language for computers” unsupported misreading of Briggs (1985) “Vedic mathematics” from the Veda unsupported sūtras not found in any Vedic text (1965 book) Ancient aircraft (Vaimānika Śāstra) unsupported text dictated 1918–1923; IISc study (1974) Heisenberg’s physics inspired by Tagore unsupported no contemporary evidence; late second-hand report Purāṇic kalpa as the age of the Earth coincidence different meanings and methods; see Chapter 2

docs.title: 19.7 “Vedic Science”: A Catalogue of Errors
docs.text:
The following claims are frequently made in popular writing and political speeches. Each is unsupported by the evidence.

  • “Vedic mathematics”. The book Vedic Mathematics (1965) by Bhāratī Kṛṣṇa Tīrtha presents sixteen short “sūtras” and techniques of mental arithmetic, which the author said he had found in the Veda. The sūtras do not occur in any known Vedic text; the techniques, though useful for quick calculation, are the author’s own. The real mathematics of the Vedic period is that of the Śulbasūtras (c. 800–200 BCE), described in Volume 11.

  • Ancient aircraft. The Vaimānika Śāstra, describing flying machines, was dictated between 1918 and 1923 by Pandit Subbaraya Shastry, who said he received it by psychic means. A study by engineers at the Indian Institute of Science in 1974 concluded that the craft described could not fly. The vimānas of the epics are mythological.

  • Plastic surgery and genetics in the epics. The elephant head of Gaṇeśa and the birth of Karṇa are myths, not evidence of transplant surgery or genetic science. The real history of Indian surgery is that of the Suśrutasaṃhitā (Volume 13).

  • The age of the universe in the Purāṇas. The coincidence between the length of a kalpa and the age of the Earth is discussed in Chapter 2.

  • Cantor in the Jain canon; Planck time in the paramāṇu; Darwin in the avatāras. See Chapters 2 and 3.

Such claims harm the tradition they intend to honour. They make Indian knowledge appear to be a matter of slogans rather than of texts, arguments and evidence, and they invite the dismissal of the real achievements along with the false ones.

docs.title: 19.8 Astrology, Superstition and the Rationalists
docs.text:
In classical India, jyotiṣa included both mathematical astronomy and the interpretation of the heavens for human affairs, and the same scholars often practised both (Pingree 1981). Horoscopic astrology, which entered India from the Hellenistic world as noted above, became part of Indian life at every level: the timing of weddings and rituals, the matching of horoscopes for marriage, the choice of auspicious moments for public acts. It remains so today, among people of every religion and level of education.

The status of astrology in modern public institutions has been contested. In 2001 the University Grants Commission invited universities to establish courses in “Vedic astrology” (jyotir vigyan). Scientists protested that astrology is not a science, and a petition was brought to the Supreme Court; in 2004 the Court declined to interfere, holding that the courses did not promote religion and that their academic value was a matter for the educational authorities. Public policy, it appeared, found it hard to distinguish between the historical study of a tradition, which belongs in a university, and the endorsement of its claims, which is a different matter. The history of Indian astrology — its Greek sources, its technical development, its social role — is a legitimate field of scholarship. The claim that the positions of the planets at birth determine character and fortune has been tested repeatedly and has not been supported.

India also has a long rationalist tradition opposed to such beliefs. Its ancestors include the Cārvāka materialists and the Buddhist critics of ritual (Volume 3); its modern representatives include Periyar’s Self-Respect Movement (Chapter 14), the rationalist associations founded in Kerala and elsewhere in the twentieth century, and campaigners who travel to villages to expose the tricks of “god-men”. The Maharashtra physician Narendra Dabholkar campaigned for many years for a law against exploitative practices of black magic and fraudulent healing; he was murdered in Pune in August 2013, and the state enacted the law, the Maharashtra Prevention and Eradication of Human Sacrifice and other Inhuman, Evil and Aghori Practices and Black Magic Act, in the same year. Other rationalist writers, Govind Pansare and M. M. Kalburgi, were killed in 2015, and the journalist Gauri Lankesh in 2017. These rationalists, too, belong to the Indian tradition of argument described in Chapter 1, and a fair account of Indian thought must include them.

docs.title: 19.9 Legitimate Comparisons
docs.text:
If anticipation is the wrong model, what comparisons between Indian thought and modern science are worthwhile? Several kinds stand out.

History of science.

The first is history itself: the study of what Indian mathematicians, astronomers, physicians and grammarians actually did, how they reasoned and how their work travelled. Kim Plofker’s Mathematics in India and George Gheverghese Joseph’s The Crest of the Peacock are examples of how this can be done without either belittlement or exaggeration (Plofker 2009; Joseph 2011).

Philosophy of mind.

Indian philosophers argued for two thousand years about the nature of consciousness, the self, perception and memory. Their arguments — Buddhist denials of a self, Nyāya defences of it, Advaita accounts of witness-consciousness, Yoga and Abhidharma analyses of mental states — can be brought into dialogue with modern philosophy of mind and cognitive science, as Jonardon Ganeri and Evan Thompson have shown (Ganeri 2012; Thompson 2015). This is a dialogue between philosophies, which may be informed by science; it is not a claim that the ancient texts contained neuroscience.

Three examples show what such dialogue can look like. First, Buddhist philosophers debated whether consciousness is “self-illuminating” (svaprakāśa) — whether every conscious state is aware of itself as well as of its object — or whether awareness of a mental state requires a second, higher-order state, as some Nyāya philosophers held; contemporary philosophers of mind debate very similar questions about self-awareness and higher-order theories of consciousness. Second, Indian discussions of dreamless sleep asked whether consciousness persists when there is no object of awareness: Advaitins held that the sleeper’s report on waking, “I slept well and knew nothing”, is a memory of a real experience of objectless consciousness, while Nyāya philosophers treated it as an inference. Thompson has brought these arguments into conversation with sleep science and the study of dreaming (Thompson 2015). Third, Buddhist analyses of the self as a series of momentary events, and their replies to the objection that memory and moral responsibility require an enduring subject, parallel modern debates about personal identity; Ganeri and Siderits have shown how the classical arguments can contribute to those debates on equal terms (Ganeri 2012; Siderits 2007). In each case the classical arguments are valuable because they are arguments, and they can be judged, accepted or rejected as arguments are.

Logic and language.

Navya-Nyāya developed a technical language for expressing precise relations, and Pāṇini a formal grammar; both invite comparison with modern logic and linguistics, as Matilal and Kiparsky have shown (Matilal 1971; Kiparsky 2009).

Contemplative practice as an object of research.

Meditation and yoga can be studied by the methods of psychology and medicine, as Chapter 20 discusses. The question there is not whether the texts anticipated science, but what effects the practices have.

Analogy and inspiration.

Finally, a scientist or writer may find in an Indian idea a fruitful analogy or a source of personal inspiration, as Schrödinger did. Such analogies are legitimate, provided they are presented as what they are: the reflections of a modern person, not the hidden meaning of an ancient text.

  • Ganeri (2012) and Thompson (2015): Indian philosophy of mind in dialogue with cognitive science.

docs.title: Chapter 20: Yoga, Meditation and Āyurveda in the Global Age
docs.text: yogaś cittavṛttinirodhaḥ Yoga is the stilling of the fluctuations of the mind. — Yogasūtra 1.2 (c. 325–425 CE)

docs.title: 20.1 Introduction
docs.text: Of all the forms of Indian knowledge, yoga, meditation and Āyurveda have travelled furthest in the modern world. Hundreds of millions of people practise some form of yoga; mindfulness meditation, derived from Buddhist practice, is taught in hospitals, schools and businesses; Āyurvedic products are sold across the world, and the Government of India promotes Āyurveda through a dedicated ministry. This global success is often cited as proof of the value of Indian knowledge. It also raises difficult questions: How much of modern yoga is ancient? What does the scientific evidence on meditation and Āyurvedic treatments show? Who “owns” these traditions? And how can the public be protected from unsafe products and exaggerated claims? This chapter addresses these questions. The classical traditions are described in Volumes 5 (yoga) and 13 (Āyurveda), and psychology in Volume 22.

docs.title: 20.2.1 Classical yoga
docs.text:
The Yogasūtra attributed to Patañjali, which Philipp Maas dates to c. 325–425 CE, defines yoga as the stilling of the mind’s fluctuations, describes an eightfold path (aṣṭāṅga) of restraints, observances, posture, breath control, withdrawal of the senses, concentration, meditation and absorption, and aims at the isolation (kaivalya) of the conscious self from matter (Maas 2013). Posture (āsana) receives three short sūtras: it should be “steady and comfortable”. Elaborate postures and breathing techniques developed later, in the haṭhayoga texts of the eleventh century onward, such as the fifteenth-century Haṭhapradīpikā, which aimed at bodily transformation and the raising of inner energy. Yoga was practised by renouncers of many sects — Śaiva, Vaiṣṇava, Buddhist and Jain — and by Sufis, and its techniques were adapted for many purposes, including worldly power.

Table 20.1 sets the eight “limbs” of Patañjali’s yoga beside the emphasis they typically receive in modern postural yoga. The contrast is not a criticism of either; it shows how much the meaning of the word has changed.

Table 20.1. The eight limbs of yoga (Yogasūtra 2.29) and modern practice (simplified) Limb In the Yogasūtra Typical modern emphasis yama five restraints: non-injury, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, non-possession often mentioned as ethics; rarely the centre of a class niyama five observances: purity, contentment, austerity, study, devotion to the Lord variable āsana a steady and comfortable seated posture (2.46) the main content: many postures and sequences prāṇāyāma regulation of the breath breathing exercises, often for relaxation pratyāhāra withdrawal of the senses from their objects seldom taught explicitly dhāraṇā fixing the mind on one place concentration exercises in some styles dhyāna continuous flow of awareness towards that object “meditation”, often brief samādhi absorption, leading to the isolation of the self rarely a stated goal

docs.title: 20.2.2 The making of modern yoga
docs.text:
Modern yoga took shape in the late nineteenth and twentieth centuries. Vivekananda’s Raja Yoga (1896) presented Patañjali’s yoga as a science of the mind and gave little place to postures, which he associated with disreputable ascetics (Chapter 10). In the early twentieth century, Indian reformers re-created posture practice as a form of physical culture and therapy. Shri Yogendra founded the Yoga Institute in Bombay in 1918; Swami Kuvalayananda founded Kaivalyadhama at Lonavla in 1924, where he studied the physiology of yoga with laboratory instruments and published a scientific journal; and T. Krishnamacharya in Mysore trained the teachers who spread posture practice worldwide (see below). Swami Sivananda’s Divine Life Society (1936) and Maharishi Mahesh Yogi’s Transcendental Meditation (from the late 1950s) carried other forms abroad.

Historians have shown how much this modern yoga owes to its time. Mark Singleton argues that the posture-based practice of today drew on European gymnastics and physical culture as well as on haṭhayoga (Singleton 2010); Joseph Alter shows how Kuvalayananda and others made yoga into a “science” of the body in the idiom of modern physiology (Alter 2004); Elizabeth De Michelis traces the influence of Western esotericism on Vivekananda’s formulation (De Michelis 2004); and Andrea Jain describes how yoga became a global consumer product (Jain 2015). These findings do not mean that modern yoga is “inauthentic”. They mean that it is a modern tradition with ancient roots, like most living traditions, and that claims that today’s studio practice is unchanged from the time of the Vedas are false.

docs.title: 20.2.3 Global recognition and its politics
docs.text: On the initiative of the Government of India, the United Nations General Assembly proclaimed 21 June as the International Day of Yoga in December 2014, and UNESCO inscribed yoga on its list of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2016. India’s Traditional Knowledge Digital Library has documented yoga postures from classical texts to prevent their being patented. Debates over ownership have taken several forms: some Hindu organisations have argued that yoga’s Hindu roots are being concealed in the West; some Christian groups have objected to yoga in schools as a Hindu practice; and attempts to copyright particular sequences of postures have been rejected by American courts. A comparative view suggests that yoga, like Buddhism, belongs to the traditions that created it and also to the many people who have made it part of their lives, and that acknowledging its origins is a matter of historical honesty, not of ownership.

docs.title: 20.2.4 Haṭha yoga before modern yoga
docs.text: Between the classical Yogasūtra and modern postural yoga lies the tradition of haṭha yoga, the “yoga of force”, which developed in the early second millennium CE, partly in tantric Śaiva and Buddhist circles and among ascetic orders such as the Nāths. Its best-known text, the Haṭhapradīpikā of Svātmārāma (c. fifteenth century), describes a small number of postures, breath-retentions, cleansing techniques and “seals” (mudrā) intended to control the vital breath and the seminal fluid, to awaken the coiled power (kuṇḍalinī) and to lead to the meditative absorption (samādhi) that the text calls rājayoga. Later texts such as the Gheraṇḍasaṃhitā (c. seventeenth–eighteenth century) increased the number of postures. Recent research, including a large anthology of translated sources by James Mallinson and Mark Singleton, has shown that haṭha yoga was more varied, older in some of its techniques and more widely practised by householders than earlier scholarship assumed (Mallinson and Singleton 2017). It has also shown that the goals of these practices were soteriological and magical — liberation, immortality, supernatural powers — rather than fitness or health in the modern sense. Modern yoga drew on this heritage selectively, as it drew on the Yogasūtra.

docs.title: 20.2.5 The Mysore lineages
docs.text: Much of the posture-based yoga practised worldwide descends from a single teacher. Tirumalai Krishnamacharya (1888–1989) taught yoga at the Jaganmohan Palace in Mysore from the 1930s under the patronage of the Maharaja Krishnaraja Wadiyar IV. Singleton has shown that the vigorous sequences taught there drew on haṭha techniques but also on the physical-culture movements of the period, including Indian wrestling and gymnastics and the Scandinavian and British systems used in Indian schools and the army (Singleton 2010). Krishnamacharya’s students carried different versions of his teaching abroad: K. Pattabhi Jois (1915–2009) developed the flowing “Ashtanga Vinyasa” system; B. K. S. Iyengar (1918–2014) a precise, alignment-based method using props, made famous by Light on Yoga (1966); Indra Devi (born Eugenie Peterson in Riga) taught Hollywood actors from the 1940s; and his son T. K. V. Desikachar adapted practice to individual needs and therapeutic purposes. The diversity of these styles, all descending from one teacher within a single lifetime, shows how recently modern postural yoga took its present forms.

docs.title: 20.2.6 Yoga and other religions
docs.text: Yoga’s spread has raised questions for adherents of other religions. In 1989 the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith of the Roman Catholic Church issued a letter on Christian meditation that warned against adopting Eastern methods in ways that would displace prayer to a personal God, while allowing that some elements could be used. In 2008 the National Fatwa Council of Malaysia advised Muslims against practising yoga that involved Hindu chanting and worship, while permitting physical exercise alone. In the United States, parents who objected to a yoga programme in the public schools of Encinitas, California, as the teaching of Hinduism lost their case; the courts held in 2013 and on appeal in 2015 that the programme, as taught, was a secular physical-education class. Christian and Muslim practitioners have developed their own adaptations. These debates mirror those within India, mentioned below. They show that whether yoga is “religious” depends less on its origins than on what is done and said in a particular class.

docs.title: 20.2.7 Yoga in India today
docs.text: In India itself, yoga has become a mass practice and an instrument of public policy. Television teachers, of whom Ramdev became the best known from the early 2000s, taught breathing exercises and postures to millions, often with claims of cures for chronic diseases that went well beyond the evidence; the business that grew from his following became one of India’s largest makers of consumer goods. The Ministry of AYUSH promotes a “common yoga protocol” for the International Day of Yoga, when mass demonstrations are held across the country, and yoga is taught in many schools. These developments have made yoga part of national identity and public health promotion. They have also revived questions about its relation to Hinduism — some Muslim and Christian organisations objected to compulsory practices such as the sun salutation and the chanting of “Om” — and about the regulation of health claims (see below).

docs.title: 20.3.1 Jung and the first encounters
docs.text: Carl Gustav Jung was among the first Western psychologists to engage seriously with Indian traditions. His seminar on Kuṇḍalinī yoga, given in Zurich in 1932 with the Indologist J. W. Hauer, interpreted the cakras as symbols of stages of psychological development (Jung 1996). He also warned that Western people should not simply imitate Eastern methods, which had grown from a different culture and could be psychologically harmful if used without understanding. The transpersonal psychology movement of the 1960s and 1970s, associated with Abraham Maslow and others, drew on Indian and Buddhist sources to describe “peak” and mystical experiences. Modern Indian psychologists have developed an “Indian psychology” that draws on the Yoga, Vedānta and Buddhist traditions, discussed in Volume 22.

docs.title: 20.3.2 From meditation to mindfulness
docs.text: Scientific study of meditation began in earnest in the 1970s, with research on Transcendental Meditation and Herbert Benson’s account of a “relaxation response” common to many meditative practices. In 1979 Jon Kabat-Zinn, a molecular biologist trained in Zen and Vipassanā meditation, founded the Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction programme at the University of Massachusetts Medical School, presenting Buddhist-derived meditation in a secular, clinical form (Kabat-Zinn 1990). Mindfulness-Based Cognitive Therapy, developed by Zindel Segal, Mark Williams and John Teasdale, combined mindfulness with cognitive therapy to prevent relapse in recurrent depression, and has been recommended for that purpose by the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence in England. Mindfulness programmes are now widespread.

docs.title: 20.3.3 What the evidence shows
docs.text:
The research literature on meditation and yoga is large and uneven. A carefully conducted meta-analysis of randomised trials of mindfulness-based interventions for psychiatric disorders by Simon Goldberg and colleagues found that they were more effective than no treatment and comparable to other active treatments such as cognitive-behavioural therapy, with the strongest evidence for depression, pain and smoking (Goldberg et al. 2018). Neuroscientific studies have reported differences in brain activity and structure in experienced meditators, such as the high-amplitude gamma-band activity found by Antoine Lutz and Richard Davidson in Tibetan monks practising compassion meditation, and differences in cortical thickness reported by Sara Lazar and colleagues (Lutz et al. 2004; Lazar et al. 2005). Many studies, however, are small, lack adequate control conditions or rely on self-report; some practitioners report adverse experiences in intensive meditation; and a group of researchers led by Nicholas Van Dam has warned against the “hype” surrounding mindfulness and called for more rigorous definitions and methods (Van Dam et al. 2018). Systematic reviews of yoga for conditions such as chronic low back pain have found small to moderate benefits.

The balanced conclusion is that meditation and yoga are useful practices for some conditions and for general well-being, on a par with other behavioural interventions, and that research on them is valuable. The evidence does not show that they cure serious disease, that they “prove” any metaphysical claim of the traditions, or that the ancient texts anticipated neuroscience. Nor does secular mindfulness reproduce the aims of the Buddhist path, which seeks liberation rather than stress reduction, a point made by Buddhist critics of the mindfulness movement.

docs.title: 20.3.4 Difficulties and context
docs.text: Two further points deserve mention. First, meditation is not free of risk. Classical texts in several traditions warn of the dangers of intensive practice — disturbing visions, “meditation sickness”, the mistaking of unusual experiences for liberation — and Aurobindo, as noted in Chapter 11, warned his disciples of the same. Modern researchers have begun to document challenging experiences reported by some practitioners, including anxiety, depersonalisation and the re-emergence of traumatic memories, particularly during intensive retreats; the scientific critique of hype in meditation research cited above calls for these effects to be monitored and reported (Van Dam et al. 2018). Second, the secular “mindfulness” taught in clinics, schools and companies has been criticised by some Buddhist teachers and scholars for detaching a technique from the ethical framework in which it was embedded — the precepts, the cultivation of compassion, the goal of liberation — and for adapting it to help people tolerate stressful working conditions rather than question them. Defenders reply that the techniques have value in their own right and that the people who learn them are free to explore their origins. The debate is a modern instance of a question that runs through this volume: what is lost, and what gained, when a practice is taken from one context and put to work in another?

docs.title: 20.4.1 From classical system to modern institution
docs.text:
The classical Āyurveda of the Carakasaṃhitā, the Suśrutasaṃhitā and Vāgbhaṭa’s Aṣṭāṅgahṛdaya is described in Volume 13; Dominik Wujastyk’s anthology is a good introduction to the texts (Wujastyk 2003). Its colonial history is outlined below. Independent India recognised Āyurveda, Unani, Siddha and Homoeopathy as systems of medicine with their own colleges and registration; a Department of Indian Systems of Medicine and Homoeopathy, later AYUSH (Āyurveda, Yoga and Naturopathy, Unani, Siddha and Homoeopathy), became a full ministry in 2014. A large Āyurvedic industry has grown up, and Āyurveda has been marketed abroad, often in forms adapted to Western wellness culture (Wujastyk and Smith 2008).

The relation between the systems in India’s public health service has been a recurring policy question. Committees appointed before and after independence debated whether Indian medicine should be integrated with biomedicine in a single course of training, developed separately in “pure” form, or confined to a supporting role; the answers changed with each generation of policy. The National Rural Health Mission, launched in 2005, sought to “mainstream” AYUSH by locating practitioners in primary health centres, partly to fill gaps in rural staffing. Proponents argued that this made use of a large trained workforce and of systems familiar to patients; critics, including many biomedical doctors, objected to AYUSH practitioners prescribing modern drugs without adequate training, a practice that several state governments have permitted and courts have repeatedly examined. The debate is not about whether Āyurveda has value, but about how a health system should combine practitioners trained in different and partly incompatible frameworks while protecting patients. Medical anthropologists have noted that patients themselves have long combined systems pragmatically, consulting different practitioners for different complaints, and that a realistic policy must start from that practice.

docs.title: 20.4.2 The classical theory in brief
docs.text: The classical system is set out in the compendia attributed to Caraka (redacted c. 100 BCE–200 CE and completed by Dṛḍhabala in the fourth or fifth century) and Suśruta (in its present form by c. 500 CE), and in the Aṣṭāṅgahṛdaya of Vāgbhaṭa (c. 600 CE), which became the most widely used textbook (Wujastyk 2003). Health is understood as the balance of three bodily “faults” (doṣa) — wind (vāta), bile (pitta) and phlegm (kapha) — which, when disturbed, cause disease; of seven bodily tissues (dhātu), from chyle and blood to semen, each formed from the one before by a process of “cooking”; and of the digestive fire (agni) on which the whole process depends. Diagnosis attends to the patient’s constitution, the season, the place, the stage of the disease and its signs. Treatment includes diet and regimen, which the texts place first; medicines, mostly of plant origin in the classical compendia, with mineral preparations becoming prominent later; purification procedures; and, in Suśruta, surgery. The texts also contain extended reflections on the method of medical reasoning and on the qualities of a good physician. Like the humoral medicine of Galen with which it is often compared, this is a coherent and sophisticated system of explanation; and like Galenic humoral theory, its explanatory concepts do not correspond to the entities of modern physiology. This is why the evaluation of Āyurveda today proceeds mainly through testing particular treatments.

docs.title: 20.4.3 Āyurveda under colonial rule
docs.text: The colonial history of Āyurveda is more complicated than a story of simple suppression. In its early decades the East India Company employed Indian practitioners, and from 1822 to 1835 the Native Medical Institution in Calcutta trained Indian students in both Western and Indian medicine, with lectures on Āyurvedic texts at the Sanskrit College. After 1835, in line with Macaulay’s policy (Chapter 8), state support was confined to Western medicine, and Indian practitioners were excluded from official medical institutions. Āyurvedic physicians responded by organising themselves: they founded associations and journals, established colleges, standardised and printed the classical texts, and set up pharmaceutical firms that manufactured remedies on a commercial scale. In doing so they also changed Āyurveda, adopting anatomy and other elements of Western medicine and turning a diverse craft into a professional system with a defined curriculum. The debates of this period — between “pure” and “integrated” Āyurveda, and over whether its practitioners should be regulated by the state — continue today (Wujastyk and Smith 2008).

docs.title: 20.4.4 Evidence
docs.text:
Some Āyurvedic herbs and formulations have been tested in clinical trials, and a few have shown promise for particular conditions; most trials, however, have been small and of limited quality, and the evidence base is far weaker than promotional literature suggests. Turmeric illustrates the difficulty. Curcumin, its main pigment, has been the subject of thousands of laboratory papers reporting effects on many biological targets; a critical review by medicinal chemists concluded that curcumin is unstable and poorly absorbed, behaves as a “promiscuous” compound that interferes with many laboratory assays, and has not been shown in well-designed clinical trials to be effective for any condition (Nelson et al. 2017). Traditional preparations combining turmeric with other ingredients may have different properties, but these too need to be tested rather than assumed.

Researchers have also investigated whether the Āyurvedic classification of constitutions (prakṛti) by the predominance of vāta, pitta and kapha corresponds to measurable biological differences. Studies led by Mitali Mukerji and colleagues at the Institute of Genomics and Integrative Biology in Delhi reported differences in gene expression and genetic variants between small groups of people classified as of extreme constitutional types (Prasher et al. 2008; Govindaraj et al. 2015). These are interesting preliminary findings in a young field. They do not validate the doṣa theory as a whole, and claims that genomics has “proved” Āyurveda go far beyond the evidence.

The Chinese experience offers a useful comparison. The Chinese scientist Tu Youyou, searching classical Chinese medical texts for leads against malaria, isolated artemisinin from sweet wormwood and received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 2015. Her success came from treating the traditional literature as a source of hypotheses to be tested by the methods of modern pharmacology, not as a body of proven cures.

docs.title: 20.4.5 Safety
docs.text:
The most serious problem in modern Āyurveda is safety. Classical Āyurveda, and especially the alchemical tradition of rasaśāstra (Volume 14), prescribes preparations of mercury, lead, arsenic and other metals, which are said to be rendered safe by purification and incineration. Studies of products sold in the United States found that about one in five Āyurvedic products bought in Boston-area shops, and a similar proportion of products sold over the internet, contained detectable lead, mercury or arsenic, some at levels that could result in intakes exceeding safety limits (Saper et al. 2004, 2008). Cases of lead poisoning linked to Āyurvedic medicines have been reported in many countries. Herbal products can also interact with prescription drugs and cause liver injury.

Health and Safety Note

Āyurvedic and other traditional preparations can contain toxic metals (lead, mercury, arsenic) and can interact with prescribed medicines. Do not take metal-based (bhasma or rasa) preparations, and do not use any traditional remedy in place of diagnosis and treatment by a qualified physician, especially for serious illness, during pregnancy or for children. Inform your doctor of any herbal products you take. Nothing in this volume is medical advice.

docs.title: 20.4.6 Research institutions
docs.text: India has built a substantial public apparatus for research in its traditional medical systems. Research councils for Āyurveda, Unani, Siddha, homoeopathy and yoga and naturopathy were established as separate bodies in 1978, when an earlier combined council was divided; the Central Council for Research in Ayurvedic Sciences runs a network of institutes and conducts clinical, pharmacological and literary research, including the editing of classical texts. An All India Institute of Ayurveda, modelled on the All India Institute of Medical Sciences, opened in New Delhi in 2017. Since 2009 clinical trials conducted in India, including trials of AYUSH interventions, have been required to be registered in advance with the Clinical Trials Registry–India, a measure intended to reduce selective reporting of results. The quality of the research produced by this apparatus varies: some studies meet international standards, while many are small, unblinded or poorly reported, and systematic reviews have repeatedly called for larger and better-designed trials. The institutions provide the means for rigorous evaluation; whether they are used for that purpose or for promotion is the question on which the credibility of the traditional systems will depend.

docs.title: 20.4.7 Why testing is difficult, and why it is still necessary
docs.text: Defenders of Āyurveda sometimes argue that the randomised controlled trial is unsuited to a system that treats each patient individually according to constitution, season and stage of disease, often with complex multi-ingredient preparations and changes of diet and regimen. The objection has some force: a trial that gives a single standardised product to every patient tests something different from what a classical physician does. But the difficulty is not unique to Āyurveda — psychotherapy, surgery and nutrition present similar problems — and methods exist to address it, including pragmatic trials of whole treatment packages, trials in which the practitioner individualises treatment within each arm, and careful observational studies. What the objection cannot justify is exemption from testing altogether. A claim that a treatment works is a claim about outcomes, and outcomes can be measured. Respect for the tradition is best shown by taking its claims seriously enough to test them.

docs.title: 20.4.8 Āyurveda and COVID-19
docs.text: The COVID-19 pandemic exposed both the potential and the dangers of Āyurveda’s place in public health. The AYUSH ministry issued advisories recommending traditional practices to support immunity and sponsored trials of some formulations. In June 2020 the company Patanjali Ayurved announced a product, Coronil, as a cure for COVID-19; the ministry asked it to stop advertising the claim until the evidence had been examined, and the episode drew sharp criticism from medical bodies. The lesson is the same as in other cases: traditional remedies may be worth testing, but claims of cure must wait for the tests.

docs.title: 20.4.9 Other systems and healing traditions
docs.text:
Āyurveda is not the only traditional medicine in India. Siddha medicine, practised mainly in Tamil Nadu and attributed to the legendary siddhar adepts, shares many concepts with Āyurveda but has its own Tamil literature and makes extensive use of mineral and metallic preparations, to which the safety concerns above apply equally. Unani medicine, of Graeco-Islamic origin, is discussed in Chapter 16. Sowa-Rigpa, the Tibetan system practised in the Himalayan regions and among Tibetan exiles, was recognised by the Government of India in 2010. Its principal text, the Four Tantras (rGyud bzhi), was compiled in Tibet in the twelfth century and combines Āyurvedic doctrine, received through translations of Vāgbhaṭa, with Chinese and Tibetan elements; the Men-Tsee-Khang, the Tibetan Medical and Astrological Institute established at Dharamsala in 1961, trains practitioners in exile. The history of Sowa-Rigpa is itself an example of the transmission and transformation of Indian knowledge across cultures, comparable to the passage of Indian astronomy into the Islamic world (Chapter 19). Homoeopathy, a German system of the early nineteenth century, is also included under AYUSH; systematic reviews by medical bodies have found no reliable evidence that its remedies work better than placebo.

Naturopathy, now grouped with yoga under AYUSH, is a European import that acquired Indian roots. The “nature cure” movements of nineteenth-century Germany, associated with figures such as Vincenz Priessnitz, Sebastian Kneipp and Louis Kuhne, prescribed water treatments, diet, fasting, fresh air and sunlight. Gandhi read Kuhne and Adolf Just in South Africa, practised nature cure on himself and his family throughout his life, and in 1946 founded a nature-cure centre at Uruli Kanchan near Pune, intended for the village poor. Indian naturopaths later combined these methods with yoga and with Āyurvedic dietary ideas. The history is a small example of the global circulation of health practices: what is now presented as traditional Indian medicine includes a German system adopted by the most famous of Indian nationalists.

Much healing in India, as elsewhere, takes place outside any formal system: at the shrines of Sufi saints, at temples famous for curing affliction by spirits, through folk healers, midwives and bonesetters. The psychoanalyst Sudhir Kakar’s study of such healing — at the Bālājī temple of Mehndipur in Rajasthan, among Sufi healers and among tantric practitioners — compared it with Western psychotherapy and argued that it addresses real psychological suffering through culturally meaningful symbols (Kakar 1982). Such healing deserves respect as a cultural practice and study as a human phenomenon; it is not a substitute for treatment of serious mental or physical illness.

docs.title: 20.4.10 Regulation
docs.text: Indian law has long restricted misleading medical claims. The Drugs and Magic Remedies (Objectionable Advertisements) Act of 1954 prohibits advertisements claiming to cure a list of serious diseases, and the regulation of Āyurvedic, Siddha and Unani drugs has been progressively strengthened, including a pharmacovigilance programme to report adverse effects. Enforcement has been uneven. In 2023–24 the Supreme Court of India, hearing a petition by the Indian Medical Association, censured a prominent Āyurvedic company for advertisements claiming cures for chronic diseases and required public apologies. Promoting traditional medicine and protecting the public are not always in harmony, and the credibility of the traditional systems themselves depends on independent regulation.

docs.title: 20.4.11 Intellectual property and biopiracy
docs.text: The value of traditional knowledge has also been contested in law. In 1995 a United States patent was granted for the use of turmeric in wound healing; the Indian Council of Scientific and Industrial Research challenged it with evidence from Sanskrit texts and earlier publications, and it was revoked in 1997. A European patent on a fungicidal use of neem was revoked in 2000. To make such challenges easier, India created the Traditional Knowledge Digital Library, which translates formulations from classical texts into a searchable database available to patent examiners. The World Health Organization’s strategy on traditional medicine calls for the integration of safe and effective traditional practices into health systems, and in 2022 the WHO and the Government of India agreed to establish a Global Centre for Traditional Medicine at Jamnagar, Gujarat. International recognition of this kind is welcome; it does not substitute for evidence of safety and effectiveness for each practice and product.

docs.title: 20.5 Assessment
docs.text: Yoga, meditation and Āyurveda show the best and the worst of the global life of Indian knowledge. At their best, they offer practices and hypotheses that have been carefully tested and found useful, and they have given millions of people a means of health and reflection. At their worst, they have been sold with false claims of antiquity, of scientific proof and of cures, and some products have harmed their users. A responsible synthesis takes from the tradition what can be shown to be valuable, describes the rest as history, and is honest about the difference.

docs.text:
