docs.title: Chapter 21: Ecology and the Arts in Global Conversation
docs.text: yat te bhūme vikhanāmi kṣipraṃ tad api rohatu mā te marma vimṛgvari mā te hṛdayam arpipam Whatever I dig from you, Earth, may that grow back quickly. May I not strike your vital points or your heart, O purifier. — Atharvaveda 12.1.35 (the hymn to the Earth)

docs.title: 21.1 Introduction
docs.text: Two further areas in which Indian traditions have entered global conversation are environmental thought and the arts. In both, Indian ideas have been genuinely influential, and in both they have been idealised. This chapter considers first the claim that Indian religions offer a distinctive ecological ethic, and the movements and critiques it has generated; it then turns to Indian aesthetic theory and to the international careers of Indian art, music and dance. The traditional knowledge of agriculture, forests and animals is the subject of Volume 15, architecture and sculpture of Volume 16, crafts of Volume 17, music, theatre and dance of Volume 9, literature and poetics of Volume 8, and the knowledge of tribal communities of Volume 23.

docs.title: 21.2.1 Textual resources
docs.text: Indian texts contain many passages that express reverence for the earth, rivers, trees and animals. The hymn to the Earth in the Atharvaveda (12.1), with its sixty-three verses, addresses the earth as a mother — “the Earth is my mother, I am the son of the Earth” (12.1.12) — and asks, in the verse quoted at the head of this chapter, that what is dug from her may grow again. Rivers, above all the Gaṅgā, were worshipped as goddesses. Trees were planted and protected for merit, and some, like the aśvattha (pipal), were sacred. The Jain and Buddhist ethics of non-injury, discussed in Chapter 7, extended moral concern to animals and, for Jains, to the elements and plants. The Arthaśāstra prescribes protected forests for elephants and sanctuaries where animals may not be harmed, and the emperor Aśoka’s fifth pillar edict lists animals that were not to be killed. Across India, villages maintained sacred groves dedicated to local deities, discussed below.

docs.title: 21.2.2 Movements
docs.text:
The Bishnois.

The Bishnoi community of western Rajasthan follows twenty-nine rules taught by Guru Jambheśvar (Jambhoji), whose sect is traditionally dated to 1485; the rules include protecting trees and animals. According to Bishnoi tradition, in 1730 a woman named Amṛtā Devī and more than three hundred others were killed at Khejarli while resisting the felling of khejṛī trees for the Maharaja of Jodhpur. The story, told in the community’s own records and songs, has become an emblem of Indian environmentalism; its details rest on tradition rather than on contemporary documents.

Chipko.

The Chipko movement began in 1973 in the Garhwal Himalaya, when villagers organised by the Dasholi Gram Swarajya Sangh, under Chandi Prasad Bhatt, prevented a sports-goods company from felling trees near Mandal by threatening to hug them (cipko, “cling”). In March 1974 at Reni, women led by Gaura Devi stopped loggers while the men of the village were away. Ramachandra Guha’s history shows that Chipko was above all a movement of hill peasants for their rights to the forests on which their livelihoods depended, against commercial forestry by the state and contractors, and that it drew on a long tradition of peasant forest protests and on Gandhian methods and workers (Guha 1989b). Later presentations of Chipko as an expression of Hindu reverence for nature, or as a movement of women defending the feminine principle (Vandana Shiva’s Staying Alive, 1988), captured some aspects of it and obscured others (Shiva 1988).

Later movements.

The campaign that saved the rainforest of Silent Valley in Kerala from a hydroelectric project (declared a national park in 1984), the Narmada Bachao Andolan led by Medha Patkar against the displacement of villagers by the Sardar Sarovar dam from the mid-1980s, and many local struggles over forests, mining and water belong to the same tradition of environmental action rooted in questions of livelihood and justice, a pattern that historians of Indian environmentalism have called an “environmentalism of the poor”.

docs.title: 21.2.3 Sacred groves
docs.text: Among the most concrete links between religion and conservation in India are sacred groves: patches of forest dedicated to a local deity, often a goddess or a village guardian, within which the cutting of trees and sometimes the gathering of any material is forbidden. They are known by many local names — devrāī in Maharashtra, kāvu in Kerala, sarnā among the Adivasi communities of Jharkhand, law kyntang in Meghalaya — and they range in size from a few trees to many hectares. Studies begun in the 1970s by Madhav Gadgil and V. D. Vartak in the Western Ghats drew attention to them as refuges for plant and animal species that had disappeared from the surrounding landscape, and thousands have since been documented across the country (Gadgil and Guha 1992). The groves show how a religious prohibition can have ecological effects. They also show the limits of such protection: many groves have shrunk or vanished as land pressure has grown, as belief has weakened, or as the worship of the local deity has been replaced by temple-building that clears the forest it was meant to protect. Their protection today depends on law and community management as much as on religion; the Biological Diversity Act and the Forest Rights Act (Chapter 22) provide some of the means.

docs.title: 21.2.4 Rivers as persons
docs.text: In March 2017 the High Court of Uttarakhand declared the Gaṅgā and the Yamunā to be legal persons with guardians who could act on their behalf, citing their sacred status among Hindus as part of its reasoning. The Supreme Court stayed the order a few months later. In the same month, New Zealand’s parliament recognised the Whanganui River as a legal person, in recognition of the Māori relationship with it; Ecuador’s constitution (2008) and Bolivian legislation (2010) recognise rights of nature. These developments show how religious and indigenous understandings of nature have entered modern law. Kelly Alley’s study of the Gaṅgā at Banaras also shows their limits: many devotees hold that the river, being divine, cannot be made impure by human waste, a belief that can coexist with severe pollution (Alley 2002).

docs.title: 21.3.1 The argument
docs.text: In 1967 the historian Lynn White argued in Science that the Judaeo-Christian doctrine of human dominion over nature lay at the historical roots of the ecological crisis. His essay encouraged a search for alternative traditions, and Indian religions — with their non-injury, sacred rivers and groves, and doctrines of the unity of all life — were widely proposed as ecological by nature. The Norwegian philosopher Arne Naess, founder of “deep ecology”, drew on Spinoza and on Gandhi’s ethic of non-violence in developing his idea of “self-realisation” as identification with all life (Naess 1989). Many Indian and Western writers have argued that Advaita Vedānta, Jain non-violence or Gandhian simplicity provide the foundations for an environmental ethic (Chapple and Tucker 2000).

docs.title: 21.3.2 The criticisms
docs.text:
These arguments have been criticised on several grounds.

  • Philosophical. Lance Nelson and others pointed out that Advaita, which regards the world as ultimately unreal and seeks liberation from it, does not obviously support concern for the natural world; the same is true of other renunciant traditions whose aim is to escape embodied existence (Nelson 1998).

  • Historical. India’s environmental history includes deforestation, the hunting of wildlife by kings and the depletion of resources long before modern industry, as well as conservation. The sacredness of a river or grove did not prevent its degradation when economic pressures were strong.

  • Political. Ramachandra Guha argued that American deep ecology, with its emphasis on wilderness preservation, was ill-suited to India, where the protection of “wilderness” had often meant the eviction of tribal and peasant communities from forests, and where the urgent environmental questions were about livelihoods and justice (Guha 1989a). Mukul Sharma has shown how religious environmentalism in India has sometimes been joined to Hindu nationalist politics, with exclusionary consequences (Sharma 2012).

docs.title: 21.3.3 What remains
docs.text: The critics do not show that Indian traditions have nothing to contribute to environmental thought. They show that the contribution must be made carefully: by attending to specific practices and communities (sacred groves, Bishnoi rules, tribal forest management, Jain non-violence) rather than to a generalised “Indian worldview”; by recognising that these traditions also had other aims; and by joining reverence for nature to justice for the people who depend on it. Gandhi’s critique of industrial civilisation and his ideal of simplicity (Chapter 12) and the movements of the poor described above may be the most valuable Indian contributions.

docs.title: 21.4.1 Rasa
docs.text:
The theory of rasa (“taste” or “relish”) is set out in the Nāṭyaśāstra attributed to Bharata, a treatise on drama, dance and music compiled over several centuries around the beginning of the Common Era (Volume 9). Its central statement is the “rasa-sūtra”:

Nāṭyaśāstra 6

vibhāvānubhāvavyabhicārisaṃyogād rasaniṣpattiḥ Rasa arises from the combination of the determinants, the consequents and the transitory states.

The Nāṭyaśāstra names eight rasas — the erotic (śṛṅgāra), the comic, the pathetic (karuṇa), the furious, the heroic, the terrible, the odious and the marvellous — each corresponding to a stable emotion (sthāyibhāva) and associated with a colour and a presiding deity: the erotic, for example, is dark blue-black (śyāma) and presided over by Viṣṇu. A ninth, the tranquil (śānta), was added later; it is first clearly listed by Udbhaṭa and was defended by Abhinavagupta. Table 21.1 sets out the scheme, and Figure 21.1 the relation between the components named in the rasa-sūtra.

Figure 21.1. The rasa-sūtra of the Nāṭyaśāstra as a diagram: the combination of determinants, consequents and transitory states, presented on the stage, brings the stable emotion to the state of rasa. The role of the stable emotion and the locus of rasa follow Abhinavagupta’s interpretation, one of several in the commentarial tradition. Table 21.1. The rasas, their stable emotions, colours and deities (Nāṭyaśāstra 6) Rasa Stable emotion (sthāyibhāva) Colour Deity erotic (śṛṅgāra) love (rati) dark (śyāma) Viṣṇu comic (hāsya) laughter (hāsa) white Śiva’s attendants (Pramathas) pathetic (karuṇa) sorrow (śoka) dove-grey Yama furious (raudra) anger (krodha) red Rudra heroic (vīra) energy (utsāha) pale gold (gaura) Indra terrible (bhayānaka) fear (bhaya) black Kāla odious (bībhatsa) disgust (jugupsā) blue Mahākāla marvellous (adbhuta) wonder (vismaya) yellow Brahmā tranquil (śānta), later addition calm (śama) or, for Abhinavagupta, knowledge of the truth — —

The Kashmiri philosopher Abhinavagupta (c. 950–1016) gave the theory its most profound interpretation in his commentary on the Nāṭyaśāstra, the Abhinavabhāratī, and in his commentary on Ānandavardhana’s Dhvanyāloka (9th century). He argued that rasa is not the emotion of a character, nor the spectator’s personal emotion, but an emotion “generalised” (sādhāraṇīkṛta) and freed from personal interest, savoured by a sensitive spectator in a state of absorbed awareness. The later theorist Viśvanātha described this experience as “a twin of the tasting of Brahman” (brahmāsvādasahodara). Ānandavardhana’s theory of suggestion (dhvani) held that the essence of poetry is a meaning that is not stated but suggested, and that rasa is always suggested (Ingalls et al. 1990; Pollock 2016; Gnoli 1956).

docs.title: 21.4.2 Comparisons
docs.text: Rasa theory invites comparison with Aristotle’s theory of tragedy and its “purgation” (katharsis) of pity and fear, with Kant’s “disinterested” pleasure in the beautiful and with modern theories of aesthetic emotion. The comparisons are illuminating, but the differences matter. Bharata’s theory was a practical analysis for the stage, concerned with the means by which a performance produces an emotional relish; Abhinavagupta’s was embedded in a Śaiva metaphysics of consciousness; and both concerned an audience of connoisseurs (sahṛdaya) whose cultivation was presupposed. Sheldon Pollock’s Rasa Reader presents the debates among the Indian theorists themselves, which were as lively as any in European aesthetics (Pollock 2016). Volume 8 treats the theory of literature and Volume 9 the performing arts.

docs.title: 21.5 Indian Art in the Eyes of the World
21.5.1 From “monsters” to masterpieces
docs.text: European visitors to India long found its religious art incomprehensible. Partha Mitter’s Much Maligned Monsters traces how early modern travellers described many-armed gods as monsters or devils, and how even sympathetic nineteenth-century critics judged Indian sculpture by the standards of Greek art (Mitter 1977). In the early twentieth century, the British art teacher E. B. Havell and the Ceylonese–English scholar Ananda Kentish Coomaraswamy (1877–1947) argued that Indian art was a spiritual art, which should be judged by its own principles. Coomaraswamy, who became a curator at the Museum of Fine Arts in Boston from 1917, interpreted the image of Śiva Naṭarāja as a symbol of cosmic rhythm in The Dance of Śiva (1918), wrote the first comprehensive History of Indian and Indonesian Art (1927), and in The Transformation of Nature in Art (1934) argued that traditional Indian, Chinese and medieval European art shared a common theory of art as the expression of a spiritual idea rather than the imitation of nature (Coomaraswamy 1918, 1927, 1934). In his later years he became a leading exponent of the “traditionalist” view that all traditional civilisations shared a single metaphysical wisdom, a view that has been influential but, like the perennial philosophy discussed in Chapter 9, contested. Tapati Guha-Thakurta has shown how museums, archaeology and art history in colonial and post-colonial India constructed the categories through which Indian art is now seen (Guha-Thakurta 2004).

docs.title: 21.5.2 Southeast Asia
docs.text: From the early centuries CE, kingdoms in mainland and island Southeast Asia adopted Sanskrit, Indian scripts, Hindu and Buddhist religion and Indian forms of kingship and art. Their monuments include Borobudur (c. 800; Figure 3.4 in Chapter 3) and Prambanan (9th century) in Java, Angkor Wat, built for the Khmer king Sūryavarman II in the twelfth century, and the temples of Bagan in Myanmar. An older scholarship spoke of the “Indianisation” of Southeast Asia, as if Indian culture had been transplanted. Historians now emphasise that Southeast Asian rulers and communities selected and transformed Indian elements for their own purposes, producing original civilisations that should not be seen as provincial versions of India. The maritime routes along which these exchanges travelled are discussed in Volume 19.

docs.title: 21.5.3 The epics in Southeast Asia
docs.text: The Rāmāyaṇa travelled with Indian culture across Southeast Asia and was retold in each society in its own way. In Java the Old Javanese Kakawin Rāmāyaṇa (9th or 10th century) adapted the Sanskrit poem to Javanese poetics; the reliefs of the Prambanan temples illustrate the story; and the shadow-puppet theatre (wayang) of Java and Bali, performed in a predominantly Muslim society, still draws on the epics. In Thailand the Ramakien, a version composed in its present form under King Rāma I at the end of the eighteenth century, is the national epic, painted on the walls of the royal temple in Bangkok; in Cambodia the Reamker and in Laos and Myanmar other versions have their own episodes and emphases. Some of these versions differ substantially from Vālmīki’s: in the Malay Hikayat Seri Rama the story is framed by Islamic elements, and in several versions Sītā is the daughter of Rāvaṇa. A. K. Ramanujan’s essay on “three hundred Rāmāyaṇas” made the point that there is no single authoritative telling (Volume 7). The Southeast Asian Rāmāyaṇas are a prime example of synthesis in the sense this volume has defended: a shared story, transformed by each culture into something of its own.

docs.title: 21.5.4 Modern Indian art
docs.text: Modern Indian art was shaped by debates about tradition and modernity similar to those described in Part II. The “Bengal School” led by Abanindranath Tagore (1871–1951), Rabindranath’s nephew, with the support of E. B. Havell, rejected the academic realism taught in colonial art schools and sought an Indian style based on Mughal and Rajput miniatures, Ajanta and Japanese ink painting. Rabindranath himself began painting in his late sixties, producing more than two thousand expressive works, shown in Paris in 1930. Amrita Sher-Gil (1913–1941), trained in Paris, combined European post-impressionism with the lessons of Ajanta and Indian miniature painting. After independence, the Progressive Artists’ Group, founded in Bombay in 1947 by F. N. Souza, S. H. Raza, M. F. Husain and others, rejected both academic realism and the Bengal School’s revivalism in favour of an international modernism with Indian subjects. Tapati Guha-Thakurta and Partha Mitter have traced these debates (Guha-Thakurta 2004; Mitter 1977).

docs.title: 21.6 Indian Literature in World Literature
docs.text:
Indian literature entered European consciousness through translation at the end of the eighteenth century. Charles Wilkins’s English Bhagavadgītā (1785) was followed by William Jones’s translation of Kālidāsa’s play Abhijñānaśākuntalam as Sacontalá, or the Fatal Ring (1789). Georg Forster’s German version of Jones’s translation (1791) captivated German readers. Goethe wrote an admiring epigram on the play in 1791, and the “Prelude in the Theatre” with which he later opened Faust is generally thought to have been suggested by the prologue between the director and the actress in Kālidāsa’s drama. Herder, Schiller and the Schlegels admired it; Jones’s translation of Jayadeva’s Gītagovinda (1792) introduced Europe to Sanskrit devotional love-poetry. The Romantic image of India as a land of poetry and dream owed much to these few texts.

In the twentieth century the traffic grew and changed direction. Tagore’s Nobel Prize of 1913 (Chapter 13) made a modern Indian poet famous worldwide. Indian writers in English — Mulk Raj Anand, R. K. Narayan, Raja Rao, and later Salman Rushdie, whose Midnight’s Children won the Booker Prize in 1981, and a large generation after him — made Indian experience part of world literature in English. Translation from the Indian languages into English, long neglected, has expanded; A. K. Ramanujan’s versions of classical Tamil poetry and of the Kannada vacanas showed readers who knew only the Sanskrit classics how varied Indian literature was. The history illustrates a point made throughout this volume: what “Indian literature” meant to the world depended on what was translated, by whom, and for what purpose.

docs.title: 21.7 Stories and Games That Travelled
docs.text: Some of India’s most far-reaching contributions to world culture travelled not as philosophy but as stories and games, often without their Indian origin being remembered. The Pañcatantra, a collection of animal fables illustrating the art of statecraft, was translated into Middle Persian in the sixth century at the court of the Sasanian king Khusraw Anūshirvān, and from Middle Persian into Arabic around 750 by Ibn al-Muqaffaʿ as Kalīla wa Dimna, named after the two jackals of its first book. From Arabic it passed into Persian, Hebrew, Latin, Greek and the vernaculars of Europe; the French fabulist La Fontaine acknowledged, in the preface to his later fables (1678), a debt to “Pilpay, the Indian sage”. The legend of the Buddha’s renunciation travelled westward through Manichaean, Arabic and Georgian versions to become the Christian romance of Barlaam and Josaphat, in which the prince Josaphat — whose name derives, through the Arabic Būdhāsaf, from bodhisattva — renounces his kingdom for a life of holiness; Josaphat came to be honoured as a saint in the Christian calendar. Chess is generally believed by historians of games to have developed in India by about the sixth century as caturaṅga, “the four limbs” of an army, and to have passed through Persia (shatranj) to the Islamic world and Europe. These are among the best-attested cases of Indian cultural transmission, and they owe nothing to inflated claims (Volume 8).

docs.title: 21.8 Architecture of Encounter
docs.text: India’s buildings record its encounters as clearly as its texts. The first mosques of the Delhi Sultanate, such as the Quwwat al-Islām mosque beside the Quṭb Mīnār (from the 1190s), were built partly from the pillars of demolished temples, and Indian craftsmen carved their arches and inscriptions; the result is at once a monument of conquest and a hybrid of two building traditions. Over the following centuries an Indo-Islamic architecture developed that combined the arch, dome and minaret of the Islamic world with Indian bracketed columns, eaves, kiosks (chhatrī) and decorative motifs. Akbar’s city of Fatehpur Sikri (1570s) mixes Persian and Rajput forms; Rajput palaces adopted Mughal gardens and halls; the Kachhwaha raja Man Singh built for Kṛṣṇa at Vrindavan in 1590 the Govindadeva temple, whose vaulted interior shows Mughal techniques; and the Taj Mahal (1632–1653) brought the synthesis to its most celebrated form. The Sikh Harimandir at Amritsar, rebuilt in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, uses a similar vocabulary of domes and kiosks. Architecture is discussed in Volume 16; here it is enough to note that the history of India’s buildings, like the history of its ideas, includes both destruction and creative synthesis.

docs.title: 21.9 Cloth: India’s Most Widely Travelled Art
docs.text:
For most of history, the Indian product that reached the largest number of people outside India was neither a text nor an idea but cloth. Indian cottons, dyed with mordants and resists in colours that did not fade, were traded across the Indian Ocean from antiquity: fragments of Gujarati block-printed cotton have been excavated at Fustat in Egypt, and Indian textiles were the principal currency of the spice trade with Southeast Asia, where they were treasured as heirlooms and ritual objects. When the European trading companies arrived, Indian cloth became their most important cargo. English words record the trade: “calico” from Calicut, “chintz” from the Hindi chīṇṭ, “dungaree” and “bandanna”. By the late seventeenth century the fashion for Indian chintz in England and France was so great that domestic wool and silk weavers demanded protection; France prohibited printed Indian cottons in 1686, and Britain restricted and then, by the Calico Act of 1721, largely banned their use.

The later history reversed the flow. Mechanised spinning and weaving in Britain, together with colonial tariff policies, flooded India with cheap machine-made cloth in the nineteenth century and contributed to the decline of many Indian weaving communities. Gandhi’s khādī movement (Chapter 12) made hand-spinning a symbol of the reversal of this history, and the spinning wheel appeared on the flag of the Indian National Congress. Indian textiles thus connect several of the themes of this volume: the global circulation of Indian craft knowledge, held by communities of weavers and dyers rather than recorded in Sanskrit texts; the role of colonial economics; and the use of tradition in nationalist politics. Volume 17 of this series treats the crafts and textiles in detail, and Volume 19 the trade.

docs.title: 21.10 Painting at the Mughal Court
docs.text:
Few episodes in Indian art show synthesis as clearly as the painting workshops of the Mughal emperors. Humāyūn brought two Persian masters, Mīr Sayyid ʿAlī and ʿAbd al-Ṣamad, from the Safavid court, and under Akbar (r. 1556–1605) they directed a large imperial atelier in which painters of Indian origin, many of them Hindus from families of craftsmen, worked alongside them. Its first great project was an illustrated Hamzanāma, the adventures of the Prophet’s uncle Ḥamza, in some fourteen hundred large paintings on cloth, produced over about fifteen years. In the 1580s the atelier illustrated the Persian translation of the Mahābhārata, the Razmnāma (“Book of War”), and of the Rāmāyaṇa, part of Akbar’s programme of translating Sanskrit works (Chapter 16) (Truschke 2016). Painters such as Basāwan and Daswanth, who came from Indian backgrounds, developed a style that combined the jewel-like colour and composition of Persian painting with Indian vitality of movement and, increasingly, with techniques learned from the European engravings and Bibles brought by Jesuit missionaries: shading, recession in space and naturalistic portraiture. Under Jahāngīr (r. 1605–1627) the emphasis shifted to portraits and to precise studies of birds, animals and plants by artists such as Abū’l-Ḥasan and Manṣūr.

Mughal painting in turn influenced the painting of the Rajput and Pahari courts, where artists applied Mughal techniques to Hindu devotional subjects — the loves of Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa, the musical modes (rāgamālā), the seasons — in styles that remained distinct and local. The history shows an art formed by Persian, Indian and European elements, produced by Muslim and Hindu artists for Muslim and Hindu patrons, and it is a better model of what samanvaya has actually meant in Indian history than any general statement about the unity of religions.

docs.title: 21.11.1 Music
docs.text:
Indian classical music became known in the West largely through the work of a few musicians in the 1950s and 1960s. The sitarist Ravi Shankar (1920–2012) and the sarod player Ali Akbar Khan, both students of Allauddin Khan of Maihar, toured Europe and America; Shankar’s recordings with the violinist Yehudi Menuhin (West Meets East, 1967) and his teaching of George Harrison of the Beatles from 1966 brought the sitar into Western popular music, and he played at the Monterey (1967) and Woodstock (1969) festivals. Ali Akbar Khan founded a college of music in California in 1967.

Comparisons between Indian and Western music have been made since the eighteenth century, when William Jones wrote an essay on the musical modes of the Hindus. The rāga is often compared with the Western mode or scale, but it is more than either: a melodic framework defined by a set of notes, characteristic ascending and descending movements, emphasised notes and typical phrases, associated in the classical theory with particular times of day, seasons and moods. The tāla is a rhythmic cycle that may run to many beats, within which performers improvise with great freedom. Indian music developed without harmony in the Western sense, but with an elaborate theory of intervals — the twenty-two śrutis of the octave described in the Nāṭyaśāstra — and a performance practice in which improvisation within strict rules is central. The meeting of the two traditions has produced both genuine collaboration and much superficial “fusion”; Volume 9 discusses the theory and history of Indian music in detail. Peter Lavezzoli’s history gives an account of this encounter and its influence on jazz, rock and minimalist composers (Lavezzoli 2006). Ravi Shankar was awarded the Bharat Ratna in 1999.

docs.title: 21.11.2 Music, nation and community at home
docs.text: The international career of Indian music had a domestic counterpart in which questions of religion, caste and nation were prominent. In the north, the leading performers of Hindustani music in the nineteenth century were largely hereditary professionals, many of them Muslim, organised in lineages (gharānā) and dependent on princely patronage. Two Maharashtrian Brahmin reformers set out to make the music respectable and teachable to the educated middle class. Vishnu Narayan Bhatkhande (1860–1936) collected compositions from hereditary musicians, published them in notation, organised all-India music conferences from 1916 and classified the rāgas into ten parent scales (thāṭ); Vishnu Digambar Paluskar (1872–1931) founded the Gandharva Mahavidyalaya at Lahore in 1901, a school that gave music a devotional Hindu framing. Janaki Bakhle has shown how these reforms, while opening classical music to new audiences, also tended to recast it as an ancient Hindu art and to marginalise the Muslim hereditary musicians who had preserved it (Bakhle 2005). In the south, the Madras Music Academy (founded 1928) and the concert culture of the city’s Brahmin middle class shaped Carnatic music in a similar way, displacing the hereditary performers, including the women of the devadāsī communities, from whom much of the repertoire came. Recent critics, among them the vocalist T. M. Krishna, have argued that the social exclusiveness of the Carnatic concert world is a continuing problem. The history of Indian music is thus a history of synthesis — of Persian and Indian, courtly and devotional, hereditary and amateur — and also of the boundaries that modern institutions drew within it.

docs.title: 21.11.3 Dance
docs.text:
Modern Indian dance was shaped by revival and reinvention. Uday Shankar (1900–1977), Ravi’s elder brother, created a modern Indian dance after touring with the Russian ballerina Anna Pavlova in the 1920s. In the 1930s Rukmini Devi Arundale, founder of the Kalakshetra academy in Madras (1936), and others reconstructed the solo temple and court dance of South India as “Bharatanatyam”, a classical art for the respectable middle classes. The revival had a cost: the hereditary women performers (devadāsī) who had carried the tradition were stigmatised, and the Madras Devadasis (Prevention of Dedication) Act of 1947 ended the institution; the history is discussed in Volume 9. Today Indian classical dance forms are taught worldwide, and choreographers such as Akram Khan have combined Kathak with contemporary dance.

The traffic in dance, as in music, ran in both directions. Western dancers drew on Indian themes before Indian dance was widely seen abroad: the American Ruth St. Denis created her solo “Radha” in 1906, an exotic fantasy of a temple dance inspired by images and descriptions rather than by Indian teachers, and Anna Pavlova’s interest in Indian dance encouraged Uday Shankar’s career. Later generations of Western students trained seriously with Indian teachers, and Indian dancers in turn absorbed the techniques of modern dance and ballet. Chandralekha (1928–2006), working in Madras, combined Bharatanatyam with yoga and the martial art of Kalarippayattu to create a contemporary dance that questioned the devotional and gender conventions of the revived classical form. The history is one of mutual influence, in which the claim of any form to timeless purity is difficult to sustain.

docs.title: 21.11.4 Film
docs.text:
India’s film industries, working in many languages, together produce more feature films each year than those of any other country. Satyajit Ray’s Pather Panchali (1955) and its sequels won international recognition, and Ray received an honorary Academy Award in 1992; the Hindi popular cinema of Bombay, often called “Bollywood”, has audiences across South Asia, the Middle East, Africa, Central Asia and the diaspora. The popular film’s blend of genres, songs and dances is sometimes compared with the classical theory of rasa, a comparison that illuminates its emotional logic but should not be pressed into a claim of direct descent.

Indian cinema has also been a powerful medium for the retelling of religious narratives. The first Indian feature film, Dadasaheb Phalke’s Raja Harishchandra (1913), told the Purāṇic story of the truthful king discussed in Chapter 7, and “mythological” films remained a major genre for decades. The television serials of the Rāmāyaṇa (1987–88) and the Mahābhārata (1988–90), broadcast on the state network Doordarshan, drew enormous audiences and created standard visual images of the epic characters for a generation. Scholars have noted that the Rāmāyaṇa serial coincided with, and was used by, the political campaign to build a temple at Ayodhya. Modern media can thus turn a plural narrative tradition — the “many Rāmāyaṇas” discussed above — into a single authoritative version, with consequences for religious and political life.

docs.title: 21.11.5 Heritage
docs.text: India has more than forty properties on UNESCO’s World Heritage List, including the Ajanta and Ellora caves, Khajuraho, Hampi, the Great Living Chola Temples, the Taj Mahal and the archaeological site of Nālandā. On the list of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity are Vedic chanting and Kūṭiyāṭṭam Sanskrit theatre (both 2008), the Rammān festival of Garhwal, Chhau dance, the Mudiyēṭṭu ritual theatre of Kerala, the Saṅkīrtana singing and drumming of Manipur, yoga (2016), the Kumbh Mela (2017), Durgā Pūjā in Kolkata (2021) and the Garbā dance of Gujarat (2023), among others. These recognitions are valuable, but they also invite caution: heritage listing can freeze living traditions into official forms and favour some communities’ practices over others.

docs.title: 21.12 Assessment
docs.text: In ecology and in the arts, Indian traditions have given the world real things: practices of conservation, movements for environmental justice, a sophisticated theory of aesthetic experience, great works of sculpture and architecture, musical and dance traditions of extraordinary refinement. They have also been used as screens for projection — of Western longing for an ecological or spiritual alternative, and of Indian longing for a flattering image of the past. The contributions are best appreciated when the projections are recognised for what they are.

docs.text:

  • Nelson (1998), Chapple and Tucker (2000) and Sharma (2012): religion and ecology in India, for and against.

  • Alley (2002): the Gaṅgā as sacred river and polluted water.

  • Pollock (2016) and Ingalls et al. (1990): Indian aesthetic theory.

  • Mitter (1977) and Guha-Thakurta (2004): Indian art in European eyes and in colonial institutions.

  • Lavezzoli (2006): Indian music in the West.

docs.title: Chapter 22: Indian Knowledge Systems Today: Samanvaya Reconsidered
docs.text: ā no bhadrāḥ kratavo yantu viśvataḥ May auspicious intentions come to us from every side. — Ṛgveda 1.89.1

docs.title: 22.1.1 Background
docs.text: This series is itself part of a movement. Since the late twentieth century, and with growing official support in the twenty-first, scholars, educators and governments in India have sought to recover and teach what are now called “Indian Knowledge Systems” (IKS): the sciences, arts, philosophies and practical skills developed in the subcontinent before and outside the colonial system of education. The movement responds to a real history. Macaulay’s Minute of 1835 (Chapter 8) expressed a contempt for Indian learning that shaped colonial education, and the institutions of traditional learning — the Sanskrit pāṭhaśālās, the madrasas, the guilds of craftsmen — lost their patronage and much of their standing. In the 1970s and 1980s the Gandhian historian Dharampal used British records to argue that India had possessed in the eighteenth century a widespread system of indigenous schools and a range of technologies, from inoculation against smallpox to the making of steel, that colonial rule had undermined (Dharampal 1971, 1983). Ashis Nandy’s The Intimate Enemy analysed the psychological effects of colonialism on the colonised (Nandy 1983), and historians of the “subaltern” and post-colonial schools, such as Partha Chatterjee and Dipesh Chakrabarty, questioned the assumption that European categories are universal (Chatterjee 1986; Chakrabarty 2000).

docs.title: 22.1.2 Policy
docs.text: India’s National Education Policy of 2020 gave the movement official form. It calls for the incorporation of “Indian Knowledge Systems”, including tribal and indigenous knowledge, into the curriculum at all levels, the promotion of classical languages and of instruction in the mother tongue, and multidisciplinary education (Ministry of Human Resource Development, Government of India 2020). An IKS Division was established in the Ministry of Education in 2020 to fund research and develop courses, and universities have introduced compulsory and elective courses in Indian knowledge; a widely used textbook for engineering students was published in 2022 (Mahadevan et al. 2022). The National Mission for Manuscripts, established in 2003, has surveyed and catalogued manuscript collections across the country, whose total size is estimated in the millions; digital projects in India and abroad — among them the Sanskrit Heritage platform developed by Gérard Huet at INRIA, the GRETIL archive at Göttingen and the SARIT library of Indic texts — have made thousands of texts searchable and developed tools for the computational analysis of Sanskrit.

docs.title: 22.1.3 The debate
docs.text: The IKS movement has been welcomed by many and criticised by many. Supporters argue that it corrects a colonial imbalance, gives students access to their own intellectual heritage and recovers knowledge of real value in fields from mathematics to ecology. Critics argue that some of what is taught under its name repeats the myths and priority claims discussed in Chapter 19; that it tends to identify Indian knowledge with Sanskrit and with the upper-caste Hindu tradition, neglecting Tamil, Persian and the vernaculars, Buddhist, Jain, Islamic and Sikh learning, and the knowledge of Dalit, Adivasi and artisan communities; and that it can serve a nationalist politics more than a scholarly purpose. Both sides are describing something real. Whether the movement succeeds as education will depend on whether it adopts the standards of evidence and argument that its best practitioners — Plofker, Matilal and the scholars cited throughout this series — have shown to be possible. The official initiative launched in 2020, and the arguments for and against it, are examined in Section 22.2.

docs.title: 22.1.4 A longer history of institutions
docs.text: The IKS movement is often presented as the first attempt to bring Indian learning into modern institutions. In fact there is a long institutional history. The East India Company founded the Calcutta Madrasa in 1781 and the Sanskrit College at Benares in 1791 to train scholars of Islamic and Hindu law; the Asiatic Society of Bengal was founded in 1784 (Chapter 8); the Sanskrit College of Calcutta followed in 1824. The Poona Sanskrit College, opened in 1821 from funds once used by the Peshwas for the patronage of Brahmin scholars, later became Deccan College, a centre of Indological and linguistic research. Indian initiatives followed: the Bhandarkar Oriental Research Institute at Pune (1917), the Oriental Research Institute at Mysore, the Adyar Library of the Theosophical Society (1886), the Sarasvati Mahal Library at Thanjavur, and in independent India the Sanskrit universities and the regional manuscript libraries. Many of these institutions did outstanding work — the Pune critical edition of the Mahābhārata is the best known example — and many have struggled for funds and successors. A new movement would do well to build on them rather than to start afresh.

docs.title: 22.2 The IKS Initiative Since 2020: Promise and Criticism
docs.text: The phrase “Indian Knowledge Systems” was in use before the policy of 2020; a two-volume collection with that title, edited by Kapil Kapoor and Avadhesh Kumar Singh for the Indian Institute of Advanced Study at Shimla, appeared in 2005 (Kapoor and Singh 2005). What changed after 2020 was the scale of official support, and with it the scale of the debate. This section describes the initiative and sets out the strongest form of the case made for it and of the objections raised against it, since both are part of the history this volume records.

docs.title: 22.2.1 What the initiative does
docs.text: The IKS Division, housed at the All India Council for Technical Education under the Ministry of Education, funds centres for the study of Indian knowledge in universities and technical institutes, research projects, internships for students, programmes for training teachers and the preparation of course materials. In 2023 the University Grants Commission issued guidelines for incorporating Indian knowledge into higher education, which recommended that students in undergraduate and postgraduate programmes take courses in Indian knowledge amounting to at least five per cent of their total credits, at least half of them related to their main discipline, and that undergraduates begin with a foundational course introducing the field (University Grants Commission 2023). The guidelines list subjects ranging from mathematics, astronomy, medicine, architecture and metallurgy to linguistics, aesthetics, philosophy, governance and agriculture. National curriculum frameworks for schools have adopted similar aims. Universities have responded unevenly: some have created substantial programmes with qualified staff, others have added short courses taught from secondary compilations.

docs.title: 22.2.2 The case for the initiative
docs.text:
Its supporters make several arguments, and the strongest of them deserve to be stated fully. The first is the argument from intellectual freedom that K. C. Bhattacharya made a century ago (Chapter 15): an educated Indian who knows Euclid and Descartes but has never read Āryabhaṭa, Pāṇini or the Tirukkuṟaḷ has been given a narrower education than he or she deserves, and the narrowness is a legacy of a colonial judgement that Indian learning had nothing to teach. The second is the argument from neglect. Manuscripts remain uncatalogued and unedited, the classical languages are taught in fewer places each decade, and the traditional scholars who could read technical texts are ageing without successors; money and institutional recognition are preconditions for reversing this. The third is pedagogical: students of engineering, medicine or management who meet the history of their own fields in Indian sources may learn that science and scholarship are human, historical and plural enterprises, and not only Western ones. The fourth concerns living knowledge: the policy explicitly includes tribal and local knowledge, and the rights of communities that hold it (Section 22.7). On this view, the errors that critics point to are reasons to do the work better, not reasons to abandon it.

These arguments have named scholarly advocates. Kapil Kapoor and Avadhesh Kumar Singh’s collection presented the classical disciplines — grammar, poetics, logic, the sciences and the arts — as systematic bodies of knowledge (śāstra) with their own concepts and methods, to be studied as knowledge and not only as cultural heritage (Kapoor and Singh 2005). Dharampal’s use of British records to document eighteenth-century schooling and technology, mentioned above, gave the movement its historical charter. A more radical argument comes from the comparative study of cultures. S. N. Balagangadhara, in The Heathen in His Blindness (1994), argued that “religion” as a category was formed within Christian theology and that Western scholarship, by looking for religions in Asia, created “Hinduism” in its own image; Indian traditions, on his view, must be described in categories drawn from their own practice (Balagangadhara 1994). Rajiv Malhotra’s Being Different (2011), the most widely read popular statement of this position, contrasted what he called the “integral unity” of the dharmic traditions with the history-centred “synthetic unity” of the Abrahamic West, and urged Indians to examine Western thought from their own standpoint rather than only being examined by it (Malhotra 2011). The textbook of Mahadevan and his colleagues translates such arguments into a university course (Mahadevan et al. 2022), and Upadhyaya’s Integral Humanism (Chapter 9) stands behind the political version of the same claim.

docs.title: 22.2.3 The objections
docs.text:
The critics’ objections also take several forms. The first concerns content. Some textbooks, lectures and popular materials circulated under the IKS label repeat the claims examined in Chapter 19 — ancient aircraft and weapons, “Vedic” anticipations of modern physics, invented verses and inflated statistics. Episodes before 2020, such as a paper on ancient Indian aviation presented at the Indian Science Congress in 2015, and claims made at the Congress of 2019 that the hundred Kaurava brothers of the Mahābhārata had been born by stem-cell and test-tube techniques, which scientists’ organisations publicly rejected, had already made many scientists wary. The second concerns scope: the objection, noted above, that “Indian” knowledge is too often equated with Sanskrit and Hindu learning, leaving out Persian and Urdu, Pali and Prakrit, Tamil and the regional languages, Islamic, Christian and Sikh learning and the knowledge of Dalit and Adivasi communities. The third concerns capacity: few universities have teachers able to read the sources in their languages, and a compulsory requirement may be met with courses that teach slogans rather than texts. The fourth concerns autonomy and purpose. Some academics have described compulsory credits as a form of indoctrination, and have argued that the initiative uses the legitimate aim of decolonising the curriculum to promote a particular cultural nationalism.

These objections, too, have a scholarly literature, and it is wider than any one author. Meera Nanda has argued that the “Vedic science” literature uses the language of postcolonial critique to shelter religious nationalism from scientific scrutiny (Nanda 2003). Historians of science approach the question differently: Gyan Prakash has shown that the claim that modern science was already Hindu was itself a product of colonial-era nationalism, and Dhruv Raina has traced how the historiography of Indian science has been shaped by the needs of successive periods (Prakash 1999; Raina 2003). The astrophysicist Jayant Narlikar, who has written appreciatively of the real achievements of Indian astronomy and mathematics, has criticised astrology and inflated claims of Vedic science as damaging to them (Narlikar 2003), and specialists such as Kim Plofker have shown in practice how the history of Indian science can be written without either belittlement or inflation (Chapter 19). The argument about the categories of Indian thought is itself contested among scholars: Sheldon Pollock’s account of a Sanskrit culture that lost its creative force in the early modern period provoked Malhotra’s reply in The Battle for Sanskrit (2016), while Jonardon Ganeri’s study of early modern Navya-Nyāya argued, on the evidence of the texts, for a vigorous “new reason” in the same centuries (Pollock 2001; Malhotra 2016; Ganeri 2011). A reader who follows these exchanges will find that the sharpest disagreements are not between Indian and foreign scholars, but between different ways of reading the evidence, on both sides.

docs.title: 22.2.4 Judging the outcome
docs.text: Neither side’s case settles the matter in advance, because the outcome depends on what is actually taught. The initiative can be judged by the same tests that this series has applied to every subject. Are students reading primary sources, in reliable editions and translations, with dates and uncertainties stated? Are claims about health, agriculture or technology tested, and are negative results reported? Do the courses include the full range of Indian languages, religions and communities, and the critics of the tradition as well as its admirers? Is the work open to review and criticism by specialists, including those outside India? The principles for teaching set out in Section 22.6 are offered in that spirit. Some of the best work described in this chapter (Section 22.10) was done long before the initiative existed, by scholars in India and abroad who held themselves to exactly these standards; whether the initiative builds on that work or bypasses it will decide whether it is remembered as a recovery of Indian learning or as another chapter in the history of its misuse.

docs.title: 22.3 Who Owns the Past?
docs.text:
The question of access runs through the history of Indian knowledge. For most of that history, Vedic learning was restricted to twice-born men, and much technical knowledge was held within particular castes and families. Modern India has changed this in ways that would have been unthinkable to the authors of the Dharmaśāstras. Sanskrit is taught in schools and universities to anyone who chooses it; women study and teach the Veda in institutions founded for the purpose; Dalit and other non-Brahmin scholars occupy chairs of Sanskrit and Indian philosophy. Some state governments have trained and appointed priests from non-Brahmin castes, including Dalits, to temples under their administration — in Kerala, where the Travancore Devaswom Board made such appointments in 2017, and in Tamil Nadu after long litigation. These changes have been resisted as well as welcomed, and they remain incomplete.

Access also has a modern form. Digitisation and open publication can make manuscripts and texts available to anyone with an internet connection, but the competence to read them — in Sanskrit, Persian, classical Tamil or Old Kannada — is scarce and unevenly distributed. A genuinely inclusive programme for Indian knowledge would invest in that competence across communities and languages, rather than in slogans about the past.

docs.title: 22.4 Many Languages, Many Classics
docs.text:
Indian knowledge was produced in many languages, and any programme to recover it must reckon with that fact. Sanskrit was the most widely used language of learning across the subcontinent for most of the first and early second millennia CE, a “cosmopolitan” language in Sheldon Pollock’s analysis, used by Buddhists, Jains and Brahmins alike and spreading across Southeast Asia (Pollock 2006). But the Buddhist canon of the Theravāda was preserved in Pali, the Jain canon in Ardhamāgadhī and other Prakrits, and a great literature of poetry, ethics and grammar in classical Tamil. From the thirteenth century Persian became a language of administration, history, poetry and science across much of the subcontinent, and Indo-Persian learning produced dictionaries, histories, medical works and translations from Sanskrit (Chapter 16). From the end of the first millennium the regional languages — Kannada, Telugu, Marathi, Bengali, Hindi and others — developed literatures of their own, often first in the hands of devotional poets who deliberately addressed people excluded from Sanskrit learning. Arabic was the language of Islamic jurisprudence and theology; Urdu and later English became languages of modern Indian thought.

The Government of India’s designation of “classical languages” reflects this plurality in part. Tamil was the first to be so designated, in 2004, followed by Sanskrit (2005), Kannada and Telugu (2008), Malayalam (2013) and Odia (2014); in 2024 Marathi, Pali, Prakrit, Assamese and Bengali were added. The inclusion of Pali and Prakrit, the languages of the Buddhist and Jain canons, is a welcome recognition that Indian classical learning is not only Brahmanical. Persian and Arabic, though they were for centuries languages of Indian learning, are not on the list: official definitions of the “Indian” heritage are themselves choices.

docs.title: 22.5 Translation as Samanvaya
docs.text:
If there is a single practice that embodies the ideal of samanvaya in the history traced by this volume, it is translation. Buddhist texts were translated from Indian languages into Chinese and Tibetan over a thousand years, with careful attention to terminology and method; the Pañcatantra passed through Middle Persian and Arabic into most of the languages of Europe (Chapter 21); al-Bīrūnī translated Patañjali and the Sāṃkhya into Arabic; Dārā Shikoh’s scholars translated the Upaniṣads into Persian, and their version, rendered into Latin, introduced the Upaniṣads to Europe (Chapter 8). Indian poets retold the epics in every regional language, not as literal translations but as new works, and the Malay, Javanese, Thai and Khmer versions continued the process abroad.

Modern India has built institutions for translation among its own languages and between them and others. The Sahitya Akademi, the national academy of letters founded in 1954, translates literary works among the Indian languages, and the National Book Trust (1957) publishes translations for a general readership. Bilingual series have made classical texts available with facing translations: the Clay Sanskrit Library (2005–2009) published some fifty-six volumes of Sanskrit literature, and the Murty Classical Library of India, launched in 2015 at Harvard University Press, publishes texts in Sanskrit, Pali, Prakrit, Persian, Tamil, Telugu, Kannada, Bengali, Hindi, Punjabi, Urdu and other languages with English translations. Such projects do the slow work that a knowledge movement needs. They also show what genuine synthesis requires: competence in more than one language, attention to difference, and the patience to let a text say what it says before deciding what it means for us.

docs.title: 22.6 Teaching Indian Knowledge Honestly
docs.text:
The introduction of courses on Indian knowledge into schools and universities raises practical questions of pedagogy, and the rules of comparison set out at the beginning of this volume (Section 1.11) translate readily into the classroom. Students learn more from sources than from slogans: a class that reads, in reliable translation with dates and context, a chapter of the Āryabhaṭīya, a dialogue from the Upaniṣads, a passage of the Tirukkuṟaḷ and a page of al-Bīrūnī will learn more than one that memorises claims of priority. Students should meet the arguments as well as the conclusions — the Cārvāka objection to inference, the Buddhist objection to the self, the Mīmāṃsaka objection to God and the Advaitin’s reply (Chapter 4) — and be asked to judge for themselves. They should meet the whole of the past: Buddhist, Jain, Islamic, Sikh and Christian learning, the regional languages, the knowledge of artisans, farmers, women and Adivasi communities, and the critics of the tradition, Phule, Ambedkar and Periyar among them, as part of the Indian intellectual heritage. And every claim should come with an account of how it is known, from which texts, inscriptions or finds and with what uncertainty, and be set where possible beside the achievements of China, the Islamic world, Greece and Europe, since comparison teaches both what was distinctive and the habit of fairness.

Table 22.1 sketches how these principles might shape an introductory university course on Indian knowledge traditions in comparative perspective. It is offered as an illustration, not a prescription; each topic is linked to the volume of this series where the reader can find the material.

Table 22.1. An illustrative introductory course on Indian knowledge traditions Unit Topic Suggested sources and questions 1 Sources and dating how texts were composed and transmitted; manuscripts, inscriptions, oral tradition (Volume 1; Chapter 1) 2 Argument and debate Nyāya on debate; the self and the means of knowledge; Buddhist and Cārvāka critiques (Volume 3; Chapter 4) 3 Mathematics place-value and zero; Brahmagupta; the Kerala series (Volume 11) 4 Astronomy and time Āryabhaṭa; the siddhāntas; Purāṇic and Jain time compared (Volume 12; Chapters 2–3) 5 Language Pāṇini’s grammar; Tamil grammar; comparison with modern linguistics (Volume 10) 6 Medicine Caraka and Suśruta; Unani and Siddha; evidence and safety today (Volume 13; Chapter 20) 7 Law and ethics dharma, caste and its critics; Aśoka; the Constitution (Volume 18; Chapter 5) 8 Craft and agriculture weavers, metallurgists, farmers; knowledge outside texts (Volumes 15, 17, 23) 9 Encounters al-Bīrūnī, Dārā Shikoh, the Orientalists (Chapters 8 and 16) 10 Modern thinkers Rammohun, Phule, Ramabai, Gandhi, Ambedkar, Tagore, Iqbal, Sayyid Ahmad Khan, K. C. Bhattacharya (Chapters 9–17) 11 Myths and how to check them “Vedic science” and invented quotations (Chapter 19; this chapter) 12 Indian knowledge today policy, rights of communities, research agenda (this chapter)

docs.title: 22.7 Knowledge Beyond Texts
docs.text: Much of the knowledge discussed in Volumes 15, 17 and 23 of this series — of crops and seeds, forests and medicinal plants, weaving and metalwork, water management and animal husbandry — is held by farmers, artisans and tribal communities rather than in texts. Recent law has begun to recognise these communities as holders of knowledge and rights. The Geographical Indications of Goods Act (1999) protects products such as Darjeeling tea and Banarasi silk associated with particular places; the Biological Diversity Act (2002) requires that communities share in the benefits when their biological resources and knowledge are used, and provides for local People’s Biodiversity Registers; and the Forest Rights Act (2006) recognises the rights of forest-dwelling communities, many of them Adivasi, to the forests they have traditionally used. These measures express in law an idea that the IKS movement often states in rhetoric: that traditional knowledge is valuable and belongs to those who created it. Their implementation has been uneven, and conflicts between conservation, development and community rights continue. An “Indian Knowledge Systems” curriculum that taught Sanskrit treatises while ignoring the living knowledge and the rights of these communities would repeat the exclusions of the past.

docs.title: 22.8 An Agenda for Research
docs.text: What would a serious programme of research on Indian knowledge systems involve? Its foundation would be editions and translations, since many important texts in Sanskrit, Persian, Tamil and other languages exist only in manuscript or in unreliable editions. On that foundation the history of Indian mathematics, astronomy, medicine and technology can be pursued with the methods that made the work of Pingree and Plofker authoritative: close reading, attention to dates and transmission, and comparison with other traditions. Knowledge recorded in the regional languages, in Persian and in oral tradition is less studied than Sanskrit learning and is disappearing faster. Where traditional knowledge makes claims about health, agriculture or the environment, those claims should be tested by the best available methods and the results reported whether positive or negative. Indian philosophical arguments should be studied as contributions to continuing debates, as Matilal, Ganeri and others have shown is possible. And the social history of knowledge — who produced, controlled and was excluded from it, by caste, gender, region and religion — belongs to the history of knowledge itself.

docs.title: 22.9 Knowledge, Identity and the Nation
docs.text:
Behind the debates about Indian knowledge lies a question about identity: whose heritage is it, and what does it mean to call it “Indian”? Several answers have been given in the history traced by this volume. For the Orientalists, the Indian heritage was above all the Sanskrit heritage, and its value lay in its antiquity. For Hindu reformers from Rammohun to Radhakrishnan, it was the Upaniṣadic and Vedāntic tradition, understood as a universal spirituality. For Hindu nationalists, it is the heritage of a Hindu nation defined by territory and ancestry. For Nehru, it was the composite inheritance of all the peoples who had lived in the subcontinent, Hindu, Buddhist, Jain, Muslim and others, layered like a palimpsest (Nehru 1946). For Ambedkar and the Dalit movement, it included above all the Buddha’s teaching and the long record of resistance to caste. For Dravidian and other regional movements, it is plural and centred in the regional languages.

These answers are not merely academic. They determine which texts are taught, which languages are funded, which monuments are protected and which histories are remembered. A comparative study cannot choose among them on behalf of its readers. It can, however, insist on two things. First, the historical record does not support any account of Indian knowledge that excludes its Buddhist, Jain, Islamic, Sikh, Christian, tribal or regional components, or the contributions of women and of castes excluded from Sanskrit learning; whatever “Indian” means, it must include them. Second, the value of a piece of knowledge — a theorem, a medical treatment, an argument about the self — does not depend on the identity of the person who discovered it. Pride in the achievements of one’s ancestors is natural, but knowledge belongs to whoever can understand and use it. The mathematicians of Kerala, like Euclid or al-Khwārizmī, are part of the heritage of humanity.

docs.title: 22.10 Examples of Good Practice
docs.text:
The research agenda above is not hypothetical; much of it is already being pursued, in India and abroad, and a few examples show what careful work can achieve.

The Kerala mathematics.

The Malayalam Yuktibhāṣā, the main source for the demonstrations of the Kerala school (Chapter 19), was published in a critical edition with English translation and detailed mathematical notes by K. V. Sarma, K. Ramasubramanian, M. D. Srinivas and M. S. Sriram (2008). The edition makes it possible for any mathematician to follow the original arguments step by step, and it has done more for the reputation of Indian mathematics than any number of claims of priority.

The census of the exact sciences.

David Pingree’s Census of the Exact Sciences in Sanskrit (five volumes, 1970–1994) listed the authors and manuscripts of Sanskrit astronomy, astrology and mathematics, laying the foundation for the work of Plofker and others (Pingree 1981; Plofker 2009).

Yoga and medicine.

Research projects at European universities in the 2010s — among them the Haṭha Yoga Project at SOAS, London, and a project on the modern history of Āyurveda and yoga at Vienna — have edited and translated previously unpublished texts and studied their modern transformations, in collaboration with Indian scholars and practitioners (Mallinson and Singleton 2017).

The epics.

The critical editions of the Mahābhārata (Pune, 1919–1966) and of the Rāmāyaṇa (Baroda, 1960–1975), produced by teams of Indian scholars from hundreds of manuscripts, remain the indispensable basis for the study of both epics, whatever their limitations.

Living knowledge.

Community biodiversity registers, participatory studies of seed varieties and documentation projects in tribal languages, many of them led by Indian non-governmental organisations and universities, show how the knowledge of farmers and forest communities can be recorded with their consent and to their benefit (Volumes 15 and 23).

These examples share the features this series has tried to embody: they work from sources, state their methods, collaborate across institutions and countries, and let the evidence decide.

docs.title: 22.11 Comparisons from Other Countries
docs.text:
India is not alone in seeking to recover and teach traditional knowledge, and the experience of other countries is instructive. China integrated Traditional Chinese Medicine into its health system after 1949, with parallel colleges and hospitals, extensive state-funded research and one Nobel Prize — Tu Youyou’s for artemisinin — as well as persistent controversy about the evidence for many treatments and the use of endangered animal products. In New Zealand, the knowledge of the Māori people (mātauranga Māori) has been incorporated into education and environmental management, and the legal personhood of the Whanganui River was negotiated with Māori communities (Chapter 21); proposals to teach it alongside science in schools provoked a public debate in 2021 about whether traditional knowledge and science are different kinds of knowledge. In Canada and Australia, indigenous knowledge has entered environmental management through formal partnerships with indigenous communities. Across Africa, “indigenous knowledge systems” have become a field of research and policy, with similar questions about evidence, ownership and the risk of romanticism.

Three lessons emerge. First, traditional knowledge is most credible when its practical claims are tested rather than assumed. Second, the communities that hold it should be partners, not merely sources. Third, the relation between traditional knowledge and science should be discussed openly: traditional knowledge can complement science, inform it and supply it with questions, but it does not replace the methods by which empirical claims are established.

docs.title: 22.12 Two Failures and How to Avoid Them
22.12.1 Uncritical celebration
docs.text: The first failure is uncritical celebration: presenting every Indian text as wise, every claim as true and every modern discovery as anticipated. Its symptoms are familiar from the preceding chapters: invented or garbled verses, quotations attributed to scientists who never wrote them, statistics without sources, the ancient aeroplane, “Vedic mathematics”, the kalpa as the age of the Earth, the claim that “all religions are one” presented as a fact about the religions. It treats the tradition as a monument to be revered rather than a conversation to be joined, and it silently excludes everyone whom the monument does not commemorate — the Śūdra excluded from the Veda, the woman denied independence, the Muslim and the Sikh whose traditions do not fit, the Buddhist who rejects Hinduism.

docs.title: 22.12.2 Colonial dismissal
docs.text: The second failure is dismissal: the assumption, inherited from Mill and Macaulay, that pre-modern Indian thought is myth and superstition, of interest only to antiquarians. It ignores the logic of Navya-Nyāya, the mathematics of the Kerala school, the grammar of Pāṇini, the medicine of Caraka and Suśruta, the ethics of the Mahābhārata, the aesthetics of Abhinavagupta, and a vast literature of argument that is as rigorous as any in the world. It also ignores the role of Indian scholars in the making of modern science and scholarship.

docs.title: 22.12.3 The path between
docs.text: Between these failures lies the path that this series has tried to follow, whose rules are stated in Section 1.11 and need not be repeated here. They are not foreign impositions. Indian intellectual traditions developed their own exacting standards of evidence (pramāṇa), textual criticism and debate, and the best of their practitioners would have recognised them.

docs.title: 22.13 How to Check a Claim
docs.text:
Those rules can be made practical. Many of the errors that circulate in writing about Indian knowledge — verses that do not exist, quotations that no one wrote, statistics without a source — could have been caught by a few simple steps, which any student or teacher can follow.

1. Find the source.

A quotation from a Sanskrit text should come with a reference precise enough to find it: the text, the edition and the chapter and verse. If the reference is missing, or if it points to a text that does not contain the passage, the quotation should not be used. “As the Vedas say” is not a reference. For modern authors, the reference should give the book or article, with the page.

2. Read the context.

A verse that has been located should be read with the verses before and after it, and with a classical commentary if one exists. Many famous “quotations” change their meaning in context: the Ṛgvedic line “what is one, the inspired poets speak of in many ways” (1.164.46) concerns the names of the gods of the Vedic sacrifice, not the unity of all religions (see the end of this chapter); and the line “for the noble-minded, the whole earth is one family” (vasudhaiva kuṭumbakam), now widely used as a motto, is spoken in a fable of the Hitopadeśa (1.71) by a jackal who wants to be accepted as the friend of a deer he plans to eat (it also occurs, in a contemplative setting, in the late Mahā Upaniṣad, 6.71). Neither modern use is illegitimate, but the reader should know the difference between the source and the slogan.

3. Date the source.

A text should be dated by the best available scholarship, with the uncertainty stated. A claim that a discovery was made “in the Vedic period” on the evidence of a medieval commentary, or that a text is “ten thousand years old” on the evidence of tradition alone, should be rejected.

4. Check the attribution.

Quotations attributed to famous scientists and writers — Einstein, Oppenheimer, Schrödinger, Twain, Voltaire, Max Müller — are especially prone to invention. They should be traced to a primary source: a book, letter or recorded speech. If the earliest source is a website or a popular book of the 1970s, the attribution is probably false.

5. Ask for the numbers.

Statistics — of manuscripts, students, patents, markets, gene variants — need a source and a date. Round numbers repeated without a source (“nine million manuscripts”, “ten thousand students”) are usually legends.

6. Distinguish analogy from history.

A resemblance between an ancient idea and a modern theory is an analogy. It becomes history only if there is evidence of a causal connection, such as a translation, a citation or a teacher. The Kerala series and the Gregory–Newton series are a striking parallel; the transmission of Indian numerals to Europe is a documented history. The two kinds of claim must be kept apart.

7. Prefer the specialist.

On any technical question — the date of a text, the meaning of a term, the effect of a medicine — the work of specialists published in reviewed journals and academic presses should be preferred to popular summaries, including this one. The Further Reading lists at the end of each chapter point to such work.

docs.title: 22.14 Questions for Further Study
docs.text: The comparative study of Indian traditions is far from finished, and the chapters of this volume leave many questions open. We still do not know exactly by which texts and persons Indian mathematics and astronomy travelled to the Islamic world and Europe, or what travelled in the other direction before the colonial period. We know far more about what learned texts taught about the cosmos, karma and rebirth than about what ordinary people believed, which inscriptions, vernacular literature and ethnography may yet reveal. The interaction of Persianate and Sanskrit learning in particular scholarly circles and households (Chapter 16) has only begun to be studied, as has the production and transmission of knowledge by women, Dalits, Adivasis and artisans who left few texts. Which traditional practices in medicine, agriculture and resource management have measurable benefits is an empirical question still largely unanswered. And the political history of Indian ideas of argument and toleration — how far they protected dissenters and minorities — and the reception of the modern thinkers in different regions and languages invite comparison with Chinese, Islamic, African and indigenous traditions as well as with European ones.

docs.title: 22.15 Synthesis in Practice: Three Places
docs.text:
General statements about synthesis are easily made; it is more instructive to look at particular places where people of different traditions have met.

Ajmer.

The shrine (dargāh) of the Chishtī saint Muʿīn al-Dīn at Ajmer in Rajasthan, who died in the 1230s, has been a place of pilgrimage for seven centuries. Akbar walked there on foot to give thanks for the birth of a son. Today it is visited by Muslims, Hindus, Sikhs and others, who offer cloths and flowers and ask for the saint’s intercession; its annual festival marks the anniversary of his death (ʿurs). The visitors do not thereby abandon their own religions, and Islamic reformers have criticised shrine practices that they regard as un-Islamic. The shrine is an example of shared devotion without doctrinal agreement.

Sabarimala and Erumeli.

Pilgrims to the hill shrine of Ayyappan at Sabarimala in Kerala traditionally stop at Erumeli to honour Vāvar, a Muslim warrior who, according to legend, became Ayyappan’s companion, and whose shrine stands in a mosque. The custom embodies a local story of friendship across communities. Sabarimala has also been the centre of a different kind of conflict: the Supreme Court’s decision in 2018 that the exclusion of women of menstruating age violated the Constitution provoked mass protests, and the question was referred to a larger bench. The same place thus displays both inter-religious accommodation and conflict between tradition and constitutional equality.

Bodh Gaya.

At the site of the Buddha’s awakening, temples and monasteries built by Buddhists from Thailand, Japan, Tibet, Bhutan, Sri Lanka, Myanmar and elsewhere surround the Mahābodhi temple, which is managed under the Act of 1949 by a committee of Buddhists and Hindus (Chapter 18). Ambedkarite Buddhists have campaigned for exclusive Buddhist control; Hindu pilgrims perform rites for their ancestors in the nearby town of Gaya. Here a single site belongs, in different ways, to a global Buddhist community, to Indian Buddhists with their own history, and to Hindus.

These three places show what samanvaya has looked like in practice: neither the dissolution of differences nor permanent hostility, but negotiated coexistence, sustained by stories, customs and institutions, and always open to renegotiation.

docs.title: 22.16 What This Volume Has Found
docs.text:
It may be useful to summarise the main findings of the comparative chapters.

Shared words, different meanings.

Hindu, Buddhist and Jain traditions shared a large vocabulary — dharma, karma, saṃsāra, mokṣa, loka, kalpa, ahiṃsā — and a common stock of images, such as Meru and Jambudvīpa. But they used them in different ways: dharma as class duty, as the Buddha’s teaching and as a medium of motion; karma as moral potency, as intention and as matter; liberation as identity with Brahman, as the blowing out of craving and as the soul’s ascent to the top of the universe (Chapters 2–7).

Argument, not consensus.

The traditions argued with one another about the most basic questions — whether there is a self, whether there is a creator, whether the Veda is authoritative, whether caste is just, whether non-violence admits of exceptions — for more than two thousand years. The modern idea of a single, harmonious “Indian worldview” obscures the very thing that makes the Indian intellectual tradition remarkable.

Encounters shaped self-understanding.

The categories through which Indian traditions are now described were shaped by long encounters: with Persian scholarship at the Mughal court, with British and German Orientalists, with missionaries and Theosophists, with modern science (Chapter 8). Modern Hindu self-understanding, in particular, was formed by reformers who answered colonial critiques by reinterpreting the tradition, often around Advaita Vedānta (Chapters 9–11).

The modern syntheses were positions.

Vivekananda’s harmony of religions, Aurobindo’s evolutionary Vedānta, Gandhi’s truth and non-violence, Radhakrishnan’s religion of the spirit, Tagore’s religion of man, Iqbal’s Islamic personalism, Madanī’s composite nationalism and Ambedkar’s Navayāna Buddhism were all creative syntheses, and all were disputed — not least by one another, and by the academic philosophers who asked what freedom in ideas required (Chapters 10–15 and 17).

India’s traditions are many.

Islam and Indo-Persian learning, Sufism, the devotional poets, Sikhism, Christianity, Adivasi religions and the smaller communities are part of Indian intellectual history, and Buddhism and Jainism have their own modern histories; none of them is a footnote to Vedānta (Chapters 14 and 16–18).

Global careers require honesty.

Indian mathematics, yoga, meditation, Āyurveda, environmental movements and arts have entered the world’s common life. Their reputation is best served by accurate history and honest evidence, not by priority claims (Chapters 19–21).

docs.title: 22.17 Samanvaya Reconsidered
docs.text:
This volume began with the Ṛgvedic verse that “what is one, the inspired poets speak of in many ways” (1.164.46), and with the Brahmasūtra’s principle of samanvaya, the coherent reading of a body of texts. It is worth returning to both in closing.

The Ṛgvedic verse, in its context, says that the poets call one divine reality by the names of several gods — Indra, Mitra, Varuṇa, Agni, Yama, Mātariśvan. It has become, in modern India, a motto of religious tolerance, cited in support of the view that all religions are paths to one truth. The verse can bear that reading, and it is a reading that has encouraged generosity. But it is a reading. The poet was speaking of the gods of the Vedic sacrifice, not of the religions of the world; and many Indians, from the Buddha to Ambedkar, from the Mīmāṃsakas to the Sikh Gurus, did not believe that the paths they rejected led to the goal they sought.

The Brahmasūtra’s samanvaya was a discipline of interpretation: the effort to show that texts which seem to disagree have a coherent meaning. Its practitioners, from Śaṅkara to Madhva, did not agree on what that meaning was, and they said so, with arguments. Perhaps that is the most useful model for a synthesis today: not the declaration that everything is one, but the patient and argued attempt to understand how different things hold together, and where they do not.

Aśoka’s twelfth rock edict, more than two thousand years old, asked the religious communities of his empire to restrain their speech about one another, to listen to one another’s teachings and to honour one another, arguing that whoever exalts his own sect by disparaging others damages it. It did not ask them to agree. A civilisation that can sustain such restraint and such listening, while continuing to argue, has achieved something rarer than uniformity. That, rather than the claim of a single “Indian worldview”, is the samanvaya this series has tried to describe.
